en: Oṃ, homage to the Omniscient One! At that time, at that moment, there was a city named Campā—[its description].
Outside that city of Campā, in the northeastern quarter, there was a shrine named Punnabhadda—[its description].
There, in the city of Campā, there was a king named Koṇika—[his description].

At that time, at that moment, there was an elder named Ārya-Sudharman, a disciple of the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, who was endowed with noble birth and noble lineage; endowed with strength, beauty, modesty, knowledge, vision, conduct, and lightness; possessed of splendor, brilliance, radiance, and glory; one who had conquered anger, conquered pride, conquered deceit, and conquered greed; who had conquered his senses, conquered sleep, and conquered the hardships of life; who was liberated from the fear of life and death; preeminent in austerity, preeminent in virtue; thus preeminent in action, conduct, restraint, determination, honesty, gentleness, lightness, patience, protection, liberation, science, mantras, celibacy, vows, logic, rules, truthfulness, purity, knowledge, vision, and conduct; noble, formidable, firm in his vows, firm in his austerities, and firm in his practice of the celibate life; one who had cast off the body, whose vast mass of heat-energy was withdrawn, a master of the fourteen *pūrvas*, possessed of the four types of knowledge, surrounded by five hundred ascetics, wandering in regular succession through villages and towns, traveling comfortably, arrived at the city of Campā and at the Pūrṇabhadra shrine. Having arrived, he took formal possession of a suitable lodging and dwelt there, disciplining himself through self-restraint and austerity.
Then, from the city of Campā, the assembly went out; Koṇika went out; the Dharma was preached; and the assembly returned to the very same direction from which it had appeared.

At that time, at that moment, the senior disciple of the venerable monk Suvrata, a monk named Ārya-Jambū of the Kāśyapa lineage—seven *ucchrayas* in height, with a symmetrical quadrangular build, possessing the *vajra-ṛṣabha-nārāca* bone-jointing, fair as the luster of refined gold, of fierce austerity, radiant austerity, burning austerity, great austerity, sublime, formidable, and even unto fiery splendor—was dwelling not far from the elder Suvrata, with his knees raised and his head lowered, absorbed in the fortress of meditation, purifying himself through self-restraint and austerity.

Then that venerable Anagāra named Jambū, having conceived faith, having conceived curiosity, having conceived wonder; having become full of faith, full of curiosity, and full of wonder; having arisen with faith, arisen with curiosity, and arisen with wonder; having fully arisen with faith, fully arisen with curiosity, and fully arisen with wonder—rose from his seat. Having risen, he approached the venerable elder Sūhamma. Having approached, he performed three circumambulations, keeping the elder to his right. Having performed them, he paid homage and saluted him. Having paid homage and saluted him, he stood near the venerable elder Sūhamma, neither too close nor too far, listening attentively, paying homage, facing him with palms joined in reverence, and serving him with humility. He spoke thus: “Venerable sir, if this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—the originator, the Tīrthaṅkara, the self-enlightened one, the lord of the world, the light of the world, the illuminator of the world, the giver of fearlessness, the giver of refuge, the giver of vision, the giver of the path, the giver of Dharma, the teacher of Dharma, the leader of Dharma, the supreme fourfold universal monarch of Dharma, the possessor of unimpeded and supreme knowledge and vision, the Conqueror, the knower, the awakened one, the awakener, the liberated one, the liberator, the one who has crossed over, the savior—who has reached and attained the eternal state that is auspicious, immovable, ageless, infinite, indestructible, free from affliction, and beyond return—if this is the meaning declared for the fifth Aṅga, then, venerable sir, what is the meaning declared for the sixth Aṅga, the *Nāyādhammakahā*?”

Then the elder Ārya-Sudharman spoke thus to the monk named Ārya-Jambū: "Indeed, Jambū, by the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, who has attained liberation, six chapters (suyakkhandha) have been taught for the sixth Aṅga, namely: the Nāyādhammakahā and the Dhammakahā."

“If, venerable sir, by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—who has attained liberation—two scriptural sections (*suyakkhandha*) have been taught for the sixth *Aṅga*, namely: the *Nāyādhammakahāo* and the *Dhammakahāo*; then, venerable sir, how many chapters (*ajjhayaṇa*) have been taught by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—who has attained liberation—for the first scriptural section, the *Nāyādhammakahāo*? “Thus indeed, Jambū, by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—who has attained liberation—nineteen chapters have been taught for the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, namely:”
Ukkhittanāga, Saṅghāḍa, Aṇḍa, Kummā, Sēlaga, Tumba, Rōhiṇī, Mallī, Māyandī, and Candimā;
Dāvaddava, Udagaṇāga, Maṇḍukka, and Tēyalī as well. // Nāyā.6 //

Nandīphala, Avarakaṅkā, Āiṇṇa, Suṃsumā, and Puṇḍarīka; these are known as the others, making nineteen in total. "If it is so, venerable sir, that the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—who has attained liberation—has proclaimed nineteen chapters of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, namely: from *Ukkhittaṇāya* up to *Puṇḍarīya*, then, venerable sir, what is the meaning proclaimed for the first chapter?"

Thus indeed, Jambū, at that time and at that season, right here on this continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, in the southern half of Bhārata, there was a city named Rājagṛha—its description [is as follows]. There was a shrine named Guṇasila—its description [is as follows]. In that city of Rājagṛha, there was a king named Śreṇika—[he was] like the great Himavat, Mahāhimavat, Malaya, Mandara, and Mahendra mountains; his description [is as follows].

King Śreṇika had a queen named Nandā, who possessed delicate hands and feet; her description is as follows. King Śreṇika had a son by Queen Nandā named Prince Abhaya. He was one whose body possessed all five senses complete and unimpaired, endowed with the qualities of auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and characteristics (*vyañjana*). His limbs were beautiful, well-formed, and perfectly proportioned according to the standards of height, girth, and measurement. He was moon-like in appearance, lovely, and pleasing to behold; he was handsome. He was well-versed in the application of the policies of conciliation, force, sowing dissension, and gifts, and was skilled in the principles of statecraft. He was an expert in the science of wealth through the fourfold intelligence consisting of innate, acquired, practical, and transformative wisdom. In many matters of business, family affairs, deliberations, secrets, mysteries, and decisions, he was the one to be consulted and questioned repeatedly by King Śreṇika. He was the central pillar, the standard, the support, the refuge, the eye, the head of the pillar, the measure, the sustenance, the foundation, and the vision for all matters. Having attained confidence in all grounds and having been granted full authority, he was the one who considered the burden of the kingdom. He himself supervised and oversaw the king’s realm, the territory, the treasury, the granaries, the army, the vehicles, the city, and the inner apartments. He dwelt there, constantly supervising them all.
King Śreṇika had a queen named Dhāriṇī, who lived there [and so forth].

Then, on another occasion, Queen Dhāriṇī, while lying upon a couch of such a kind—furnished with pillars that were well-proportioned, polished, and beautifully shaped, rising up like excellent, choice *śālabhañjikā* figures; adorned with bright jewels, gold, and gems; featuring lattices and half-lattices from which fragrant sandalwood smoke was wafting out; decorated with golden *candraśālikā* (dormer-windows) and artistic panels; beautified by the color of fresh, pure minerals; plastered, smoothed, and polished on the outside, and with exquisite, well-finished paintings on the inside; having a floor made of various five-colored jewels and gems; its ceiling decorated with lotus-clusters, flowering creepers, and varieties of choice blossoms; its doorways shining with fresh lotuses and well-fashioned golden *vandana-kalaśas*; its door-surfaces beautifully arranged with hanging strings of pearls and gems; providing delight to the heart with decorations of soft, feathery eyes made of fragrant, choice flowers; delightful with the sweet, wafting fragrance of burning camphor, cloves, Malaya sandalwood, black agallochum, and the finest *kundurukka* and *turukka* incenses; perfumed with the scent of excellent fragrances as if it were a center of a perfume-shop; its darkness dispelled by the rays of jewels; in short, a magnificent dwelling that rivaled the celestial chariots of the gods—in such a place, upon a couch that was well-proportioned, with pillows on both sides, high at both ends but deep in the middle, resembling the sands of the Ganges’ banks, covered with a spread of fine *kṣauma* and *dukūla* cloth, adorned with fresh *malaya*, *navataya*, *kusatta*, *limba*, and *siṃhakesara* flowers, provided with a well-made canopy, draped in red silk, and as soft to the touch as camel-hair, wool, cotton, or fresh butter—at the time between the first and last watches of the night, while she was dozing off and waking again, she saw a great being, resembling a mass of silver, beautiful and of lovely form, moving playfully in the sky, yawning, and with its mouth wide open, and she woke up.

Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having seen this noble, auspicious, propitious, fortunate, excellent, beautiful, and great dream, awoke. With a heart thrilled and delighted, joyful and gladdened, supremely happy, her heart overflowing with joy, and the hair on her body bristling like a *kalamba* flower struck by rain, she took note of that dream. Having taken note of it, she rose from her bed; having risen, she stepped down from the footstool; having stepped down, with a gait that was unhurried, steady, unflustered, and unhindered—like that of a royal swan—she went to where King Śreṇika was. Having approached, while conversing with King Śreṇika in words that were desirable, lovely, dear, agreeable, pleasing, noble, auspicious, propitious, fortunate, excellent, beautiful, heart-stealing, heart-delighting, soft, sweet, resonant, deep, and majestic, she awakened him. Having awakened him, being permitted by King Śreṇika, she sat down upon an auspicious throne variegated with patterns of various jewels, gems, and gold. Having sat down, composed, confident, and seated comfortably upon the excellent couch, she placed her joined palms over her head in salutation and spoke thus to King Śreṇika:

"Thus indeed, O beloved of the gods! today, while lying upon that couch in the Tārāśaka chamber, embracing the pillow, I fell asleep and, having seen an elephant entering my own mouth as it appeared in a dream, I woke up. Therefore, O beloved of the gods! what auspicious distinction of fruit and result do you think will come from this sublime and auspicious dream?"

Then King Śreṇika, having heard and reflected upon this matter from Queen Dhāriṇī, with a heart filled with joy and satisfaction, his body bristling like a cluster of fragrant flowers on a tree drenched by rain, and the hairs on his body standing on end, grasped that dream. Having grasped it, he entered into it; having entered, he determined the meaning of that dream through his own natural, intellect-born wisdom and discernment. Then, repeatedly consoling Queen Dhāriṇī with words that were delightful to the heart, gentle, sweet, resonant, deep, and majestic, he spoke as follows:

"O beloved of the gods! A magnificent dream has been seen by you; indeed, O beloved of the gods, an auspicious dream has been seen by you. It is a propitious, fortunate, auspicious, and beautiful dream, O beloved of the gods! It brings about health, prosperity, long life, and all that is auspicious and favorable. O Queen, a gain of wealth awaits you, O beloved of the gods; a gain of a son awaits you, O beloved of the gods; a gain of sovereignty awaits you, O beloved of the gods; a gain of enjoyments and happiness awaits you, O beloved of the gods! Truly, O beloved of the gods, when nine months have passed and seven and a half nights have elapsed, you will give birth to a boy who is a banner for our clan, a lamp for our clan, a mountain for our clan, a pinnacle for our clan, an ornament for our clan, a bringer of fame to our clan, a bringer of livelihood to our clan, a source of joy to our clan, a bringer of glory to our clan, a support for our clan, a tree for our clan, and one who causes the increase of our clan—a child with delicate hands and feet, and so forth, endowed with great beauty. And when that boy has cast off childhood and reached the age of discretion, having attained youth, he will become a king, a lord of the realm, heroic, brave, valiant, possessing vast and extensive power and forces. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, a magnificent dream has been seen by you... [it is] a dream, O Queen, that brings about health, prosperity, long life, and all that is auspicious and favorable. Having said this, he repeated his words again and again.

Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having been thus addressed by King Śreṇika, with a heart joyful, satisfied, and gladdened, her heart overflowing with the force of delight, placed her joined palms upon her head in salutation and spoke as follows:

"O beloved of the gods, it is even so; O beloved of the gods, it is exactly so; O beloved of the gods, this is not otherwise; O beloved of the gods, this is beyond doubt; O beloved of the gods, this is desired; O beloved of the gods, this is acceptable; O beloved of the gods, this is both desired and acceptable. O beloved of the gods, this matter which you speak is indeed true. Having said this, she accepted that dream correctly. Having accepted it, being permitted by King Śreṇika, she rose from her auspicious throne, which was variegated with the inlaid patterns of various jewels, gems, and gold. Having risen, she went to where her own couch was, and having approached, she sat down upon her own couch. Having sat down, she spoke thus:

Thinking, "May this supreme, excellent, and auspicious dream not be thwarted by other evil dreams," she remains awake throughout the night, keeping watch over her sleep with virtuous, righteous, and auspicious discourses concerning the deities and elders.

Then King Śreṇika, at the time of dawn, summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Prepare and cause to be prepared the outer assembly hall today so that it is exceptionally beautiful, sprinkled with scented water, swept clean, and smeared with plaster; adorned with heaps of fresh, fragrant flowers of five colors scattered about; made delightful by the rising of fragrant, sweet-smelling odors from burning black aloe, excellent kundurukka, and turukka incense; perfumed with the finest fragrances until it becomes a veritable center of fragrance. Then those household officials, being thus addressed by King Śreṇika, were pleased and delighted, and they carried out the command and reported back to him.

Then, when the night had turned into dawn, King Śreṇika rose from his bed at sunrise—the sun which was as pale-white as a blooming blue lotus gently opening; which possessed the radiance of the red Aśoka, the Kiṃśuka, the beautiful face of a parrot, the half of a Guñjā berry, the Bandhujīvaka flower, the eye of a pigeon, the deep-red eyes of a francolin partridge, the Jāsumaṇa flower, a mass of fire, molten gold, the Kalamasa fruit, and vermilion; and which was exceedingly beautiful, radiant, and surpassing all other forms. When the darkness had been dispelled by the succession of the rays of that maker of day, and the world of living beings appeared as if inlaid with the saffron of the morning glow, and when the world was clearly revealed by the expanding vision of those whose eyes were following the objects of sight, and when the thousand-rayed sun, the maker of day, had risen like a cluster of blooming lotus groves and was blazing with splendor, he arose from his couch. Having arisen...

He went to where the gymnasium was, and having arrived, he entered the gymnasium. While he was exhausted from various exercises involving stretching, contracting, pressing, and wrestling, he was massaged with *abhyaṅga* (oil rubs) prepared with one hundred and one thousand varieties of fragrant and excellent oils—oils that were nourishing, invigorating, exhilarating, intoxicating, and delightful, bringing joy to all the senses and the body. Once massaged, while his fatigue had subsided, the king was then rubbed with a fourfold massage—beneficial for the bones, the flesh, the skin, and the hair—by men who were skilled, expert, diligent, noble, intelligent, clever, proficient in their craft, tireless, and perfected in the arts of rubbing, kneading, and stroking. Having been thus relieved of his fatigue, the lord of men emerged from the gymnasium.

He went to where the bathing hall was; having arrived, he entered the bathing hall. Having entered, he sat comfortably upon a bathing throne—which was delightful with its floor paved with various jewels and gems, beautiful with a lattice-work of complete designs, and adorned with patterns of diverse jewels and gems—in the charming bathing pavilion. He was bathed again and again according to the auspicious and excellent ritual of bathing, using pure waters, perfumed waters, flower-infused waters, and clear waters. At the conclusion of that auspicious and excellent bathing ceremony performed with hundreds of various auspicious rites, his body was rubbed with fine, soft, fragrant *kāśāya* (yellowish) powders. He was well-draped in a very costly, new, and precious silk garment (*duṣyavastra*). His limbs were anointed with fresh, fragrant *gośīrṣa* sandalwood paste. He wore clean garlands, unguents, and cosmetics; he was adorned with gold and jewels. He shone with beautifully fashioned necklaces, half-necklaces, and armlets hanging down like streaks of lightning. His waist was graced by a well-fashioned girdle hanging down in folds. He wore a breast-band (*gevejja*) and bracelets (*aṅgulējaga*), and his limbs were beautified by lovely ornaments. His arms were supported by various jewel-studded bracelets and armlets. Possessing supreme beauty and splendor, his face was illuminated by earrings, and his head was radiant with a crown. His chest was beautifully decorated with a necklace and a breast-ornament. His fingers were marked by rings and red lac-dye. A well-fashioned lower garment hung down in folds. He wore a hero’s bracelet (*vīravalaya*), which was made of various jewels, gold, and gems—spotless, most worthy, skillfully crafted, shimmering, well-fitted, distinguished, long, well-proportioned, and excellent. What more need be said? The king was like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), perfectly adorned and embellished.

With a white umbrella adorned with a cluster of *koraṇṭa* flowers being held over him, his body fanned by the waving of four chowries, while the world around him proclaimed auspicious cries of "Victory!", the King—surrounded by numerous troop-commanders, district governors, royal officials, provincial chiefs, city prefects, barons, householders, ministers, chief ministers, astrologers, priests, counselors, servants, eunuchs, heralds, citizens, guild-leaders, army generals, caravan leaders, envoys, and treaty-makers—emerged from the bathhouse like the moon amidst a host of planets, stars, and constellations shining in the sky, appearing like a great white cloud. Having emerged, he went to the outer assembly hall and, having arrived, sat down upon an excellent lion-throne facing the east.

Then King Śreṇika had eight auspicious thrones (*bhadra-āsana*) prepared not far from himself in the northeastern quarter; they were covered with white cloth, consecrated with the auspicious rites of *siddhārtha* seeds and other protective ceremonies. Having had them prepared, he had an inner curtain (*javaṇikā*) hung, which was adorned with various jewels and gems, of exceedingly beautiful appearance, made of costly fine silk, featuring hundreds of delicate and variegated patterns, and decorated with designs of *īhāmṛga*, bulls, horses, men, crocodiles, birds, serpents, *kinnaras*, *rūru* deer, *sarabhas*, yak-tails, elephants, forest creepers, and lotus creepers; its edges were finished with exquisite goldwork. Having had that hung, he had a throne for Queen Dhāriṇī prepared—one stuffed with cotton, *maüa*, and *masūra* fibers, covered with white cloth, possessing a most distinguished and pleasant touch to the limbs, and very soft. Having had it prepared, he summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus:

"Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Summon the readers of the *Aṣṭāṅga-mahānimitta-sūtra*, who are skilled in various treatises and proficient in the science of dreams; having summoned them, report back to me immediately that this command has been carried out."

Then those householders' men, being thus addressed by King Śreṇika, were delighted, thrilled, joyful, and their hearts overflowing with the weight of joy; they joined their ten fingers together in an añjali at their heads, turning it toward the king, and with devotion and humility replied, "So be it, Your Majesty. Having thus assented to his command, they departed from the presence of King Śreṇika. (2) Proceeding through the middle of the city of Rājagṛha, they went to where the houses of the dream-interpreters were, and having arrived, they summoned the dream-interpreters.

Then those dream-interpreters, having been summoned by the king Seniya’s household servants, were delighted, joyful, and gladdened in heart, their hearts overflowing with joy. Having bathed, performed their ritual offerings (*balikamma*), and completed the auspicious purificatory rites (*kautuka-maṅgala-prāyaścitta*), they adorned their bodies with many costly ornaments. With their heads bound in turbans decorated with green sprouts and *siddhārtha* (white mustard) seeds, they departed from their respective homes. They proceeded through the center of the city of Rājagṛha and arrived at the gate of King Seniya’s palace pavilion. Having arrived, they gathered together; having gathered, they entered through the gate of King Seniya’s palace pavilion. Having entered, they went to the outer assembly hall where King Seniya was, and upon arriving, they greeted him with cries of "Victory! and "Triumph! Being honored, saluted, revered, esteemed, respected, and welcomed by King Seniya, they each sat down on the previously prepared auspicious seats. Then King Seniya stationed Queen Dhāriṇī behind a curtain. Having done so, with his hands full of flowers and fruits, he addressed those dream-interpreters with the utmost humility: [End of excerpt]

"Thus indeed, O beloved of the gods, Queen Dhāriṇī today, while lying upon such a bed as that, having seen such a great dream, has awakened. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, what auspicious and distinguished result do you think will come from this magnificent, glorious, and beautiful great dream?"

Then those dream-interpreters, having heard and understood this matter in the presence of King Śreṇika, were thrilled, delighted, and joyful, their hearts overflowing with the weight of rapture. They thoroughly grasped that dream, entered into its investigation, and deliberated upon it together. Having attained the meaning of that dream, having questioned about its meaning, having mastered its meaning, having determined its meaning, and having fully comprehended its meaning, they recited the treatises on dreams before King Śreṇika and spoke as follows:

"Indeed, Master, in our manual of dream interpretation, forty-two dreams, thirty great dreams, and seventy-two all-dreams have been seen. Among them, Master, when an embryo of an Arhat or an embryo of a Cakravartin is entering the womb, the mother of the Arhat or the mother of the Cakravartin awakens after seeing these fourteen great dreams, namely:
an elephant, a bull, a lion, anointing, a garland, the moon, the sun, a banner, and a pitcher."
The lotus lake, the ocean, the celestial palace, the mountain, the jewel-mine, and the fire. // Nāyā.16 //

"The mother of a Vāsudeva, when a Vāsudeva is descending into her womb, wakes up after seeing any seven of these fourteen great dreams. The mother of a Baladeva, when a Baladeva is descending into her womb, wakes up after seeing any four of these fourteen great dreams. The mother of a Maṇḍalika king, when a Maṇḍalika king is descending into her womb, wakes up after seeing any one of these fourteen great dreams. And now, Lord, this one great dream has been seen by Queen Dhāriṇī; it is indeed auspicious, Lord, that such a dream was seen by Queen Dhāriṇī—up to—it is a dream, Lord, that brings about health, joy, long life, prosperity, and auspiciousness for Queen Dhāriṇī. There will be gain of wealth, Lord; gain of a son, Lord; gain of a kingdom, Lord; gain of enjoyments, Lord; gain of happiness, Lord. Truly, Lord, after nine months have fully elapsed, Queen Dhāriṇī will give birth to a boy. And that boy, having cast off childhood, being mature and of sound mind, having reached youth, will become a powerful, heroic, valiant, and sovereign king with vast and extensive forces and vehicles; or he will become a monk of purified soul. Thus, Lord, the dream seen by Queen Dhāriṇī is indeed auspicious," up to "it was seen"—having said this, they celebrated it again and again.

Then King Śreṇika, having heard and reflected upon this matter from those dream-interpreters, with a heart joyful, satisfied, and delighted, and with his heart overflowing with the weight of joy, joined his palms [in reverence] and spoke thus: "It is so, O beloved of the gods, it is exactly as you say. Having said this, he accepted that dream correctly. He honored and respected those dream-interpreters with abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, as well as garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments; having honored and respected them, he gave them a generous gift of affection suitable for their livelihood, and having given it, he dismissed them.

Then King Śreṇika rose from his lion-throne and went to where Queen Dhāriṇī was; having approached her, he spoke thus to Queen Dhāriṇī: "O beloved of the gods, in the science of dreams there are forty-two types of dreams... [as before] ...up to one great dream, which he repeatedly interprets. Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having heard and understood this matter from the presence of King Śreṇika, with a heart joyful, delighted, gladdened, and overflowing with the weight of joy, properly accepted that dream. She went to her own quarters, bathed, performed the ritual offerings, and remained there.

When two months had passed for Queen Dhāriṇī and the third month was underway, at the time of the pregnancy-longing, this kind of longing for untimely rains arose in her: "Blessed indeed are those mothers; fulfilled indeed are those mothers; successful indeed are those mothers; meritorious indeed are those mothers; fortunate indeed are those mothers; well-obtained indeed is the fruit of human birth and life for them—those who, when the clouds have risen up, become upright, swollen, towering, thundering, flashing with lightning, sprinkling rain, and rumbling; which possess the luster of polished silver plates, marks, conchs, the moon, jasmine, and heaps of rice-powder; which possess the luster of *cikura*, *hariyāla*, *bhēya*, *campaga*, *saṇa*, *kōraṇṭa*, *sarisava*, and *paümaraya*; which possess the luster of fresh lac-juice, red *kiṁsuya*, *jāsumaṇa*, red *bandhujīvaga*, *jātihiṅgulaya*, fresh saffron, and the blood of a ram; which possess the luster of peacock feathers, blue *guliyā* birds, *sugacāsa* wings, *bhiṅga* leaves, *sāsaga* flowers, blue lotuses, clusters of new *sirīsa* blossoms, and fresh petals; which possess the luster of natural collyrium, *bhiṅga* minerals, *riṭṭhaga* gems, swarms of bees, dark *guliya* minerals, and lampblack; which flash with lightning and thunder; which move restlessly across the vast sky driven by the wind; where the pure, excellent streams of water fall, and the wind, being struck and driven, scatters and pours down from above; which are greenish-red; where the surface of the earth is cooled by the falling showers; where the groves of trees in the green sky are sprouted; where the creepers and vines have spread; where the heights are elevated and beautiful; where the mountain torrents have burst forth from the slopes and ridges of Mount Vēbhāra; where the mountain rivers flow with turbid water, agitated by foam as they rush and tumble; where the gardens are filled with *sajja*, *juṇa*, *nīvakuḍaya*, *kandala*, and *silindha* plants; where the peacocks, delighted and thrilled by the taste of the rain, utter cries of joy with throats loosened by ecstasy; where the gardens emit the fragrance of *mayaja*, young *taruṇasahaya*, *ripaṇa*, fresh *surabhi*, *silindha*, *kuḍaya*, *kandala*, and *kalamba* flowers; where the air is crowded with the humming of *parahuya* birds; where the red *indagōvaya* and *thōvaya* birds cry out piteously; where the grounds are adorned with bent grass and made resonant by frogs; where the regions are buzzing with swarms of intoxicated bees and honey-bees hovering over the nectar of the flowers; where the paths of the moon, sun, planets, and constellations have vanished; where the sky is like a banner bound with Indra’s bow (the rainbow) and beautified by rows of soaring cranes; and when the rainy season has arrived, bringing longing to the *kāraṇḍaga*, *cakravāka*, and *kalahaṁsa* birds—I too would fulfill my longing. Then, when two months had passed for Queen Dhāriṇī and the third month was underway, at the time of the pregnancy-longing, this kind of longing for untimely rains arose in her: "Blessed indeed are those mothers; fulfilled indeed are those mothers; successful indeed are those mothers; meritorious indeed are those mothers; fortunate indeed are those mothers; well-obtained indeed is the fruit of human birth and life for them—those who, when the clouds have risen up, become upright, swollen, towering, and standing high; thundering, flashing with lightning, sprinkling rain, and rumbling; possessing the luster of polished silver plates, marks, conchs, the moon, jasmine, and heaps of rice-powder; possessing the luster of *cikura*, *hariyāla*, *bhēya*, *campaga*, *saṇa*, *kōraṇṭa*, *sarisava*, and *paümaraya*; possessing the luster of fresh lac-juice, red *kiṁsuya*, *jāsumaṇa*, red *bandhujīvaga*, *jātihiṅgulaya*, fresh saffron, and the blood of a ram; possessing the luster of peacock feathers, blue *guliyā* birds, *sugacāsa* wings, *bhiṅga* leaves, *sāsaga* flowers, blue lotuses, clusters of new *sirīsa* blossoms, and fresh petals; possessing the luster of natural collyrium, *bhiṅga* minerals, *riṭṭhaga* gems, swarms of bees, dark *guliya* minerals, and lampblack; flashing with lightning and thunder; moving restlessly across the vast sky driven by the wind; where the pure, excellent streams of water fall, and the wind, being struck and driven, scatters and pours down from above; which are greenish-red; where the surface of the earth is cooled by the falling showers; where the groves of trees in the green sky are sprouted; where the creepers and vines have spread; where the heights are elevated and beautiful; where the mountain torrents have burst forth from the slopes and ridges of Mount Vēbhāra; where the mountain rivers flow with turbid water, agitated by foam as they rush and tumble; where the gardens are filled with *sajja*, *juṇa*, *nīvakuḍaya*, *kandala*, and *silindha* plants; where the peacocks, delighted and thrilled by the taste of the rain, utter cries of joy with throats loosened by ecstasy; where the gardens emit the fragrance of *mayaja*, young *taruṇasahaya*, *ripaṇa*, fresh *surabhi*, *silindha*, *kuḍaya*, *kandala*, and *kalamba* flowers; where the air is crowded with the humming of *parahuya* birds; where the red *indagōvaya* and *thōvaya* birds cry out piteously; where the grounds are adorned with bent grass and made resonant by frogs; where the regions are buzzing with swarms of intoxicated bees and honey-bees hovering over the nectar of the flowers; where the paths of the moon, sun, planets, and constellations have vanished; where the sky is like a banner bound with Indra’s bow (the rainbow) and beautified by rows of soaring cranes; and when the rainy season has arrived, bringing longing to the *kāraṇḍaga*, *cakravāka*, and *kalahaṁsa* birds—I too would fulfill my longing. Having bathed, performed the ritual offerings, and completed the auspicious purificatory rites, she put on excellent garments, anklets, jeweled belts, necklaces, bracelets, small armlets, and various beautiful bangles that adorned her arms; her face was illuminated by earrings; her limbs were decorated with jewels; she wore a garment with a texture and color so pleasing it surpassed the scent of breath, captivating to the eye, and as soft as a horse's saliva, with ends inlaid with white gold and a luster like clear crystal; she wore fine silk upper garments and had her head adorned with fragrant flowers and excellent garlands of all seasons; she was perfumed with black aloe incense; dressed in a manner equal to Śrī herself; mounted upon the excellent scent-elephant Sēyaṇaya; with a parasol bearing a cluster of *kōrēṇṭa* flowers held over her; fanned by four whisks with handles of moonstone, diamond, and pure beryl, appearing like conchs, jasmine, frost, or a mass of foam; accompanied by King Śreṇika, who sat upon the back of the elephant; followed closely behind by a fourfold army—a great cavalry, elephant corps, chariot corps, and infantry—with all its splendor, majesty, and the sound of loud proclamations, she looked upon Rājagṛha city with its crossroads, trijunctions, quadrangles, squares, and main roads, all sprinkled, swept, cleaned, dusted, and smeared, fragrant with the finest scents and like a whirlpool of perfume; while being cheered by the citizens, she wandered all around the lovely foothills of Mount Vēbhāra, which were covered with clusters of shrubs, creepers, trees, and thickets, thus fulfilling her longing. "If I too, when the clouds have risen up... [could fulfill

Then, while that longing remained unfulfilled, Queen Dhāriṇī—her desire unattained, unsatisfied, and unhonored—became parched, hungry, fleshless, emaciated, and physically exhausted; she grew weak and frail, her lotus-like face and eyes drooping, her countenance pale like a *campaka* garland crushed in the palm of a hand; devoid of luster, with a dejected and discolored face, she took no pleasure in appropriate flowers, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, or necklaces; she abandoned all playful and pleasurable activities, and being distressed, despondent, joyless, with her gaze fixed upon the ground, she brooded with a troubled mind and intent.

Then the inner personal attendants and female slave-girls of Queen Dhāriṇī, seeing her dejected and brooding, spoke thus: "Why, O beloved of the gods, are you so dejected, with such a dejected body, and why do you brood?
Then Queen Dhāriṇī, being thus addressed by those inner personal attendants and female slave-girls, neither acknowledged nor paid heed to them; not acknowledging or paying heed, she remained silent.

Then those inner personal attendants and female slave-maids spoke thus to Queen Dhāriṇī a second and a third time: "Why, O beloved of the gods, are you dejected, with a dejected body, and so on, until you are brooding? Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having been addressed thus by those inner personal attendants and female slave-maids a second and a third time, neither heeded nor acknowledged them; not heeding and not acknowledging them, she remained silent. Then those inner personal attendants and female slave-maids, being neither heeded nor acknowledged by Queen Dhāriṇī, became agitated as before and departed from the presence of Queen Dhāriṇī. Having departed, they went to where King Śreṇika was, and having approached him, with palms joined together [in reverence], and so on, they greeted him with cries of "Victory! Victory! and having greeted him, they spoke thus: "Truly, Lord, today Queen Dhāriṇī is somehow dejected, with a dejected body, and so on, until she is brooding, overcome by anxious meditation."

Then King Śreṇika, having heard and understood this matter from those female attendants, became agitated in that very way; quickly, hurriedly, restlessly, and anxiously, he went to where Queen Dhāriṇī was. Having arrived, he saw Queen Dhāriṇī distressed, her body languid, and so on, up to being absorbed in anxious meditation (*ārtadhyāna*). Having seen her, he spoke thus: "Why, O beloved of the gods, are you distressed, your body languid, and so on, up to being absorbed in anxious meditation? Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having been addressed thus by King Śreṇika, neither acknowledged nor accepted it, but remained silent.

Then King Śreṇika said this to Queen Dhāriṇī a second and a third time: "Why, O beloved of the gods, are you so distressed, with a body so emaciated, [and] brooding while overcome by anxious meditation? Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having been addressed thus by King Śreṇika a second and a third time, neither acknowledged nor accepted it, but remained silent.

Then King Śreṇika made Queen Dhāriṇī swear an oath, and having made her swear, he spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods, why did you keep this mental anguish of mine secret, when I was not even worthy to hear of such a matter? Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having been made to swear by King Śreṇika, spoke thus to King Śreṇika: "Truly, my lord, after three full months had passed since that magnificent and great dream of mine, this kind of longing for unseasonable rain arose within me: 'Blessed are those mothers, fortunate are those mothers, who—having wandered all around the base of the peaks of Mount Vebhāra—fulfill their longings. If I too, O Lord, were to fulfill my longing while the clouds have risen and so forth, then, my lord, because this unseasonable longing remains unfulfilled, I am dejected and brood in the fire of anxiety."

Then King Śreṇika, having heard and understood this matter from Queen Dhāriṇī, spoke thus to Queen Dhāriṇī: "O beloved of the gods, do not be distressed, nor even dwell in the meditation of anguish; I shall act in such a way that you will attain the fulfillment of this desire for an untimely longing. Having said this, he consoled Queen Dhāriṇī with words that were desirable, lovely, dear, agreeable, and pleasing. Having consoled her, he went to the outer assembly hall and sat down upon an excellent lion-throne facing the east. While reflecting again and again upon Queen Dhāriṇī’s untimely longing through many methods and means—through the fourfold types of intelligence consisting of the innate, the acquired, the karmic, and the transformative—he could find no means, method, stability, or origin for that longing. With his mind and intentions dejected, he remained there, dwelling in meditation.

Immediately thereafter, Prince Abhaya, having bathed, performed his ritual offerings, and adorned himself with all ornaments, set out to pay his respects at the feet [of the king]. When Prince Abhaya arrived where King Śreṇika was, he saw that the king was dejected in mind and intent, brooding. Upon seeing this, there arose within him this internal reflection, thought, conviction, and mental consideration: "On other occasions, when King Śreṇika saw me approaching, he would welcome me, acknowledge me, honor me, respect me, converse with me, speak with me, invite me to share half his seat, and smell my head. But now, King Śreṇika does not welcome me, does not acknowledge me, does not honor me, does not respect me, does not converse with me, does not speak with me, does not invite me to share half his seat, and does not smell my head; rather, he is somewhat dejected in mind and intent, brooding. There must be some reason for this. It would be well for me to ask King Śreṇika about this matter. Having reflected thus, he approached King Śreṇika, joined his palms in reverence over his head, and after saluting him with cries of "Victory! and "Prosperity!", he spoke as follows:

"Previously, my dear ones, when you saw me approaching, you welcomed me, recognized me, and even kissed me on the head; but now you do not welcome me, nor do you kiss me on the head. You are dejected in mind and intent upon something else, even to the point of brooding. Therefore, there must be some reason for this. So, my dear ones, without concealing, hiding, denying, or being evasive regarding this matter, explain it to me exactly as it is, truly, and without doubt. Then I shall find the end of that cause. Then King Śreṇika, having been addressed thus by Prince Abhaya, spoke to Prince Abhaya: "It is indeed so, my son. When two months of Queen Dhāriṇī, your younger mother’s pregnancy had passed and the third month was underway, at the time of her longing, this kind of longing arose: 'Blessed are those mothers... [all should be told in full] ...until I am delivered. Then, my son, because I could not find a way to fulfill Queen Dhāriṇī’s untimely longing through many means and methods, I became dejected in mind and intent upon something else, even to the point of brooding. I did not even know that you had arrived. It is for this reason, my son, that I am dejected in mind and intent upon something else, even to the point of brooding."

Then Prince Abhaya, having heard and understood this matter from King Śreṇika, with a heart glad, joyful, and delighted, his heart overflowing with the force of joy, spoke thus to King Śreṇika: “Do not, O King, be dejected in mind and intent upon [grief] as you are brooding; I shall act in such a way that my younger mother, Queen Dhāriṇī, shall attain the fulfillment of her heart’s desire regarding this unseasonable longing. Having said this, he comforted King Śreṇika with those words, which were pleasing and so forth. Then King Śreṇika, being addressed thus by Prince Abhaya, with a heart glad, joyful, and delighted, his heart overflowing with the force of joy, honored and respected Prince Abhaya and dismissed him.

Then, having been honored, respected, and dismissed by King Śreṇika, Prince Abhaya departed from the king’s presence. Having departed, he went to his own palace and sat down upon his lion-throne. Then, this reflection arose within Prince Abhaya: “It is certainly not possible to fulfill my younger mother, Queen Dhāriṇī’s unseasonable longing through any human means; it can only be done through a divine means. Now, there is a god who was formerly associated with me, a resident of the Saudharma Kalpa, possessing great power and great happiness. Therefore, it would be well for me to enter the fasting hall, observing the *poṣadha* vow, practicing celibacy, abstaining from perfumes, garlands, and ointments, laying aside weapons and ornaments, alone and without a companion, lying on a bed of *darbha* grass, undertaking the eighth meal-fast (*aṣṭama-bhakta*), and dwelling there while keeping that former associate, the god, in mind.”

Then that deity who had been his former associate thought, "I shall satisfy this pregnancy-longing of my younger sister’s wife, Dhāriṇī, which has arisen regarding unseasonable clouds. Having reflected thus, he went to the fasting hall (*pōsahasālā*). Upon arrival, he swept the fasting hall; having swept it, he inspected the area for excrement and urine; having inspected it, he ascended a bed of *dabbha* grass; having ascended it, he undertook the eighth-meal fast (*aṭṭhamabhatta*). Having undertaken the fast, he remained in the fasting hall, observing celibacy and keeping the former associate deity constantly in mind. Then, as Abhayakumāra’s eighth-meal fast was concluding, the seat of the former associate deity shook.

Then that former acquaintance, a god dwelling in the Saudharma realm, perceived his seat shaking. Having perceived it, he exercised his clairvoyant vision (*avadhi-jñāna*). Then, this kind of reflection arose within that former acquaintance, the god: "It is indeed thus: my former acquaintance, the prince named Abhaya, in the city of Rājagṛha in the southern half of Bhārata on the continent of Jambūdvīpa, having undertaken an eighth-meal fast in the fasting hall, remains there constantly keeping me in mind. Therefore, it is well for me to manifest myself in the presence of Prince Abhaya."

Reflecting thus, he departed toward the north-eastern direction. Having departed, he underwent a transformation-body emission (*vaikriyasamudghāta*). Having undergone it, he projected a staff (*daṇḍa*) extending for many *yojanas*. It consisted of: gems, diamonds, beryls, rubies, emeralds, *haṃsagarbha*, *pulaka*, *saugandhika*, *jyotīrasa*, *aṅka*, *añjana*, silver, gold, *añjanapulāka*, crystal, and *riṣṭha* stones. He shed the grosser matter particles (*pudgala*) accordingly; having shed them, he took up the subtler matter particles. Out of compassion for Abhayakumāra, and because of the sorrow born from the affection, love, and respect produced by their former births, he descended from that excellent celestial palace, the *Puṇḍarīka*, which was made of the finest jewels. As he moved swiftly toward the surface of the earth, his crest-jewel—a pinnacle of pure gold—was tilted, appearing magnificent. Adorned with clusters of many gems, gold, and jewels, his body was variegated with artistic patterns, producing joy through its human qualities. His beautiful face shone with swinging, exquisite, and lovely earrings, creating a gentle appearance like the rising moon on a night of the *Kauṃudī* festival, situated between Saturn, Mars, and Jupiter. He was a delight to the eyes, like the autumn moon, radiant with the brilliance of celestial herbs, possessing the full splendor of the moon’s beauty, and delightful with the wafting fragrance of incense. Like Meru, the king of mountains, he moved through the midst of the oceans and islands of countless names and dimensions, illuminating the world of living beings with pure radiance. Wearing a divine form, he descended into the presence of Abhaya at the excellent city of Rājagṛha.

Then that god, stationed in the sky and wearing excellent garments of ten colors adorned with small bells, spoke thus to Prince Abhaya: "O beloved of the gods, I am a god of great power dwelling in the Saudharma Kalpa, with whom you shared a former connection. Because you remained in the fasting hall having undertaken the eighth-meal fast while keeping me in mind and meditating upon me, I have come here quickly, O beloved of the gods. Command me, O beloved of the gods: what shall I do? What shall I give? What shall I offer? Or what is desired by your heart? Then Prince Abhaya, seeing that god of former connection stationed in the sky, was thrilled and delighted; he concluded his fast, and having done so, he joined his palms in reverence from his hands up to his head and spoke thus:

"Indeed, O dear one! This kind of untimely longing has arisen in my younger mother, Queen Dhāriṇī: 'Blessed are those mothers who, as previously described, wander all around at the foot of the slopes of Mount Vebhāra, and by so wandering, satisfy their longings. If I too, when the clouds have risen, [could likewise] satisfy my longing, then you, O dear one, must satisfy this kind of untimely longing for my younger mother, Queen Dhāriṇī. When the god was thus addressed by Prince Abhaya, he was delighted and joyful, and he spoke to Prince Abhaya as follows: "O dear one, remain well-composed and at ease; I shall satisfy this kind of untimely longing for your younger mother, Queen Dhāriṇī. Having said this, he departed from the presence of Prince Abhaya. Having departed, he directed a transformation-body emission (*vaikriyasamudghāta*) toward the north-eastern side of Mount Vebhāra. Having performed the emission, he very quickly manifested the divine splendor of the rainy season, accompanied by thundering, lightning, and flashes of light, adorned with the rumbling of five-colored clouds. Having manifested it, he approached Prince Abhaya and spoke to him as follows:

"Indeed, O dear one! For the sake of your pleasure, I have manifested this divine splendor of the rainy season, accompanied by thunder, rain, and lightning. Therefore, O dear one, you must satisfy this unseasonable longing of your younger mother, Queen Dhāriṇī. Then Prince Abhaya, having heard and understood this matter from that deity who was formerly associated with him and dwells in the Sōhamma heaven, became joyful and delighted. He departed from his own palace, went to where King Śreṇika was, and upon arrival, he placed his joined palms over his head in salutation and spoke thus: "Indeed, Father, for my sake, a deity dwelling in the Sōhamma heaven—who was formerly associated with me—has swiftly manifested this divine splendor of the rainy season, accompanied by thunder, lightning, and rain, and adorned with the sounds of five-colored clouds. Therefore, Father, you must satisfy this unseasonable longing of my younger mother, Queen Dhāriṇī."

Then King Śreṇika, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the presence of Prince Abhaya, was joyful and delighted. He summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, prepare and cause to be prepared the city of Rājagṛha—on its crossroads, triple-ways, quadrangles, junctions, and great highways—sprinkled with water, swept, cleaned, and smeared, [and so on] until it is fragrant with the finest scents, becoming as if a whirlpool of perfume. Report back when this command has been carried out. Then those household officials [did as they were told] and reported back. Then King Śreṇika summoned his household officials for a second time and spoke to them thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, equip the fourfold army consisting of horses, elephants, chariots, and elite foot-soldiers; and prepare the scent-elephant Śvetana! They did exactly that and reported back.

Then King Śreṇika went to where Queen Dhāriṇī was and, having approached her, spoke thus to Queen Dhāriṇī: "O beloved of the gods, indeed, the glory of the rainy season has appeared with thundering clouds and so forth; therefore, O beloved of the gods, fulfill this unseasonable longing of yours. When Queen Dhāriṇī had been addressed thus by King Śreṇika, she was delighted and joyful. She went to the bathing chamber, and having entered it, she bathed within the inner apartments, performed the offering of oblations, and completed the auspicious rites and purificatory ceremonies. Then, adorned with excellent foot-ornaments, anklets, jeweled girdles, necklaces, and various bracelets and bangles upon her arms—her arms supported by beautiful armlets—and wearing garments as radiant as the surface of the sky, she mounted the scent-elephant Śvetanaka. Being fanned on all sides by white chowries that resembled masses of foam from the nectar-ocean, she set out. Then King Śreṇika, having likewise bathed and performed the offering of oblations, mounted the back of an elephant and followed behind Queen Dhāriṇī, holding a parasol adorned with a cluster of *koreṇṭa* flowers while four chowries were being waved for him.

Then Queen Dhāriṇī, followed closely behind by King Śreṇika as he sat upon the neck of a state elephant, accompanied by a fourfold army consisting of the best of horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry, surrounded by a great multitude of soldiers, attendants, and followers, with all her splendor and glory, and amidst the sound of drums and the clamor of music, was being cheered and welcomed by the citizens of the city of Rājagṛha at the crossroads, triple-forked roads, quadrangles, junctions, and highways. She proceeded toward Mount Vaibhāra; having arrived, she wandered about on all sides at the foot of Mount Vaibhāra—through groves, gardens, forests, thickets, clusters of trees, shrubs, bushes, creepers, climbing plants, caves, ravines, peaks, herds, marshes, rivers, confluences, and glens—stopping here and there, looking about, bathing, gathering leaves, flowers, fruits, and sprouts, measuring them, smelling them, enjoying them, distributing them, and sharing them, thus fulfilling her pregnancy longing at the foot of Mount Vaibhāra. Then Queen Dhāriṇī became one whose longing was honored, whose longing was satisfied, whose longing was fulfilled, and whose longing was attained.

Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having mounted the elephant Seṇiya, a scent-elephant, followed closely behind by King Śreṇika as he stood upon the shoulder of his own elephant, proceeded with the noise of horses, elephants, and so forth, toward the city of Rājagṛha; having arrived there, she entered through the very center of the city of Rājagṛha and went to her own palace. Having arrived, she dwelt there enjoying extensive human pleasures and delights.

Then that Prince Abhaya went to the fasting hall; having arrived, he honored and respected the deity with whom he had a prior connection, and having honored and respected him, he dismissed him. Thereupon, that deity withdrew the divine splendor of the rainy season—which was accompanied by thunder, lightning, and hail, and adorned by clouds of five colors—and having withdrawn it, he departed in the same direction from which he had appeared.

When Queen Dhāriṇī had thus fulfilled that untimely longing, having had her desire honored, she remained for the sake of protecting the fetus: she stayed alert, sat alert, and slept alert; and even when taking food, she took it neither too bitter, nor too pungent, nor too astringent, nor too sour, nor too sweet, but such food as was beneficial, moderate, and desired for that fetus, eating at the proper place and time; being free from excessive passion, grief, delusion, fear, and anxiety, and with her worries, sorrows, delusions, fears, and anxieties departed, she carried that fetus comfortably by means of seasonal comforts—delicious foods, clothing, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.

Then, when nine months and seven and a half nights had fully elapsed, Queen Dhāriṇī gave birth at the hour of midnight to a boy whose hands and feet were delicate and who was beautiful in every limb. When the female attendants saw that Queen Dhāriṇī had given birth to a boy whose hands and feet were delicate and who was beautiful in every limb—having seen this—they went quickly, swiftly, hurriedly, and fleetly to where King Śreṇika was. Having approached, they greeted King Śreṇika with cries of "Victory! and "Triumph! Having greeted him, they placed their joined palms over their heads in salutation and spoke thus: "O Lord, Queen Dhāriṇī has indeed given birth to a boy whose hands and feet are delicate and who is beautiful in every limb, after nine months had fully elapsed. We announce this pleasant news to you, O Lord; may it be pleasing to you."

Then King Śreṇika, having heard and understood this matter from those female attendants, was delighted and joyful. He honored and respected those female attendants with sweet words and with an abundance of flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments; he washed their heads, provided them with a livelihood for themselves and their descendants, and having done so, dismissed them. Then King Śreṇika summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Have the city of Rājagṛha sprinkled [with water] and swept, and have it adorned; have the prisons cleaned; and having done so, increase the measures and weights. Having fulfilled this command, report back to me. They reported back accordingly.

Then King Śreṇika summoned the eighteen provincial governors and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Go, dear friends! In the city of Rājagṛha, both inside and outside, perform and cause to be performed for ten days the festival of the installation (sthāpanā), free from anxiety, free from tumult, free from the entry of royal officers, without the sounding of drums or small drums, without fines, without imprisonment, without the beating of drums, with unfading garlands of flowers, adorned with the finest courtesans and actors, attended by many musicians, delightful with joyful sports, according to the custom of the installation as is appropriate. And report back this command. They did exactly so and reported back accordingly. Then King Śreṇika, seated upon an excellent lion-throne in the outer assembly hall facing the east, remained there while distributing, causing to be distributed, and receiving gifts by the hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands. And he passed his time in this manner.

Then his parents performed the birth-rite on the first day; on the second day, they held a vigil; on the third day, they performed the ceremony of showing the moon and sun. When the impure birth-rites had been completed and twelve days had passed, they prepared an abundance of solid food, soft food, chewable food, and lickable food. Having prepared it, they invited their friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, connections, and many officials, including the *gaṇanāyakas* and others. Then, having bathed, performed their offerings, and completed the auspicious purificatory rites, and being adorned with all ornaments, they entered a vast and magnificent dining hall. There, together with their friends, kinsmen, *gaṇanāyakas*, and others, they partook of, relished, distributed, and consumed that abundant solid food up to lickable food, and so they remained. When they had finished eating and were satisfied, refreshed, pure, and rendered supremely clean, they honored and respected their friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, connections, retinue, and many officials, including the *gaṇanāyakas* and the *sandhivālas*, with an abundance of flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. And having done so, they spoke as follows:

"Since this longing arose for our son even while he was still in the womb during unseasonable rains, let our son be named Meha. Thus his parents gave the boy that appropriate name, Meha, derived from his specific quality. Then the boy Meha was attended by five nurses, namely: the milk-nurse, the bath-nurse, the play-nurse, the adornment-nurse, and the lap-nurse. Furthermore, he was surrounded by a retinue of many female attendants—dwarfs, Cilātīs, Vāmanīs, Vaḍabhīs, Babbarīs, Baūsīs, Jōmiyās, Pallaviyās, Īsiṇiyās, Thārugiṇiyās, Lāsiyās, Laüsiyās, Dāmilīs, Siṁhalīs, Ārabīs, Pulindīs, Pakkaṇīs, Bahalīs, Maruṇḍīs, Sabarīs, and Pārasīs—women from various countries adorned with foreign ornaments, who understood gestures, thoughts, and desires, wore the dress and attire of their respective regions, were skillful and disciplined, and formed a circle of handmaidens, umbrella-bearers, chamberlains, door-keepers, and eunuchs. Being passed from hand to hand, cradled from lap to lap, being sung to, and fondled, he grew up in great comfort upon a delightful jeweled floor, like a *campaka* tree nestled in a mountain cave, free from wind and obstruction. Then, in due course, the parents of the boy Meha performed his naming ceremony, the first feeding of solid food, the first walking, and the tonsure ceremony with great wealth, honor, and grandeur.

When Prince Megha was a little over eight years old, his parents presented him to a teacher of the arts during an auspicious eighth month of pregnancy, on a day marked by favorable astrological conjunctions and moments. Then that teacher of the arts instructed and trained Prince Megha in the seventy-two arts, both in their theory (*sutta*), their meaning (*attha*), and their practical application (*karaṇa*), from writing (*lēha*) up to the cries of birds (*saüṇaruya*). They were as follows: writing, arithmetic, drawing, dancing, singing, instrumental music, the science of musical scales (*saragaya*), the science of drumming (*pōkkharagaya*), rhythmic clapping (*samatāla*), gambling, popular lore (*jaṇavāya*), logic (*pāsaya*), the art of debate (*aṭṭhāvaya*), the art of storytelling (*pōrēkavva*), the preparation of water-pastes (*dagamaṭṭiya*), the rules for food, the rules for drink, the rules for clothing, the rules for ointments, the rules for beds, riddles (*ajja*), enigmatic verses (*pahēliya*), *Māgadhī* verses, *Gāhā* verses, songs (*gīiya*), poetry (*silōya*), the application of silver, the application of gold, the application of perfumes (*cuṇṇajutti*), the rules for jewelry, the grooming of young women (*taruṇīpaḍikamma*), the characteristics of women, the characteristics of men, the characteristics of horses, the characteristics of elephants, the characteristics of oxen, the characteristics of cocks, the characteristics of umbrellas, the characteristics of staffs, the characteristics of swords, the characteristics of gems, the characteristics of coins (*kāgaṇi*), architecture (*vatthuvijja*), the measurement of military camps (*khandhāramāṇa*), the measurement of cities (*nagaramāṇa*), military arrays (*vūha*), counter-arrays (*paḍivūha*), scouting (*cāra*), counter-scouting (*paḍicāra*), the wheel-array (*cakkavūha*), the eagle-array (*garulavūha*), the cart-array (*sagaḍavūha*), combat (*juddha*), wrestling (*nijuddha*), hand-to-hand combat (*juddhāijuddha*), fighting with sticks (*aṭṭhijuddha*), boxing (*muṭṭhijuddha*), arm-wrestling (*bāhujuddha*), sword-fighting (*layājuddha*), archery (*īsattha*), the science of missiles (*charuppavāya*), the science of the bow (*dhaṇuvēya*), the refining of silver, the refining of gold, ball-games (*vaṭṭakhēḍḍa*), string-games (*suttakhēḍḍa*), pipe-games (*nāliyākhēḍḍa*), leaf-cutting (*pattacchējja*), wood-carving (*kaḍacchējja*), living models (*sajjīva*), lifeless models (*nijjīva*), and the cries of birds.

Then that teacher of the arts taught and instructed Prince Megha in the seventy-two arts—beginning with writing and culminating in the cries of birds—in their rules, their meanings, and their practical applications. Having taught and instructed him, he presented him to his parents. Then the parents of Prince Megha honored and respected that teacher of the arts with sweet words and with abundant clothing, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments; having honored and respected him, they gave him a generous gift of affection appropriate for his livelihood, and then dismissed him.

Then that prince Mēha became proficient in the seventy-two arts, well-versed in the ninefold scriptures (*navaṅgasutta*), an expert in the eighteen types of regional dialects (*dēsībhāsā*), a lover of song, skilled in music and dance, a warrior on horseback, a warrior on elephant, a warrior in chariot, a warrior with his arms, a crusher of arms, capable of enjoying pleasures, daring, and a wanderer at night. Then the parents of the prince Mēha, seeing that their son Mēha had become proficient in the seventy-two arts and had become a wanderer at night, caused eight magnificent palaces (*pāsāyavaḍiṁsaē*) to be built. They were lofty and towering, as if laughing; variegated with patterns of jewels, gold, and gems; adorned with fluttering victory banners (*vijaya-vējayantī*), flags, and parasols above parasols; high, with peaks reaching toward the surface of the sky; shimmering like a cluster of gems through the lattice windows; with jeweled and golden pillars like blooming white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*); shining like half-moons made of *tilaka* gems; adorned with garlands of various jewels; smooth inside and out; with floors spread with golden sand and strewn with beautiful pebbles; pleasant to the touch, lovely in form, delightful, and so forth, even unto being peerless. And they caused one great mansion to be built, supported by many hundreds of pillars, featuring graceful standing statues of women (*sālabhañjiyā*). It was beautiful with lofty, well-fashioned archways (*toraṇa*) and excellent statues of women; with very polished, distinguished, elegant, and well-proportioned pillars of *vairuliya* (cat’s-eye) gems; inlaid with various jewels, gold, and gems; with a floor that was bright, very level, well-divided, and delightful; variegated with designs of wild animals and deer; charming with archways and railings rising from the pillars; appearing like a pair of twin Vidyādharas joined together; worthy of being garlanded by thousands of rays of light; possessed of thousands of forms; shimmering, dazzling, and captivating to the eyes; pleasant to the touch, lovely in form, with pillars of gold, jewels, and gems; its upper peaks adorned with bells and flags of five colors; emitting white camphor smoke; smeared, plastered, and perfumed like a fragrant paste; delightful, worth seeing, beautiful, and peerless.

Then, on an auspicious day, at a favorable conjunction of the lunar mansions and moment, the parents of Prince Meha had him take the hand of eight excellent princesses in marriage on a single day; they were brought from royal families of equal status, of similar age, stature, and endowed with similar qualities of beauty, form, youth, and virtue, and were accompanied by the auspicious recitations of the eightfold blessings for a bride and the presentation of bridal gifts.

Then his parents gave this kind of gift of joy to that Mēha: eight crores of gold coins, eight crores of gold [pieces]—this should be recited according to the sequence of the verses—up to female messengers; and furthermore, abundant wealth consisting of bullion, gold, gems, jewels, pearls, conch shells, crystals, coral, red jewels, and all kinds of excellent, precious, and valuable things, sufficient to give as much as desired, to enjoy as much as desired, and to distribute as much as desired, down to the seventh generation of the family line.

Then Prince Meha gave to each of his wives one hundred million pieces of gold, and so on, until he gave each a female servant; furthermore, he distributed vast amounts of wealth, gold, and so forth, providing for them all. Then Prince Meha, staying in his excellent upper palace, being sung to by thirty-two musical ensembles accompanied by beautiful young women playing cymbals and drums, being fanned and entertained, dwelt enjoying the abundant human pleasures of desirable sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and scents.

At that time, on that occasion, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, wandering in regular succession through villages and towns, traveling comfortably, arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and stayed at the Guṇasilaka shrine.

Then, in the city of Rājagṛha, from the crossroads up to the great sound of the people, many *uggas* and *bhogas* were departing in one direction toward a single goal through the very center of the city of Rājagṛha. And Prince Megha, staying atop his excellent palace with the tops of his towers resounding, enjoying human sensual pleasures, and repeatedly gazing down at the royal highway, was thus passing his time.

Then Prince Meha saw those many *ugras*, *bhogas*, and others departing toward a single direction; having seen them, he summoned his chamberlain and spoke thus: "O dear sir, what is it today in the city of Rājagṛha—is there a festival for Indra, or a festival for Skanda, or likewise for Rudra, Vaiśramaṇa, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, rivers, lakes, trees, shrines (*caityas*), or mountains, or a festival for a garden, a mountain, or a spring, such that these many *ugras*, *bhogas*, and others are departing toward a single direction? Then that chamberlain, having received news of the arrival of the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra, spoke thus to Prince Meha:

"Indeed, O beloved of the gods, there is no festival for Indra, nor [any other festival] up to the pilgrimage to Mount Girija, in the city of Rājagṛha today, such that these *uggas*, *bhogas*, and others are departing in one direction, toward one goal. Rather, O beloved of the gods, the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra—the founder, the Tīrthaṅkara—has arrived here in this region, has reached here, and is staying in a manner appropriate to the occasion at the Guṇasilaka shrine in this very city of Rājagṛha. Then, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the mouth of his chamberlain, Prince Megha was delighted and overjoyed. He summoned his household servants and spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods, quickly prepare a four-bell chariot drawn by horses! "So be it," they replied, and prepared it.

Then that Mēha, having bathed and being adorned with all ornaments, mounted a horse-chariot with four bells; while a parasol decorated with *kōraṇṭa* flowers and garlands was held over him, and surrounded by a great retinue of soldiers, attendants, and followers, he went out through the very center of the city of Rājagṛha. Having gone out, he approached the Guṇasilaka shrine. Upon arriving, he saw the successive layers of parasols and flags, as well as the Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and Jambhakas, both descending and ascending. Having seen them, he descended from his four-belled horse-chariot. Having descended, he approached the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, with a fivefold approach, namely: by removing animate objects, by not removing inanimate objects, by arranging his upper garment over one shoulder (*ekasāṭikottarāsaṅga*), by joining his palms at the sight [of the Teacher], and by concentrating his mind on a single point. He went to where the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was, and having gone there, he performed three circumambulations from left to right. Having performed them, he paid homage and saluted him. Having paid homage and saluted him, he waited upon the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, nearby yet not too far away, listening attentively, with palms joined, facing him, and with humility.

Then the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra, standing in the midst of that great and vast assembly, proclaimed the manifold Dharma—how living beings awaken, how they are liberated, and how they become defiled; the discourse on Dharma should be related [in full] until the assembly had departed.

Then that prince Megha, having heard and reflected upon the Dharma from the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, was joyful and delighted. He performed three circumambulations, keeping the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, to his right; having done so, he paid homage and reverence. Having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: "I have faith, O Lord, in the Nirgrantha doctrine; I believe it, I am pleased with it, and I accept it, O Lord. This Nirgrantha doctrine, O Lord, is indeed so; this, O Lord, is exactly so; this, O Lord, is not otherwise; this, O Lord, is desired; this, O Lord, is accepted; this, O Lord, is both desired and accepted. It is just as you say, O beloved of the gods. However, O beloved of the gods, I shall first take leave of my parents; thereafter, having shaved my head, I will go forth from the home to the homeless state. "As it pleases you, O beloved of the gods; do not delay," [the Blessed One replied].

Then the prince Meha paid homage and reverence to the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra; having paid homage and reverence, he went to where his four-bell chariot was, and having gone there, he mounted the four-bell chariot. With a great retinue of troops and followers, he proceeded through the very center of the city of Rājagṛha to his own palace. Having arrived, he descended from the four-bell chariot; having descended, he went to where his mother and father were, and having gone there, he prostrated at the feet of his mother and father and spoke thus:

"Thus indeed, mothers, have I heard the Dharma in the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra; and that Dharma has been desired, accepted, and approved by me. Then his parents said this to him: "Blessed are you, my son! You are fulfilled, my son! You have achieved your purpose, my son! You are one of auspicious marks, my son! Since you have heard the Dharma in the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, and since that Dharma has been desired, accepted, and approved by you. Then the youth Meha said this to his parents for a second time: "Thus indeed, mothers, have I heard the Dharma in the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra; and that Dharma has been desired, accepted, and approved by me. Therefore, mothers, I desire with your permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness, having become a monk in the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra."

Then Queen Dhāriṇī, having heard and reflected upon those harsh words—which were undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, unpleasing, and never before heard—was overcome by a great mental anguish born of grief for her son. With the hair on her body standing on end and her limbs trembling from the weight of her sorrow, she was tearful, her face dejected and despondent like a lotus garland crushed in the palm of a hand. At that moment, her bodily luster and beauty faded and vanished; her ornaments became loose, her white bracelets slipped and crumbled, and her upper garment fell away. Her delicate locks of hair became disheveled, and she fainted from the force of her emotion. Heavy as if weighed down by a fallen axe, like a Champaka creeper cut down at its root, or like Indra’s staff dropped from the sky, her joints and ligaments gave way, and she fell with a thud, her entire body collapsing onto the floor. Then Queen Dhāriṇī, being quickly sprinkled with a stream of cool, pure water flowing from the mouth of a golden pitcher by the attendants of the harem, had her body revived. Fanned by the breeze produced by the waving of fans, and touched by the attendants, she was comforted. As tears flowed from her breasts like a string of pearls, she, piteous, despondent, and miserable, weeping, wailing, sobbing, grieving, and lamenting, spoke thus to Prince Meha: [The rest of the text follows...]

"My son, you are our only son—beloved, dear, pleasing, charming, delightful, trustworthy, affectionate, esteemed, highly cherished, and approved. You are like a casket of treasures, a jewel among jewels, the very breath of our life, the source of joy to our hearts, and as rare to hear of as the *umbara* flower; how much more so to behold! Indeed, my son, we cannot bear even a moment's separation from you. Therefore, enjoy these abundant human pleasures while we still live. After we have passed away, when we are old and our lineage has been firmly established, you may then, free from anxiety, go forth from the home into the homeless state under the guidance of the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra."

When Prince Megha had been addressed thus by his parents, he spoke to them in this way: "O mother and father, it is exactly as you say to me: 'You, my son, are our only child... [and so on] until... you will go forth as a monk without concern for us. Indeed, mother and father, human existence is unstable, impermanent, and insecure; it is overwhelmed by calamities and afflictions, as flickering as a flash of lightning, transient, like a bubble on water, resembling a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass, similar to the hue of a twilight cloud, comparable to the sight of a dream, subject to the nature of crumbling, falling, and destruction; it must inevitably be abandoned both later and sooner. Who, mother and father, knows who shall go first and who shall go last? Therefore, mother and father, I desire, with your permission, to go forth as a monk under the Blessed One."

Then his parents spoke thus to Prince Megha: "My son, these wives of yours are similar, equal in complexion, equal in age, and endowed with similar beauty, form, youth, and virtues; they have been brought from royal families of equal status. Therefore, my son, enjoy extensive human pleasures together with them; later, having experienced those pleasures, you may go forth as a śramaṇa."

Then Prince Megha spoke thus to his mother and father: "O mothers and fathers, it is exactly as you say to me: 'My son, these [wives] are suitable for you... until you go forth into the religious life under the Blessed One. Indeed, O mothers and fathers, human sensual pleasures are impure; they flow with vomit, bile, phlegm, lymph, and blood. They are filled with foul exhalations and inhalations, and with foul urine, feces, pus, and many other things. They originate from feces, urine, phlegm, snot, tears, bile, lymph, and blood. They are unstable, non-eternal, non-permanent, subject to decay, falling apart, and destruction. They must inevitably be abandoned both later and sooner. Who knows, O mothers and fathers, who will go first and who will go last? Therefore, O mothers and fathers, I wish to go forth into the religious life. Then his mother and father spoke thus to Prince Megha: "My son, here is your wealth inherited from your ancestors, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers—abundant gold, silver, bronze, cloth, jewels, pearls, shells, crystals, corals, and red gems, along with a vast store of treasures. Enough of it to give, enjoy, and distribute as much as you like, even down to the seventh generation of your lineage. So, my son, enjoy this extensive human prosperity and honor while it lasts; then, after you have experienced these blessings, you may go forth into the religious life in the presence of the Blessed One Mahāvīra."

Then Prince Meha spoke thus to his parents: "O mothers and fathers, it is exactly as you say to me: 'These are your ancestors, your great-grandparents,' and so on, until 'you shall go forth after having experienced prosperity. But indeed, O mothers and fathers, gold and so forth, up to wealth, is subject to fire, subject to thieves, subject to kings, subject to heirs, and subject to death; it is common to fire and so on, up to common to death; it is of the nature of crumbling, falling, and destruction; and it must inevitably be abandoned both later and earlier. Who knows, O mothers and fathers, who will go first and who will go last? Therefore, I wish to go forth [into the religious life]."

When the parents of Prince Meha were unable to persuade him through many conciliatory explanations, instructions, admonitions, and entreaties that were favorable to sensual pleasures, they then instructed him with teachings unfavorable to sensual pleasures that were intended to produce fear of self-restraint, saying this: "My son, this Nirgrantha doctrine is true, unsurpassed, absolute, perfect, leading, pure, a thorn-remover, the path to perfection, the path to liberation, the path of deliverance, the path to *nirvāṇa*, the path to the cessation of all suffering. It is like a snake seen only at one end; it is like a razor with a single edge; it must be steered like iron arrows; it is as tasteless as a mouthful of sand; it is like the Ganges, a great river, flowing against the current; it is like the great ocean, difficult to cross with one's arms; it must be traversed with sharpness, endured with heaviness, and practiced like walking on the edge of a sword. Indeed, my son, it is not permitted for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, to eat or drink food that is procured by them, or prepared specifically for them, or bought, or stored, or prepared, or food given during a famine, or food from a wilderness, or food given during a storm, or food for the sick, or food consisting of roots, tubers, fruits, seeds, or green vegetables.
