And you, my son, are accustomed to comfort and not accustomed to hardship; you are not capable of enduring cold, heat, hunger, thirst, or various diseases and ailments arising from wind, bile, phlegm, or their combination; nor are you capable of properly enduring the many and varied hardships and afflictions that are thorns to the village. Therefore, my son, enjoy human sensual pleasures first; afterwards, having enjoyed them, you may go forth as a Śramaṇa."

When Prince Megha had been addressed thus by his parents, he spoke to them as follows: “It is exactly so, mothers, as you say to me: ‘O son, this Nigaṇṭha doctrine is true and unsurpassed... [repeating the same] up to: ‘...thereafter, having enjoyed worldly pleasures, you shall go forth from the home life into homelessness under the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra. But indeed, mothers, this Nigaṇṭha doctrine is difficult for the lazy, the faint-hearted, the base, those bound to this world, and those who have no thirst for the next world; it is difficult for ordinary people, but not at all for one who is steadfast, resolute, and self-controlled. What is difficult for such a person to do in this matter? Therefore, mothers, I desire, with your permission, to go forth as an ascetic under the Lord Mahāvīra.”

When the parents were unable to persuade Prince Meha by means of many exhortations, instructions, admonitions, and entreaties—both favorable to the objects of the senses and contrary to them, whether to inform him, instruct him, admonish him, or entreat him—they then, against their own will, spoke thus to Prince Meha: "Dear son, we wish to see even a single glimpse of your royal splendor. Then Prince Meha, complying with his parents, remained silent. Thereupon King Śreṇika summoned his household officials and said to them: "O beloved of the gods, quickly prepare for Prince Meha a grand, costly, magnificent, and extensive royal consecration ceremony."

Then those householders presented [the items]. Then King Śreṇika, surrounded by many chief ministers and so forth, up to the boundary-guardians, together with eight hundred golden jars, silver jars, jeweled jars, gold-and-silver jars, gold-and-jeweled jars, silver-and-jeweled jars, gold-and-silver-and-jeweled jars, and earthen jars—with all kinds of water, all kinds of clay, all kinds of flowers, all kinds of perfumes, all kinds of unguents, all kinds of medicinal herbs, and *siddhārthaka* seeds; with all prosperity, all splendor, all power, and with the sound of drums and the noise of music, performed the great royal consecration (*rājābhiṣeka*) upon Prince Megha. Having consecrated him, and having joined his palms [in reverence], he spoke thus: "Victory, victory, O Nanda! Victory, victory, O Bhadra! Victory, victory, O Nanda! May it be well with you! Conquer what is unconquered! Protect what is conquered! Dwell in the midst of the conquered! Conquer the faction of enemies that is unconquered! Protect the faction of friends that is conquered! And as Bharata was for men, so may you exercise sovereignty over the city of Rājagṛha, and over many other villages, towns, cities, and settlements, and dwell [there]. Having said this, they raised a cry of "Victory, victory! Then that King Megha became like the Great Himavat mountain and dwelt [in glory].

Then the parents of King Megha spoke thus to King Megha: "Speak, my son! What shall we give? What shall we bestow? Or what power do you desire in your heart? Then King Megha spoke thus to his parents: "I desire, O mothers, that a dust-removing broom and an alms-bowl be brought from a barber's shop, and that a barber be summoned."

Then King Śreṇika summoned his household officials and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Go, dear friends, take three hundred thousand [pieces of gold] from the treasury; with two hundred thousand, purchase a water-strainer and an alms-bowl from a shopkeeper, and with one hundred thousand, summon the barber Kāśyapa."

Then those householders, being thus addressed by King Śreṇika, were delighted and joyful; taking three hundred thousand [pieces of gold] from the treasury, they brought a raincoat and an alms-bowl for two hundred thousand, and with one hundred thousand, they summoned the Kāśyapa.

Then that Kāśyapa, having been summoned by those householders, was joyful, satisfied, and delighted in heart; his mind overflowing with joy, he bathed, performed his ritual offerings, completed the auspicious purificatory rites, put on clean, excellent garments, and adorned his body with many costly ornaments. He went to where King Śreṇika was, and upon arriving, he placed his joined palms over his head in salutation before King Śreṇika and spoke thus: "Command me, O Lord, as to what must be done by me."

Then King Śreṇika said this to the barber Kāśyapa: "Go, dear sir! With fragrant scented water, wash your hands and feet; bind your mouth with a white four-cornered cloth, and shave the crown hair of Prince Mehara that is suitable for the renunciation ceremony, leaving a space of four finger-breadths. When the barber Kāśyapa had been thus addressed by King Śreṇika, he was delighted, satisfied, joyful, and his heart overflowing with gladness; he gave his assent. Having assented, he washed his hands and feet with fragrant scented water, bound his mouth with a clean cloth, and with great care shaved the crown hair of Prince Mehara that was suitable for the renunciation ceremony, leaving a space of four finger-breadths.

Then the mother of Prince Meha received his hair with a highly precious cloth marked with the sign of a swan; having received it, she washed it with fragrant scented water; having washed it, she applied a paste of fresh Gośīrṣa sandalwood; having applied it, she bound it with a white turban; having bound it, she placed it in a jeweled casket; having placed it in the casket, she put it into a chest. Shedding tears as bright as strings of pearls from *hāra*, *vāridhāra*, and *sinduvāra* flowers, weeping repeatedly, wailing, and lamenting, she spoke thus: "This shall be the final sight of our Prince Meha on occasions of prosperity, festivals, births, auspicious days, celebrations, sacrifices, and holy days. Having said this, she placed it at the foot of the head of the bed.

Then the parents of Prince Mēha had the *uttarāvakkamaṇa* lion-throne prepared; they bathed Prince Mēha for a second and a third time with white and blue pitchers. Having bathed him, they rubbed his limbs with soft, delicate *gandhakāsāiya* powder. Having rubbed them, they anointed his limbs with fresh *gōsīsa-candana*. Having anointed them, they dressed him in a silken garment (*paḍasāḍaga*) marked with the swan-sign, which was as pure as the breath from the nostrils. Having dressed him, they fastened upon him a necklace (*hāra*), a half-necklace (*addhahāra*), and likewise a single-string necklace (*ēgāvali*), a pearl necklace (*muttāvali*), a gold necklace (*kaṇagāvali*), a jewel necklace (*rayaṇāvali*), a long pendant (*pālamba*), a foot-pendant (*pāyapalamba*), bracelets (*kaḍaga*), armlets (*tuḍiga*), upper-arm bracelets (*kēūra*), finger-rings (*aṅguliya*), a set of ten seals (*dasamuddiyāṇantaya*), a waist-band (*kaḍisuttaya*), earrings (*kuṇḍala*), a crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*), and a crown (*maüḍa*) adorned with jewels. Having fastened these, they made him like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkhaga*), adorned and decorated with the fourfold types of ornaments: knotted (*ganthima*), woven (*vēḍhima*), stuffed (*pūrima*), and sewn (*saṅghāima*).

Then King Śreṇika summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Have a palanquin prepared—a palanquin supported by hundreds of pillars, adorned with graceful *sālabhañjikā* figures, decorated with patterns of elephants, bulls, horses, men, crocodiles, birds, serpents, *kinnaras*, *ruru* deer, *sarabhas*, yak-tails, elephants, forest creepers, and lotus creepers; possessing a sweet and charming sound from rows of bells; beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold; encircled by a network of tinkling gem-studded chimes set with skillfully inset, glittering jewels; delightful with its lofty diamond railings; appearing like a pair of *vidyādhara* youths joined together; radiant with thousands of garlands of light, endowed with thousands of forms, shimmering and sparkling, a delight to the eyes, pleasant to the touch, of auspicious appearance, swift, rapid, and agile, and carried by a thousand men. Then those household officials, joyful and delighted, prepared the palanquin—supported by hundreds of pillars, and so forth—and presented it.

Then Prince Meha mounts the palanquin; having mounted it, he sits down upon an excellent lion-throne facing the east. Then Prince Meha’s mother—having bathed, performed the ritual offerings, and adorned her body with many costly ornaments—mounts the palanquin; having mounted it, she sits on a throne at Prince Meha’s right side. Then Prince Meha’s wet-nurse, taking a broom and an alms-bowl, mounts the palanquin; having mounted it, she sits on a throne at Prince Meha’s left side.

Behind Prince Meha stood one exquisite young woman, charmingly attired in the colors of love and beauty, skilled in the arts of graceful movement, laughter, speech, gesture, amorous play, conversation, and polite conduct. Her breasts were firm, full, lovely, well-shaped, and closely set, like a pair of joined *āmēlaka* fruits. Holding a white sunshade (*āyavatta*) as bright as jasmine and moonlight, adorned with a cluster of *kōrēṇṭa* flowers and a garland of blossoms, she stood gracefully waving it back and forth. Then two other exquisite young women, likewise charmingly attired in the colors of love and beauty and skilled in all such arts, mounted the palanquin. Once seated, they stood on either side of Prince Meha, gracefully waving back and forth two chowries (*cāmara*). These chowries had handles made of various jewels, gold, gems, and highly refined, glittering, variegated gold; they were radiant, possessed soft and long hairs, and were as white as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, snow, silver, or a mass of foam. They stood there, gracefully waving them back and forth.

Then, a certain excellent young woman, adorned with ornaments and skilled [in her duties], mounted the palanquin for Prince Meha; having mounted it, she stood to the east of Prince Meha, holding a fan with a handle made of moonstone, diamond, and pure beryl. Then, another excellent young woman, likewise skilled, mounted the palanquin for Prince Meha; having mounted it, she stood to the southeast of Prince Meha, holding a water-pot made of silver, pure and filled with water, shaped like the great face of an elephant in rut. Then, Prince Meha’s father summoned his household servants and spoke to them thus:

"Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Summon a thousand young, excellent householders who are similar in appearance, similar in age, and who have taken up identical ornaments and equipment. They summoned them. Then those young, excellent householders, having been summoned by the king's officers, were delighted; they bathed, adorned themselves with all their finery, took up identical ornaments and equipment, and went to where King Śreṇika was. Having arrived, they spoke thus to King Śreṇika: "Command us, O beloved of the gods, what we should do."

Then King Śreṇika said to those thousand young householders: "Go, dear friends, and carry the palanquin for Prince Megha, which is borne by a thousand men. Then that thousand of young householders, being thus addressed by King Śreṇika, were delighted and carried the palanquin for Prince Megha, which was borne by a thousand men. When Prince Megha had mounted the palanquin borne by a thousand men, these eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalaka) proceeded first before him in due order: namely, the *svastika*, the *śrīvatsa*, the *nandyāvarta*, the *vardhamānaka*, the *bhadrāsana*, the *kalaśa*, the *matsya*, and the *darpaṇa*. [And] many people seeking wealth, [with various desires], [praising him] with those desirable things, [and so forth], continuously congratulating and extolling him, spoke thus: "Victory, victory, O Nanda! Victory, victory, O Bhadra! Victory, victory, O Nanda! May it be well with you! Being unconquered, conquer the senses; having conquered them, protect the duty of a śramaṇa. Having conquered obstacles, dwell, O Lord, in the midst of perfection (*siddhi*). Destroy the enemies of passion and hatred with austerity, having firmly girded your loins with fortitude. Crush the enemies of the eight karmas with supreme, pure meditation. Being vigilant, attain stainless, unsurpassed, absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*). Go to liberation (*mokṣa*), the supreme, eternal, and unshakable state. Alas! Be fearless toward the armies of hardships (*parīṣaha*) and undaunted by afflictions and calamities. May there be no obstacle to your Dharma! Having spoken thus, they repeatedly raised cries of auspiciousness and victory. Then Prince Megha, proceeding through the very center of the city of Rājagṛha, went to the Guṇasilaka shrine. Having arrived, he descended from the palanquin borne by a thousand men.

Then the parents of the prince Meha placed Meha before them and approached the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra. Having approached, they performed three circumambulations—clockwise and counter-clockwise—around the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra; having done so, they paid homage and bowed down to him. Having paid homage and bowed down, they spoke thus: “O Devāṇuppiyas, this is our only son, Meha, dear and beloved, [our very] breath of life, the joy of our hearts, as rare to hear of as an *umbara* flower, let alone to behold. Just as a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white water-lily, though born in the mud and raised in the water, is not defiled by the mud nor defiled by the water; even so, Meha, though born among sensual pleasures and raised among enjoyments, is not defiled by passion for sensual pleasures, nor is he defiled by passion for enjoyments. O Devāṇuppiyas, Meha is terrified of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and is afraid of birth, old age, and death. He desires, O Devāṇuppiyas, to go forth from the home into the homeless state under you, having shaved his head. We offer ourselves as alms for disciples to the Devāṇuppiyas; may the Devāṇuppiyas accept this alms for disciples.”

When the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, had been thus addressed by the parents of Prince Meha, he correctly accepted this matter. Then Prince Meha departed from the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, toward the north-eastern direction; he himself removed his ornaments, garlands, and finery. Then the mother of Prince Meha caught the ornaments, garlands, and finery in a cloth-strip marked with the swan-sign; having caught them, shedding tears like a stream of water, like a *sinduvāra* flower, or like a string of pearls—shedding them again and again, weeping, wailing, and lamenting—she spoke thus: "O son, you must strive! O son, you must exert yourself! O son, you must persevere! And in this matter, you must not be negligent! May this very path be ours as well! Having said this, the parents of Prince Meha paid homage and reverence to the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra; and having paid homage and reverence, they returned to the very direction from which they had come.

Then the prince Mēha himself performed the tonsure of five handfuls of hair; having done so, he approached the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra. Having approached, he circumambulated the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, three times, keeping him to his right; he paid homage and reverenced him. Having paid homage and reverenced him, he spoke thus: “Blessed One, the world is ablaze; Blessed One, the world is set on fire; Blessed One, the world is both ablaze and set on fire by old age and death. It is just as if some householder, while his house is burning, were to take whatever goods there are that are of little weight but great value, and depart for a secluded place, thinking: ‘Once this has been secured, it will later and earlier be for my welfare, happiness, peace, total security, and future benefit. Even so, I too have a certain asset of the self that is desirable, lovely, dear, pleasant, and agreeable; once this has been secured, it will bring about the end of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, O beloved of the gods, I desire that you yourself initiate me, yourself shave me, yourself instruct me, yourself teach me, and yourself explain the Dharma concerning conduct, scope, discipline, modesty, behavior, practice, and the observance of the rules of life.”

Then the Blessed Śramaṇa Mahāvīra himself initiated Prince Megha and himself taught him the conduct and the Dharma, saying: "O beloved of the gods! You must proceed thus; you must stand thus; you must sit thus; you must lie down thus; you must eat thus; you must speak thus; and having risen from your seat, you must restrain yourself with self-restraint toward living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings; and in this matter, you must not be negligent. Then Prince Megha correctly accepted this religious instruction from the presence of the Blessed Śramaṇa Mahāvīra; according to that command, he proceeded thus, stood thus, sat thus, lay down thus, ate thus, spoke thus, and having risen from his seat, he restrained himself with self-restraint toward living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings.

On the very day that Prince Meha, having shaved his head, went forth from the home life into homelessness, in the afternoon of that same day, while the beds and bedding were being distributed among the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, according to their seniority, a bed and bedding was assigned to Prince Meha at the door. Then, during the time between the first watch and the last watch of the night, as the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, were coming and going for the purpose of recitation, questioning, rehearsing, and reflection on the Dharma, or for the sake of voiding urine or excrement, some of them brushed against Prince Meha with their limbs; likewise, some brushed against him with their feet, heads, bellies, or bodies; some stepped over him, some stepped upon him, and some covered him with the dust and dirt of their feet. During such a great night, Prince Meha was not able to close his eyes even for a moment.

Then, this kind of reflection arose within the mind of Prince Megha: "Indeed, I am the son of King Śreṇika and Queen Dhāriṇī, known as Megha... up to the point of being heard of. While I was living in the midst of the household, the Śramaṇas and Nirgranthas used to welcome me, recognize me, honor me, and respect me; they explained to me points of doctrine, reasons, questions, causes, and answers; and they conversed with me in pleasant, lovely, and charming words. But from the moment I shaved my head and went forth from the household life into homelessness, the Śramaṇas and Nirgranthas no longer welcome me, nor do they converse with me. Furthermore, during the latter part of the night, at the time of recitation and questioning, [they keep me awake] until such a late hour that I am unable to close my eyes even for a moment. Therefore, it would be better for me, tomorrow at dawn when the night has passed and the sun is blazing with its radiance, to take leave of the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra and return once more to live in the midst of the household. Having thus reflected, his mind overcome by the eight worldly concerns, he spent that night as if in hell. When the dawn had broken and the night was pure, while the sun was blazing with its radiance, he went to where the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra was. Having approached, he performed three circumambulations around the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra from left to right, and having done so, he paid homage, bowed down, and waited upon him.

Then, the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, spoke thus to the youth Megha: "Megha, it is indeed true that during the latter part of the night, while you were with the ascetics, the Nirgranthas, for the purpose of recitation and questioning—and while this very long night lasted—you were unable to close your eyes even for a moment. Then, Megha, there arose within you this kind of internal reflection: 'When I lived as a householder, the ascetics, the Nirgranthas, honored me... [and so on] ...and acknowledged me. But from the time I shaved my head and went forth from home into homelessness, the ascetics, the Nirgranthas, have no longer honored me... nor acknowledged me. Furthermore, during the night, some of the ascetics, the Nirgranthas, have covered me with dust and dirt from their feet while they were reciting... Therefore, it would be best for me, when tomorrow morning has dawned, to take leave of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, and to return once more to live as a householder. Having reflected thus, you spent the night with a mind overwhelmed by distress and grief; having spent the night, you have come here quickly to where I am. Is this matter, Megha, indeed possible? "Yes, it is possible."

"Thus indeed, Mēha! In this very third previous birth, at the foot of the Vēyaḍḍha mountain, you were a king of elephants named Sumēruprabha. You were created by the forest-dwellers with a name and title; you were white, bright as a conch, pure, stainless, and radiant like the mass of curd, cow’s milk, foam, and moonlight; seven cubits in height, nine in length, and ten in circumference; established on seven limbs, lovely, handsome, with a head raised high in front, a beautiful seat, and a boar-like hindquarters; with a belly that was not sunken, not protruding, and not pendulous, yet with long, hanging lips and trunk; with a back distinguished by the curve of a bow-staff; with limbs that were well-proportioned, rounded, and stout; with a tail well-proportioned and measured; with full, beautiful, and moving hooves; with twenty nails that were white, perfectly clean, smooth, and unblemished; and you had six tusks. There, Mēha, surrounded by many male and female elephants, calves and female calves, you lived as the leader of a thousand elephants, the guide, the pioneer, the instigator, the lord of the herd, increasing its prosperity, exercising authority over many other solitary male and female elephant calves, and so forth."

Then, O Megha, you—who were constantly heedless, sleeping in marshy thickets, delighting in playfulness, prone to infatuation, insatiable, and addicted to sensual pleasures—surrounded by many elephants and others, wandered happily and without fear or anxiety at the foot of the Veyaddha mountains. You roamed among the hills, caves, hollows, caverns, waterfalls, springs, ravines, pits, marshes, thickets, mountain ridges, mountain-side marshes, slopes, plateaus, cliffs, peaks, summits, precipices, meadows, garlands, forests, groves, forest clusters, forest rows, rivers, riverbanks, lakes, confluences, ponds, lotus pools, oblong lakes, canals, lakes, series of lakes, and forest ranges. Surrounded by many elephants and others, you enjoyed yourself comfortably in various places where there were young shoots of trees, abundant water, and grass. Then, O Megha, after some time had passed, when the five seasons of the rainy, autumnal, winter, spring, and summer had elapsed in succession, during the summer season in the month of Jyeṣṭha-Mūla, a great and terrifying forest fire broke out. It was fanned by a wind joined with dry grass, leaves, and chaff. As the edges of the forest were engulfed in flames, the quarters of the sky were filled with smoke, and the thickets of trees were shattered by the force of a great wind. As the hollow trees collapsed and burned from within, the forest edges were reduced to a state where the water in the streams was exhausted, becoming muddy with the remains of dead, putrid, and decomposed worms. The cries of the distressed and wretched birds echoed like the sound of small bells. The trees were scorched by harsh, rough, unpleasant, and calamitous winds, their bark peeling away. Flocks of birds shrieked with parched throats, their wings and feet trembling, their tongues and palates exposed, and their beaks agape. Afflicted by the heat of the summer and fierce, harsh winds, the wild animals wandered about, parched with thirst. On the great mountains, which bore banners of thirst, whirlwinds swirled, crushing deer, rabbits, and reptiles. With their mouths wide open and tongues lolling out, with ears drooping like large gourds, with shriveled, thick, and fat trunks and raised tails, they let out loud, piercing, and discordant roars that seemed to split the vault of heaven. With the stamping of their feet, they made the surface of the earth tremble. Shedding cold spray all around, they tore through creepers and twigs and uprooted thousands of trees. There, amidst the destruction, like a fallen king or a ship driven by the wind, whirling like a whirlwind, repeatedly discharging masses of dung, you fled in every direction along with many elephants and others.

Thereupon, O Megha, you—old, with a body worn out by age, sick, exhausted, thirsty, weak, weary, deprived of your herd, bewildered regarding the directions, separated from your own herd, and overcome by the flames of a forest fire—being assailed by heat, thirst, and hunger, frightened, terrified, anxious, seized by fear, and running and wandering about in all directions, entered a certain great lake that had little water and was full of mud, descending to drink at a place where there was no ford. There, O Megha, having reached the bank but not yet reached the water, you sank into the mud; there, O Megha, thinking "I shall drink the water," you stretched out your hand, but even that hand did not reach the water. Then, O Megha, thinking "I shall lift my body up again," you sank even deeper into the mud. Then, O Megha, on another occasion, a certain young bull-elephant who had long since been driven away from his own herd, being afflicted by blows from the trunks, feet, tusks, and trunks of others, entered that same great lake to drink water. There, that young elephant saw you; having seen you, he remembered his former enmity. Remembering it, he became enraged, furious, angry, fierce, and blazing with wrath. He went to where you were, and having approached, he struck you three times on the back with his sharp tusks like pestles. Having struck you and thus avenged his former enmity, he drank the water with a joyful heart, and having drunk, he departed in the same direction from which he had come.

Then, Mēhā, intense, vast, harsh, deep, fierce, painful, and unbearable sensations arose within your body; your body was overcome by bilious fever, and you remained afflicted by a burning heat. Then, Mēhā, having experienced that intense, unbearable sensation for seven days and nights, and having lived out your full lifespan of one hundred and twenty years, you passed away at the time of death while distressed, tormented, and overwhelmed by suffering. Right here on this continent of Jambūdvīpa, in Bhāratavarṣa, in the southern half of Bhārata, on the southern bank of the great river Gaṅgā, at the foot of the Vindhya mountains, you were conceived as a young elephant in the womb of an excellent female elephant by a single pre-eminent scent-elephant. Then, after nine months, during the spring month, that female elephant gave birth to you. Then, Mēhā, once released from the dwelling in the womb, you became a young elephant—delicate as a red lotus, with the color of the red *jāsumana* flower, the *pāliya* fruit, lac-dye, fresh saffron, or the glow of twilight. You were beloved by your own herd-leader, surrounded by many hundreds of elephants, and you roamed happily in delightful mountain forests like a *gaṇiyāra*, *kaṇeru*, or *kōttha* elephant.

Then, Mēha, when you had cast off childhood and reached youth, and the leader of the herd had been joined by the law of time (had died), you yourself took over that herd. Then, Mēha, you became a pre-eminent elephant-king with four tusks, named by the forest-dwellers, and originating from Mount Mēru; there, Mēha, you were established with seven limbs [perfectly proportioned], and so on, until: "you were beautiful"; there, Mēha, you enjoyed the leadership of a herd of seven hundred elephants, and so on, until: "you delighted therein."

Then, Mēha, at another time during the summer season, in the month of Jyeṣṭha or Āṣāḍha, when the forest edges were set ablaze by forest fires, the quarters of the sky filled with thick smoke, and you were wandering about like a whirlwind—frightened, terrified, agitated, and seized with fear—you fled in every direction along with many elephants and even up to young female elephants. Then, Mēha, upon seeing that forest fire, there arose within you this kind of internal reflection: "Where, I wonder, have I previously experienced such a terrifying conflagration as this?"

Then, O Megha, as your mental dispositions (*leśyā*) were being purified by your excellent and auspicious resolve, and through the subsidence and destruction of the karma obscuring knowledge, while you were engaged in reflection, deliberation, investigation, and search, there arose in you the recollection of a previous birth. Then, O Megha, you correctly understood this matter: "In a former second existence, here indeed in Jambudvīpa, in Bhāratavarṣa, at the foot of the Veyaddha mountain... [until] I was a king of elephants named Sumēruprabha. There, I experienced such a calamity involving fire. Then, O Megha, on the afternoon of that very day, you arrived together with your own herd. Then, O Megha, you were a seven-cubit-tall elephant named Sumēruprabha, possessing four tusks and endowed with the recollection of a previous birth. Then, O Megha, there arose in you this internal reflection: "It would be well for me now, on the southern bank of the great river Gaṅgā at the foot of the Vindhya mountains, to clear a vast circle of land by means of my own herd for the purpose of preventing forest fires. Having thus reflected, you dwelt there in comfort.

Then, Mēha, on another occasion during the first rains when a great mass of rain had fallen, you were surrounded by many elephants—up to female calves—and seven hundred elephants near the great river Gaṅgā. You formed a great circle measuring one *yojana* in circumference; it was vast and immense. Whatever grass, leaves, wood, thorns, creepers, vines, stumps, trees, or shrubs were there, you gathered them all up three times with your trunk and tossed them aside with your foot, took them with your trunk, and piled them away to one side. Then, Mēha, not far from that very circle, on the southern bank of the great river Gaṅgā at the foot of the Vindhya mountains, you roamed happily among the hills and so forth.

Then, Mēha, at another time during the middle of the rainy season, when a great downpour of rain has fallen, you go to that very circle and, having arrived, you strike the circle for a second time; likewise, during the final rainy season, while a great downpour of rain is falling, you go to that very circle and, having arrived, you strike the circle for a third time, until you dwell in complete ease.

Then, Mēha, at another time, when the five seasons had passed by in due course during the summer season in the month of Jyeṣṭha-Mūla, when the herds of deer, wild beasts, flocks of birds, and reptiles were being driven together by the heat arising from the friction of the trees and were fleeing in all directions, you, along with those many women, set out toward that same circular enclosure. There, many other lions, leopards, bears, hyenas, tigers, jackals, wolves, dogs, foxes, hares, *kokantikās*, *ciccās*, and *cillalās*—having previously entered [the enclosure] and being terrified by the fear of fire—were staying together in a state of huddling within their burrows.

Then, Mēha, you went to that very circle and, having arrived, stood together with those many lions and so forth, including the *cilla*s, in the manner of sharing a cave. Then, Mēha, thinking, "I will scratch my foot," you lifted your foot; and in that interval, while being repeatedly pushed away by other powerful beings, a hare entered it. Then, Mēha, after scratching your body, you thought, "I will put my foot back down," but seeing that hare had entered, out of compassion for living beings, compassion for creatures, compassion for souls, and compassion for sentient beings, you held up that foot right there and did not set it down. Then, Mēha, through that compassion for living beings, up to compassion for sentient beings, your wandering in *saṃsāra* was shortened and a human lifespan was secured. Then that forest fire burned that forest for two and a half days and nights; having burned it, it became exhausted, ceased, subsided, and was extinguished.

Then those many lions, up to and including the jackals, seeing that forest fire extinguished, ceased, and calmed, were freed from the fear of fire; yet, being overcome by thirst and hunger, they emerged from that circle and scattered in every direction. Then those many elephants, up to and including [the deer], being overcome by thirst and hunger, emerged from that circle and scattered in various directions. Then you, Megha, old, your body worn out by age, with limbs covered in loose wrinkles, weak, exhausted, parched, thirsty, powerless, feeble, and lacking strength or prowess—standing there, thinking "I shall scatter with speed," as you stretched out your legs, you fell prostrate upon the surface of the earth with all your limbs, like a flash of lightning striking the peak of the Jewel Mountain. Then, Megha, intense pain arose in your body, burning and so forth, and you remained in a state of feverish affliction. Then you, Megha, having endured that intense, unbearable pain for three days and nights, and having lived out your full lifespan of one hundred years, have been reborn right here in Jambudvīpa, in Bhāratavarṣa, in the city of Rājagṛha, in the womb of Queen Dhāriṇī, the wife of King Śreṇika, to become a prince.

"Then, Mēha, when you had emerged from the womb in due course, having cast off childhood and attained youth, you went forth from the household life into homelessness under me, having become shaven-headed. If even then, Mēha, while you were still in the state of a lower birth (*tirikkhajōṇiya*), having not yet obtained the jewel of right conviction (*sammatta*), you maintained that foot out of compassion for living beings and creatures, and did not set it down—how much more so now, Mēha, since you have been born into a noble family, possess an unimpaired body and the faculties of the five senses, and are endowed with such exertion, strength, heroism, manly vigor, and prowess; having gone forth from the household life into homelessness under me as a monk among the *Nirgrantha* ascetics, why do you not properly endure, tolerate, bear, and acquiesce to the clashing of hands and feet, and even the being covered by dust and dirt, as you go in and out for the sake of recitation and the contemplation of the Dharma during the first and last watches of the night? Then, having heard and reflected upon this matter in the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, Mēha’s thoughts became purified through auspicious transformations and commendable mental dispositions, and as his defilements (*lēśyā*) were becoming pure, through the subsidence and destruction of the karma obscuring knowledge, he performed inquiry, investigation, search, and examination, whereby the memory of his previous births arose as previously experienced, and he correctly understood this matter. Then, Mēha the prince, whose past lives had been recalled by the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, felt redoubled spiritual agitation (*saṃvēga*); his face was filled with tears of joy, his heart expanded with the force of rapture, and the hairs on his body stood on end like a *kalambaka* flower struck by rain. He paid homage and saluted the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, and having done so, spoke thus: "From this day forward, O Venerable One, my entire body, with the exception of my two eyes, is surrendered to the *Nirgrantha* ascetics. Having said this, he again paid homage and saluted the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, and having done so, spoke thus: "I desire, O Venerable One, now for a second time to be ordained by myself, to be shaven by myself, to be instructed by myself, to be taught by myself, and to be explained the Dharma concerning conduct, sphere of activity, and the duties of a householder."

Then the Blessed Śramaṇa Mahāvīra himself initiated Prince Meha and taught him the Dharma pertaining to the practice of the proper conduct of life: "O beloved of the gods, one must proceed thus; one must stand thus; one must sit thus; one must lie down thus; one must eat thus; one must speak thus; and having risen from one's seat, one must exercise restraint with regard to living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings."

Then that Megha correctly received this religious instruction from the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra; having received it, he proceeded accordingly and conducted himself accordingly, until he restrained himself through self-restraint. Then that Megha became an ascetic (anagāra)—the description of an ascetic should be recited [as follows]: he was one who was restrained in his movements (iryā-samita), and so forth. Then that ascetic Megha studied the eleven Angas, beginning with the Sāmāyika, in the presence of the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra and those elders of such a kind; having studied them, he wandered about while cultivating himself through many fasts of the sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth [meals], as well as month-long and half-month-long penances. Then the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra departed from the city of Rājagṛha and the Gumśilā shrine, and having departed, he wandered for the benefit of the people in the regions outside.

Then, on another occasion, that ascetic Mēha paid homage and reverence to the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra; having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: "Venerable Sir, I wish, being authorized by you, to undertake and dwell in the month-long *bhikṣu-pratimā*. [Mahāvīra replied: "As it pleases you, dear one! Do not hesitate. Then, being authorized by the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra, that ascetic Mēha undertook and dwelt in the month-long *bhikṣu-pratimā*. He correctly practiced, observed, beautified, fulfilled, and proclaimed the month-long *bhikṣu-pratimā* according to the Sūtra, according to the rule, and according to the path, through his own body. Having correctly practiced, observed, beautified, fulfilled, and proclaimed it through his own body, he again paid homage and reverence to the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra; having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus:

“I desire, venerable sir, with your permission, to undertake and dwell in the two-month mendicant’s vow (bhikkhu-paḍimā). “As is agreeable to you, dear one; do not hesitate. As was the first formula, so it was for the second, third, fourth, sixth-month, seventh-month, first seven-night, second seven-night, third seven-night, one-day-and-night, and one-night [vows]. Then that anagāra Mēha, having properly touched, observed, beautified, fulfilled, and proclaimed the twelve mendicant’s vows, again paid homage and saluted him; having paid homage and saluted him, he spoke thus: “I desire, venerable sir, with your permission, to undertake and dwell in the austerity-practice of the ‘Year of the Jewels of Virtue’ (guṇarayaṇasaṃvacchara). “As is agreeable to you, dear one; do not hesitate.”

Then that ascetic Mēha, during the first month, performed the practice of fasting for four days at a time (*caütthaṃ-caütthēṇaṃ*) with uninterrupted austerity; by day he remained on the ground for self-mortification (*āyāvaṇabhūmī*), squatting (*ṭhāṇukkuḍuē*) and facing the sun, and by night he sat in the *vīrāsana* posture, uncovered (*avāuḍaēṇaṃ*). During the second month, he fasted for six days at a time; during the third month, for eight days at a time; during the fourth month, for ten days at a time—with uninterrupted austerity, by day squatting on the ground facing the sun for self-mortification, and by night sitting in the *vīrāsana* posture, uncovered. In this same manner, during the fifth month, he fasted for twelve days at a time; during the sixth month, for fourteen days at a time; during the seventh month, for sixteen days at a time; during the eighth month, for eighteen days at a time; during the ninth month, for twenty days at a time; during the tenth month, for twenty-two days at a time; during the eleventh month, for twenty-four days at a time; during the twelfth month, for twenty-six days at a time; during the thirteenth month, for twenty-eight days at a time; during the fourteenth month, for thirty days at a time; during the fifteenth month, for thirty-two days at a time; and during the sixteenth month, for thirty-four days at a time—with uninterrupted austerity, by day squatting on the ground facing the sun for self-mortification, and by night sitting in the *vīrāsana* posture, uncovered. Then that ascetic Mēha practiced the austerity of the "Year of Virtuous Joy" (*guṇaraya-saṃvaccharaṃ tavōkammaṃ*) according to the scriptures, correctly experiencing it with his body, guarding it, beautifying it, fulfilling it, and proclaiming it; according to the scriptures and according to the rule, until he had proclaimed it. Having done so, he paid homage and reverence to the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra; having paid homage and reverence, he continued to dwell there, transforming himself through various austerities such as the sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth-day fasts, and through monthly and half-monthly penances.

Then that ascetic Mēha, by means of that sublime, vast, beautiful, diligent, sustained, auspicious, peaceful, blessed, propitious, exalted, noble, supreme, and majestic practice of austerity, became emaciated, withered, fleshless, shriveled, reduced to skin and bone, lean, and with veins standing out; he moved only with great effort and remained standing only with great effort. When he had spoken, he was exhausted; while speaking, he was exhausted; and thinking "I shall speak," he was exhausted. He was like a cartload of charcoal, or a cartload of wood, or a cartload of leaves, or a cartload of sesame husks, or a cartload of castor seeds—when placed in the heat and dried, they move with a sound and stand with a sound. Even so, Mēha, covered as it were by a mass of light, stood shining exceedingly, shining exceedingly with the splendor of his austerity and the power of his heat.

At that time, on that occasion, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra—the founder of the order, the Tīrthaṅkara—wandering in regular succession from village to village, traveling comfortably, arrived at the city of Rājagṛha. Having arrived, he went to the Guṇasilaka shrine; having gone there, he accepted a suitable lodging and dwelt there, disciplining himself through self-restraint and austerity.

Then, while that ascetic Megha was practicing spiritual vigilance during the latter part of the night, this reflection arose within his mind: "Indeed, while I possess such sublime [strength], and so forth, until 'I shall speak these words,' as long as I have exertion, action, power, vigor, manly effort, and valor; as long as I have faith, fortitude, and spiritual urgency; and as long as these teachers of the Dharma, instructors of the Dharma, the venerable Śramaṇa Mahāvīra, the Jina, remains dwelling in good health—then it is well for me to rise tomorrow at dawn, when the night has passed and the sun, the thousand-rayed maker of day, is blazing with its splendor, to pay homage and reverence to the venerable Śramaṇa Mahāvīra. Having been authorized by the venerable Śramaṇa Mahāvīra, having myself undertaken the five great vows, and having asked forgiveness from the Śramaṇas and Nirgranthīs headed by Gautama, I shall slowly ascend Mount Vipula together with elders of similar character. Having personally inspected a stone slab resembling a thick cloud, and having practiced self-mortification through refinement, having renounced food and drink, having entered the state of total fasting, I shall dwell there without longing for death."

Reflecting thus, and having reflected, when the night had turned into the clear dawn and the thousand-rayed sun, the maker of day, was blazing with its brilliance, he went to where the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra was. Having approached, he performed three circumambulations from left to right around the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra; having done so, he paid homage and reverence. Having paid homage and reverence, neither too near nor too far, desiring to hear, paying homage, facing him, with humility and palms joined in reverence, he waited upon him. Then the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, spoke thus to the mendicant Mēha: “Mēha, it is certainly true that last night, during the time between the first and last watches of the night, while you were awake practicing the vigilance of Dharma, this kind of internal reflection and thought arose in you: ‘Indeed, by means of this sublime practice of austerity, I have become emaciated... [and so on] ...until I have come here quickly. Is this purpose of yours, Mēha, indeed correct? “Yes, it is so. “As you wish, dear one; do not let there be any hesitation.”

Then that ascetic Mēha, being permitted by the venerable Lord Mahāvīra, became joyful, satisfied, and delighted in heart; his heart overflowing with joy, he rose up. Having risen, he performed three circumambulations of the venerable Lord Mahāvīra from left to right, and having done so, he paid homage and reverence. Having paid homage and reverence, he himself undertook the five great vows (*pañca-mahāvratāni*). Having undertaken them, he asked forgiveness from the ascetics and nuns, Gautama and the others. Having asked forgiveness, he slowly and carefully ascended Mount Vipula together with elders such as Kaḍa and others. Having ascended, he himself inspected a stone slab that resembled a mass of clouds. Having inspected it, he inspected the area for excrement and urine. Having inspected it, he spread out a layer of *darbha* grass. Having spread it, he ascended the *darbha* mat. Having ascended, he sat down cross-legged facing the east. Placing his joined palms over his head in a gesture of reverence, he spoke thus:

"Homage be to the Arhats, who have attained the state named the destination of perfection (siddhigati); homage be to my spiritual teacher, the ascetic [Mahāvīra], who desires to attain that very state named the destination of perfection. I pay homage to the Blessed One who is there; may the Blessed One, remaining there, see me here. Having said this, he pays homage and reveres him. Having paid homage and revered him, he spoke thus: "Previously, in the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed Mahāvīra, I renounced all killing of living beings, false speech, taking what is not given, unchastity, and possession; anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, aversion, quarreling, slander, calumny, backbiting, discontent and delight, deceitful lying, and the thorn of false view. Now, too, in his very presence, I renounce all killing of living beings, up to the thorn of false view. I renounce all fourfold food—edibles, drinks, chewables, and tastables—for as long as life lasts. And as for this body—which is desirable, lovely, dear, and so forth—I shall cast it away with my final inhalations and exhalations when various diseases, ailments, hardships, and afflictions touch it. Having said this, he practices self-mortification through austerity, having rejected food and drink, has undertaken the vow of fasting, and dwells awaiting the time of death without longing for it."

Then those venerable elders performed service for the ascetic Megha without weariness. Then that ascetic Megha, having studied the eleven *aṅgas* beginning with the *Sāmāyika* in the presence of the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra and such like elders, having completed a full twelve years of the stage of asceticism (*śrāmaṇya*), having emaciated himself through a month-long process of purification (*saṃlekhanā*), having terminated sixty meals by means of fasting, and having confessed and repented, with his thorns extracted and having attained meditative composure (*samādhi*), passed away in due course.

Then those venerable elders saw that the ascetic Mēha had passed away in due course; having seen this, they performed a *kāyotsarga* for the sake of his final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*). Having performed it, they took Mēha’s requisites and descended very slowly from the great mountain. Having descended, they went to the Guṇasilaka shrine where the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra was, and upon arriving, they paid homage and saluted the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra. Having paid homage and saluted him, they spoke thus: “Indeed, O Lord, the disciple of the Exalted Ones named Mēha was naturally auspicious, [virtuous,] up to being disciplined. With the permission of the Exalted Ones, he asked forgiveness from the ascetic *nirgranthas* and *nirgranthīs*, headed by Gautama. Then, together with us, he slowly ascended Mount Vipula. He himself inspected a stone slab resembling a dense cloud; having inspected it, he renounced food and drink and passed away in due course. This, O Exalted Ones, is the ascetic equipment of the ascetic Mēha.”

"Venerable Sir," [said] the Blessed Gautama, "he pays homage and obeisance to the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra; having paid homage and obeisance, he spoke thus: 'It is indeed so, O Devānupriya: your disciple, the ascetic named Meha—O Venerable Sir, where has that ascetic Meha gone after passing away at the time of death? Where has he been reborn? The Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra spoke thus to the Blessed Gautama: 'It is indeed so, Gautama! My disciple, the ascetic named Meha, who was naturally virtuous and disciplined, studied the eleven Angas beginning with the Sāmāyika under such elder monks. Having studied them, he practiced the twelve vows of the monk and the year-long austerity of the Jewel of Virtue (Guṇarayaṇa) through his body. Having fulfilled these and being permitted by me, Gautama, he apologized to the elder monks, slowly climbed the Vipula mountain, spread out a bed of Darbha grass, and having ascended the bed of Darbha, he himself recited the five Great Vows. Having completed the twelve years of the stage of a śrāmaṇa, and having purified himself through a month-long process of emaciation (saṃlekhanā), he cut off sixty meals by means of fasting. Then, rising upwards to a great distance—many yojanas, many hundreds of yojanas, many thousands of yojanas, many hundreds of thousands of yojanas, many crores of yojanas, and many koṭākoṭis of yojanas, beyond the moon, sun, planets, constellations, and stars—he passed through the celestial realms of Saudharma, Īśāna, Sanatkumāra, Māhendra, Brahma, Lāntaka, Mahāśukra, Sahasrāra, Ānata, Prāṇata, Āraṇa, and Acyuta, and further through three hundred and eighteen Vimānas of the Graiveyaka heavens. He was reborn as a god in the great Vimāna Vijaya. There, the lifespan of some gods is declared to be thirty-three sāgaropamas; there, the lifespan of the god Meha is also thirty-three sāgaropamas. 'Venerable Sir, when this god Meha departs from that divine world at the exhaustion of his life-span, his tenure, and his existence, where will he go? Where will he be reborn? 'Gautama, in Mahāvideha he will attain perfection, awaken, be liberated, reach final nirvana, and bring an end to all suffering. Thus, Jambū, this is the meaning of the first narrative chapter (Nāyādhyayana), which was taught by the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra—the pioneer, the Tīrthaṅkara, who has reached the state known as the destination of the Siddhas—for the purpose of self-examination. Thus I speak."

"If, venerable sir, this is the meaning set forth by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for the first chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo, then what, venerable sir, is the meaning set forth for the second chapter?"

Thus indeed, Jambū, at that time and at that occasion, there was a city named Rājagṛha—[its] description. Outside that city of Rājagṛha, in the north-eastern direction, there was a shrine named Guṇasilaka—[its] description. Not far from that Guṇasilaka shrine, there was also a large, old garden; it had dilapidated temples, crumbling archways and gate-houses, and was shaded by various trees, clusters, shrubs, creepers, and vines; it was a place fit for the gathering of many hundreds of children. In the very middle of that old garden, there was also a large, ruined well. Not far from that ruined well, there was also a large Māluyā thicket; it was black, with a black luster, and so on, delightful, like the dense mass of a great cloud, covered and overspread with many trees, clusters, shrubs, creepers, vines, grasses, *kuśa* grass, and clumps of earth; it was hollow within and deep without, and it was also a place fit for the gathering of many hundreds of children.

There, in the city of Rājagṛha, lived a caravan leader named Dhana, who was wealthy, opulent, and possessed of abundant food and drink. That caravan leader Dhana had a wife named Bhadrā, whose hands and feet were delicate, whose body possessed all five senses complete and unimpaired, and who was endowed with the qualities of auspicious marks and characteristics. She was perfect in height, girth, and proportion, with all her limbs beautifully formed and lovely in every part; she was as beautiful as the moon, charming and pleasant to behold, and of handsome appearance. Her waist was slender with three folds measured by the palms of her hands; the lines on her cheeks were like the curves of earrings; her face was full and moon-like like the radiance of the autumn moon; she was elegantly dressed and graceful in her bearing, even to the point of being peerless. Yet she was barren, unable to bear children, and remained until her knees were covered by her upper garment.

That caravan leader Dhana had a servant boy named Panthaka, who was handsome in all his limbs, well-fleshed, and skilled in youthful sports. Now, that caravan leader Dhana became like an eye for many city-dwellers, guild-leaders, merchants, and caravan leaders in Rājagṛha, as well as for the eighteen classes of military commanders and sub-commanders, regarding many affairs and counsels; he even became like an eye for his own family regarding many affairs and counsels.

Now, in that city of Rājagṛha, there was a thief named Vijaya—evil, of Caṇḍāla appearance, performing most terrible and cruel deeds, with eyes red and blazing with rage, possessing a large, protruding, and terrifying beard, with lips curled upward and a prominent nose, having the color of a swarm of bees or Rāhu, merciless, without remorse, cruel, fearsome, suspicious, pitiless, with a gaze fixed on one object like a snake, with a single-edged blade like a razor, greedy for meat like a vulture, devouring all like fire, seizing everything like water; abounding in deception, fraud, trickery, guile, hypocrisy, and deceit; long accustomed to the corrupt conduct, character, and behavior of the city; addicted to gambling, liquor, food, and meat; cruel, heartless, daring, a breaker of walls, a stealer of deposits, a betrayer of trust, skilled in breaking open the gates of friends and holy places, swift-handed in seizing the property of others, constantly intent upon it, and full of intense enmity toward the city of Rājagṛha. He was well-acquainted with many entrances and exits, gates and side-gates, breaches and gaps, city embankments, narrow passages, turnings, and junctions; with gambling-halls, taverns, brothels, haunts of thieves, strongholds of thieves, crossroads, triple-forks, quadrangles, marketplaces, temples of Nāgas, temples of Bhūtas, shrines of Yakṣas, assembly halls, pleasure-houses, shops, and empty houses.

Constantly watching, spying, seeking, and searching for the weak points, difficulties, misfortunes, calamities, festivals, births, deaths, ceremonies, celebrations, sacrifices, and holidays of many people; seeking and searching for those who are intoxicated, heedless, distracted, busy, happy, or sorrowful, as well as those traveling abroad or living away from home—seeking their path, weakness, separation, and opportunity—he wanders about in this manner. Furthermore, outside the city of Rājagṛha, he wanders about in this manner, seeking and searching for the weak points and opportunities of many people in gardens, parks, ponds, lotus pools, oblong lakes, groves, lakes, rows of lakes, ruined parks, broken wells, thickets of *māluya* creepers, cemeteries, mountain caves, shelters, and resting places.

Then, on another occasion, during the time between the latter part of the night and the early part of the morning, while she was keeping watch over the household duties, this reflection arose within Bhadrā’s wife: “For many years, together with the merchant Dhanaka, I have lived enjoying human sensual pleasures—sounds, touches, tastes, smells, and forms. Yet, I have not given birth to a son or a daughter. Blessed indeed are those mothers, and truly well-attained is the fruit of their human birth and life, those mothers whose own womb-born infants, greedy for breast milk, sweetly babbling and speaking with charming voices, crawl from the base of the breasts toward the armpits; who drink at the breast, and then, taking them with hands soft as lotuses, place them upon their laps and give them sweet, very pleasant, and repeatedly tender words. I, however, am unfortunate, meritless, and lacking auspicious marks; I have not obtained even one such child. Therefore, it is best for me that tomorrow, when the night has turned to dawn and the sun has risen, blazing with a thousand rays, I shall take leave of the merchant Dhanaka, and being permitted by him, I will have prepared a great abundance of food, drink, snacks, and delicacies. Taking a vast quantity of flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, surrounded by many female friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, and attendants, I shall go to the shrines outside the city of Rājagṛha—to the Nāgas, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, Indras, Khaṇḍas, Rudras, Śivas, and Vaiśramaṇas—and there, having performed a fitting flower-worship before the many images of the Nāgas up to the Vaiśramaṇas, I shall prostrate myself with knees and forehead touching the ground and speak thus:”

"If, O beloved of the gods, I give birth to a son or a daughter, then I shall increase for you your income, your wealth, your property, and your inexhaustible treasury"—having said this, she made a proposal. Having reflected thus, when the next day dawned and the sun was shining, she went to where the merchant Dhanaka was and spoke to him as follows: "Truly, O beloved of the gods, for many years I have shared with you much conversation—sweet, dear, and repeatedly uttered in charming tones. Yet, unfortunate, meritless, and lacking auspicious marks as I am, I have not obtained even one of these things. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, I desire, with your permission, to prepare a grand feast and provide an inexhaustible treasury by increasing your food and so forth."

Then Dhanna the caravan leader said this to his wife Bhaddā: "O beloved of the gods, it is also my very same desire: how might you give birth to a son or a daughter? Bhaddā the caravan leader consented to this matter. Then Bhaddā the caravan leader, having been permitted by Dhanna the caravan leader, was joyful, satisfied, delighted in heart, and with a heart overflowing with the weight of joy; she had abundant solid food, drinks, chewables, and delicacies prepared. Having had them prepared, she took a great quantity of flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Having taken them, she departed from her own house and went through the middle of the city of Rājagṛha. Having gone out, she approached the lotus pond. Having approached, she set down on the bank of the pond a great quantity of flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Having set them down, she entered the pond. Having entered, she bathed. Having bathed, she played in the water. Having played, she bathed, performed the ritual offerings (*balikamma*), and, wearing her wet upper garment, she gathered whatever blue lotuses there were, up to the thousand-petaled lotuses. Having gathered them, she emerged from the pond. Having emerged, she took that great quantity of flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Having taken them, she went to where the temples of the Nāgas were, and so on, up to the temple of Vaiśramaṇa. Having gone there, she looked upon the images of the Nāgas, and so on, up to the images of Vaiśramaṇa, and paid homage. She bowed slightly; having bowed, she took hold of a brush of hair (*lomahatthaga*). Having taken hold of it, she wiped the images of the Nāgas, and so on, up to the images of Vaiśramaṇa, with the hair-brush. Having wiped them, she sprinkled them with a stream of water. Having sprinkled them, she rubbed their bodies with fine, soft fragrant paste (*gandhakāsāī*). Having rubbed them, she performed the offering of costly garments, garlands, and perfumes. Having performed these, she burned incense. Having burned it, she fell with knees to the ground, palms joined in reverence, and spoke thus:

"If I give birth to a boy or a girl, then I shall raise them [and so on] until they are grown," she said, and having made this vow, she went to the lotus pond. Having arrived, she remained there enjoying that abundant food, drink, soft food, and delicacy, and so forth. When she had finished eating and was purified, she returned to her own home. Furthermore, on the fourth, eighth, and full-moon days, Bhadrā, the merchant's wife, prepared abundant food, drink, soft food, and delicacies; and while honoring and paying homage to many Nāgas and so on up to the Vaiśramaṇas, she continued to live in this manner.

Then, at another time, after some interval, Bhaddā the merchant’s wife became pregnant. When two months of that pregnancy had passed and the third month was underway, a longing of this nature arose within Bhaddā the merchant’s wife: “Blessed indeed are those women, and fortunate indeed are those women, who—taking abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, as well as a great quantity of flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments—surrounded by their friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, and female attendants, go out through the very center of the city of Rājagṛha, proceed to the lotus pond, enter the lotus pond, bathe, perform their ritual offerings, adorn themselves with all ornaments, and while tasting and enjoying abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, satisfy their longing. Reflecting thus, she rose early while the sun was shining, went to where Dhanaka the merchant was, and having approached him, spoke to the merchant Dhanaka as follows: “It is indeed so, O Lord! Regarding that pregnancy of mine... [as above] ...they satisfy their longing. Therefore, O Lord, I desire, with your permission, to go and enjoy myself in that manner.”

"As you wish, dear ones! Do not hesitate. Then Bhaddā, having been granted permission by the caravan leader Dhanā, was thrilled, delighted, and joyful in heart; her heart overflowing with rapture, she had abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies prepared. Having had them prepared, and having bathed and so forth, dressed in a lower garment and an upper robe, she went to the Nāga temple and offered incense. Having offered it, she paid homage. Having paid homage, she went to the lotus pond.

Then those friends, kinsmen, and so forth, up to the city women, adorned Bhaddā, the caravan leader’s wife, with all her ornaments. Then Bhaddā, the caravan leader’s wife, together with those friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, and city women, satisfied her longing by partaking of and enjoying that abundant food, drink, chewables, and delicacies; having satisfied it, she departed in the same direction from which she had appeared.

Then Bhaddā, the merchant’s wife, having her pregnancy-longings fulfilled, carried that fetus comfortably until it was time. When nine months and seven and a half nights had passed, Bhaddā, the merchant’s wife, gave birth to a son with delicate hands and feet, [and so on]. Then the boy’s parents performed the birth-rites on the first day; in the same manner, they prepared abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, and after feeding his friends, kinsmen, and relatives, they bestowed upon him a name derived from his qualities and based on his characteristics: "Since this child of ours was obtained through the favor of many images of Nāgas and even images of Vaiśramaṇa, let this child of ours be named Devadinna. Then the boy’s parents gave him the name Devadinna. Thereafter, the boy’s parents increased his wealth, his property, his possessions, and his inexhaustible treasury.

Now that Pathaka became the foster-attendant for the boy Devadatta; taking the boy Devadatta upon his hip, he took him and enjoyed himself, surrounded by many boys and girls, children and children, and youths and maidens.

Then, on a certain occasion, that merchant’s wife Bhaddā bathed her son Devadinna, performed the ritual offerings, the auspicious rites, and the purificatory ceremonies, and adorned him with all his ornaments; having done so, she placed him in the hands of the servant-boy Panthaka.

Then that servant-boy Panthaka, taking the boy Devadatta from the hands of the noble woman Sattavāhī and placing him upon his hip, departed from his own house. Surrounded by many boys and girls, as well as youths and maidens, he went to the royal highway. Having arrived, he set the boy Devadatta aside and, surrounded by those many boys and girls as far as the maidens, he wandered about in a state of negligence.

And in this Vijaya, the thief, searching for and seeking out many entrances, exits, gates, and side-doors of the city of Rājagṛha, as well as empty houses, arrived right where the boy Devadatta was. Having arrived, he saw the boy Devadatta adorned with all his ornaments; seeing him, he became infatuated, captivated, greedy, and obsessed with the boy’s jewelry and decorations. He saw the servant-boy Panthaka standing off guard; seeing him, he looked around, and having looked around, he took the boy Devadatta, placed him under his arm, covered him with his upper garment, and quickly, hurriedly, and swiftly departed through a side-gate of the city of Rājagṛha. Having departed, he went to the ruined park and to the broken well. Having arrived, he deprived the boy Devadatta of life; having deprived him of life, he took the jewelry and ornaments and threw the body of the boy Devadatta—devoid of breath, motionless, and abandoned by life—into the broken well. Then he went to the Māluyā thicket; having entered the Māluyā thicket, he remained there motionless, still, and silent, passing the day.

Then, after a short while, that servant Panthaka went to the very place where the boy Devadatta had been set down. Upon arriving, not seeing the boy Devadatta at that spot, he wept, wailed, and lamented; he conducted a search and inquiry for the boy Devadatta in every direction and on all sides. Failing to obtain any news, report, or information regarding the boy Devadatta anywhere, he went to his own house where the caravan leader Dhana was, and having arrived, he spoke thus to the caravan leader Dhana: "Indeed, Master, the caravan leader’s wife Bhadrā bathed the boy Devadatta, adorned him with all ornaments, and placed him in my hands. Then I took the boy Devadatta upon my hip, and [carrying him] I conducted a search and inquiry. Therefore, Master, it is not known whether the boy Devadatta has been led away, carried off, or snatched away by someone. Thus he informed the caravan leader Dhana, falling at his feet.

Then, having heard and reflected upon these words of the servant Panthaka, the caravan leader Dhana was overcome by great grief for his son; like a *campaka* tree struck by an axe, he fell with all his limbs onto the surface of the earth with a loud crash. After a moment, the caravan leader Dhana recovered, regained his breath, and began a search and inquiry for the boy Devadinna in every direction and on all sides. Finding no news, report, or information regarding the boy Devadinna anywhere, he went to his own home. Having arrived there, he took a valuable gift and went to the city guards. Upon arriving, he presented that valuable gift and spoke as follows:

"O beloved of the gods, my son Devadatta, the son of Bhadrā his wife, was dear to me... [as before] ...as rare as an *umbara* flower even to hear of, let alone to see. Then Bhadrā, having bathed Devadatta and adorned him with all ornaments, placed him in the hands of Pathaga and, prostrating at my feet, informed me of it. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, I desire that a search and inquiry for the boy Devadatta be made in every direction. Then those city guards, being thus addressed by the caravan leader Dhana, equipped themselves with armor and breastplates, fastened their quivers and belts, and took up various weapons. Together with the caravan leader Dhana, they set out from the city of Rājagṛha, searching and inquiring among many roads, paths, and crossroads. Having departed from the city of Rājagṛha, they went to the ruined park (*jiṇṇujjāṇa*) where the broken well was located. Upon arriving, they saw the body of the boy Devadatta—lifeless, motionless, and abandoned by the soul. Seeing this, they cried out, "Alas! Alas! Oh, what a tragedy! and lifted the boy Devadatta out of the broken well, placing him in the hands of the caravan leader Dhana.

Then those city guards, following the tracks of the thief Vijaya, arrived at the Māluyā thicket; having arrived, they entered the Māluyā thicket, and having entered, they seized the thief Vijaya alive—along with his weapons, his stolen goods, and his neck-ornament. Having seized him, they broke and bruised his limbs with blows from their fists, elbows, knees, and forearms; having done so, they made him face downward and bound him. Having bound him, they took the ornaments of the boy Devadinna and fastened them around the neck of the thief Vijaya. Having fastened them, they emerged from the Māluyā thicket and went to the city of Rājagṛha. Having gone there, they entered the city of Rājagṛha; having entered, they paraded him through the triple-forked roads, trijunctions, crossroads, squares, and main highways of the city of Rājagṛha, striking him with whips, sticks, and canes, while scattering ashes, dust, and husks over him. Shouting with a great clamor, they proclaimed thus: [The rest of the text follows the proclamation.]

"O beloved of the gods, this is the criminal named Vijaya—[who is] like a vulture devouring raw flesh, a slayer of children, a murderer of children. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, neither a king, nor a prince, nor a royal minister commits any offense against him; rather, it is his own past deeds that commit offenses here. Having said this, they went to the prison cell, and having arrived, they placed him in fetters and bonds. Having done so, they cut off his food and drink. Then, thrice daily, they remained there inflicting upon him blows with whips, blows with sticks, and blows with canes. Then the caravan leader Dhana, together with his friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, and attendants, weeping, crying out, and lamenting, performed the funeral rites for the body of the boy Devadinna with great pomp and honor. Having performed many worldly funeral ceremonies, after some time, he became free from grief.

Then, at another time, that caravan leader Dhanaka became implicated in a minor offense against the king. Thereupon, the city guards seized the caravan leader Dhanaka; having seized him, they went to the prison, entered it, and having placed him inside, they bound him hand and foot along with the thief Vijaya.

Then, at dawn when the sun had risen, Bhadrā his wife prepared an abundant supply of food, drink, snacks, and delicacies. Having prepared them, she made a package of food, placed the various dishes inside, and sealed it with a mark and a seal. She then filled a fragrant water-vessel with pure water and called her servant, Panthaka. Having called him, she spoke thus: "Go, dear one, and deliver this abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies to Dhanah, the caravan leader, at the prison-house."

When Panthaka had been thus addressed by Bhadrā the caravan-leader’s wife, he was delighted and glad; he took that basket of food and that water-vessel filled with fragrant, excellent water. Having taken them, he departed from his own house and, proceeding through the middle of the city of Rājagṛha, went to where the prison hall was and to where Dhanaka the caravan-leader was. Having arrived, he set down the basket of food, opened it, took the vessels, and arranged the vessels. He provided hand-washing water, and then served Dhanaka the caravan-leader with that abundant solid and soft food, consisting of eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables.

Then that thief Vijaya spoke thus to the caravan leader Dhana: "O beloved of the gods, please share some of this abundant food—consisting of eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—with me. Then the caravan leader Dhana spoke thus to the thief Vijaya: "Even if I were to give this abundant food—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—to dogs or to scavengers, or even if I were to throw it away into a rubbish heap, I would certainly not share from this abundant food—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—with you, the killer of my son, the murderer of my son, my enemy, my adversary, my foe, and my opponent. Then the caravan leader Dhana consumed that abundant food—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—and sent the traveler on his way. Then the servant-boy Panthaka took that basket of food and, having taken it, departed in the very same direction from which he had appeared.

Now, when that caravan leader Dhanaka had consumed that abundant food—consisting of eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—urine and excrement arose within him. Then the caravan leader Dhanaka spoke thus to the thief Vijaya: "Come here for a moment, Vijaya, let us go to a secluded spot so that I may dispose of my urine and excrement. Then the thief Vijaya said this to the caravan leader Dhanaka: "O beloved of the gods, you who have consumed such abundant food—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—may indeed have urine or excrement; but as for me, O beloved of the gods, while being overwhelmed by these many blows from whips, blows from sticks, blows from creepers, and by thirst and hunger, I have no need for any urine or excrement. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, please go to a secluded place and dispose of your urine and excrement according to your wish."

When the caravan leader Dhana was thus addressed by the thief Vijaya, he remained silent. After a short while, as Dhana the caravan leader was being oppressed by increasingly severe urges for excrement and urine, he spoke thus to the thief Vijaya: "Come, Vijaya, let us go to a secluded spot so that I may relieve myself. Then the thief Vijaya said to the caravan leader Dhana: "If, dear sir, you will share with me a portion of that abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, then I shall go with you to a secluded place."

Then Dhanasārthavāha spoke thus to the thief Vijaya: "I shall give you a share of this abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies. Then that thief Vijaya accepted this proposal from Dhanasārthavāha.

Then that caravan leader Dhana, having gone aside with the robber Vijaya, voided excrement and urine; having returned, being clean and rendered perfectly pure, he approached that very spot and stayed there. Then, when it was morning and the sun was shining, Bhaddā prepared an abundant supply of food and drink and served it.

Then that caravan leader Dhanaka distributed a share of those abundant foods—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—to the thief Vijaya; thereafter, the caravan leader Dhanaka dispatched his servant, the slave Panthaka.

Then that Panthaka, taking the basket of food, departed from the prison. Having departed, he went through the middle of the city of Rājagṛha to his own house, and arriving there, he approached Bhadrā, the merchant’s wife, and spoke to her thus: “O beloved of the gods, the merchant Dhanaka is indeed distributing a share of abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies to the executioner, your enemy and the slayer of your son.”

Then Bhaddā, the merchant’s wife, having heard this matter from the mouth of the servant Panthaka, became furious, enraged, angry, and fierce; burning with indignation, she bore a grudge against the merchant Dhanaka.

Then, on another occasion, that merchant Dhana had himself released from his royal duties by his friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, and retinue, as well as by his own wealth. Having been released, he departed from the prison cell; having departed, he went to the hall of ornaments. Having gone there, he performed the work of adorning himself. Having performed it, he went to the lotus pond. Having gone there, he took washed clay, and having taken it, he entered the pond. Having entered, he performed a bath in the water. Having bathed and performed the ritual offerings (*balikamma*), he proceeded until he entered the city of Rājagṛha. Having entered, he set out toward his own house, traveling through the very middle of the city of Rājagṛha.

When they saw the caravan leader Dhana approaching, many people in the city of Rājagṛha—merchants, guild-leaders, wealthy householders, caravan leaders, and others—welcomed him, recognized him, honored him, paid him respect, rose up for him, and inquired after his physical well-being. Then the caravan leader Dhana went to his own house. There, whatever his outer circle of attendants was—whether slaves, servants, laborers, or sharecroppers—they too saw the caravan leader Dhana approaching; falling at his feet, they inquired after his health and welfare. And whatever his inner circle of attendants was there—whether mother, father, brother, or sister—they too saw the caravan leader Dhana approaching; they rose from their seats, embraced him neck-to-neck, and shed tears.

Then Bhaddā saw the caravan leader Dhanaka approaching; having seen him, she did not welcome him nor acknowledge him. Not welcoming him and not acknowledging him, she remained silent and turned away. Then the caravan leader Dhanaka spoke thus to his wife Bhaddā: "Why is it, dear lady, that you have no satisfaction, no joy, or no gladness, now that I have liberated myself from the king's business by means of my own wealth?"

Then Bhaddā said this to the caravan leader Dhaṇa: "How, O beloved of the gods, could there be for me satisfaction, joy, or gladness, that you should offer a share of that abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies to the slayer of my son, even to my enemy?"

Then that caravan leader Dhanaka said this to his wife Bhadrā: "My dear lady, it was certainly not for the sake of dharma, nor for the sake of austerity, nor for the sake of a reciprocal favor, nor for worldly custom, nor for family tradition, nor for friendship, nor for a companion, nor for a well-wisher, that I shared those abundant foods—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—with the thief Vijaya; it was for no purpose other than the care of my own body.
