Then Bhadrā, having been addressed thus by the caravan leader Dhanaka, was delighted and thrilled; she rose from her seat, embraced him neck-to-neck, and inquired after his welfare and health. Having bathed and performed her religious observances, she continued to live there, enjoying abundant pleasures.

Then that criminal Vija, while being tormented in the prison cell by those bonds, beatings, lashes of whips, and so forth, as well as by thirst and hunger, passed away at the time of death and was reborn among the hell-beings in the hells. There he was born as a hell-being, black with a black appearance, and dwelt experiencing such agony.

Having transmigrated from there, he will wander through the beginningless, endless, long-lasting, fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*. Just so, Jambū, any monk or nun of ours who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness after shaving their head in the presence of a teacher and preceptor, becomes greedy for an abundance of jewels, pearls, wealth, gold, and precious gems—they too are exactly like that.

At that time, at that moment, the venerable elders—endowed with noble birth and [all other auspicious qualities]—wandering in regular succession, arrived at the city of Rājagṛha. They went to the Guṇasilaka shrine and, having taken formal possession of a suitable dwelling, dwelt there, disciplining themselves through self-restraint and austerity. The assembly went out, and the Dharma was preached. Then, having heard this matter from the mouths of many people and having reflected upon it, this thought arose within the caravan leader Dhana: "Truly, the venerable elders, endowed with noble birth, have arrived here and reached this place. I wish to pay homage and reverence to those venerable elders. Having thus reflected, he bathed and, having dressed in clean, pure, and auspicious garments, proceeded on foot toward the Guṇasilaka shrine where the venerable elders were staying. Upon arrival, he paid them homage and reverence. Then the venerable elders expounded the manifold Dharma to Dhana.

Then that caravan leader Dhana, having heard the Dharma, spoke thus: "I have faith, O Venerable One, in the teaching of the Nirgranthas," and so on, until he went forth as a monk. Having practiced the stage of asceticism for many years, having renounced food, having withered himself through a month-long process of mortification (*saṃlekhanā*), and having terminated sixty meals by means of fasting, he passed away at the time of his death and was reborn as a god in the *Saudharma* heaven. There, the lifespan of certain gods is declared to be four *palyopamas*; the lifespan of that god Dhana was four *palyopamas*.

Then that god Dhana, upon the exhaustion of his lifespan, the exhaustion of his stay, and the exhaustion of his existence, having fallen from that celestial world immediately after death, will attain perfection in Mahāvideha, and so on, until he makes an end to all suffering.

"Just as, Jambū, the caravan leader Dhanaka did not give that abundant food, drink, chewables, and delicacies to the thief Vijaya as a religious gift (*dharma*), nor for any such purpose, but solely for the sake of protecting his own body; even so, Jambū, when we—whether monks or nuns who have gone forth—having abandoned bathing, rubbing with unguents, flowers, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and finery, consume that abundant food, drink, chewables, and delicacies not for the sake of beauty, nor for the sake of form, nor for the sake of strength, nor for the sake of sensual pleasure, but solely for the sake of sustaining knowledge, vision, and conduct; then in this very world he becomes worthy of worship by many monks, many nuns, many laymen, and many laywomen, up to being worthy of being served. And in the next world, he will not undergo many cuttings of hands, cuttings of ears, cuttings of noses, nor likewise the extraction of hearts, the extraction of entrails, or hanging from hooks. Furthermore, he will cross over the beginningless, endless, long-lasting, fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*—just like that caravan leader Dhanaka. Thus indeed, Jambū, has this meaning of the second *Nāyādhyayana* been proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained perfection. Thus I say.

"If, venerable sir, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, for the second chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahā*, then what, venerable sir, is the meaning declared for the third chapter of the *Nāya*? "Thus it was, Jambū: at that time, in that period, there was a city named Campā—[its description]. Outside that city of Campā, in the northeastern quarter, there was a park named Subhūmibhāga, abounding in all kinds of flowers and fruits, very beautiful, like the Nandana grove, endowed with pleasant, fragrant, and cool shade. To the north of that Subhūmibhāga park, in a certain place, there was a thicket of *māluya* creepers—[its description]. There, a certain wild peahen laid two eggs—well-formed, mature, white as a tortoise-shell, flawless, unblemished, and the size of a closed fist. Having laid them, she dwelt there, guarding, protecting, and incubating them with her own wings."

There, in the city of Campā, two sons of caravan leaders lived, namely: the son of Jinadatta and the son of Sāgaradatta. They were born together, raised together, and played with dust together; they saw each other’s wives, were devoted to one another, faithful to one another, compliant with each other’s wishes, and performed for one another whatever was desired for their welfare. They dwelt performing their duties and obligations in each other’s households.

Then, on another occasion, when those two caravan-leader’s sons had come together, met, sat down, and were seated in one place, this kind of conversation arose between them: "O dear ones, whatever happiness or suffering, or renunciation, or departure to a foreign land may befall us, we shall overcome it by meeting together. Having thus agreed upon this mutual pact, they each returned to their respective duties.

There, in the city of Campā, lived a courtesan named Devadattā—wealthy, possessing abundant food and drink, skilled in the sixty-four arts, endowed with the sixty-four qualities of a courtesan, delighting in twenty-nine special charms, preeminent in twenty-one qualities of lovemaking, expert in the thirty-two services toward men, well-versed in the ninefold treatises, proficient in the eighteen regional dialects, beautiful in her graceful appearance and attire, skilled in the proper application of gestures, laughter, speech, conduct, amorous play, conversation, and discourse, bearing a raised banner, receiving a thousand [pieces of gold], granted an umbrella, chowries, and fans, and having a *kaṇīrahu* tree as her birthplace; she exercised authority over many thousands of courtesans and lived there.

Then, on another occasion, at a time in the late afternoon, when those two merchant’s sons had finished their meal and returned from eating, having bathed, being clean and perfectly purified, and were seated comfortably upon excellent seats, this kind of conversation arose between them: "It would indeed be well for us, dear friends, tomorrow at dawn while the sun is shining, to have prepared an abundant supply of food, drink, edibles, and delicacies; and taking that abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies, along with incense, flowers, perfumes, garments, garlands, and ornaments, we shall go together with the courtesan Devadattā to enjoy the splendor of the Subhūmibhāga park. Having said this, they agreed to one another's proposal. Then, when the night had turned into dawn, they summoned their household servants and spoke to them thus:

"Go, dear ones, and prepare an abundant supply of food, drink, edibles, and delicacies. Having prepared that abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies, take incense, flowers, perfumes, garments, garlands, and ornaments, and go to the Subhūmibhāga park. Upon arriving at the Nandā lotus pond, construct a pavilion of pillars not far from the Nandā lotus pond; have it sprinkled, swept, and plastered, and make it fragrant and adorned with flowers. Then remain waiting for us. And so they waited.

Then those caravan-leader’s sons called for their household servants a second time; having called them, they spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Prepare and bring forth a carriage yoked with light equipment, drawn by excellent young bulls characterized by even hooves and tails, with well-trimmed sharp-pointed horns, adorned with silver bells, fine ropes, and exquisite gold-inlaid ornaments, with blue lotuses tied to their necks, and encircled by a network of various jewels, gems, and gold; it must be endowed with the most excellent marks. They brought it just as they were told. Then those caravan-leader’s sons, having bathed and prepared their bodies, mounted the carriage; having mounted it, they went to the house of the courtesan Devadattā. Having arrived, they descended from the carriage and entered the house of the courtesan Devadattā.

Then that courtesan Devadattā saw the merchant’s son approaching; seeing him, she was thrilled and delighted, rose from her seat, followed him for seven or eight paces, and having followed him, spoke thus to the merchant’s son: “May my lords deign to tell me: what is the purpose of your visit here?”

Then those two merchant’s sons said this to the courtesan Devadattā: “O beloved of the gods! We wish to enjoy the splendor of the Subhūmibhāga park together with you. Then Devadattā consented to this request of the two merchant’s sons; having consented, she bathed, performed her duties, and—adorned with excellent [garments] and dressed in a magnificent, glorious attire—went to where the two merchant’s sons were.

Then those two merchant’s sons, having mounted the carriage together with the courtesan Devadattā, proceeded through the middle of the city of Campā. They arrived at the Subhūmibhāga park, and from there at the Nandā lotus-pond. Having arrived, they alighted from the carriage; having alighted, they entered the Nandā lotus-pond and performed their ablutions. Having bathed, they engaged in water-sports. Having finished their sports and being well-bathed, they emerged from the Nandā lotus-pond together with Devadattā. They went to the Thūṇāmaṇḍava pavilion and entered it. Adorned with all ornaments, relaxed, confident, and seated comfortably upon excellent seats together with Devadattā, they enjoyed, relished, distributed, and partook of that abundant food—solid, soft, chewable, and tastable—as well as incense, flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Thus they lived. And when they had finished eating and were satisfied, they continued to live enjoying abundant sensual pleasures together with Devadattā.

Then, in the late afternoon, those two merchant’s sons, together with the courtesan Devadattā, departed from the Thūṇā pavilion. Having departed, they wandered about in the Subhūmibhāga garden, enjoying the splendor of the park, moving hand-in-hand through many pleasure-houses—namely, plantain houses, creeper-arbor houses, resting houses, viewing houses, dressing rooms, intoxicating rooms, *sāla* houses, lattice houses, and flower houses.

Then those two merchant’s sons set out toward that very *māluyā* thicket. When the forest peahen saw the two merchant’s sons approaching, she became terrified and frightened; emitting loud, piercing cries of "kekā," she emerged from the *māluyā* thicket. Having emerged, she perched upon the branch of a tree and remained there, gazing at the two merchant’s sons and the *māluyā* thicket with an unblinking gaze.

Then those two caravan-leader’s sons called out to one another, and having called out, they spoke thus: "O dear ones, since this wild peahen, seeing us approaching, became frightened, terrified, alarmed, and agitated, and fled while standing and staring at us with unblinking eyes from within the *māluyā* bower, there must surely be a reason for this. Having said this, they entered the interior of the *māluyā* bower. There they saw two eggs that were round and well-formed, and having seen them, they called out to one another and spoke thus: "It would indeed be well, O dear ones, if we were to place these two wild peahen eggs among the eggs of our own domestic hens. Then those domestic hens will take care of and protect these eggs along with their own by means of their own brooding and wings. Thus, we shall have two young peahens here as playthings for ourselves. Having agreed upon this matter, they called out to their respective servant boys and spoke thus: [The rest of the passage follows the same structure regarding the boys' actions and the subsequent events.]

"Go then, dear ones, take these eggs and place them among the eggs of the hens of the Jātimanta breed that you keep. When they had placed them there, those two merchant’s sons, together with the courtesan Devadattā, enjoyed the splendor of the Subhūmibhāga park and remained there. Then, mounting their carriage, they went toward the city of Campā, specifically to the house of the courtesan Devadattā. Having arrived, they entered Devadattā’s house; having entered, they gave the courtesan Devadattā a generous gift of affection appropriate for her livelihood. Having given it, they honored and respected her; having honored and respected her, they departed from Devadattā’s house. Having departed, they went to their respective homes, and upon arrival, they became engaged once again in their own occupations.

There, the merchant’s son Sāgaradatta, having risen early while the sun was shining, went to where that peahen’s egg was. Having arrived, he became suspicious, anxious, filled with doubt, seized by fear, and clouded in mind regarding that peahen’s egg, thinking: "Could this be a young peahen for my amusement here, or could it not be? Thinking thus, he repeatedly turned it over, rolled it about, shook it, tossed it, moved it, stirred it, agitated it, disturbed it, and repeatedly made a *ṭiṭṭiya* sound at its base.
Then that peahen’s egg, being repeatedly turned over and incubated, became fully developed.

Then, on another occasion, that merchant’s son Sāgaradatta went to where his peahen’s egg was; having gone there, he saw that very peahen’s egg cracked. Thinking, "Alas! My peacock chick, intended for play here, has not been born," he became dejected in mind and remained brooding. In the same way, O venerable ascetic, a Nirgrantha or Nirgranthī who, having gone forth in the presence of the Ācāryas and Upādhyāyas, becomes doubtful regarding the five great vows, the six classes of living beings, and the Nirgrantha doctrine—becoming [further] agitated and clouded in mind—is in this very life an object of contempt, reproach, ridicule, censure, and humiliation for many monks, many nuns, many laymen, and many laywomen; and in the next world as well, he undergoes many punishments and will wander through the cycle of existence.

Then that son of Jinadatta went to where that peahen’s egg was; having gone there, being free from doubt, free from uncertainty, and free from hesitation regarding that peahen’s egg, he thought, "A young peahen shall be born here for my amusement," and so he repeatedly turned it over and did not let it sit [on its own], nor did he cause it to be disturbed. Then, as that peahen’s egg was being turned over and not allowed to sit, in the course of time, at the proper moment, the young peahen was hatched and born there.

Then that son of Jinadatta, seeing that peacock chick, was delighted and thrilled; he summoned the peacock-keepers and spoke to them thus: "O dear ones, you must carefully protect, guard, and nourish this peacock chick in due course with many substances suitable for raising peacocks, and teach it the art of dancing. Those peacock-keepers accepted this request of the son of Jinadatta; they took the peacock chick and went to their own homes, where they taught the peacock chick everything up to the art of dancing.

Then that peacock chick, having shed its childhood, reached the stage of maturity and attained youth; endowed with the qualities of auspicious marks and characteristics, with its wings and plumage fully developed in size, measure, and proportion, possessing variegated feathers, a hundred moons [on its tail], a blue throat, and a nature inclined toward dancing—it roamed about making hundreds of warbles and hundreds of cries of "kekā" whenever it was struck once by a hand-clap. Then those peacock-keepers, seeing that peacock chick having shed its childhood and so forth, making hundreds of cries of "kekā," seized that peacock chick and presented it to Jinadatta’s son.

Then, seeing that peacock chick who had emerged from childhood and was uttering hundreds of cries, the merchant’s son Jinadatta, delighted and joyful, gave them a generous gift of wealth suitable for their livelihood; having given it, he dismissed them.

Then, as soon as that peacock chick was struck by Jinadatta’s son with a single pinch of the fingers, it shook its neck and head, spread its white wings, displayed its tail-fan, and danced while emitting hundreds of cries.

Then that son of Jinadatta, with that peacock, wandered about in the city of Campā, winning victories at the crossroads and thoroughfares through wagers of hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands. "In the same way, O venerable one, a monk or a nun of ours who, having gone forth from the home to the homeless state under a teacher and preceptor, becomes shaven-headed and remains free from doubt, free from uncertainty, and free from hesitation regarding the five great vows, the six classes of living beings, and the Nirgrantha doctrine—even in this very life, he will surpass many monks and many nuns," and so on, until: "he will pass beyond. Thus indeed, Jambū, has this meaning of the third chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo* been declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—the pioneer, the Tīrthaṅkara, who has attained the station named the realm of the Siddhas. Thus I say.

“If, venerable sir, this is the meaning of the third chapter on knowledge as taught by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, then what is the meaning of the fourth chapter on knowledge as taught by him? “Thus it was, Jambū: At that time, in that period, there was a city named Vāṇārasī, [described] in detail. To the north-eastern quarter outside that city of Vāṇārasī, on the bank of the great river Gaṅgā, there was a lake named Mayaṅgatīraddaha. Its water was well-formed in succession, deep, cool, clear, pure, and covered with a film; it was overspread with leaves, flowers, and foliage, and filled with many blue lotuses, pink lotuses, white lotuses, night-blooming lotuses, beautiful lotuses, fragrant lotuses, white lotuses, great white lotuses, hundred-petaled, thousand-petaled, and filamented flowers. It was lovely, beautiful to behold, charming, and exquisite. There, many herds of fish, tortoises, crocodiles, sharks, and *suṃsumāra* monsters—by the hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands—dwelt without fear, without anxiety, delighting in great happiness. Not far from that Mayaṅgatīraddaha lake, there was a large *māluyā* (creeper) thicket, [described] in detail. There dwelt two wicked hunters (*pāvasiyāla*), who were evil, fierce, cruel, impetuous, reckless, blood-thirsty, seeking flesh, carrying flesh, fond of flesh, greedy for flesh, searching for flesh, wandering at night and at twilight, and remaining hidden during the day.”

Then, on another occasion, when the sun had long set, during the flickering twilight and when people were sparse—while they were resting and returning from their work—two turtles, seeking food and searching for nourishment, slowly emerged from that very Mayaṅgatīra lake. Wandering all around its perimeter, they roamed about, making their living. Immediately thereafter, those two wicked hunters, also seeking food and searching for nourishment, emerged from the Māluyā thicket; having emerged, they went to where the Mayaṅgatīra lake was, and wandering all around its perimeter, they roamed about, making their living.

Then those wicked jackals saw those tortoises; having seen them, they set out toward where those tortoises were in order to attack them. Then those tortoises saw those wicked jackals approaching; having seen them, being afraid, terrified, alarmed, agitated, and seized by fear, they withdrew their hands, feet, and limbs into their respective bodies; having withdrawn them, they remained motionless, still, and silent.

Then those wicked hunters went to where those tortoises were; having arrived, they rolled them over from all sides, turned them around, tossed them about, shifted them, shook them, struck them, agitated them, crushed them with their claws, and gnawed at them with their teeth; yet they were not able to cause even the slightest harm, injury, or wound to the bodies of those tortoises, nor were they able to inflict any laceration of their skin.

Then those wicked hunters turned those tortoises over and over again from all sides, but they were not at all able to do anything with them; thereupon, exhausted, weary, distressed, and despondent, they slowly withdrew, moved aside to one side, and remained motionless, still, and silent.

Then, perceiving that those wicked jackals had gone far away and were out of sight, the tortoise very slowly withdrew one leg. When those wicked jackals saw that the tortoise had very slowly withdrawn one leg, they approached with a leaping gait—swift, rapid, impetuous, fierce, and forceful—and came right up to where the tortoise was. Having arrived, they tore at that leg of the tortoise with their claws, gnawed it with their teeth, and then devoured both the flesh and the marrow. Having eaten it, they rolled the tortoise over in every direction, yet they were not able to cause even the slightest affliction or injury to the body of that tortoise, nor could they inflict a wound upon its skin. Though they shook it, struck it, made it tremble, agitated it, tore at it with their claws, and gnawed at it with their teeth, they still could not cause any affliction or injury to the tortoise’s body. A second time, they retreated to one side; and in this manner, they did so for all four legs until finally, the tortoise very slowly withdrew its neck.

Then those wicked jackals, seeing that the tortoise had slowly and carefully extended its neck, quickly, swiftly, fleetly, fiercely, violently, and with great speed—[acting] as before—tore at its neck with their claws, split open its shell with their teeth, and having split it open, they deprived the tortoise of life; and having deprived it of life, they consumed its flesh and blood.

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic, if a monk or a nun who has gone forth in the presence of the teachers and preceptors does not guard the five senses, he will, even in this very life, become an object of contempt for many monks, many nuns, many laymen, and many laywomen; and in the next world as well, he will undergo many punishments and continue to wander through the cycle of rebirths—just like that tortoise whose senses were unguarded. Then those wicked hunters went to where that second tortoise was, and having arrived, they turned it over on all sides and bit it with their teeth; yet they were not able to cause even the slightest harm or injury to the body of that tortoise.

Then those fishermen tried to turn that tortoise over a second and a third time, but they were unable to cause even the slightest affliction, injury, or even a wound to the body of that tortoise. Consequently, exhausted, weary, overcome, and despondent, they returned to the very same direction from which they had come.

Then, knowing that those two wicked jackals had gone far away and were out of sight, that tortoise slowly extended his neck; having extended it, he surveyed the directions; having surveyed them, he extended all four feet simultaneously; having extended them, moving along with that most excellent gait of a tortoise, he arrived at Lake Mayaṅgatīra. Having arrived, he was reunited with his friends, kinsmen, relatives, blood relations, and attendants.

In the same way, O venerable ascetic, if a monk or a nun, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness under the presence of a teacher or preceptor, possesses five guarded senses—just as that tortoise had its senses guarded—it is indeed thus, Jambū, that this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, in the fourth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*. Thus I say.

"If, venerable sir, this meaning has been declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for the fourth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, what meaning, venerable sir, has been declared for the fifth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*?"

Thus indeed, Jambū, at that time and in that era, there was a city named Bāravatī. It extended eastward and westward, and was broad northward and southward; it was nine yojanas wide and twelve yojanas long. It was built by the wise Dhanavaī, possessing excellent ramparts of refined gold and beautified by multi-colored turrets made of various jewels. Resembling the city of Alakā, it was full of joy and sport, appearing like a manifest world of the gods. Outside that city of Bāravatī, in the northeastern quarter, there was a mountain named Revataga. It was lofty, with peaks scraping the surface of the sky, covered with various kinds of shrubs, bushes, creepers, and climbing plants, and frequented by flocks of swans, deer, peacocks, cranes, sārasa birds, cakravākas, mayanasa birds, and cuckoos. Abounding in many banks, ridges, caves, waterfalls, springs, and peaks, it was a place of constant resort for throngs of celestial nymphs, hosts of gods, cāraṇas, and pairs of vidyādharas. It was auspicious, fortunate, pleasant to behold, beautiful, delightful, lovely to see, charming, and perfect.

Not far from that Mount Revataka, there was a garden named Nandanavana; it was abundant with all kinds of flowers and fruits, delightful, resembling the Nandana grove, beautiful, lovely to behold, charming, and exquisite.

In the very center of that park was a yakṣa shrine named Surappiya, divine in appearance. There, in the city of Dvārāvatī, resided King Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva. He ruled there over Samudravijaya and the other ten Daśārhas; Baladeva and the other five Mahāvīras; sixteen thousand chieftains headed by Ugrasena; three million and a half princes headed by Pradyumna; sixty thousand "unsubdued" warriors headed by Śamba; twenty-one thousand heroes headed by Vīrasena; fifty-six thousand soldiers headed by Mahāsena; thirty-two thousand women headed by Rukmiṇī; many thousands of courtesans headed by Anaṅgasenā; and many others, including lords, high officials, and caravan leaders. He dwelt there exercising sovereignty and protection over the southern half of Bharata, from the Vaitāḍhya mountains to the edge of the ocean, and over the city of Dvārāvatī.

There, in the city of Bāravaī, there lived a householder’s wife named Thāvaccā—wealthy, [and so on], until: unassailable. That householder’s wife Thāvaccā had a son, a caravan-leader’s son named Thāvaccāputta, who was delicate of hand, [and so on], until: handsome.

Then, when that housewife Thāvaccā knew that the boy had become more than eight years old, she presented him to a teacher of the arts during an auspicious conjunction of the lunar day, the karana, the asterism, and the moment. When she knew he was capable of enjoyment, she had him take the hand of thirty-two maidens from wealthy families on a single day; there was a gift of thirty-two [villages], and so forth, until he lived enjoying a vast abundance of sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells together with those thirty-two maidens from wealthy families.

At that time, at that moment, the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi—the founder of the order, the Tīrthaṅkara—of the same description [as previously mentioned], ten *dhanus* in height, with the complexion of a blue lotus, an ox-head, or a *gulikā* flower, surrounded by eighteen thousand ascetics and forty thousand female ascetics, wandering in regular succession, arrived at the city named Dvārāvatī. He went to Mount Revataka, to the Nandana grove park, to the shrine of the Yakṣa Surapriya, and to the noble Aśoka tree; having arrived, he took up a suitable lodging and dwelt there, purifying himself through self-restraint and austerity. The assembly went out, and the Dharma was preached.

When Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva had grasped the meaning of this speech, he summoned his household servants and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! In the Sudharmā assembly hall, beat the drum of the spring season, which has a deep and sweet sound like the rumbling of a mass of clouds."

When those householders had been thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, they were delighted and overjoyed; bowing their heads with palms joined in reverence, they assented to his command with humble words, saying, "So be it, Lord. Having assented, they departed from the presence of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva. They went to the Sudharmā assembly hall, and to where the Kōmudikā drum was located. Arriving there, they struck that Kōmudikā drum, which produced a deep, sweet sound like the rumbling of a mass of clouds. Then, as the Kōmudikā drum was being struck, its resonance—like the thundering of a rain-cloud with a soft, sweet, and deep echo—reverberated through the city of Dvārakā. Measuring nine yojanas in width and twelve yojanas in length, the sound of that Kōmudikā drum, filling the intersections, tri-junctions, crossroads, squares, caves, grottoes, openings, hollows, mountain peaks, city gates, palaces, doors, houses, temples, and monasteries, spread throughout the thousands of dwellings, pervading the entire city of Dvārakā, both inside and out, in every direction on all sides.

Then, in the city of Dvārāvatī, which was nine yojanas wide and twelve yojanas long, the ten *daśārhas* headed by Samudravijaya, as well as the thousands of courtesans—having heard and perceived the sound of the celestial drum *kaumudikā*—were joyful, delighted, and gladdened in heart; having bathed and adorned themselves with wreaths and garlands of choice flowers, their bodies anointed with sandalwood paste and dressed in unwashed garments, some mounted on horses, some on elephants, some in chariots, palanquins, or litters, and others proceeding on foot surrounded by a throng of men, appeared in the presence of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.

Then, seeing Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva and the ten Dāśārhas headed by Samudravijaya approaching his presence, he was thrilled, delighted, and joyful in heart; with his heart overflowing with joy, he summoned his household servants and spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, prepare the fourfold army and bring forth the scent-elephant Vijaya! They did so, saying "So be it," and he paid them his respects.

Thāvaccāputta also went forth, and just as Meha had done, having heard and reflected upon the Dharma, he approached Thāvaccā, the householder’s wife. Having approached, he grasped her feet; and just as with Meha, so too was the formal announcement made. Then, when Thāvaccā, the householder’s wife, was unable—through many declarations, explanations, persuasions, and entreaties, both favorable to the objects of the senses and contrary to them—to declare, explain, persuade, or entreat him, she then, though against her will, consented to the renunciation of her son Thāvaccāputta, saying only, "Let us see the consecration of his renunciation. Thereupon, Thāvaccāputta remained silent.

Then that housewife Thāvaccā rose from her seat; having risen, she took up a gift of great significance, high value, and great worth, worthy of a king. Surrounded by her friends and [other attendants], she went to the area of the main gate of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva’s excellent palace. Having arrived, she proceeded along the path indicated by the doorkeeper to where Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was. Having approached, she saluted him with palms joined [in reverence] and, having saluted him, presented that gift of great significance, high value, and great worth, worthy of a king. Having presented it, she spoke as follows:

"Truly, O beloved of the gods! I have an only son, a dear child named Thāvaccāputta, who is [dear] unto me... Now, O beloved of the gods! he, being terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, desires to go forth as a monk under the Arhat Ariṭṭhanemi... Therefore, I shall perform the ceremonial honors for his renunciation. Thus, O beloved of the gods! I desire that the parasol, the crown, and the fly-whisks be granted to Thāvaccāputta as he goes forth."

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to the householder Thāvacca: "Stay here, dear lady, well-composed and at ease; I myself shall perform the ceremonial honors for the renunciation of the young Thāvacca-putta."

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, mounted upon the elephant-treasure Vijaya and accompanied by his fourfold army, went to the residence of the householder’s wife Thāvaccā. Having arrived, he spoke thus to Thāvaccāputra: “O beloved of the gods, do not become a shaven-headed ascetic and go forth into homelessness! O beloved of the gods, enjoy the abundant human pleasures of the senses, which are protected by the shade of my arm! I am simply unable to prevent the wind-element from passing over you; however, O beloved of the gods, whatever affliction or injury may arise for you, I shall ward all of that off.”

When Thāvaccāputta had been thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, he spoke to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva as follows: "If, O beloved of the gods, you could ward off death as it approaches to take my life, or if you could ward off old age—which destroys the beauty of the body—and the decay of the body as it advances, then indeed I would dwell enjoying the vast human pleasures of the senses under the protection of your arms."

When Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva had been addressed thus by Thāvaccāputta, he spoke to Thāvaccāputta as follows: "O Devānuppiya! These [obstacles] are impossible to overcome; indeed, they cannot be warded off even by a very powerful god or dānava, except through the exhaustion of one's own karma. Therefore, O Devānuppiya, I wish to effect the exhaustion of my own karma, which has been accumulated through ignorance, false belief, lack of self-restraint, and the passions."

When Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva had been thus addressed by Thāvaccāputta, he summoned his household servants and said to them: "Go, dear friends! In the city of Dvārāvatī, at the intersections of three roads, four roads, and crossroads—[and so on]—mounted upon the backs of excellent elephants, proclaim with a very loud voice this proclamation: 'Listen, dear friends! Thāvaccāputta, terrified of the cycle of existence and afraid of birth, old age, and death, desires to go forth as a monk under the presence of the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi after having shaved his head. Therefore, dear friends, if there is a king, a crown prince, a queen, a prince, a lord, a high official, a provincial governor, a wealthy merchant, a guild-leader, a general, or a caravan leader who follows Thāvaccāputta when he goes forth, Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva grants him permission; moreover, for that person's parents, friends, and kinsmen, [Kṛṣṇa] shall provide security and prosperity. Having made this proclamation, proclaim it! And so they proclaimed it. Then, out of affection for Thāvaccāputta, a thousand men, having bathed and adorned themselves with all ornaments, mounted individual palanquins carried by a thousand men each, and surrounded by their friends and kinsmen, appeared in the presence of Thāvaccāputta.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva saw a thousand men appearing before him; having seen them, he summoned his household servants and spoke to them as follows: "Just as was the consecration for the renunciation of Megha, in that same manner they bathe him with white and blue [waters], and so on, until they see the parasol over the parasol and the banner over the banner of the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi; having seen them, and having seen the Vidyādharas and Cāraṇas, and so on, he descends from the palanquin."

Then that Kṛṣṇa or Sudēva, placing Thāvaccāputta in front, [went] right there where the Arhat Ariṣṭanēmi was; all that [he did], including the laying aside of his ornaments, was exactly as described before.

Then that housewife Thāvaccā received her jewelry, garlands, and ornaments with a swan-patterned cloth, while shedding tears as bright as a necklace of pearls from a *vāridhāra* jasmine flower; and shedding them again and again, she spoke thus: "O daughter, you must strive! O daughter, you must exert yourself! O daughter, you must persevere! And in this matter, you must not be negligent. Having said this, she departed in the same direction from which she had appeared. Then Thāvaccāputta, together with a thousand men, performed the tonsure of five handfuls of hair himself; having done so, he went to where the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi was, and upon arrival, he circumambulated the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi three times, keeping him to his right; he paid homage and reverence, and then went forth as a monk.
Then that ascetic Thāvaccāputta became one who was restrained in his movements (*īryā-samita*) and restrained in his speech (*bhāṣā-samita*), and so on, until he lived [his life].

Then that Thāvaccāputta studied the fourteen *pūrvas*, beginning with the *Sāmāyika*, in the presence of the Tīrthaṅkara Ariṣṭanemi and such-like elders; having studied them, he lived while cultivating himself through many fasts of the fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth [meals], as well as monthly and half-monthly penances.
Then the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi gave those one thousand ascetics, headed by the merchant’s son, into the charge of the ascetic Thāvaccāputta as his disciples.

Then, on another occasion, that Thāvaccāputta paid homage and reverence to the Arhat Ariṭṭhanemi; having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: "I wish, O Venerable One, with your permission, to wander at my pleasure. Then that Thāvaccāputta wandered for the alms-round in the countryside together with a thousand ascetics.

At that time, in that period, there was a city named Śelakapura. There was a park called Subhūmibhāga, and King Śelaka reigned there. Queen Paumāvatī and Prince Maṇḍuka were the crown prince. King Śelaka had five hundred ministers, headed by Panthaka, who were endowed with the fourfold intelligence—innate, acquired, karmic, and transformative—and who managed the affairs of the kingdom.

When Thāvaccāputta had arrived at Selagapura, the king went out [to meet him]. A discourse on the Dharma was given. Having heard the Dharma, [the king said]: "Just as many *uggas*, sons of *uggas*, *bhogas*, and so forth, up to *ibbhas* and sons of *ibbhas*, have renounced gold and wealth and gone forth under the Venerable Ones, so too am I unable to go forth. However, O Venerable One, I shall become a lay follower (*śramaṇopāsaka*) under you, observing the five minor vows (*pañcāṇuvratika*), and so forth—[becoming] one who has understood the nature of living beings and non-living beings, and so forth, dwelling while cultivating his soul. With Panthaga at their head, five hundred ministers became lay followers.
Thāvaccāputta was wandering on a tour through the countryside outside [the city].

At that time, at that moment, there was a city named Sōgandhiyā—[its description follows]—and a garden named Nīlāsōya—[its description follows]. There, in the city of Sōgandhiyā, lived a leading merchant (nagaraseṭṭhī) named Sudarśana, who was wealthy and so forth, up to being beyond reproach.

At that time, in that period, there was a wandering mendicant named Sūrya. He was skilled in the sixty branches of learning, including the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda; he was proficient in the conventions of the conch-shell and had attained the essential meaning [of these scriptures]. He proclaimed and expounded the ten-fold religion of the wandering mendicants, which is rooted in purity and consists of the five vows and five rules, as well as the duty of giving, the duty of purification, and ritual bathing at sacred fords. Dressed in excellent yellow garments, carrying a triple staff, a water-pot, an umbrella, a pair of sandals, a bamboo staff, a hook, a broom, and a lion’s tail, and surrounded by a thousand wandering mendicants, he arrived at the city of Śrāvastī and went to the dwelling of the wandering mendicants. Having arrived, he deposited his belongings in the mendicants' quarters and dwelt there, purifying himself according to the conventions of the conch-shell.

Then, in the city of Sogandhikā, at the crossroads and other places, many people spoke thus to one another: "Indeed, the wandering mendicant Sūrya has arrived here and is staying [in such-and-such a place]. The assembly went out; Sudarśana also went out.

Then that wandering mendicant Sudaṃsaṇa gave an exposition to that assembly, to Sudarśana, and to many others regarding the calculation [of purification]: "Indeed, O Sudarśana! Our doctrine is proclaimed to have its root in water. That water is also proclaimed to be of two kinds, namely: material water (*dravyasōya*) and spiritual water (*bhāvasōya*). Material water consists of water and clay; spiritual water consists of *darbha* grass and mantras. Whatever is impure for us, O dear sir, all that is smeared with sacrificial ground (*sajjōpuḍhavī*) and then washed with pure water; thus that which was impure becomes pure. In this way, indeed, living beings who purify themselves with ablutions in water go to heaven without obstacle."

Then Sudarśana, having heard the Dharma from the mouth of Suya, was delighted and joyful; he received the Dharma rooted in self-restraint from Suya, and having received it, he continued to dwell there, providing the wandering mendicant Suya with abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, as well as clothing and other necessities.
Then that wandering mendicant Suya departed from the city of Śrāvastī and went to wander in the countryside outside.

At that time, on that occasion, there was a gathering of Thāvaccāputta; the assembly had gone out, and Sudarśana also went out, paid homage and reverence to Thāvaccāputta, and having paid homage and reverence, spoke thus: "In what is your Dharma rooted? When Sudarśana had spoken thus, Thāvaccāputta replied to Sudarśana as follows: "Sudarśana! Dharma is taught to be rooted in discipline (*vinaya*). And that discipline is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the discipline of the householder and the discipline of the homeless ascetic."

Therein, that which is the discipline of the householder consists of the five minor vows (*aṇuvvaya*), the seven rules of training (*sikkhāvaya*), and the eleven lay practitioner’s observances (*uvāsagapaḍimā*). Therein, that which is the discipline of the homeless ascetic consists of the five great vows (*mahavvaya*), namely: abstention from all killing of living beings, abstention from all false speech, abstention from all taking what is not given, abstention from all unchastity, and abstention from all possessions, up to abstention from the thorn of wrong view; as well as the tenfold renunciation, the twelve ascetic observances (*bhikkhupaḍimā*), and so forth. By means of this twofold Dharma rooted in discipline, through gradual practice, they exhaust the eight types of karmic matter and become established at the summit of the universe.

Then Thāvaccāputta said this to Sudarśana: “Sudarśana, what is the root of the Dharma as it has been proclaimed for you? “O Devānupriya, for us the Dharma is proclaimed to have its root in ritual bathing (sōya); by means of it, people go to heaven.”

Then Thāvaccāputta said this to Sudarśana: "Sudarśana, suppose there were a man who washed a large cloth stained with blood using nothing but water; Sudarśana, would there be any purification of that blood-stained cloth by washing it with water alone? No, this is not possible. In the very same way, Sudarśana, for you as well, there is no purification from the taking of life, up to the thorn of wrong view, just as there is no purification for that blood-stained cloth when it is washed with nothing but water, Sudarśana."

"Just as if, Sudarśana, some man were to smear a large cloth stained with blood with salt-water, and having smeared it, were to place it on a stove, and having placed it there, were to heat it, and then afterwards wash it with pure water; would that cloth stained with blood, Sudarśana, which had been smeared with salt-water, placed on the stove, and heated, become clean when washed with pure water? "Yes, it would," [he replied]. "In exactly the same way, Sudarśana, for us there is purity through abstention from taking life, up to abstention from the dart of wrong view; just as there is purity for that second cloth stained with blood when it is washed with pure water. Then, Sudarśana, having become fully enlightened, he paid homage and reverence to Thāvaccāputta. Having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: 'I wish, O Venerable One, to hear and understand the Dharma in your presence,' and so on, until he became a lay follower (*śrāvakopāsaka*), having comprehended the nature of living beings and non-living beings, and so forth. [The narrative continues: Thus, Sudarśana, having abandoned the doctrine of purification (*śaucadharma*), accepted the Dharma rooted in discipline (*vinayamūla*). [Gosāla thought: "It would be well for me to turn Sudarśana away from this view and to explain the Dharma rooted in purification once more. Having reflected thus, he set out with a thousand followers toward the city of Sōgandhiyā, to the residence of the wandering ascetics (*parivrājaka*). Upon arriving, he deposited his belongings in the ascetics' quarters. Wearing excellent saffron-colored robes and surrounded by a few wandering ascetics, he departed from the ascetics' quarters, went through the middle of the city of Sōgandhiyā, and arrived at the house of Sudarśana, where Sudarśana was.

Then Sudarśana saw that Śuka approaching; having seen him, he did not rise up, nor go forward to meet him, nor show respect, nor acknowledge him, nor salute him, but remained sitting in silence. Then Śuka the wandering ascetic, seeing Sudarśana not rising up [and so forth], spoke thus: "Sudarśana, formerly when you saw me approaching, you would rise up and even salute me. But now, Sudarśana, seeing me approaching, you do not salute me. For what reason, Sudarśana, have you adopted such a dharma rooted in discipline?"

When Sudarśana had been addressed in this way by the wandering mendicant Suya, he rose from his seat. Having risen, with palms joined [in reverence], he spoke thus to the wandering mendicant Suya: “It is indeed so, dear sir! The disciple of the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi named Thāvaccāputta, a houseless ascetic, has arrived here and is currently staying in the Nīlāśa grove. It is from him that I have accepted the Dharma rooted in discipline.”

Then that wandering mendicant Suva said this to Sudarśana: "Come, Sudarśana! Let us go into the presence of your spiritual teacher, Sthavirāputra, and appear before him. We shall ask him these kinds of matters, reasons, questions, and explanations. If he explains these matters to me, then I shall pay him homage and revere him; but if he does not explain these matters to me, then I shall resolve those very matters, reasons, questions, and explanations [in his favor]."

Then Suva, together with that thousand of wandering mendicants and the merchant Sudarśana, went to the Nīlāśoka grove where the ascetic Thāvaccāputta was; having arrived, he spoke thus to Thāvaccāputta: "Is your journey well, venerable sir? Is your sustenance sufficient, venerable sir? Are you free from affliction, venerable sir? Is your dwelling comfortable, venerable sir? Then, being thus addressed by the wandering mendicant Suva, the ascetic Thāvaccāputta spoke thus to the wandering mendicant Suva: "Suva, my journey is indeed well; my sustenance is indeed sufficient; I am indeed free from affliction; and my dwelling is indeed comfortable."

Then Suṣeṇa said this to Thāvaccāputta: "What, venerable sir, is your 'exertion' (jattā), son? "Son, that which consists of effort through the applications of knowledge, vision, conduct, austerity, and restraint—that is your exertion. "What, venerable sir, is your 'sustenance' (javaṇijja)? "Son, sustenance is declared to be of two kinds, namely: sustenance of the senses (indiyajavaṇijja) and sustenance not of the senses (nōindiyajavaṇijja)."

What is that which pertains to the restraint of the senses (*indriyajavaṇijja*)? O Śrutas! It is when my ear-sense, eye-sense, nose-sense, tongue-sense, and body-sense remain under control, unimpaired; that is what pertains to the restraint of the senses. What is that which pertains to the restraint of the non-senses (*noindriyajavaṇijja*)? O Śrutas! It is when my anger, pride, deceit, and greed are destroyed, stilled, and do not arise; that is what pertains to the restraint of the non-senses.

"What, venerable sir, is freedom from affliction (*avyābādha*)? O Śuka, it is when various diseases and ailments—arising from wind, bile, phlegm, or their combination—do not arise within me; that is freedom from affliction. What, venerable sir, is a pure dwelling (*phāsuya-vihāra*)? O Śuka, it is when I dwell having taken up, as provided for the occasion, beds, couches, mattresses, and bedding in groves, gardens, temples, assembly halls, or mountain caves—abodes free from women, cattle, and eunuchs; that is a pure dwelling."
"Venerable sir, are *sarisava* seeds edible or non-edible? "O Śuka, *sarisava* seeds are both edible and non-edible."

"For what reason, O Venerable One, is it said that *sarṣapas* (mustard seeds) are both edible and non-edible? O Śruta! *Sarṣapas* are declared to be of two kinds: namely, *mitra-sarṣapas* (friend-seeds) and *dhānya-sarṣapas* (grain-seeds). Among these, those which are *mitra-sarṣapas* are declared to be of three kinds: namely, those born together, those grown up together, and those who played with dust together; these are non-edible. Among these, those which are *dhānya-sarṣapas* are declared to be of two kinds: namely, those transformed by fire (*śastra-pariṇata*) and those not transformed by fire. Among these, those which are not transformed by fire are non-edible for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas. Among these, those which are transformed by fire are declared to be of two kinds: namely, pure (*prāsuka*) and impure (*aprāsuka*). O Śruta! Those which are impure are not to be eaten. Among these, those which are pure are declared to be of two kinds: namely, acceptable (*eṣaṇīya*) and unacceptable (*aneṣaṇīya*). Among these, those which are unacceptable are non-edible. Among these, those which are acceptable are declared to be of two kinds: namely, prepared (*jāita*) and unprepared (*ajāita*). Among these, those which are unprepared are non-edible. Among these, those which are prepared are declared to be of two kinds: namely, obtained (*laddha*) and unobtained (*aladdha*). Among these, those which are unobtained are non-edible. Among these, those which are obtained are edible for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas. For this reason, O Śruta, it is said that *sarṣapas* are both edible and non-edible."

In this same way, the *kulattha* beans are also to be described; however, there is this distinction: there are female *kulattha* beans and grain *kulattha* beans. Female *kulattha* beans are declared to be of three kinds, namely: the wife of the family, the mother of the family, and the daughter of the family. The grain *kulattha* beans are exactly like that.

The same applies to months; however, there is this distinction: months are declared to be of three kinds, namely—time-months (*kālamāsa*), wealth-months (*atthamāsa*), and grain-months (*dhaṇṇamāsa*). Among these, those that are time-months are declared to be of twelve kinds, namely—Sāvaṇa, Bhaddava, Āsōya, Kattiya, Maggasira, Pōsa, Māha, Phagguṇa, Cetta, Vaīsāha, Jēṭṭhāmūla, and Āsāḍha. These are not to be consumed. Wealth-months are of two kinds—silver-months and gold-months—and these are not to be consumed. Grain-months are exactly as before.

“Are you one, sir? Are you two, sir? Are you many, sir? Are you indestructible, sir? Are you unchangeable, sir? Are you immutable, sir? Are you one who has become manifold and will also become manifold? “Suyā! I am indeed one; I am also two, and so on, up to being one who has become manifold and will also become manifold. “For what reason, venerable sir, are you one, and so on, up to being one who will also become manifold? “Suyā! From the standpoint of substance (*dravyārthatayā*), I am one. From the standpoint of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśanārthatayā*), I am two. From the standpoint of space-points (*pradeśārthatayā*), I am indestructible, I am unchangeable, and I am immutable. From the standpoint of functional consciousness (*upayogārthatayā*), I am one who has become manifold and will also become manifold. Thereupon, Suyā, having attained full awakening, paid homage and reverence to Thāvaccāputta. Having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: “I wish, venerable sir, to hear the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins in your presence. [The Teacher] should then deliver the discourse on the Dharma.

Then that wandering ascetic Sūrya, having heard and reflected upon the Dharma in the presence of Thāvaccāputta, spoke thus: "Venerable sir, I desire, together with my thousand wandering ascetics, to go forth into homelessness and become shaven-headed in the presence of the Devānuppiya. "As it pleases you, Devānuppiya," [Thāvaccāputta replied]. Then the wandering ascetic Sūrya stepped out toward the north-eastern direction; he set aside his triple staff and so forth, as well as his saffron-colored robes, in one place; he himself plucked out his hair, and having plucked it out, he went into the presence of Thāvaccāputta, became shaven-headed, and went forth into homelessness. He studied the fourteen Pūrvas, beginning with the Sāmāyika.
Then Thāvaccāputta assigned a thousand anagāras to Suyasa as his disciples.

Then Thāvaccāputta departed from the city of Sōgandhikā, from the Nīlāsōya garden; having departed, he wandered through the countryside outside. Then Thāvaccāputta, accompanied by a thousand ascetics, went to Mount Puṇḍarīka. Having arrived, he slowly ascended Mount Puṇḍarīka. Having ascended, he sat down in the paryanka posture upon a stone slab that resembled a dense cloud and was strewn with celestial flowers.

Then that Sthavirāputra, having fulfilled the course of the ascetic life for many years, having purified himself through a month-long process of emaciation, having terminated sixty meals by means of fasting, and having produced supreme, perfect knowledge and vision, thereafter became perfected, liberated, and passed beyond all suffering.

Then, at another time, that son went to the city of Śailapura, to the Subhūmibhāga park, where there was an assembly; the people came out, and Śailaka also came out. Having heard the Dharma, he said: "O Venerable One! Only this remains: I wish to take leave of my five hundred ministers, with Panthaka as their chief, and to establish Prince Maṇḍuka on the throne. After that, O Venerable One, I shall go forth from the home to the homeless state in the presence of the Venerable Ones. [The Teacher replied: "As it pleases you."

Then King Śailaka entered the city of Śailakapura; having entered, he went to his own house, specifically to the outer assembly hall, and sat down upon the lion-throne. Then King Śailaka summoned the five hundred ministers, headed by Panthaka, and spoke to them thus: "O beloved of the gods, I have heard the Dharma in the presence of Suya. That Dharma has been desired, accepted, and approved by me. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, being terrified of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), I intend to go forth [into the religious life]. What will you do, O beloved of the gods? What do you resolve? Or what is desired by your hearts? Then those five hundred ministers, headed by Panthaka, said to King Śailaka: "If you, O beloved of the gods, being terrified of the cycle of existence, intend to go forth, then what other support or refuge can we have, O beloved of the gods? We too, O beloved of the gods, being terrified of the cycle of existence, intend to go forth. Just as you, O beloved of the gods, have been like an eye to us in many affairs and matters, so shall you be even when we have gone forth, in many affairs and matters. Then King Śailaka said to the five hundred ministers, headed by Panthaka: "If you, O beloved of the gods, being terrified of the cycle of existence, intend to go forth, then go, O beloved of the gods! Establish your eldest sons in the midst of your respective households, mount carriages drawn by a thousand men, and appear before me. They did exactly so and appeared before him.

Then King Śailaka saw those five hundred ministers appearing; having seen them, he was joyful and satisfied, and he summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, prepare the great royal consecration for Prince Maṇḍuka! The household officials [prepared] the royal consecration for Prince Maṇḍuka and consecrated him; Maṇḍuka became king and lived [in happiness].

Then Seḷaga asked King Maṇḍuka for permission. Then King Maṇḍuka summoned his household officials and said to them: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Have the city of Seḷagapura swept and prepared until it is like a heap of fragrant incense; do this yourselves and have others do it as well, and report back that this command has been fulfilled. Then Maṇḍuka spoke to his household officials a second time: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Perform the grand and magnificent consecration of departure for King Seḷaga, exactly as it was done for Meha. However, Queen Paumāvatī herself receives the first locks of hair; she takes the alms-bowl herself, mounts the palanquin, and the rest is exactly as before, up until he studies the eleven Angas beginning with the Sāmāyika, and having studied them, he dwells practicing the various vows from the fourth [meal-interval] onwards."

Then Suva gave those five hundred ascetics, headed by Panthaka, to Selaga the houseless one as his disciples. Then, at another time, Suva departed from the city of Selapura, from the Subhūmibhāga park; having departed, he wandered on a tour through the countryside outside.

Then, on a certain occasion, that disciple, the ascetic Suṣeṇa, surrounded by those thousand ascetics, wandering in regular succession from village to village, traveling comfortably, reached Mount Puṇḍarīka and, having attained liberation, was freed from all suffering and became perfected (siddha).

Then, as a result of those final, extreme, meager, coarse, tasteless, flavorless, cold, hot, untimely, and excessive meals, a pain arose in the body of the royal sage Sela—which was naturally delicate and accustomed to comfort—that was intense, even unto unbearable; and he wandered about with his body overcome by itching, burning, and bilious fever. Then, due to that affliction of disease, Sela became emaciated and famished.

Then, on another occasion, while that Śailaka was wandering in regular succession through the countryside, he eventually reached the Subhūmibhāga park and stayed there; the assembly went out, and Maṇḍuka also went out, paid homage to and reverenced the ascetic Śailaka, and waited upon him.

Then King Maṇḍuka, seeing the body of the ascetic Sela—dried up, emaciated, free from all affliction, yet still subject to disease—spoke thus: "Venerable sir, I shall have medical treatment provided for you by physicians acting according to their practice, with medicines, remedies, food, and drink as prescribed. Venerable sir, please come and stay in my carriage-sheds, taking possession of pure and acceptable seats, benches, beds, and bedding."
Then that ascetic Śailaka accepted this matter from King Maṇḍuka, saying, "So be it.
Then Maṇḍuka paid homage and reverence to Śailaka; having paid homage and reverence, he departed in the same direction from which he had appeared.

Then, at dawn when the sun was shining, Sela, taking his own goods, utensils, and equipment, entered the city of Selaga together with five hundred ascetics led by Panthaka. Having entered, he went to the carriage shed belonging to Maṇḍuka, and having arrived, he stayed there using pure and acceptable seats and so forth.

Then that King Maṇḍuka summoned those physicians and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! You must attend to Śailaka’s medical treatment with wholesome and permissible food and drink. Then those physicians, being thus addressed by King Maṇḍuka, were delighted and joyful; they attended to Śailaka’s medical treatment with medicines, drugs, food, and drink as prescribed, and they also administered a purgative to him.

Then, for that Śailaka, through those [medicines] as prescribed and by means of drinking intoxicants, his ailment was indeed pacified; he became healthy, his body like that of a wrestler, and his ailment vanished. When that ailment had subsided, Śailaka became infatuated with, attached to, greedy for, and obsessed with that abundant food, drink, snacks, delicacies, and intoxicants. He became indolent, living indolently; he became a lax follower of the path, living as a lax follower; he became negligent, living negligently; he became defiled, living in a defiled manner; he remained bound to seasonal beds, planks, and mattresses. Thus living negligently, he was unable to return the comfortable and permissible bed and so forth, nor was he able to take leave of King Maṇḍuka to wander abroad in the countryside.

Then, on a certain occasion, while those five hundred ascetics—excluding Panthaka—were staying together and keeping the vigil of the Dharma during the time between the latter part of the night and the early part of the morning, this reflection arose within their minds: "It is indeed true that the royal sage Śailaka has renounced his kingdom and gone forth into homelessness; yet, being intoxicated by abundant food, drink, edibles, delicacies, and wine, he is unable to continue his practice. O beloved of the gods! It is not fitting for ascetics who are heedless to remain in such a state. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, it would be well for us to ask leave of the royal sage Śailaka tomorrow, return the borrowed seats, benches, beds, and bedding, appoint the ascetic Panthaka as the attendant to the ascetic Śailaka, and then wander abroad in the countryside with unrestrained travel. Having thus reflected, they asked leave of the royal sage Śailaka the following day, returned the borrowed seats, benches, beds, and bedding, appointed the ascetic Panthaka as the attendant to the ascetic Śailaka, and then wandered abroad in the countryside.
Then that Panthaka performed service for Śailaka with diligence and humility, providing him with bedding, mats, excrement, urine, phlegm, nasal mucus, food, drink, medicine, and remedies as needed.

Then, on a certain occasion during the four-month rainy season retreat of Kārttika, Śailaka had consumed a large amount of solid and soft food—consisting of various kinds of eatables and drinks—and having drunk much intoxicating liquor, he fell into a deep sleep in the late afternoon.

Then, during the Kaumuda four-month period, while that Panthaka had performed his kāyotsarga and was performing the daily pratikramaṇa, desiring to perform the four-month pratikramaṇa, he touched the feet of the royal sage Śailaka with his head for the purpose of asking forgiveness.

Then, as that path-maker touched the feet of Śailaka with his head, he became enraged and, burning with anger, stood up. Having stood up, he spoke thus: "Who is this, O sir, who desires what is undesirable... who is so ill-behaved that he touches me with his foot while I am sleeping soundly? When the path-maker was addressed in this way by Śailaka, he became afraid, terrified, and anxious. With palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus: "O Venerable One, I am the path-maker; having performed *kāyotsarga*, I was performing the daily *pratikramaṇa*, offering the four-monthly salutations, and bowing to the Lord. Thus, I have touched your feet with my head. Therefore, I beg pardon from you, O Venerable One! May the Venerable One forgive me! It is right for the Venerable One to forgive me! I shall not do such a thing again. Having said this, he repeatedly begged forgiveness from the ascetic Śailaka for that matter with proper humility.

When Panthaka had spoken thus to the royal sage Śelaga, this reflection arose within him: "Indeed, having renounced my kingdom and so forth, I have gone forth as a monk; yet I remain settled in luxury, using a bedstead during the rainy season and so on. This is not permitted for the Nigrantha ascetics who are beyond reproach... [and so on] until: 'it is not fitting to live in such a manner. Therefore, it is better for me to request leave from King Maṇḍuka tomorrow, return the borrowed bedstead, plank, mattress, and bedding, and then, together with the monk Panthaka, wander abroad in a wandering life through the countryside. Having reflected thus, he did so the following day and wandered forth.

In the very same way, venerable ascetic, any monk or nun who is indolent, living in indolence, and so forth, who dwells heedlessly even regarding his bedding—such a person, in this very world, becomes an object of contempt for many monks, many nuns, many laymen, and many laywomen, and so on; [the rest] regarding the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) should be recited as before.

Then those five hundred ascetics, with the exception of Panthaka, having understood the meaning of this report, called out to one another; having called out, they spoke thus: "It is indeed so, dear friends! The royal sage Śailaka is wandering outside together with Panthaka, and so forth. Therefore, dear friends, it is well for us to dwell having taken up residence under the royal sage Śailaka. Having reflected thus, they took up residence under the royal sage Śailaka and dwelt there.

Then those five hundred ascetics, with Śailaka at their head, having completed the course of the ascetic life for many years, went to Mount Puṇḍarīka; having arrived there, they attained perfection (siddha) in exactly the same manner as Thāvaccāputta. In this very way, O venerable monk, a Nirgrantha or a Nirgranthī who wanders through the countryside with resolute conduct becomes in this very world worthy of reverence by many monks [and so forth] up to being worthy of worship, and even in the next world he shall cross over the wilderness of the fourfold saṃsāra.
"Thus indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, regarding the fifth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo; so I say.

If, O Venerable Sir, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, regarding the fifth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo, then what is the meaning declared, O Venerable Sir, regarding the sixth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo?"

Thus indeed, Jambū! At that time, at that moment, there was a gathering in Rājagṛha; the assembly had gone out. At that time, at that moment, the senior disciple of the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, the monk named Indrabhūti, was dwelling not far from the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, having attained the meditations on purity (*śukladhyāna*). Then, that monk named Indrabhūti, having conceived faith, spoke as follows: "How, O Venerable One, do living beings quickly attain heaviness or lightness?"

“Gautama! Suppose, for example, there were a certain man who took a large, dry, unblemished, and undamaged gourd and wrapped it with *dabha* grass and *kuśa* grass; having wrapped it, he coated it with a layer of clay, and having coated it, he placed it in the heat. Once it was dry, he wrapped it a second time with *dabha* grass and *kuśa* grass, coated it with a layer of clay, and placed it in the heat. Once it was dry, he wrapped it a third time with *dabha* grass and *kuśa* grass and coated it with a layer of clay. In this manner, by this method—wrapping it in between, coating it in between, and drying it in between—he coats it with eight layers of clay. Then, he would cast it into water that is deep, bottomless, and waist-deep. Surely, Gautama, because of the weight, the heaviness, and the heavy-weightedness of those eight layers of clay, that gourd, having sunk down through the water, comes to rest upon the surface of the earth below. In exactly the same way, Gautama, living beings, having accumulated the eight types of karma in succession—from killing living beings up to the thorn of wrong view—because of the weight, the heaviness, and the heavy-weightedness of those [karmas], when they die at the time of death, they sink down through the surface of the earth and come to rest upon the surface of hell below. Thus indeed, Gautama, living beings quickly attain heaviness.”

"Indeed, Gautama! When that [lotus] of yours has risen slightly above the surface of the earth while still in its first coating of clay—which is bitter, putrid, and decaying—and remains there; and immediately thereafter, it rises again from the second coating of clay and remains there; and thus, by this very method, when those eight coatings of clay have been worn away until it is freed from all bonds, it descends below the surface of the earth and becomes established upon the surface of the water. In exactly the same way, Gautama, living beings—by abstaining from taking life, up to abstaining from the dart of wrong view—gradually exhaust the eight types of karma, rise up into the expanse of the sky, and become established at the summit of the universe. Thus indeed, Gautama, do living beings attain lightness quickly."
Thus indeed, Jambū! by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained [liberation], this is the meaning declared in the sixth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo; thus I say.

“If, venerable sir, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, in the sixth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, what, venerable sir, is the meaning declared in the seventh chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*? “Thus it was, Jambū: at that time, in that period, there was a city named Rājagṛha. There was a park named Subhūmibhāga. In that city of Rājagṛha, there lived a caravan leader named Dhana, who was wealthy, prosperous, and beyond reproach. His wife was Bhaddā, whose body possessed all five senses intact and who was beautiful. That caravan leader Dhana had four sons by his wife Bhaddā, who were caravan leaders’ sons: namely, Dhanapāla, Dhanadeva, Dhanagopa, and Dhanarakṣita. That caravan leader Dhana had four daughters-in-law as wives for his four sons: namely, Ujjhitā, Bhogavatī, Rakṣitā, and Rohiṇī.”

Then, on another occasion, at a time between the earlier and later parts of the night, this thought arose in the caravan leader Dhana: "Indeed, in the city of Rājagṛha, I am one whom many lords, up to the most eminent, as well as my own household, consult regarding many affairs, matters, domestic concerns, deliberations, secrets, mysteries, and legal disputes; I am the one to be asked for advice, the one to be consulted repeatedly—the pillar, the standard, the support, the refuge, the eye, the foundation, the authority, the resort, and the witness—acting as the foundation, the authority, the support, the refuge, and the witness for all undertakings and their success. Therefore, it is not known by me what will become the support, the refuge, or the reliance for this household if I should go away, pass away, die, perish, be ruined, fall, depart to a foreign land, or live abroad. It would be well for me, tomorrow when the sun is blazing with its heat, to have abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies prepared; to invite my friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, and attendants, as well as the circles of the families of my four daughters-in-law; and having honored and respected that circle of friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, and attendants, along with the family circles of my four daughters-in-law, with abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, and with incense, flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, I shall give five *akṣas* of rice to each of my four daughters-in-law in the presence of those friends, kinsmen, and the family circles of my four daughters-in-law, for the purpose of testing them, so that I may know which of them will protect, preserve, or increase [the rice]."

Reflecting thus, and having reflected, when the night had turned to dawn, [he] invited his circle of friends, kinsmen, and so forth, up to the circles of the families of his four daughters-in-law. Having invited them, he had abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies prepared. Then, having bathed and seated himself upon an excellent, comfortable throne in the dining hall, together with that circle of friends, kinsmen, and the circles of the families of his four daughters-in-law, he partook of that abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, and honored them. Having honored them, in the presence of that very circle of friends, kinsmen, and the circles of the families of his four daughters-in-law, he took five *akṣas* (measures) of śāli rice. Having taken them, he summoned his eldest daughter-in-law, Ujjhitā; having summoned her, he spoke thus: "My daughter, take these five *akṣas* of śāli rice from my hand; preserve and protect them in due order. My daughter, whenever you give birth to these five *akṣas* of śāli rice, then you must return these five *akṣas* of śāli rice to me. Having said this, he placed them in his daughter-in-law's hand and dismissed her.

Then Ujjhitā agreed to this matter, saying "So be it" to Dhanasārthavāha. Having agreed, she took those five measures of rice from the hands of Dhanasārthavāha; having taken them, she stepped aside. Having stepped aside, there arose in her this internal reflection, extending to [the thought] that was produced: "In my father’s granary, many baskets full of rice remain. Therefore, when my father asks me for these five measures of rice, at that time I shall take other five measures of rice from another basket and give them to him. Having reflected thus, she hid those five measures of rice in a secret place and became engaged in her own work.
In the same way, for the sake of enjoyment as well; however, she chewed, and having chewed, she swallowed; and having swallowed, she became engaged in her own work.

Even though she guarded them in this way, however, while she was taking them and retiring to a secluded spot, there arose within her a reflection such as this: "Indeed, my father summoned me in the presence of these friends, kinsmen, and so forth, up to the four daughters-in-law and their families, and said: 'My son, take from my hand these five measures of śāli rice; preserve and protect them in due order as you live. When I am gone, my son, you must return these five measures of śāli rice to me. Having said this, he placed the five measures of śāli rice into my hand. There must be a reason for this," she thought. Having reflected thus, she tied those five measures of śāli rice in a clean cloth, placed them inside a jewel casket, set it down at the foot of her head, and lived watching over them vigilantly three times every day.

Then that caravan leader Dhanaka, together with his friends, kinsmen, and so forth, up to the fourth [time], reflected: "This must surely be the reason for this matter; it is indeed better for me to protect, guard, and increase these five *akṣas* of rice," and having thus reflected, he summoned the men of his family house and spoke to them as follows:

"O beloved of the gods, take these five thousand grains of śāli rice; once you have taken them, when the first monsoon season has arrived and the great mass of rain has fallen, prepare a small, well-cultivated field. Having prepared it, sow these five thousand grains of śāli rice. After sowing, harvest them twice and thrice. Having done so, perform the transplanting into the enclosure. Then, protecting and guarding them, cause them to grow in due succession."

Then those householders agreed to this matter of Rohiṇī; they took five measures of śāli rice and guarded and protected them in succession. Then, when the first monsoon season had arrived and a great rain had fallen, those householders prepared a small field well-tilled and sowed the five measures of śāli rice. A second and a third time they performed the sowing and harvesting; they constructed a fence around it and dwelt there, guarding, protecting, and cultivating it in succession.

Then those rice plants, being protected, guarded, and nurtured in due succession, grew up—black, with a black luster, and so on until they became thickets; they were lovely, beautiful to behold, handsome, and perfect in form.

Then those rice plants became leafed, stalked, budded, ripened, fragrant, milky, set fruit, ripe, fully matured, ready for the sickle, ready for the sickle, and ready for the reaper; they were born again and again. Then those householders, knowing that the rice had become leafed up to fully matured, ready for the sickle, and ready for the sickle, harvested it with sharp, newly whetted sickles; having harvested it, they threshed it in their hands, and having threshed it, they winnowed it. There, a Magadhan measure of rice was produced—grains that were clean, unbroken, uncrushed, and free from chaff.

Then those householders put that new rice into jars; having put it in, they seal them; having sealed them, they mark them with seals; having marked them with seals, they place them in a certain part of the granary; and having placed them there, they dwell guarding and protecting them.

Then, during the second rainy season, when the first monsoon rains had fallen as a great downpour, those householders prepared a small field, making it well-tilled; they sowed the rice, and a second time they plucked out the weeds and leveled the ground, until finally they reaped it with sickles. Having reaped it, they threshed it with their feet, and having threshed it, they winnowed it. There, they stored many measures (*kuḍava*) of that rice in one place; having stored it, they dwelt there, guarding and protecting it.

Then, during that third rainy season, when there was heavy rainfall, those householders prepared many well-cultivated fields, and so on, until they reaped them; having reaped them, they threshed them; having threshed them, they made a threshing floor; they winnowed them, and so on, until many jars were produced. Then those householders placed that rice in a granary on a platform, and so on, until they lived [in comfort]; in the fourth rainy season, many hundreds of jars were produced.

Then, as the fifth year of Dhana’s [household] was drawing to a close, during the time of transition between the latter part of the night and the early part of the day, this kind of reflection arose within him: "Indeed, five years ago from now, for the purpose of testing my four daughters-in-law, I placed five handfuls of śāli rice in each of their hands. It would be well for me, tomorrow when the sun has risen, to go and inspect those five handfuls of śāli rice, so that I may know how they have been guarded, preserved, or increased.
