Having thus reflected, he rose the next morning when the sun had risen, prepared an abundant meal, and after honoring his friends, kinsmen, and the circles of families belonging to his four daughters-in-law, he summoned his eldest daughter-in-law, Ujjhikā, in the presence of that circle of friends, kinsmen, attendants, and the families of his four daughters-in-law, and spoke to her thus:

"In this way, my son! Five years ago, in the presence of these friends, kinsmen, attendants, and the group of four daughters-in-law with their families, I placed five grains of śāli rice in your hand and said: 'My son, when you have produced these five grains of śāli rice, then you shall return these five grains of śāli rice to me,' and having said this, I gave them into your hand. Is this matter not indeed true, my son? Yes, it is true. Therefore, my son, you must return those grains of śāli rice to me."

Then Ujjhitā consented to this matter of the caravan leader Dhana; she went to the storehouse, took five *akṣas* of rice from the granary, and having taken them, she went back to where the caravan leader Dhana was and spoke thus to the caravan leader Dhana: "Here are those five *akṣas* of rice," and saying this, she placed those five *akṣas* of rice into the hand of Dhana.
Then Dhanā, the caravan leader, made Ujjhitaka swear an oath; having made him swear, he spoke thus: "My son, are these the very same five thousand measures of rice, or are they others?"

Then Ujjhitā said this to the caravan leader Dhana: "Truly, dear father, five years ago in the past, you said to me: 'Go, my daughter, to such-and-such a village where the caravan leader Dhana dwells; having gone there, speak thus to him: "Dear father, please stay here for five years; then I shall give you five measures of śāli rice. Then I agreed to this matter of yours and took those five measures of śāli rice, retiring to a secluded place. Thereupon, this reflection arose within me: 'Truly, while my father’s granary is full, I am also unacquainted with the art of winnowing. Therefore, dear father, these are not those same five measures of śāli rice; these are others. Then the caravan leader Dhana, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the mouth of Ujjhitā, became enraged and, burning with indignation, placed Ujjhitā in front of her friends, kinsmen, and the four daughters-in-law, as well as before the assembly of the family household, and appointed her to the tasks of clearing out the dung-hill, the manure-heap, the refuse-heap, the sweepings, the dust-heap, the water-drawers, the bath-attendants, and the female servants who perform external chores.

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic! if a Nirgrantha or a Nirgranthī who has gone forth [into the religious life] abandons the five great vows, then in this very life he becomes an object of contempt for many monks, many nuns, many laymen, and many laywomen, and so on, until he wanders through the wilderness of *saṃsāra*—just like that discarded woman.

In the same way, O venerable ascetic, even a woman who manages the household—only that she appoints another as the one who grinds, pounds, and husks; likewise, the one who supervises, cooks, serves, and distributes food, acting as the internal messenger and head cook—even so, O venerable ascetic, the monk for whom our five great vows have been shattered will, in this very life, become an object of reproach for many monks and many nuns, and so on, until he wanders through the fourfold wilderness of saṃsāra, just like that woman who manages the household.

Having guarded it in this manner, he returned to the very same bedroom; having arrived, he opened the chest, took those five hundred thousand grains of śāli rice from the jewel-casket, and having taken them, he went to where the merchant Dhana was and, having arrived, placed the five hundred thousand grains of śāli rice into Dhana’s hand.

Then Dhanasārthavāha said this to Rakkhiyā: "My daughter, are these the same five measures of rice, or are they others? Then Rakkhiyā said this to Dhanasārthavāha: "These are indeed those same five measures of rice, not others. How so, my son? Because, my son, it was necessary for me to do so; thinking 'this must be the reason,' I bound those five measures of rice in a clean cloth and remained there, keeping watch over them three times a day. For that reason, these are those same five measures of rice, not others."

Then, having heard this matter from Rakkhiyā, the caravan leader Dhana was delighted and satisfied; he appointed her as the treasurer for that family’s gold, bronze, cloth, abundant wealth, and all other assets up to the silver.

"In the very same way, O venerable ascetic! as long as his five great vows (*mahāvratas*) are guarded, he indeed becomes here in this very life worthy of worship by many ascetics... [as before] ...just as that [cow] was guarded. Rohiṇīya is exactly the same, with this difference: 'Will you give me a very large quantity of carts and wagons, so that I may return those five hundred thousand measures of rice to you?
Then the caravan leader Dhanaka spoke thus to Rohiṇī: 'How, my daughter, will you transport those five hundred thousand measures of rice by means of carts and wagons?'"

Then Rohiṇī said this to the caravan leader Dhanaka: "Truly, dear one! In the fifth year past from now, many hundreds of jars of these very same grains were produced by you in this same manner. Truly, dear one! I shall transport those five hundred thousand measures of rice (*sāli*) by means of wagons and carts. Then the caravan leader Dhanaka gave Rohiṇī a great quantity of wagons and carts. Taking that great quantity of wagons and carts, Rohiṇī went to her own family home; having arrived, she opened the storehouses, uncovered the granaries, filled the wagons and carts, and proceeded through the middle of the city of Rājagṛha toward her own house where the caravan leader Dhanaka was. Now, in the city of Rājagṛha, in the crossroads, streets, and highways, many people spoke thus to one another: "Blessed indeed, O beloved of the gods, is the caravan leader Dhanaka, whose daughter-in-law Rohiṇī transports five hundred thousand measures of rice by means of wagons and carts!"

Then that caravan leader Dhanā saw those five hundred thousand measures of rice being transported by means of wagons and carts; seeing this, he was delighted and joyful, and having accepted them, he established Rohiṇī—his daughter-in-law—as one to be consulted in many affairs, even up to secret matters, and as one who had been raised to a position of authority and trust before his circle of friends, kinsmen, and the families of his four daughters-in-law.

"In this very same way, O venerable ascetic! when those five great vows have been fully developed, he indeed, even in this very life, [becomes worthy of honor] for many ascetics... and shall cross over the wilderness of the fourfold saṃsāra—just like that Rohiṇī.
Thus indeed, Jambū, has this meaning of the seventh lesson of the Nāyādhammakahāo been proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra; so I say."

"If, venerable sir, this meaning has been proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for the seventh lesson of the Nāyādhyayana, then what meaning, venerable sir, has been proclaimed for the eighth?"

Thus indeed, Jambū, at that time and at that moment, right here on this continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the region of Mahāvideha, to the west of Mount Mandara, to the north of the Nisadha range of boundary mountains, to the south of the great river Sītodā, to the west of the Su-hāvaha range of secondary mountains, and to the east of the western salt-water ocean—therein lies the Vijaya (province) named Salilāvatī. In that Vijaya of Salilāvatī is the royal capital named Vītasōgā, nine yōjanas in extent, [and so forth], which is like a direct manifestation of the world of the gods.
To the northeast of that capital city Vītasōgā was a park named Indakumbha. There, in the capital city Vītasōgā, was a king named Bala, who had a thousand queens, of whom Dhāriṇī was the chief.

Then, on another occasion, Queen Dhāriṇī, having seen a lion in a dream, awoke; [and so on] until a son was born named Mahābala. When he had cast off childhood and reached the age of maturity capable of enjoying pleasures, his parents had him take the hand of five hundred excellent royal maidens, headed by Kamalaśrī, all on the same day. He lived enjoying human sensual pleasures, possessing five hundred palaces and five hundred wives, and so forth.

At that time, at that moment, the Elders arrived at the Indrakumbha garden. The assembly went out; Bala also went out. Having heard and reflected upon the Dharma, he thought: "Only after I have established Prince Mahābala on the throne... [and having done so], he became a master of the eleven Angas. After practicing the stage of asceticism for many years, he attained perfection (siddhi) on Mount Cāru by means of a month-long fast.

Then, on another occasion, Kamalaśrī, having seen a lion in her dream, awoke; [in due course] Prince Balabhadra was born, and he even became the crown prince (*yuvarāja*). Now, King Mahābala had these six childhood companions as kings, namely: Ayala, Dharaṇa, Pūraṇa, Vasu, Vaiśramaṇa, and Abhicandra. Being co-born, they agreed upon this matter, saying, "We must cross over [this world] together," and they consented to this purpose one with another.

At that time, in that period, the Elders arrived at the Indrakumbha park. The assembly went out. Having heard the Dharma from Mahābala, [the king thought], "Only this remains: I shall take leave of my six childhood friends and install Prince Balabhadra on the throne. He then took leave of those six childhood friends. Then those six childhood friends spoke thus to King Mahābala: "If you, O Lord, go forth, what other means of subsistence will we have? We too shall go forth."

Then King Mahābala spoke thus to those six childhood companions: "If you will renounce the world along with me, then go and establish each of your own sons in their respective kingdoms. When the litters carried by a thousand men had appeared, King Mahābala saw that his six childhood companions had also appeared; seeing them, he was joyful and satisfied. He summoned his household officials and [performed] the consecration of Balabhadra, and finally took leave of King Balabhadra.

Then that Mahābala, having gone forth with great magnificence together with his six childhood friends, became a knower of the eleven Angas and wandered about, practicing various austerities such as the fourth [meal-interval], while cultivating meditative states.

Then, on a certain occasion, while those seven ascetics, headed by Mahābala, were staying together, this conversation arose among them: "Friends, since one of us, dear sirs, dwells having undertaken the practice of austerity, therefore all of us should dwell having undertaken the practice of austerity. Having thus agreed to this matter with one another, they listened to each other's words, and having so agreed, they practiced for many days, [observing] the fourth [meal-interval], and so forth.

By this cause, that ascetic Mahābala produced karma for the name and status of a woman: if those six ascetics, excluding Mahābala, were to dwell having undertaken the fourth [fast], then the ascetic Mahābala would dwell having undertaken the sixth; if those six ascetics, excluding Mahābala, were to dwell having undertaken the sixth, then the ascetic Mahābala would dwell having undertaken the eighth. In this manner—whether from the eighth to the tenth, or from the tenth to the twelfth—and by these twenty causes being practiced and frequently cultivated, they produced the karma for the name and status of a Tīrthaṅkara [as follows]:

Devotion toward the Arhats, the Siddhas, the Doctrine, the Preceptors, the Elders, the learned, and the ascetics; and likewise, constant application toward their [teachings] and toward the utilization of knowledge. // Nāyā.77 Being free from transgression regarding right view, discipline, the essential duties (āvaśyaka), and the vows of conduct.
Through momentary and fleeting service, through service rendered at the proper time, and through meditative composure;
// Nāyā.78 Through the acquisition of unprecedented knowledge, devotion to the scriptures, and the promotion of the teaching—by these causes, he indeed attains the state of a Tīrthaṅkara. // Nāyā.79

Then those seven ascetics, headed by Mahābala, having undertaken the practice of the monthly alms-round, lived [thereby], up to the practice of the one-night fast. Then those seven ascetics, headed by Mahābala, having undertaken the minor "lion’s play" (*khuḍḍāga-sīhanikkīliya*) penance, lived [thereby]. It was as follows: they performed the fourth [meal-fast] and completed it with all sensory enjoyments; they performed the sixth and then the fourth; they performed the eighth and then the sixth; they performed the tenth and then the eighth; they performed the twelfth and then the tenth; they performed the fourteenth and then the twelfth; they performed the sixteenth and then the fourteenth; they performed the eighteenth and then the sixteenth; they performed the twentieth and then the eighteenth; they performed the eighteenth, the twentieth, and the sixteenth; they performed the eighteenth, the fourteenth, the sixteenth, and the tenth; they performed the twelfth, the fourteenth, the tenth, and the sixth; they performed the eighth, the fourth, the sixth, and the fourth; and having performed them, they completed them everywhere with all sensory enjoyments.

Thus, indeed, this first cycle of the minor lion’s sport ascetic practice (*khuddāga-sīhanikkīliya-tavokamma*) is accomplished according to the scripture in six months and seven days and nights. Immediately following that, they perform the second cycle, undertaking the fourth meal (fasting for three days), with the difference that they break their fast by avoiding solid foods (*vigai*). Likewise the third cycle, with the difference that at the time of breaking the fast they consume food free from oily substances (*alēvāḍa*). Likewise the fourth cycle, with the difference that at the time of breaking the fast they break it with rice and molasses (*āṃbila*).

Then those seven monks, headed by Mahābala, having performed the "Little Lion’s Play" (*khuḍḍāga-sīhanikkīliya*) penance according to the scriptures for two years and twenty-eight days, up to fulfilling the command, approached the venerable elders. Having approached, they paid homage and reverence to the venerable elders; having paid homage and reverence, they spoke thus: "Venerable sirs, we wish to perform the 'Great Lion’s Play' (*mahālaya-sīhanikkīliya*) in the same manner as the Little one, with this difference: thirty-four [days] are subtracted; it is completed in a single round in one year, six months, and eighteen days; and the entire Great Lion’s Play is completed in six years, two months, and twelve days."

Then those seven ascetics, headed by Mahābala, having performed the great lion’s sport according to the scriptures and so forth until they had attained perfection, went to where the venerable elders were; having approached, they paid homage and reverence to the venerable elders, and after paying homage and reverence, they dwelt for many [periods], practicing from the fourth [fast] onwards.

Then those seven ascetics, headed by Mahābala, through that sublime practice of austerity, became emaciated and famished—just as in the case of Skandaka—with this difference: having taken leave of their elders, they ascended Mount Cāru and, after performing a two-month period of internal refinement (*saṃlekhanā*) by fasting for one hundred and twenty meals, they completed eighty-four hundred thousand years of the stage of a monk (*śrāmaṇya-paryāya*), lived out their full lifespan of eighty-four hundred thousand *pūrva*s, and were reborn as gods in the Jayanta celestial mansion.

Therein, the lifespan of some gods is declared to be thirty-two *sāgaropamas*. Therein, the lifespan of the six gods excluding Mahābala is slightly less than thirty-two *sāgaropamas*, while the lifespan of the god Mahābala is a full thirty-two *sāgaropamas*. Then those six gods, excluding Mahābala, having fallen from the Jayanta heaven due to the exhaustion of their life-span, the exhaustion of their existence, and the exhaustion of their lifespan, immediately after passing away, were reborn here in Jambūdvīpa, in the land of Bhārata, in royal lineages of pure paternal descent, each as a prince. They were as follows: Pratibuddhi, king of the Ikṣvākus; Candracchāya, king of Aṅga; Śaṅkha, king of Kāśī; Rūpī, lord of Kuṇālā; Adīnasattu, king of Kuru; and Jitasattu, lord of Pañcālā.

Then that god Mahābala, endowed with those various omens—when the planets had ascended to high positions; when the quarters were bright, free from darkness, and pure; when the birds were joyful; when the wind blew favorably and clockwise along the ground; when the earth was rich with ripened crops; and when the people were delighted and sporting—at the time of midnight, under the conjunction of the asterism *Assiṇī*, in the fourth month of winter, in the eighth fortnight, on the fourth day of the bright half of the month of Phalguna, he descended from the celestial vehicle *Jayanta*, after passing away from a life-span of thirty-two *sāgaropamas*. He entered the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the consort of King Kumbha in the capital city of Mithilā, within this very continent of Jambudvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, through the descent of food, the descent of existence, and the descent of the body. On that night, fourteen great dreams appeared [as described], followed by the husband’s narration, the inquiry of the dream-interpreters, and so forth, until she dwelt [in her pregnancy].

When three months of Queen Pabhāvatī’s pregnancy had fully elapsed, this kind of longing arose within her: “Blessed indeed are those mothers who, seated and reclining upon a couch strewn and covered with five-colored flowers—both aquatic and terrestrial, radiant and abundant—spend their time in delight; and who, smelling a great cluster of garlands (*śrīdāmagaṇḍa*) consisting of *pāṭala*, *mallikā*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṇṇāga*, *nāga*, *maruyaka*, *damanaka*, *anōjja*, and *kōjjaya* flowers—exquisite to the touch, beautiful to behold, and emitting a great mass of fragrance—fulfill their longings. Then, seeing that such a longing had arisen in Pabhāvatī, the attendant Vāṇamantara gods immediately brought into King Kumbha’s palace both aquatic and terrestrial [radiant and abundant] five-colored flowers, by the measure of jars and by the measure of loads; and they presented a great cluster of garlands, as described above, emitting a great mass of fragrance. Then Queen Pabhāvatī fulfilled her longing with those aquatic and terrestrial flowers, and she continued to live with her longing satisfied.

Then, when nine months and seven and a half nights had fully elapsed, Queen Pabhāvaī gave birth to the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara, who was healthy and free from illness, during the first month of winter, in the second fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on its eleventh day, at the time of transition from the latter part of the night to the early part of the morning, while the moon was in conjunction with the asterism Āśvinī, the planets were in their exalted positions, and the people were joyful and sporting.

At that time, in that period, the eight Great Goddesses of the Quarters (Disākumāris) residing in the lower world arrived, as described in the *Jambuddīvapaṇṇattī* regarding the birth festival; however, the specific reference to Mithilā, King Kumbha, and Queen Prabhāvatī must be joined here. [The narrative continues] until the grand celebration on Mount Nandīśvara. Then, when the consecration for the birth of the Tīrthaṅkara had been performed by many gods, from the Bhavanapatis up to the Vaimānikas, and the birth rites and naming ceremony were completed, they declared: "Since the pregnancy longing (*doḷaha*) of this girl’s mother was fulfilled upon her lying on a bed of *malla* flowers, let our daughter’s name be Mallī. Thus she grew up, just like Mahābalā, until she reached maturity.
That blessed lady, fallen from the world of the gods and possessed of incomparable splendor,
grew up surrounded by female and male servants and attended by chamberlains.
With hair like a sword-blade, beautiful eyes, lips like the bimba fruit, and rows of white teeth—

Her limbs were as tender as a choice lotus, and her breath was fragrant like a blooming blue lotus. (Nāyā. 84) Then that Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha, having cast off childhood, became exceedingly distinguished in beauty, youth, and loveliness; indeed, she possessed a most excellent body. Then, when she was nearly sixteen years old, Mallī remained constantly surveying those six kings with her vast clairvoyant power (*avadhi-jñāna*), namely: Pratibuddhi, and so on, up to Jitasatru, the lord of Pañcāla.

Then Mallī summoned her household servants and said, "O dear ones, construct in the Aśoka grove a great house of enchantment (*mōhaṇaghara*), furnished with many hundreds of pillars. In the very center of that house of enchantment, construct a lattice chamber (*jālagharaya*). In the very center of that lattice chamber, construct a jeweled pedestal (*maṇipēḍhiyā*)," and so on, until they had completed the task and reported back.

Then Mallī, upon that jeweled pedestal, fashioned a golden statue resembling herself—equal in form, equal in age, and endowed with similar beauty, appearance, youth, and qualities—with a hole at its head and a lotus as a lid. Having made it, she would take one morsel each day from the abundant food, drink, chewables, and delicacies she consumed, and while living her life, she would place those pleasant morsels of food, drink, chewables, and delicacies into the head of that golden statue with the hole in its top.

Then, as each individual lump was being placed into that golden statue with the hole in its head, a certain odor emanated; it was like the smell of a dead snake, or [other such things]—indeed, even more unpleasant, even more disagreeable, and even more offensive than those.

At that time, in that era, there was a district named Kosala; therein was a city named Sāgaya. To the northeast of that city was a great Naga temple—divine, true, possessing true efficacy, and endowed with manifest miracles. In that city of Sāgaya lived the Ikṣvāku king named Pratibuddhi, together with Queen Padmāvatī and the minister Subuddhi, who dwelt there, being well-versed in the principles of policy and skilled in the application of conciliation, force, intimidation, and generosity.

Then, at another time, there occurred for Queen Padmāvatī a festival in honor of the Nāgas (nāgajaṇṇa). When Queen Padmāvatī learned that the festival in honor of the Nāgas had arrived, she approached King Prati-buddhi with her hands joined in reverence and spoke thus: "Truly, my lord, tomorrow there will be a festival in honor of the Nāgas for me. Therefore, my lord, I desire with your permission to go to the festival in honor of the Nāgas; may you also, my lord, come along with me to the festival in honor of the Nāgas. Then Prati-buddhi consented to this request of Padmāvatī.

Then Paumāvatī, having been granted permission by King Paḍibuddhi, was joyful and delighted. She summoned her household servants and spoke to them thus: "O beloved of the gods! Tomorrow there will be a Nāga festival for me. Therefore, summon the florists and tell them: 'Tomorrow there will be a Nāga festival for Queen Paumāvatī; therefore, O beloved of the gods, bring various flowers of ten colors from both water and land to the Nāga temple, and present a great, magnificent cluster of auspicious garlands.'"

Then, let them construct a vast, costly, and magnificent flower-pavilion (*puṣpamaṇḍapa*) adorned with five-colored flowers from both water and land, beautifully fashioned with various artistic designs, and featuring representations of swans, deer, peacocks, *koñca* cranes, *sārasa* cranes, ruddy geese (*cakravāka*), *madanasāla* birds, and cuckoos, as well as other such figures. In its very center, let them suspend from the ceiling a great cluster of garlands (*śrīdāmagaṇḍa*)—replete with fragrant perfumes—emitting a cloud of scent. Let them remain waiting for Queen Padmāvatī. Then those householders remained waiting for Queen Padmāvatī.

Then Queen Padmāvatī, having summoned her household officials early in the morning, spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, have the city of Sāgaya, both inside and outside, sprinkled, swept, and smeared with plaster," and so on, until they reported back that it was done. Then Queen Padmāvatī, having summoned her household officials once more, spoke thus: "Quickly prepare a magnificent religious chariot, yoked with light horses," and so on; they likewise prepared it accordingly.

Then Queen Padmāvatī, having bathed within the inner apartments and mounted her righteous carriage, set out from the city of Sāgaya through its very center, surrounded by her own retinue. She approached the lotus pond, entered it, and performed her ablutions. Having become supremely purified and wearing wet garments, she gathered the blue lotuses and other flowers found there. She then proceeded toward the Nāga temple. Behind Queen Padmāvatī followed many female servants, carrying trays of flowers in their hands and censers of incense in their hands.

Then Queen Padmāvatī, with full royal splendor, went to where the Nāga temple was; having arrived, she entered the Nāga temple, took hold of a hair-cloth (*lōmahatthaga*), burned incense, and remained there waiting again and again for Prativuddhi.

Then that Paḍibuddhi, having bathed, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, being fanned with white, excellent yak-tail whisks adorned with koraṇṭa flowers and the like, accompanied by a magnificent array of horses, elephants, chariots, and foot-soldiers, and surrounded by a vast multitude of troops, chariots, and crowds, departed through the middle of the city of Sāgēya. Having departed, he went to where the Nāga-shrine was; having arrived, he dismounted from the elephant’s back, made a respectful salutation toward the shrine, and entered the flower-pavilion. Having entered, he saw there a great cluster of garlands of glory.

Then Paḍibuddhi gazed upon that cluster of auspicious garlands for a very long time; having become filled with wonder regarding that cluster of auspicious garlands, he spoke thus to the minister Subuddhi: "O beloved of the gods, you have traveled through many villages, towns, and even settlements as my second [companion], and you have entered the houses of many kings, lords, and even caravan leaders and so forth. Have you ever before seen anywhere such a cluster of auspicious garlands as this cluster of auspicious garlands belonging to Queen Paumāvatī?"

Then Subuddhi spoke thus to King Paḍibuddhi: "Indeed, my lord, on another occasion I went with you to the royal capital of Mithilā. There, during the annual festival of purification (*saṃvacchara-paḍilehaṇaga*), I previously beheld a divine cluster of garlands of glory belonging to Mallī, the daughter of King Kumbha and Queen Pabhāvatī. Compared to that cluster of garlands of glory, this cluster of garlands of glory belonging to Queen Paumāvatī does not equal even a hundred-thousandth part of it. Then Paḍibuddhi spoke thus to the minister Subuddhi: "Of what sort, O beloved of the gods, is Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, for whom a cluster of garlands of glory—even one that makes the cluster of garlands of glory belonging to Queen Paumāvatī worth less than a hundred-thousandth part—exists during her annual festival of purification? Then Subuddhi spoke thus to Paḍibuddhi, the Ikṣvāku king: "Indeed, my lord, Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, has well-set, high, and beautiful feet... [and so on] ...she is of perfect form."

Then Paḍibuddha, having heard and reflected upon this matter in the presence of the minister Subuddhi, his laughter provoked by the cluster of garlands of glory (*siridāmagaṇḍa*), summoned a messenger and spoke thus: "Go, dear sir, to Mithilā, the royal capital; there, request Mallī, the daughter of King Kumbhaka and granddaughter of Pabhāvatī, the excellent princess of Videha, for me to be my wife, even though she herself is the dowry for the kingdom. When the messenger had been thus addressed by King Paḍibuddha, he was delighted and joyful, and he gave his assent. Having assented, he went to his own house and to the four-bell chariot; having arrived, he had the four-bell chariot prepared. Having had it prepared, he mounted it and, accompanied by a great multitude of horses, elephants, and a vast host of soldiers, departed from Sākeya and set out toward the Videha country and the royal capital of Mithilā.

At that time, in that period, there was a district named Aṅga; therein was a city named Campā. In that city of Campā, there was a king of Aṅga named Candracchāya. In that city of Campā, many sea-faring ship-traders, headed by Arahaṇṇaga, resided—wealthy, [and so on], until: not despised by the multitude. Now, that Arahaṇṇaga was also a lay follower of the ascetics (*śramaṇopāsaka*), who had understood the nature of living and non-living beings, and so forth, as described in the [standard] description.

Then, on a certain occasion, while those merchants of the caravan led by Arahaṇṇaka were gathered together, this conversation arose among them: "It would indeed be well for us to take merchandise—goods to be counted, weighed, measured, and bartered—and set out upon the salt ocean by ship. Having agreed to this proposal with one another, they took the fourfold merchandise. They prepared their wagons and carts; having prepared them, they loaded the wagons and carts with the fourfold merchandise. On an auspicious day, at a favorable conjunction of time, lunar mansion, and moment, they had abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies prepared. At the time of the meal, they fed their friends, kinsmen, and relatives, and then took leave of them. Having taken leave, they yoked their wagons and carts and departed through the center of the city of Campā. Having departed, they went to the port of Gambhīrā and arrived there. Upon arrival, they unyoked their wagons and carts and prepared the ship. They loaded the ship with the fourfold merchandise. They filled the ship with rice, sugar, oil, ghee, molasses, milk products, the four kinds of water, vessels, medicinal herbs, drugs, grass, wood, armor, weapons, and many other articles suitable for a sea voyage. On an auspicious day, at a favorable conjunction of time, lunar mansion, and moment, they had abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies prepared. At the time of the meal, they fed their friends, kinsmen, relatives, associates, and retinue. Having fed them, they took leave of their friends and retinue, went to the shipyard, and arrived there.

Then the retinue of those Arhaṇṇakas and merchants, up to the point of being gladdened and praised by those dear and pleasing words, spoke thus: "O father, uncle, brother, nephew! May you live long and may it be well with you, as you are not being abandoned by the Blessed Ocean. We shall see you again when you have achieved your goal, fulfilled your duty, and returned safely and intact to your own home. Having said this, they stood for a moment gazing with gentle, long, longing, and tearful eyes. Then, when the offerings of flowers had been prepared, when the fresh red sandalwood paste had been applied to the five-toed palms, when the incense had been raised, when the sea-vessels had been honored, when the bali-offerings had been distributed, when the white banners were hoisted, when the musical instruments were sounding loudly, when all the auspicious omens had appeared, and when the royal edicts had been received, the merchants, making the earth seem like the roaring of the great ocean with a great, loud lion’s roar and other sounds, boarded the ship in one direction. Then Puṣyamāṇava uttered these words: "Ho there! Success in your goals has arrived for all of you; auspicious things are present and all evils are averted. Puṣya is joined [with the moon], the hour is victorious, and this is the right time and place. When Puṣyamāṇava had spoken these words, the helmsmen, the steersmen, the sailors, the ship-owners, and the merchants, joyful and delighted, set the ship—its bow full and its stern full—free from its moorings.

Then that ship, its moorings released, driven by the force of the wind, like a young female Garuḍa with outspread wings and uplifted tail-feathers, being tossed about again and again by the sharp currents and velocities of the Ganges waters, and encountering thousands of successions of waves and billows, after several days and nights had passed, entered many hundreds of yojanas into the salt ocean. Then, as those merchants led by Arahaṇṇaga had entered many hundreds of yojanas into the salt ocean, hundreds of portents appeared: unseasonable thundering, unseasonable lightning, and unseasonable peals of thunder; and celestial nymphs danced repeatedly in the sky. And they saw a great palm-demon (tālapisāya) with legs as long as palm trees, with arms reaching up to the heavens, dark as collyrium, a buffalo, or black as a cloud, with a large hanging lip, protruding teeth, a pair of lolling tongues, his cheeks and face bloated, a flat nose like a Chinese person's, eyebrows distorted and broken, eyes glowing red like fireflies, terrifying, broad-chested, with a vast and pendulous belly, his limbs twitching, shaking, and manifesting, dancing, slapping his arms, bowing down, and roaring; emitting repeated "aṭṭaṭṭa" laughs; having the luster of blue lotuses, emeralds, or black bees, and holding a sword with a razor-sharp edge, he was seen rushing toward them.

Then those merchants, together with their ship, saw a great palm-demon (*tālapisāya*). They beheld it with legs like palm trees, its head struck by arms raised toward the sky; it was like a heap of excellent flesh, black as a buffalo, with the color of a full cloud, possessing beautiful nails, a tongue like a sickle, and hanging lips. Its mouth was covered with white, round, smooth, sharp, firm, thick, and curved fangs. It had a pair of wide-open, sharp-edged tusks, and its thin, flickering tongue lolled from its throat, moving restlessly and rapidly, repeatedly licking its tip. Its large, protruding, hideous tongue was dripping with saliva, making its red palate appear like a cave in a mountain of vermilion filled with soot. Its face was like a flame of fire devouring the peak of a mountain of collyrium. Its cheeks were covered with skin and leather, and its nose was thin, wrinkled, crooked, and broken. With its nostrils flared and its breath hissing fiercely and harshly in anger, its face was terrifying and distorted with a gaping snarl. Its ears were like large, hairless, dangling balls, and its long, moving ears hung down. Its eyes were tawny and glowing; its forehead was furrowed with wrinkles. It wore a crest bound with a garland of human heads and a girdle well-fastened with various snakes. It was adorned with a variegated cloak made of slithering, hissing snakes, scorpions, lizards, mongooses, and jackals. It had earrings of black serpents hissing and writhing, and its shoulders were draped with cats and jackals. Its hair was disheveled and smoking, and it let out a fierce, loud laugh that was terrifying and heart-rending for cowards. Its body was filthy and smeared with fat, blood, pus, flesh, and grime; it was vast-chested and terrifying. Seeing that form of a palm-demon approaching—its nails, mouth, eyes, and ears torn apart, wearing a tiger-skin loincloth and a fresh-bloodied elephant-hide spread and raised upon its pair of arms—they saw it threatening them with harsh, rough, unkind, impure, unpleasant, and loathsome cries. Upon seeing it, they became terrified and seized with fear; clutching one another’s bodies, they stood there reciting hundreds of protective charms (*uvāiya*) to many Indras, Skandas, Rudras, Śivas, Vaiśravaṇas, Nāgas, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, and Ārya-Koṭṭakiriyas.

Then that lay follower Arahanṇaka saw that divine Piśāca form approaching; having seen it, he remained fearless, untroubled, unmoving, undisturbed, unperturbed, and undismayed, with the color of his face and eyes unchanged. With a mind neither dejected nor despondent, he wiped the ground in one part of the ship with a cloth, and having wiped it, he stood in that place. Joining his palms, he spoke thus: "Homage be to the Arhats, up to those who have attained perfection. If I am released from this calamity, then it is permissible for me to break my fast; but if I am not released from this calamity, then I must renounce food accordingly. Having said this, he renounced food with specific conditions.

Then that spirit-form went to where the lay follower Arahaṇṇaga was, and having approached him, spoke to Arahaṇṇaga thus: "Ho there, Arahaṇṇaga! You who desire what is undesired... [and so on] ...you who have avoided [evil]. It is certainly not permissible for you to cause your vows of morality, restraints, virtues, abstinences, fasts, and observances to waver, to be shaken, to be broken, to be shattered, to be cast aside, or to be abandoned. Therefore, if you do not abandon your vows of morality and so forth, then I shall take this ship with my two fingers, lift it up into the air to the height of seven or eight palm trees, and plunge it into the water; thereby, overcome by distress and agony, deprived of self-composure, you shall be deprived of life prematurely."

Then that lay follower Arhaṇṇaka addressed that deity with his mind alone, saying: "O beloved of the gods, I am the lay follower named Arhaṇṇaka, one who has understood the nature of living beings and non-living beings. Indeed, no god whatsoever—[not even] Śakra—is able to cause me to waver, disturb, or turn away from the teaching of the Nirgranthas. You may do whatever faith you have. Having said this, he remained fearless, with the color of his face and eyes undiminished, his mind neither dejected nor despondent, motionless, unshakable, silent, and absorbed in the meditation on Dharma.

Then that divine being in the form of a Piśāca spoke thus to Arahaṇṇaka, the lay follower of the ascetics, a second and even a third time: "Ho, Arahaṇṇaka! [But he remained] until, with a mind free from distress, he continued to dwell motionless, unshaking, silent, and absorbed in the meditation on the Dharma.

Then that divine spirit in the form of a Piśāca saw Arahaṇṇaka absorbed in the meditation on Dharma; having seen him, becoming even more intensely enraged, he seized that ship with two fingers and, having lifted it up through seven or eight stories, spoke thus to Arahaṇṇaka: "Ho there, Arahaṇṇaka! You who desire what is undesired, it is truly not fitting for you—though you remain absorbed in the meditation on Dharma—to violate your vows and observances, and so forth."

When that *piśāca* form was unable to move Arahaṇṇaka away from the doctrine of the Nirgranthas, or [to cause him] anything else up to [despair], it then became calm and despondent; it slowly raised that ship above the water, and having raised it, withdrew its divine *piśāca* form and manifested a divine celestial form. Having manifested it, he stood in the air, wearing tinkling ornaments and so forth, and spoke thus to the lay follower Arahaṇṇaka: "O Arahaṇṇaka, lay follower! You are fortunate, O beloved of the gods! Your life has borne fruit, since you have attained, reached, and fully realized such a state of devotion toward the doctrine of the Nirgranthas."

"Thus indeed, O beloved of the gods, Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the gods, in the Sōhamma realm, in the Sōhamma-pavilion, in the Sudhamma assembly hall, seated in the midst of many gods, speaks with a very great voice, declares, proclaims, and expounds thus: 'Indeed, O gods, in Jambudvīpa, in the land of Bhārata, in the city of Campā, there is the lay disciple Arahaṇṇaka, who has understood the nature of living beings and non-living beings. Truly, no god or Dānava—nor anyone else—is able to move, disturb, or even transform him from the doctrine of the Nirgranthas.'"

"O Devānupriya! I did not believe, trust, or find pleasure in this matter of Sakka, the Lord of Devas, the King of Devas. Then, O Devānupriya, there arose within me this internal reflection, extending even to a thought: 'I shall go into the presence of Arahaṇṇaga and appear before him so that I may know: Is Arahaṇṇaga one who loves the Dharma or not? Is he firm in the Dharma or not? Will his virtues of conduct and vows waver, or will he not abandon them? Having reflected thus, I employed my limited knowledge (*avadhi-jñāna*). Having employed it, O Devānupriya, I perceived you with my *avadhi* vision. Having perceived you, I departed toward the north-eastern quarter, assumed a northern celestial form, and with that most exalted divine speed, I went to where the salt ocean was, and to where you, O Devānupriya, were. Having arrived, I caused you harassment. Yet, O Devānupriya, you were neither afraid nor [distressed], and so forth. Therefore, what Sakka, the Lord of Devas, the King of Devas said is indeed true. This power, splendor, fame, and prowess—attained, acquired, and fully realized—belong to you, O Devānupriya. Thus, I beg forgiveness from you, O Devānupriya! Forgive me, O Devānupriya! Never again shall I act in such a way. Having said this, with palms joined and prostrating at your feet, he repeatedly begged forgiveness for this matter with humility, and gave two pairs of earrings to Arahaṇṇaga. Having given them, he returned to the very same direction from which he had appeared."

Then Arhaṇṇaka, concluding that there were no obstacles, completed his meditative posture (*paḍima*). Then those merchants, headed by Arhaṇṇaka, with a favorable wind from the south, arrived at the port of Gambhīrā. Having arrived, they moored the ship; having moored it, they prepared their wagons and carts; having prepared them, they transferred the goods to be counted, weighed, measured, and bartered onto the wagons and carts; having transferred them, they yoked the wagons and carts; having yoked them, they proceeded toward Mithilā. Having arrived at Mithilā, the capital city, they unloaded their wagons and carts in the outer garden. Having unloaded them, they took up a great, costly, precious, and abundant royal gift, as well as a divine pair of earrings. Having taken these, they entered the capital city of Mithilā. Having entered, they approached King Kumbha. Having approached, with palms joined in reverence, they presented that great, costly, and precious royal gift, along with the divine pair of earrings.

Then King Kumbha received [the message] from those merchants, and having received it, he summoned Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha. Having summoned her, he fastened that divine pair of earrings upon Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha; having fastened them, he dismissed [the merchants].

Then King Kumbha provided abundant food, clothing, perfumes, and so forth, along with great hospitality, to those merchants headed by Arhannaka; having provided these things, he assigned them lodgings situated along the royal highway, and having done so, he dismissed them.

Then the merchants Arhaṇṇaka and his companions went to their encampment situated along the royal highway; having arrived, they conducted the exchange of goods, took the merchandise in return, and loaded it onto their carts and wagons. Having loaded them, they went to the deep seaport; having arrived, they prepared the ship and transferred the goods onto it. With a favorable wind from the south, they went to the port of Campā; having arrived, they moored the ship and readied the carts and wagons. They transferred the goods—those to be counted, weighed, measured, and bartered—onto the carts and wagons. Then, taking the tribute and the divine pair of earrings, they went to King Candracchāya of Aṅga and presented that great wealth to him.

Then Candracchāya, the King of Aṅga, accepted that great gift and the divine pair of earrings; having accepted them, he spoke thus to those led by Arahanaka: "O dear ones, you wander through many villages, towns, and settlements, and you frequently navigate the salt ocean by ship. Have you ever seen anywhere any such marvel? Then those led by Arahanaka spoke thus to Candracchāya, the King of Aṅga:

"It is indeed so, Master! We are many sea-faring ship-merchants residing right here in the city of Campā, headed by Arahaṇṇaga. On a certain occasion, we took up goods to be counted, weighed, measured, and bartered; having acquired them in full measure and quantity, we presented them to King Kumbhaka. Then King Kumbhaka fastened that divine pair of earrings upon Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, and having fastened them, he dismissed us. Thus, Master, it was in the palace of King Kumbhaka that we beheld the wonders of Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha. Truly, there is no other celestial maiden, nor any such as she, who is like Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha. Then Candracchāya honored and respected Arahaṇṇaga and the others, and having honored and respected them, he dismissed them."

Then Candracchāyā, having caused laughter among the merchant folk, summoned a messenger; and having summoned him, [she said] up until: "Even though she herself is fond of sovereignty," then that messenger, joyful and delighted, set out for the journey.

At that time and in that season, there was a district named Kuṇālā; there was a city there named Sāvatthī. There, King Rūppi, the lord of Kuṇālā, reigned. He had a daughter, a girl named Subāhū, born of Queen Dhāriṇī. She was delicate in her hands and feet, and she was preeminent in beauty, youth, and loveliness, possessing an exceedingly excellent body. On another occasion, the four-monthly bathing festival of the girl Subāhū took place.

Then Rūpī, the lord of Kuṇālā, knowing that the four-monthly bathing festival for the maiden Subāhū had arrived, summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "O dear ones, tomorrow will be the four-monthly bathing festival for the maiden Subāhū. Therefore, you must collect water and land flowers of ten colors and varieties at the crossroads leading to the royal highway, and so on, until they form a mass of auspicious garlands."

Then Rūppi, the lord of Kuṇālā, summoned a guild of goldsmiths and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! In the flower-pavilion situated at the edge of the royal highway, draw a city with rice grains of various five colors; in its very center, fashion a rug," and so on, until they reported back [that it was done].

Then Rūpī, the lord of Kuṇālā, mounted upon the neck of an elephant, surrounded by a fourfold army and encircled by a great multitude of warriors, chariots, and throngs of followers, accompanied by his harem and retinue, placed the maiden Subāhū at his front, proceeded along the royal highway to the Flower Pavilion, and having arrived, descended from the elephant’s shoulder; having descended, he entered the Flower Pavilion and sat down upon an excellent lion-throne facing the east.

Then those women of the inner apartments place the maiden Subāhū upon a palanquin; having placed her there, they bathe her with white and yellow jars; having bathed her, they adorn her with all ornaments; and having so adorned her, they bring her to pay homage at her father’s feet. Then the maiden Subāhū goes to where King Rūppi is, and having approached him, she grasps his feet.

Then King Rūppi placed the maiden Subāhū on his lap; having placed her there, he was filled with wonder at the maiden Subāhū’s beauty, youth, and loveliness, and he summoned his chamberlain and spoke to him thus: "O dear one, you enter many villages, hamlets, cities, and houses as my second [minister]. Have you ever before seen such a bathing pavilion for anyone—whether a king or a lord—as this bathing pavilion belonging to this maiden Subāhū?"

Then that chamberlain, having grasped Rūpin the king by the hands with palms joined, spoke thus: "Truly, my lord, on another occasion when I had gone to Mithilā along with you, I saw there Mallī, the Videhan princess, daughter of King Kumbhaka and Queen Pabhāvatī, at her bathing festival. The bathing festival of this maiden Subāhū is not worth even a hundred-thousandth part of that bathing festival. Then King Rūpin, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the mouth of the chamberlain, did exactly as before; and with a smile born of the news regarding the bathing festival, he summoned a messenger and spoke thus: "Go directly toward the city of Mithilā."

At that time, in that era, there was a region named Kāsī; there was a city there named Vārāṇasī; and there was a king of Kāsī named Saṅkha. Then, at another time, the joint of that divine pair of earrings belonging to Mallī, the daughter of the excellent Videha king, became dislodged.

Then King Kumbha summoned the guild of goldsmiths and spoke to them thus: "O beloved of the gods! Join together the seam of this divine pair of earrings. Then that guild of goldsmiths agreed to this matter, saying, "So be it. Having agreed, they took that divine pair of earrings and went to where the goldsmiths' workbenches were; having arrived, they placed them upon the goldsmiths' workbenches. Though they applied many efforts and exerted themselves to the utmost in their attempts, they desired to join the seam of that divine pair of earrings, yet they were simply not able to join it.

Then that guild of goldsmiths went to where King Kumbha was; having approached him and, with palms joined [in reverence], offered their salutations, they spoke thus: "It is indeed so, Lord! Today you summoned us... until [you said] 'having opened the seam, report back this command. Then we took that divine pair of earrings; having taken them, we went to where the goldsmith's benches were, but we were not able to open the seam. Therefore, Lord, we shall fashion another pair of earrings similar to this divine pair of earrings."

Then King Kumbha, having heard and reflected upon this matter from that guild of goldsmiths, became enraged and furious; knitting his brows into a triple furrow upon his forehead, he spoke thus: "Who are you that call yourselves artisans, you who are unable to join the seam of this divine pair of earrings? He then ordered those goldsmiths to be banished.

Then those goldsmiths, having been ordered by King Kumbha to leave the country, went to their respective homes. Having arrived, they took their goods, wares, and equipment and departed through the very center of the capital city of Mithilā. They traveled through the middle of the Videha territory until they reached the Kāśī territory and the city of Vārāṇasī. Upon arrival, they unloaded their carts and wagons at the main park; having unloaded them, they took with them a great and valuable gift-offering. Then, entering through the very center of the city of Vārāṇasī, they went to where Saṅkha, the King of Kāśī, was located. Having arrived, they joined their palms [in reverence] and spoke as follows:

“Lord, we have indeed been ordered by King Kumbha to leave the kingdom of Mithilā; having been so commanded, we have come here quickly. Therefore, Lord, we wish to dwell here in great comfort, free from fear and anxiety, sheltered under the protection of your arms. Then Śaṅkha, the King of Kāśī, said to those goldsmiths: “Why, dear friends, have you been ordered by King Kumbha to leave the kingdom?”

Then those goldsmiths said this to King Śaṅkha of Kāśī: "Truly, Lord, the joint of the pair of earrings belonging to Mallī—the daughter of King Kumbha and the daughter of Queen Pabhāvatī—has come apart. Thereupon, King Kumbha summoned the guild of goldsmiths [and punished them], up until they were ordered to be banished from the country. For this reason, Lord, we have been ordered by King Kumbha to be banished."

Then King Śaṅkha of Kāśī said to those goldsmiths: "O beloved of the gods, what is Mallī, the Videhan princess, the daughter of King Kumbhaka and Queen Prabhāvatī, like? Then those goldsmiths said to King Śaṅkha of Kāśī: "Indeed, my lord, there is no other divine maiden or Gandharva maiden who is even like Mallī, the Videhan princess."
Then King Śaṅkha of Kāśī, his laughter provoked by the earrings, summoned a messenger and set out on that very path for Hastināpura.

At that time and at that moment, there was a district named Kuru, and in the city of Hastināpura, there reigned a king named Adīnasattu. Meanwhile, in Mithilā, the son of King Kumbhaka and Queen Pabhāvaī, born after Mallī [was conceived], a prince named Malladinna, who was the crown prince, lived there.

Then, on a certain occasion, Prince Malladinna summoned his household servants and spoke to them thus: "Go, prepare for me a large picture gallery in my pleasure grove, furnished with many hundreds of pillars... [and so on, until] "...they reported back [that it was finished]. Then Prince Malladinna summoned a guild of painters and spoke to them thus: 'O dear ones, paint the picture gallery with figures endowed with gestures, expressions, charms, and amorous graces; having painted it, report back that this command has been fulfilled.'"

Then that guild of painters accepted this matter, saying "So be it. Having accepted it, they went to their respective homes; having gone there, they took their brushes and pigments. Having taken them, they entered the picture gallery; having entered, they prepared the floor area and leveled the ground. Having leveled it, they set about painting the picture gallery with various gestures and expressions.

Now, that painter possessed such a skill as a master artist—attained, reached, and fully mastered—such that whenever he saw even a single part of a biped, a quadruped, or a winged creature, he would produce its likeness according to that specific part. Then, through the lattice-work of the curtain behind which Mallī was hidden, the painter caught sight of her big toe. Thereupon, this reflection arose within the mind of that painter: "It would indeed be well for me to create a form for Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha, corresponding to her big toe, [and so on] up to one endowed with all her qualities. Having thus reflected, he prepared the ground; having prepared it, he created a form for Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha, corresponding to her big toe, [and so on] up to a form endowed with all her qualities.

Then that group of painters decorated the picture-gallery with various gestures and expressions, and having finished the decoration, they approached Prince Malladinna and reported that their instructions had been carried out.

Then that Prince Malladinna honored and respected the guild of painters; having honored and respected them, he gave them a generous gift suitable for their livelihood as a token of affection, and having given it, he dismissed them. Then that Prince Malladinna, having bathed and being surrounded by his retinue of women, together with his nurse, went to where the picture-gallery was. Having arrived, he entered the picture-gallery. While looking again and again at the figures endowed with gestures, expressions, charms, and coquettish movements, he directed his gaze toward the figure of Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha, which had been fashioned according to her own likeness. Then, seeing the figure of Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha, fashioned according to her likeness, this reflection arose within him: "This is indeed Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha. Thinking thus, he became ashamed, abashed, and embarrassed, and he slowly backed away.

Then, seeing Prince Malladinna withdrawing very slowly, his nurse said this to him: "Why, my son, do you withdraw so slowly, acting ashamed, embarrassed, and bashful? Then Prince Malladinna said this to his nurse: "Is it proper, mother, for my eldest sister—who is like a teacher to me and worthy of my respect—to enter my picture-gallery? Then the nurse said this to Prince Malladinna: "Indeed, this is not the princess Mallī, the daughter of the eminent King of Videha; rather, this is a likeness of the princess Mallī created by a painter in her own image."

Then, having heard and reflected upon this matter from his nurse, Prince Malladinna became enraged and spoke thus: "Who is this Citrāra, O sir!—this one who prays for what is undesirable, and so forth, until 'is to be avoided'—who has portrayed my eldest sister, who is like a tutelary deity to me, and so forth, as 'one who has brought [this] about'? Having said this, he ordered that the painter be executed."

Then that group of painters, having understood this matter, went to where Prince Malladinna was; having approached, they saluted him with palms joined together [in reverence] and spoke thus: "Truly, Lord, that painter has attained, acquired, and mastered such a skill of painting that he can produce the likeness of any two-legged being, and so forth. Therefore, Lord, do not order that painter to be executed. Instead, Lord, impose upon that painter some other punishment appropriate to the situation. Then Prince Malladinna had the painter's thumb-nail cut off and ordered him to be banished from the country.

Then that painter Malladinna, having been ordered by Prince Malladinna to be dismissed, departed from the city of Mithilā with his goods, belongings, and equipment. Having departed, he traveled through the middle of the Videha country until he reached the Kuru country, and within it, the city of Hastināpura; there he went to King Adīnasattu. Having arrived, he set down his goods, prepared a painting board, and fashioned the likeness of Mallī, the noble princess of Videha, following the proportions of her big toe. Having completed it, he tucked it under his arm, took a great gift-offering, and proceeded through the center of the city of Hastināpura to where King Adīnasattu was. Having arrived, he saluted the king with palms joined in reverence and presented the gift-offering. Having presented it, he spoke thus: "Indeed, my lord, I am a painter who has been ordered to be dismissed by Prince Malladinna—the son of King Kumbhaga and the nephew of Queen Pabhāvaī—from the capital city of Mithilā; I have come here in haste. Therefore, my lord, I wish to dwell under the protection of your arms."

Then King Adīṇasattu said this to that painter: "Why, dear sir, have you been ordered by Malladinnā to be banished? Then that painter said this to King Adīṇasattu: "It is indeed so, my lord. On a certain occasion, Prince Malladinnā summoned the guild of painters and, having summoned them, spoke thus: 'You, dear sirs, [must paint] my picture-hall... (and so on, everything should be recited as before) "...until he had his pincers cut off, and having had them cut off, he ordered me to be banished from the country. It is indeed so, my lord; I have been ordered by Prince Malladinnā to be banished."

Then King Adīṇasattu said this to that painter: "O beloved of the gods, what kind of form has been produced by you for Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, corresponding to her [beauty]? Then that painter took the painting-board out from his armpit; having taken it out, he presented it to King Adīṇasattu and spoke thus: "This, O Lord, is some representation of the form, appearance, and configuration corresponding to Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, which has been produced. Indeed, it is not possible for any god or [other being] to produce a form corresponding to Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha."

Then that Adīṇasattu summoned an envoy who was handsome and capable of inspiring laughter; having summoned him, he spoke thus: [the same as before] up to "set out for the journey. At that time, in that period, in the kingdom of Pañcāla, in the city of Kampillapura, there was a king named Jiyasattu, the sovereign of Pañcāla. To that Jiyasattu, there were a thousand queens in his harem, of whom Dhāriṇī was the chief. Now, in Mithilā, there was a female ascetic named Cokkhā, who was well-versed in the Ṛgveda and so forth, and who had attained complete perfection.

Then that wandering ascetic Cokkhā wandered about in Mithilā, in the presence of many kings, ministers, and even caravan leaders, proclaiming, teaching, expounding, and demonstrating the duty of giving (*dāna-dharma*), the duty of austerity (*śauca-dharma*), and ritual bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha-abhiṣeka*). Then, on a certain occasion, Cokkhā took up her triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), her water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), and so forth, including her saffron-colored robes; having taken these, she departed from the dwelling of the wandering ascetics. Surrounded by a few wandering ascetic women, she went through the very center of the capital city of Mithilā to the palace of King Kumbhaka, to the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*), and to where Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, was. Having arrived, she sat down upon a seat (*bhisī*) covered with Darbha grass and touched by the morning sun. Seated there, she proceeded in front of Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, to proclaim and so forth [the duties] until she wandered about.

Then Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, spoke thus to the female ascetic Cokkhā: “O Cokkhā, what is the root of the Dharma taught by you? Then that female ascetic Cokkhā spoke thus to Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha: “O beloved of the gods! We teach a Dharma rooted in water. Whatever impure thing we may have, we purify it with water and clay, and thus we go to heaven without obstacle.”

Then Mallī, the excellent daughter of the King of Videha, said this to the female ascetic Cokkhā: "Cokkhā! Suppose, for example, there were a certain man who washed a blood-stained garment with blood itself; is there, Cokkhā, any purification of that blood-stained garment by washing it with blood? No, this is not possible. Even so, Cokkhā, for you there is no purification whatsoever from the taking of life up to the thorn of false belief, just as there is no purification of that blood-stained garment by washing it with blood itself. Then, having been addressed thus by Mallī, the daughter of the King of Videha, the female ascetic Cokkhā became doubtful, perplexed, hesitant, and overcome by fear. She was unable to utter even a word of rebuttal to Mallī and remained silent.

Then, many handmaidens of Mallī, the Videha princess, reviled, censured, despised, and reproached Cokkhā; some mocked her, some made faces at her, some imitated her gestures, and some, scolding and striking her, drove her out. Thus, being reproached and reviled by the handmaidens of Mallī, the Videha princess, Cokkhā became enraged and, burning with indignation, conceived a grudge against Mallī, the Videha princess. She took her seat-cushion, departed from the inner apartments of the palace, left Mithilā, and surrounded by female wanderers, traveled to the Pañcāla country. Arriving at Kampillapura, she wandered about, preaching her doctrines to many kings, ministers, and others.

Then, on another occasion, while Jiyasattu was staying in his excellent lion-throne, surrounded by the retinue of his inner apartments, the female ascetic Cokkhā, accompanied by her followers, entered the palace of King Jiyasattu where King Jiyasattu was, and having entered, she greeted him with cries of "Victory! and "Success! (jayaṃ vijayaṃ).

Then Jiyasattu saw the female wanderer Cokkhā approaching; having seen her, he rose from his lion-throne, and having risen, he honored and respected Cokkhā. Having honored and respected her, he invited her to sit on a seat. Then Cokkhā sat down on a cushion spread over darbha grass moistened with water. Having sat down, she asked King Jiyasattu about the welfare of his kingdom and even his harem. Then Cokkhā remained there, demonstrating to King Jiyasattu the duty of giving (*dāna-dharma*) and so forth.

Then Jiyasattu, filled with wonder upon seeing his own palace, spoke thus to Cokkha: "O beloved of the gods! You have wandered through many villages, towns, and settlements, and you have entered the houses of many kings, ministers, caravan leaders, and others. Have you ever before seen such a palace as this one of mine?"

When the female ascetic Cokkhā had been addressed thus by Jiyasattu, she smiled slightly and spoke as follows: "Are you indeed like that frog from the well, O beloved of the gods? Who, O beloved of the gods, is this frog from the well? "Jiyasattu! Suppose there were a frog from a well. Born there and grown up there, not having seen another well, lake, pool, pond, or ocean, he would think: 'This [well] alone is a well'... up to '...an ocean. Then, another ocean-frog would suddenly arrive at that well. Thereupon, the well-frog would speak thus to that ocean-frog: 'Who are you, O beloved of the gods? Or from where have you come here? Then the ocean-frog would speak thus to that well-frog: 'Indeed, O beloved of the gods, I am an ocean-frog. Then the well-frog would speak thus to that ocean-frog: 'How large, O beloved of the gods, is that ocean? Then the ocean-frog would speak thus to that well-frog: 'Very large, O beloved of the gods, is that ocean.'"

Then that well-dweller dragged a line with his foot, and having dragged it, he spoke thus: "Is the ocean, O beloved of the gods, very large? Then that well-dweller dragged the line with his foot, and having dragged it, he spoke thus: "Is that ocean, O beloved of the gods, so very large? "It is not so; that ocean is indeed very large. Then that well-dweller, leaping from the eastern shore, went to the western shore; having gone there, he spoke thus: "Is that ocean, O beloved of the gods, so very large? "It is not so; it is not possible [to measure it]. "In exactly the same way, you too, Jiyasattu, while not seeing the wife, sister, daughter, or daughter-in-law of many other kings, lords, and even caravan-leaders, think: 'The kind of beauty I have is not found in others. But this is the truth: in the city of Mithilā, there is Mallī by name, the daughter of King Kumbha and granddaughter of Pabhāvatī. In beauty and youth—and so on—there is truly no other celestial maiden or the like who is like Mallī, the noble daughter of the King of Videha. Compared to her, even a hundred thousandth part of the splendor of your own harem does not equal even a single toe of hers. Having said this, she departed in the same direction from which she had appeared.
Then Jiyasattu, provoked to laughter by the female wanderer, summoned a messenger and dispatched him to go and strike [the king].

Then the messengers of those six kings, headed by Jitasatru, set out for Mithilā. Those six messengers arrived at Mithilā, entered the city’s principal garden, and each established his own military camp. Having done so, they entered the capital city of Mithilā and approached King Kumbhaka. Upon arrival, they each took hold of his hands with both palms joined and reported the words of their respective kings.

Then Kumbhaka, having heard this matter from those messengers, became enraged and, knitting his brows into three folds, spoke thus: "I will not give Mallī, the excellent daughter of the King of Videha, to you! Having said this, he dismissed all six messengers without honor or respect, turning them out through a non-gate.

Then those messengers of the six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, having been neither honored nor respected by King Kumbha and having been expelled through an improper gate, went to their respective territories, to their respective cities, and to their respective kings. Having arrived, they joined their palms in reverence and spoke thus: "Truly, O Lord, we are the messengers of the six kings headed by Jiyasattu; we arrived at Mithilā simultaneously and [were treated as described] until he expelled us through an improper gate. Therefore, O Lord, Kumbha does not give Mallī to any of the kings. Thus they reported this matter to each of their respective kings.

Then those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the mouths of their messengers, became enraged and dispatched messengers to one another. Having done so, they spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! Messengers from us six kings have been sent simultaneously, and [having been received] they have been driven out. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, it is well for us to launch an expedition against Kumbhaka. Having agreed to this proposal with one another, they bathed, armored themselves, and mounted the backs of elephants. Adorned with garlands of *koreṇṭa* flowers and excellent jasmine, and being fanned with white, choice yak-tail whisks, they set out from their respective cities with great pomp and a tumultuous roar, accompanied by a fourfold army consisting of excellent horses, elephants, chariots, and foot soldiers. Having departed, they converged at one place and set out toward Mithilā.

When King Kumbha had grasped the meaning of this report, he summoned his commander-in-chief and, having summoned him, spoke thus: "Quickly [prepare] the cavalry force... [and so on] until they reported back."

Then King Kumbha, having bathed and armored himself, mounted upon the back of a preeminent elephant, adorned with a *koreṇṭa* flower [garland], and being fanned by white, excellent yak-tail whisks, proceeded through the very center of Mithilā with great [royal pomp]. Having marched out, he established his military camp at the border of the country, right through the middle of the Videha territory. There, he remained waiting for battle, fully prepared for war, while awaiting the six kings headed by Jitasattu.

Then those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, went to where King Kumbhaka was and engaged in combat with him. Then those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, drove King Kumbhaka in every direction—his horses slain, his preeminent heroes killed, his banners, flags, and pennants torn away, and his life-breath barely remaining.

Then, having been defeated, humiliated, and driven out by the six kings headed by Jiyasattu, Kumbhaka—being powerless, weak, and devoid of heroism, and concluding that he was unable to withstand them—quickly and hurriedly returned to Mithilā. Upon arriving, he entered Mithilā, closed its gates, and remained ready for defense.
Then those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, went to Mithilā; having arrived, they stood surrounding the royal city of Mithilā on all sides, making it completely inaccessible and devoid of movement.

Then King Kumbhaka, learning that the capital city of Mithilā was besieged, sat upon his excellent lion-throne in the inner audience hall. Finding no vulnerabilities, no gaps, no openings, and no vital points among those six kings headed by Jitasattu, he reflected again and again through various means and stratagems—through intuitive, discursive, practical, and synthetic forms of intelligence—but failing to find any advantage or expedient, he remained with a dejected mind and intent, brooding in distress.

And now Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, having bathed and so forth, surrounded by many hunchbacked women, approached Kumbhaka. Having approached, she grasped Kumbhaka’s feet. Then Kumbhaka neither welcomed nor acknowledged Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, but remained silent. Then Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, spoke thus to Kumbhaka: “O father, on other occasions you would come out to meet me as I approached and so forth, and escort me inside; why then do you today sit here dejected and brooding?”

Then Kumbha spoke thus to Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha: "Truly, my son, regarding your marriage, messengers were dispatched by six kings, headed by Jitasattu. They were treated with disrespect by me and eventually driven away. When those kings, headed by Jitasattu, heard this matter from the mouths of those messengers, they became enraged and have laid siege to the capital city of Mithilā, making it inaccessible. Therefore, my son, being unable to find any opening among those six kings, headed by Jitasattu, I sit brooding in the fire of anxiety."

Then Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, spoke thus to King Kumbhaka: "O father, do not be dejected in mind and intent, nor dwell upon [this sorrow]. O father, send secret messengers one by one to each of those six kings, headed by Jitasatru, and say to each of them: 'I give Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, to you. Having said this, at the time of twilight, when people are few and have settled down and retired, enter the capital city of Mithilā one by one; having entered, place them in the inner apartments; having placed them there, close the gates of the capital city of Mithilā; and having closed them, remain ready for battle."

Then Kumbhaka remained ready with Rohā. Thus, everything occurred exactly as before until they caused her to enter. Then, at dawn when the night had turned to light, those six kings, headed by Jitasattu, [arrived] and so forth; everything happened exactly as before until they caused her to enter. Through the lattice-windows, they saw the golden statue with a hole in its head and a lotus-closure on top. Thinking, "This is indeed Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha," they became infatuated, greedy, and utterly absorbed by the beauty, youth, and loveliness of Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha. They stood gazing at her with unblinking eyes.

Then Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, having bathed and performed her purificatory rites, adorned with all her ornaments and surrounded by many hunchbacked women and others, went to the lattice-window where the golden statue was located. Having arrived, she removed that lotus from the head of the golden statue. Then a stench issued forth—just like the smell of a dead snake, or even more foul than that. Overwhelmed by that foul odor, Jitasatru and the other kings covered their faces with their upper garments and stood with their backs turned.

Then Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, spoke thus to those kings headed by Jitasattu: "Why, O beloved of the gods, do you stand with your faces turned away, each with his own upper garment [covering his nose]?

Then those kings headed by Jitasattu said this to Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha: "It is indeed because we are overwhelmed by this foul odor, O beloved of the gods, that we stand each with our own [upper garments over our noses], and so forth."

Then Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, spoke thus to those kings headed by Jitasattu: "O beloved of the gods! If, for this golden image [and so forth], every single morsel of pleasant food—eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted—is thrown into it day after day, such a foul transformation of matter (*asubha-poggala-pariṇāma*) occurs; what kind of transformation, then, will there be for this physical body (*orāliya-sarīra*), which exudes saliva, vomit, bile, phlegm, and blood, which is full of pus, urine, and excrement, which has foul inhalations and exhalations, and whose nature is to decay and so forth? Therefore, O beloved of the gods! Do not become attached to, enamored of, greedy for, infatuated with, or obsessed by human sensual pleasures. Indeed, O beloved of the gods! In our third previous birth, in the land of Aparavideha, in the city of Salilavatī in the realm of Vītaśoka, we seven kings, headed by Mahābala, were brothers born together [and so forth] until we all went forth as ascetics. Then, O beloved of the gods! For this reason, I brought about the karma of a female name (*itthī-nāma-gōya*): 'If you practice the fourth [meditative stage] and dwell therein, then I shall practice the sixth and dwell therein. Everything else was exactly the same. Then, O beloved of the gods! Having passed away at the time of death, you were reborn in the Jayanta celestial palace. There, your lifespan was slightly less than thirty-two *sāgaropamas*. Then, having fallen from that divine world immediately after its expiration, you have been reborn right here on the continent of Jambudvīpa, each having attained his own respective kingdom and dwelling therein. As for me, O beloved of the gods! My lifespan in that divine world having expired [and so forth] until I have come here to be your daughter."
What indeed have you forgotten, O noble Jayanta, that you have dwelt for a time bound by convention? O gods, remember your former births! // Nāyā.94 //

Then, having heard and reflected upon this matter in the presence of Mallī, the excellent princess of Videha, those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, through a favorable transformation, a praiseworthy mental disposition, and as their *leśyās* were being purified, there arose within them a realization of the truth regarding the obstruction-covering karmas, etc., up to the attainment of the *saṃjñī* state; they thus correctly grasped this matter.

Then the Arhat Malli, having recognized that Jiyasattu and the other six kings had attained the recollection of their former births (*jātismaraṇa*), opened the doors of the inner apartments. Then those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, went to where the Arhat Malli was. At that time, the seven childhood friends, headed by Mahābala, were also gathered together in one place. Then the Arhat Malli spoke thus to those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu: "O dear ones, it is indeed because I am terrified of the fear of *saṃsāra*... that I am going forth into the religious life. Therefore, what will you do? What do you resolve? Or what power for your own welfare do you possess? Then the six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, spoke thus to the Arhat Malli: "If you, O dear one, being terrified of the fear of *saṃsāra*... are going forth, then, O dear one, who else would be our support, our sustenance, or our bond? Just as you, O dear one, in this third birth from us, were the pillar, the authority, and so on, up to the bearer of the burden of Dharma in many affairs; even so now, O dear one, you shall remain the bearer of the burden of Dharma. We too, O dear one, terrified of the fear of *saṃsāra* and afraid of births and deaths, shall go forth with you, O dear one, having shaved our heads and so on."

Then the Arhat Mallī spoke thus to those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu: "If you are terrified of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and so forth, and wish to go forth with me, then go, dear friends! Establish your respective kingdoms in the hands of your eldest sons; having done so, mount chariots drawn by a thousand men and appear before me. Then those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, accepted this proposal of the Arhat Mallī. Then the Arhat Mallī, taking those six kings headed by Jiyasattu, went to where Kumbhaka was; having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of Kumbhaka. Then Kumbhaka honored and respected those kings, headed by Jiyasattu, with abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies, as well as flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments; having honored and respected them, he dismissed them.

Then those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, having been dismissed by King Kumbha, went to their respective kingdoms and their respective cities; having arrived, they entered and settled in their respective kingdoms and lived there. Meanwhile, at the end of the year, the Arhat Malli formed the thought: "I shall go forth into the religious life."

At that time, on that occasion, the throne of Śakra trembled.
