Then Śakra, the lord of gods and king of the gods, seeing his throne tremble, exercised his clairvoyance (*avadhi-jñāna*); having exercised it, he perceived the Arhat Mallī through his clairvoyance, and upon perceiving her, this kind of reflection arose within him:

Thus, indeed, on the island of Jambudvīpa, in the region of Bhāratavarṣa, in the city of Mithilā, Mallī the Arhat—the daughter of King Kumbha and granddaughter of Queen Pabhāvatī—formed the resolve: "I shall go forth. It is the established custom for the Śakras, Arhats, and Blessed Ones of the past, present, and future who are going forth to bestow such a gift of wealth, namely: Three hundred crores, eighty-eight crores, and eighty thousand; these Indras bestow upon the Arhats. (Nāyā. 97)

Reflecting thus, and having reflected, he summoned the god Vessamaṇa and spoke to him as follows: “It is indeed so, dear sir! In Jambudvīpa, in the land of Bhārata... [and so on] ...grant eighty hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Therefore, go, dear sir, to Jambudvīpa, to the land of Bhārata, to the capital city of Mihilā, to the palace of King Kumbhaga, and deliver this kind of gift of wealth. Having delivered it, quickly report back to me that this command has been carried out.”

When the god Vessamaṇa had been thus addressed by Sakka, the lord of gods and king of gods, he was delighted and joyful; with palms joined together [in reverence], he gave his assent. Having given his assent, he summoned the Jambha gods and said this: "Go, O beloved of the gods! To the continent of Jambudvīpa, to the land of Bhārata, to the capital city of Mihilā, into the palace of King Kumbhaga, bring three hundred and eighty-eight million and eighty thousand [pieces] of such wealth. Having brought it, report back to me that this command has been carried out."

Then those Jambhaka gods, having been thus addressed by the god Vaiśramaṇa, and so on, having assented, departed toward the north-eastern direction; and so on, they manifested superior magical forms (*uttaravaikriya-rūpa*). Having manifested them, traveling with that most excellent divine gait, as they proceeded, they arrived at the continent of Jambūdvīpa, at the region of Bhārata, at the royal capital of Mithilā, and at the palace of King Kumbhaka. Having arrived, they deposited three hundred koṭis [of gold] and so on within the palace of King Kumbhaka. Having deposited them, they returned to where the god Vaiśramaṇa was, and having arrived, they reported back to him with palms joined, and so on.
Then that god Vaiśramaṇa approached where Śakra, the lord of gods and king of gods, was; having approached, with palms joined together [in reverence], he reported back that command.

Then, Mallī Arhat, day after day, until the Magadhan mealtime, distributed this kind of wealth-gift—consisting of one koṭi of gold and no less than eight hundred thousand [pieces of gold] each—to many people: those with protectors and those without protectors, travelers, wayfarers, beggars, and mendicants.

Then King Kumbha had many great kitchens constructed here and there in various places throughout the capital city of Mithilā. There, many men, provided with wages for their labor, prepared abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies. Whosoever arrived—whether travelers, wayfarers, carriers, mendicants, heretics, or householders—to him they distributed and served that abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies as he sat at ease, confident, and comfortably seated upon an excellent seat. Then, in the city of Mithilā, at the crossroads and along the highways, a great multitude of people spoke thus to one another: "O dear ones, in the palace of King Kumbha, abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies—possessing every quality and desired by all—are being served to many ascetics and others, even down to the mendicants."
"Let the proclamation 'Choose what you desire' be sounded; let manifold gifts be given at the renunciation of those honored by gods, asuras, deities, dānavas, and lords of men. // Nāyā.
99 // Then Mallī, the Arhat, having bestowed this kind of wealth-gift—three hundred and eighty-eight koṭis and eighty lakhs for one year—set his mind upon renunciation, thinking: "I shall go forth."

At that time, at that moment, the world-guardian deities (lokiyā devā) in the Brahma-world (bambhalōē kappa), in the Riṣṭa celestial abode (riṭṭhe vimāṇapatthaḍē), were dwelling in their respective celestial palaces (vimāṇēhiṁ) and their respective magnificent mansions (pāsāyavaḍiṁsaēhiṁ), surrounded by four thousand personal attendants (sāmāṇiya-sāhassīhiṁ), three assemblies (parisāhiṁ), seven divisions of the army (aṇiēhiṁ), seven commanders of the divisions (aṇiyāhivaīhiṁ), sixteen thousand protective deities (āyarakkha-dēvasāhassīhiṁ), and many other world-guardian deities; they were sporting, enjoying vast pleasures and enjoyments amidst the great sound of music, dance, song, and instrumental performance.
The Sārassaya, Māicca, Vaṇhī, Varuṇa, and Gaddatoya; the Tusita, Avvāvāha, Aggicca, and Riṭṭha. // Nāyā.102 //

Then, the seats of those world-protector deities (*lokaṃtiya*) each shook; [the rest is] just as before, up until: "We shall perform an awakening for the Arhats as they are departing. Thinking, "Let us also go and perform an awakening for the Arhat Malli," they reflect thus. Having reflected, they move toward the north-eastern direction and perform a transformation-projection (*vaikriya-samudghāta*). Having performed it, they extend their staff-like bodies (*daṇḍa*) for a measurable number of *yojanas*, just as the *jambhakas* do, up until: where the capital city of Mithilā is, where the palace of King Kumbha is, and where the Arhat Malli is, there they arrive. Arriving, they stand in the sky, wearing excellent garments including tinkling bells, with palms joined [in reverence], and with those pleasing words, they speak thus: "Awaken, O Blessed One! Lord of the World! Set in motion the ford of Dharma, which will bring about welfare, happiness, and ultimate liberation for living beings. Having said this, they say it a second and a third time. They pay homage to and revere the Arhat Malli, and having paid homage and revered him, they depart back in the same direction from which they appeared.

Then Malli, the Arhat, having been exhorted by those world-protector deities, went to where his maternal grandfather was; having arrived, with palms joined [in reverence], he spoke thus: "O mother and father! I desire, being permitted by you, to become shaven-headed and go forth into the religious life. "As it pleases you, dear one! Do not create an obstacle."

Then King Kumbha summoned his household officials and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Prepare eight thousand golden jars, up to eight thousand earthen jars, and other items of great value, for the consecration of a Tīrthaṅkara. And so they prepared them.

At that time, at that moment, Camara the lord of the Asuras, and so on, arrived, with the gods of the Acyuta heaven at their head. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods and king of the devas, summoned the Abhiyogika gods and spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Prepare eight thousand golden jars... and that vast array for the consecration of a Tīrthaṅkara. They likewise prepared it, and those jars merged back into those very same jars. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods and king of the devas, together with King Kumbhaka, seated the Arhat Mallī upon a lion-throne facing the east and performed the Tīrthaṅkara-consecration with eight thousand golden jars, and so forth.

While the consecration of the Blessed Malli was thus taking place, some gods ran all around Mithilā, both inside and outside, in every direction and on all sides. Then King Kumbha had the second northward-advancing lion-throne prepared; having done so, he adorned it with every ornament. Having done so, he summoned his household officials and, having summoned them, spoke to them thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, bring forth the beautiful palanquin! They, too, brought it forth.

Then Śakra, the lord of gods and king of the gods, summoned the Abhiyogika gods and spoke thus: "Quickly prepare a palanquin that is supported by many hundreds of pillars, [and so on] up to one that is delightful. They too prepared it, and Queen Sāvitrī entered that very same palanquin.

Then the Arhat Mallī rose from his lion-throne; having risen, he went to where the Manorama chariot was; having approached, while circumambulating the Manorama chariot, he ascended it. Having ascended, he sat down upon the excellent lion-throne facing the east. Then Kumbhaka summoned the eighteen generals and sub-generals and spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! Having bathed and being adorned with all ornaments, you must carry the chariot of Mallī. And they likewise carried it.

Then Śakra, the lord of gods and king of the gods, took hold of the upper right arm of the beautiful palanquin; Īśāna took hold of the upper left arm; Camara took hold of the lower right arm; and Bali took hold of the lower left arm. The remaining gods carried the beautiful palanquin according to their respective rank. Previously it was lifted by humans with their hair standing on end from joy;
afterwards, the lords of the Asuras, the lords of the Suras, and the lords of the Nāgas carried the palanquin. (Nāyā. 104)
Wearing swaying and trembling earrings, and bearing ornaments created at will, the lords of gods and the lords of demons carry the palanquin of the Lord of Jinas. // Nāyā.105 //

Then, as the Arhat Malli was mounting his beautiful palanquin, these eightfold auspicious symbols proceeded before him in their proper sequence; his departure was just like that of Jamāli. Then, as the Arhat Malli was departing, some gods made the city of Mithilā—both inside and out—sprinkled, swept, scrubbed, cleaned, with its streets, gardens, and groves prepared, and so on, until they ran about.

Then the Arhat Mallī went to the Sahasrāmavana park, to where the noble Aśoka tree stood; having arrived, he descended from the palanquin. Having descended, he removed his ornaments and jewelry, which Prabhāvatī received. Then the Arhat Mallī himself performed the tonsure with five handfuls of hair. Then Śakra, the lord of gods and king of the gods, caught Mallī’s hair; having caught it, he cast it into the Ocean of Milk.

Then the Arhat Malli, having said "Homage be to the Siddhas," undertook the conduct of equanimity (*sāmāyika-cāritra*). At the very moment the Arhat Malli undertook the conduct of equanimity, at that same moment the clamor of gods and humans, the sound of musical instruments, and the noise of singing and instrumental music vanished by the command and message of Śakra. And at the moment the Arhat Malli had undertaken the conduct of equanimity, at that same moment, a supernormal knowledge of the minds of others (*manahparyāya-jñāna*) superior to human capacity arose in the Arhat Malli.

In the second month of winter, in the fourth fortnight of the bright half of the month of Pauṣa, on the eleventh day of that bright half of Pauṣa, during the forenoon, while observing the eighth meal (fasting) without water, under the conjunction of the asterism Āśvinī, Mallī, the Arhat, together with three hundred women as his inner retinue and three hundred men as his outer retinue, shaved his head and went forth into the homeless life.
These eight princely youths followed Mallī, the Arhat, into the religious life.
Nandi, Nandimitra, Sumitra, Balamitra, Bhānumitra, Amarapati, Amarasena, and Mahāsena as the eighth.

Then those gods of the Bhavanavāsin, Vānamantara, Jyotiṣka, and Vaimānika classes performed the great festival for the renunciation of the Arhat Malli; having performed it, they went to the island of Nandīśvara and performed the eight-day festival there, after which they returned to that same direction from which they had come.

Then, on that very day when Mallī Arhat had gone forth, during the afternoon, while he was seated comfortably upon a choice stone slab beneath the noble Aśoka tree, through a state of well-being, with praiseworthy mental dispositions (*adhyavasāna*) and purifying, praiseworthy passions (*leśyā*), he entered the unprecedented refinement (*apūrvakaraṇa*) which effects the destruction of the dust of karma obscuring knowledge; and thereupon infinite, supreme, excellent knowledge and vision (*kevalavarajñānadarśana*) arose within him.

At that time, at that moment, the thrones of all the gods shook; they assembled and listened to the Dharma. Having listened, they went to the island of Nandīśvara. Having gone there, they performed the eight-day festival (aṣṭāhnikā-mahimā). Having performed it, they returned to the very same direction from which they had appeared. Kumbhaka also went out.

Then those six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, having established their eldest sons in the kingdom, mounted palanquins carried by a thousand men and, with full royal splendor, went to where the Arhat Malli was and paid him homage.

Then the Arhat Malli preached the Dharma to that great and vast assembly, to King Kumbha, and to those kings headed by Jiyasattu. The assembly departed in the same direction from which it had come. King Kumbha became a lay follower of the ascetics (*śramaṇopāsaka*) and returned; so too did Prabhāvatī. Then the six kings, headed by Jiyasattu, having heard and reflected upon the Dharma, spoke thus: "We are, O Venerable One, [afflicted] by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair... [and so on] until they went forth as ascetics, became masters of the fourteen *pūrvas*, attained infinite, perfect knowledge (*kevala*), and subsequently reached liberation (*siddha*)."
Then the Arhat Malli departed from the Sahasrāmravana grove; having departed, he wandered on a tour through the countryside outside.

The Arhat Malli had twenty-eight assemblies and twenty-eight *gaṇadharas*, headed by Bhiṣaja. Under the Arhat Malli, there were forty thousand monks at the maximum, headed by Bandhumati; fifty-five thousand nuns at the maximum; one hundred and eighty-four thousand laymen (*śrāvaka*); three hundred and sixty-six thousand female lay devotees (*śrāvikā*); six hundred who possessed the knowledge of the fourteen *pūrvas*; two thousand who possessed clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñāna*); thirty-two hundred who possessed omniscience (*kevalajñāna*); thirty-five hundred who possessed the power of transformation (*vaikriya*); eight hundred who possessed mind-reading knowledge (*manahparyāyajñāna*); fourteen hundred eloquent preachers (*vādī*); and two thousand who were reborn in the highest heavens (*anuttaropapātika*).

For the Arhat Malli, there were two kinds of stages for ending [existence]: the stage of ending at the end of a *yuga* (generation) and the stage of ending at the end of the [monastic] career. The stage of ending at the end of a *yuga* lasted until the twentieth generation of men; he brought about the end [of existence] after a two-year monastic career.

The Arhat Mallī was twenty-five *dhanus* in height; in complexion he was like the *piyaṅgu* flower; his body was symmetrical and quadrangular in shape (*samacaturaṃsa-saṃsthāna*), and his skeletal structure was that of the "diamond-like" *vajra-ṛṣabha-nārāca* type. Having lived in perfect ease in the central region, he went to Mount Sammeta. Upon reaching the summit of Mount Sammeta, the Arhat Mallī resolved upon fasting unto death. The Arhat Mallī spent one hundred years in the household life and fifty-nine thousand years less one hundred years in the career of a *kevalin*. Having completed a total lifespan of fifty-nine thousand years, in the first month of winter, in the second fortnight of the bright half of Caitra, on the fourth day of that bright fortnight of Caitra, under the conjunction of the *Bharaṇī* constellation at the hour of midnight, surrounded by five hundred female ascetics (*ajjikā*) in the inner assembly and five hundred male mendicants (*anagāra*) in the outer assembly, with his hands and feet extended and his food and drink ceased, having observed a month-long fast without water, his *vedanīya*, *āyuṣka*, *nāma*, and *gotra* karmas were exhausted, and he became perfected (*siddha*). In this manner, the great festival of his final liberation (*parinirvāṇa-mahimā*) should be described as it is in the *Jambūdvīpaprajñapti*. On the island of Nandīśvara, the eight-day festivals concluded. Thus indeed, O Jambū, this is the meaning of the eighth chapter of the *Nāyādhyayana* as taught by the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra. Thus I speak.

"If, venerable sir, this is the meaning set forth by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained liberation, as contained in the eighth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, then what, venerable sir, is the meaning set forth in the ninth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*? "Thus it was, Jambū: At that time, in that period, there was a city named Campā and a shrine named Punnabhadda. There lived a caravan leader named Māyandī, who was wealthy. His wife was named Bhaddā. She had two sons, both caravan leaders, namely Jinapāliya and Jinarakkhia."

Then, on another occasion, a conversation of this nature arose among those sons of Māgandika as they sat together: "Indeed, dear ones, we have already crossed the salt ocean by ship eleven times; on every occasion we achieved our purpose, accomplished our task, and returned safely and quickly to our own homes. Therefore, dear ones, it would be well for us to embark upon the salt ocean by ship for a twelfth time. Having said this, they agreed to one another's proposal. Having agreed, they went to where their parents were, and having approached them, they spoke thus.

"Indeed, mothers! Eleven times we have already gone out to sea and returned safely to our own homes. Therefore, mothers, we wish with your permission to embark upon the twelfth voyage across the salt ocean by ship. Then the parents of the two Māgandiya youths spoke thus: "My sons, you have these [jewels]—enough for your study, enjoyment, and distribution. So, my sons, enjoy this abundant human wealth and honor! Why do you seek to cross the salt ocean, which is fraught with danger and devoid of support? Truly, my sons, the twelfth expedition is full of perils. Therefore, my two sons, do not embark upon the salt ocean for the twelfth time; let there be no harm to your bodies."

Then those parents of the Māgaṃdīya boys spoke thus to them a second and even a third time: "In this way, indeed, O mothers and fathers! we have plunged into the salt ocean eleven times, up until the twelfth time we shall plunge into the salt ocean. When those parents of the Māgaṃdīya boys were unable—through many exhortations and persuasions—to either exhort or persuade them, they then, though unwilling, gave their consent to this matter.

Then those Māgaṃdiya merchants, having been granted permission by their parents, took up merchandise to be counted, weighed, measured, and bartered; as in the case of Arahannaka, they entered the salt ocean at many hundreds of yojanas.

Then, as those sons of Māgandiya had traveled many hundreds of *yojanas*, many hundreds of portents appeared to them, such as: unseasonable thundering, and so forth, up to the sound of peals of lightning; and a dark storm (*kāliyavāta*) arose, and so forth. Then that ship, being tossed about and shaken by that dark storm, being agitated and convulsed, battered by the sharp force of the waters, was tossed here and there like a *tinduka* fruit struck against the surface of a terrace. It rose up as if a young Vidyādhara maiden rising from the earth with her magic power (*vidyā*), and descended as if a young Vidyādhara maiden fallen from the sky after losing her magic power. It fled away like a noble serpent maiden terrified by the speed of a great Garuḍa; it ran about like a female horse (*āsakisorī*) who has lost her place, panicked by the clamor of a great crowd of people. It whirled about like a well-born maiden whose heavy offense has been seen by her elders; it reeled like one struck by hundreds of blows from the waves. It wept like a young bride whose husband has passed away, her support gone from the sky; it lamented like a great city besieged by a foreign army, overcome by supreme terror. It meditated like a female ascetic (*parivrājikā*) engaged in the practice of deceptive transformations; it sighed like an elderly woman exhausted by wandering through a great wilderness. It grieved like a noble celestial maiden at the time of her fall, her enjoyment of merit exhausted by asceticism. With its keel shattered, its masts broken, its thousand-fold rigging torn, its curved frames pierced by spikes, its iron fittings bursting and cracking between the planks, its joints splitting apart, its ropes frayed and falling from every limb, it became like an unbaked earthen pot. Like the unfulfilled desires of an unfortunate person when being contemplated, it was filled with the cries of "Alas! Alas! from the sailors, merchants, laborers, and servants. Filled with various kinds of gems and merchandise, and with hundreds of men weeping, crying out, grieving, fainting, and lamenting, it struck a great mountain peak within the water. With its masts and arches crushed, its flagstaffs broken, and its hundred rings shattered, it went to its destruction right there with a crashing sound.
Then, as that boat was breaking apart, those many men, having taken a vast quantity of merchandise and goods, were submerged within the water.

Then those sons of Māgandiyā—skilled, dexterous, experienced, wise, proficient in their craft, having gained mastery through many voyages by sea, victorious, undeluded, and with unerring hands—reached a large piece of timber. At the very spot where that ship had wrecked, there was a great island named Ratnadvīpa, many yojanas in length and breadth, and many yojanas in circumference; its regions were adorned with various groves of trees, beautiful as the moon, lovely to behold, pleasing, and exquisite.
In its central region, there was a great palatial mansion—towering, lofty, and radiant, possessing a beautiful form, delightful, lovely to behold, charming, and exquisite.
In that palatial mansion dwelt a goddess named Ratnadvīpa-devatā—one who is wicked, fierce, cruel, malicious, and murderous.

On the four sides of that palace-tower there were four groves, black and darkly radiant. Then those sons of Mākandika, being repeatedly tossed about by that fragment of a plank, were eventually driven onto the Jewel Island. Thereupon, the sons of Mākandika found a place to rest; after a short interval they took heart, set down the fragment of the plank, and stepped onto the Jewel Island. They searched for and sought out fruits, ate the fruits, searched for and sought out coconut trees, split open the coconuts, and anointed each other’s limbs with coconut oil. They entered the lotus ponds, bathed, and emerged from the lotus ponds. They sat down upon a stone slab on the ground; having sat down, refreshed, at ease, and comfortably seated, they brooded over and reflected upon the city of Campā, their departure from their parents, their crossing of the salt ocean, the storming of the black wind, the shipwreck, the drifting on the fragment of the plank, and their arrival at the Jewel Island. Thus, with depressed minds and intentions, they remained lost in thought.

Then that goddess of the Jewel Island perceived those sons of Mākandika through her clairvoyance; with a sword and shield in hand, she rose into the air to a height of seven or eight *tala*-measures. Having risen, moving along with that exalted, divine gait, she approached the sons of Mākandika. Arriving there, enraged, she addressed the sons of Mākandika with harsh, rough, and cruel words, saying this:

"O sons of Māgandikā! You who pray for what should not be prayed for: if you dwell with me, enjoying abundant sensual pleasures, then you shall have life; but if you do not dwell with me, enjoying abundant sensual pleasures, then with this sword—blue-lotus-colored, as dark as a young elephant’s trunk, and sharp-edged as a razor—I shall strike off your heads, which are as red as the flesh of a goat's cheek and as tender as a palm fruit, and cast them aside. Then those sons of Māgandikā, having heard this matter from the presence of the deity of the Jewel Island, became terrified. With palms joined together, they spoke thus: "Whatever the beloved one commands, we shall abide by his instruction, his command, his word, and his direction."

Then that goddess of the Jewel Island took those sons of Māgandika and went to the palace turret; there she drew out impure matter and infused pure matter, and thereafter, enjoying extensive sensual pleasures with them, she dwelt there, bringing nectar-like fruits to them every day.

Then that goddess of the Jewel Island (Rayaṇadīvadēvayā), by the command and message of Śakra, was appointed with these instructions: "The Lord of the Salt Ocean (Lavaṇāhivaï) has commanded that the Salt Ocean must be circled twenty-one times by Suṭṭhiya. Whatever there may be therein—grass, leaves, wood, husks, filth, impurity, or foul-smelling, unclean things—all that must be gathered up repeatedly and cleared away twenty-one times to one side. Having been thus appointed, the goddess of the Jewel Island spoke to those sons of Māgandiya: "O dear ones, it is indeed by the command and message of Śakra that I have been appointed, and so forth, until: 'I have been appointed. Therefore, O dear ones, remain right here at Pāsāvayaḍaṃsa, enjoying yourselves happily, until I have finished clearing the Salt Ocean. If, in the meantime, you should become anxious, distressed, or agitated, then you should go to the eastern forest grove. There, two seasons are always available: namely, the rainy season (pāusa) and the monsoon (vāsāratta)."

There, the rainy season is like a noble elephant: its tusks are the *u-kandala* and *silindha* flowers; its trunk is thick with the excellent blossoms of the *nīpa*; it gives forth a fragrant scent like the *kuṭaja* and *arjuna*; and it possesses the *asāhī* creeper.
There, moreover, it is variegated with gems like the eyes of Indra’s elephant, and resounds with the cries of families of frogs and the noise of waterfalls.
With his head encircled by a peacock’s tail-feathers, he has the rainy season as his garment at his disposal. (Nāyā. 115)

There, O beloved of the gods, you may dwell, delighting yourselves in great ease, among many ponds and so forth, up to rows of lakes; and among many groves of *ālī* plants, groves of *mālī* plants, and so forth, up to groves of flowers. If, however, you should become anxious, distressed, or agitated even there, then you should go to the northern forest grove. There, two seasons are always at your disposal, namely: autumn and winter.
There, the cowherd possesses a plow as bright as the color of gold, with a handle like a blue lotus, a lotus, or a water-lily;
he has the cry of cranes, ruddy geese, and peacocks, and the autumn season is at his command.
// Nāyā.117 There, the cowherd possesses a plow as bright as the color of gold, with a handle like a blue lotus, a lotus, or a water-lily.
The cry of cranes and ruddy geese resounds; the autumn season is ever at his disposal.

And there, the winter season with its moon—whose light is as white as a jasmine flower, whose surface is adorned by groves of flowering lodhra trees, and whose thick rays are like streams of dew—is always at his disposal. (Nāyā. 117–118)

"There, O beloved of the gods, you may sport in the ponds and so forth. If you should become anxious or even longing there, then you should go to the upper forest grove; there two seasons are always at your disposal, namely: spring and summer.

There, the king of the spring season is at your disposal, with its beautiful mango trees as necklaces, its *kiṃśuka*, *karṇikāra*, and *aśoka* flowers as crowns, and its uplifted *tilaka*, *bakula*, and *āmrātaka* trees. // Nāyā.120 //

There, the ocean of the summer season has the *yapāḍala* and *śirīṣa* flowers as its foam, the *mallikā* and *vāsantī* jasmine as its white waves, and the cool, fragrant, dark-blue clouds as its sea-monsters; it is under the sovereign command of the summer. // Nāyā.121 //

"There, O beloved of the gods, you may stay for many days... if, however, you should become anxious or restless there, then you should go to Pāśākhyapaṭaṃsaka and remain waiting for me again and again; do not go to the southern forest grove. There dwells a certain great serpent of fierce venom, violent venom, terrible venom, and great venom; one of immense body and great size, like a mass of fire, black as ink, buffalo-horn, or a black vessel; his eyes are filled with the poison of wrath; he has the luster of a heap of powdered collyrium; he has red eyes and twin, flickering, trembling tongues; he is like a braid upon the surface of the earth; he is skilled in spreading out his expanded, stiff, crooked, knotted, hard, and wide hood; he makes a sound like the roaring of a smelting furnace; he possesses unrestrained, fierce, and intense anger; and he blows violently, swiftly, and restlessly with his breath—this serpent, whose very glance is poisonous, dwells there. Lest there be harm to your bodies, O Māgandika’s sons! Having spoken thus a second and a third time, he undergoes a transformation by means of a *samudghāta* (an expansion of his vital energy). Having undergone that transformation, he set out through the sky with that supreme divine speed to circumambulate the salt ocean twenty-one times.

Then, after a short while, those sons of Māgandikā, finding neither comfort, nor pleasure, nor mental stability in their palatial mansions, spoke thus to one another: "O dear ones, the goddess of the Jewel Island has indeed spoken to us in this way:"

"In this way, indeed, by the command and message of Sakka, and because of the well-being of the Lord of the Ocean, until [the danger] shall be averted, it is indeed best for us, O beloved of the gods, to go to the eastern grove. They consented to this matter to one another; having consented, they went to where the eastern grove was, and there they enjoyed themselves in the ponds and so forth, and sported in the bowers of creepers and so forth.

Then those sons of Mākandika, not finding even a place to sleep there, went to the northern grove; there they stayed in the ponds and so forth, up to the huts for water-sports. Then those sons of Mākandika, not finding even a place to sleep there, went to the western grove and stayed there, and so forth.

Then those sons of Māgandiya, while there, spoke thus to one another: "O dear ones, the goddess of the Jewel Island spoke to us thus: 'O dear ones, I have been appointed by Suṭṭhiya, the lord of the salt ocean, on the command and message of Śakra... [until] lest there be harm to your bodies; therefore, there must be a reason for this. It would be well for us to go toward the southern grove... [until] to strike right there. Then a scent wafted forth, such as the smell of a dead snake, or even more unpleasant than that."

Then those sons of Māgandikā, overcome by that foul odor, covered their noses with their respective upper garments. Having done so, they went to where the southern grove was; there they saw a great slaughter-ground crowded with hundreds of heaps of bones, terrifying to behold. And there they saw a man impaled on a stake, uttering piteous, discordant, and wailing cries. Terrified and seized with fear, they approached the man on the stake and spoke to him thus:

"O beloved of the gods! Whose abode is this? Who are you, and from where have you come here so quickly? Or by whom has such a calamity as this been suffered? Then that man impaled on the stake spoke thus to the sons of Māgandiya: "O beloved of the gods! This is the abode of the goddess of the Jewel Island (Ratnadvīpa). As for me, O beloved of the gods, I came from Jambudvīpa, from the land of Bhārata, from the city of Kākaṇdī, having set out upon the salt ocean with a ship carrying a vast cargo of merchandise for trade. Then, due to the wrecking of the ship, my goods and wealth were submerged; I clung to a piece of timber. While being tossed about by the waves, I was carried to the vicinity of the Jewel Island. Then the goddess of the Jewel Island saw me with her supernatural vision (avadhi-jñāna); having seen me, she took hold of me, and having taken me, she dwells with me, enjoying manifold pleasures."

Then, on another occasion, that goddess of the Jewel Island, having become enraged at a very slight offense, brought such a calamity upon me; therefore, O beloved of the gods, it is not known what kind of calamity might befall even your bodies.

Then those two sons of Mākandika, having heard and understood this matter from the presence of that man on the stake, became even more terrified and filled with fear; they spoke thus to the man on the stake: "O beloved of the gods! How might we escape safely from the hands of the goddess of the Jewel Island? Then that man on the stake spoke thus to the two sons of Mākandika:

"O beloved of the gods! In the eastern grove, at the abode of the yakṣa Śailaka, there dwells a yakṣa named Śailaka who assumes the form of a horse. On the fourteenth, eighth, and full moon days, when the time has arrived and the occasion has come, that yakṣa Śailaka utters with a very loud voice: 'Whom shall I deliver? Whom shall I protect? Therefore, O beloved of the gods, go to the eastern grove and perform a grand floral worship of the yakṣa Śailaka. Having done so, remain there in humble attendance, kneeling with your hands joined in reverence. When that yakṣa Śailaka, at the arrived time and on the occasion, says, 'Whom shall I deliver? Whom shall I protect?', you must say: 'Deliver us! Protect us! Then the yakṣa Śailaka will personally rescue you from the hand of the goddess of the Jewel Island. Otherwise, I know not what calamity may befall these bodies of yours."

Then those sons of Māgandikā, having heard and understood this matter from the presence of that man impaled on the stake, quickly, fiercely, restlessly, swiftly, and hurriedly went to the eastern grove where the lotus pond was; having arrived, they entered the lotus pond, bathed in the water, and gathered whatever blue lotuses and other flowers were there. Having taken them, they went to the shrine of the Yakṣa Śailaka; having arrived, they offered salutations toward the direction [of the deity], performed a grand worship with flowers, and, kneeling with their knees touching the ground, waited upon him with devotion and reverence.

Then that yakṣa Śailaka, the time having arrived and the opportunity having presented itself, spoke thus: "Whom shall I rescue? Whom shall I protect? Then those sons of Mākandika rose up from their seats; having risen, they joined their palms [in reverence] and spoke thus: "Rescue us! Protect us! Then that yakṣa Śailaka spoke to those sons of Mākandika as follows: "Indeed, dear ones, as you are passing through the middle of the salt ocean with me, that goddess of the Jewel Island—wicked, fierce, cruel, base, and violent—will inflict many obstructions upon you through harsh and gentle words, both favorable and unfavorable, and through seductive and piteous provocations. Therefore, dear ones, if you should accept, acknowledge, or pay heed to this matter of the goddess of the Jewel Island, then I shall cast you off from my back. But if you do not accept, acknowledge, or pay heed to this matter of the goddess of the Jewel Island, then I shall personally deliver you from her hands."

Then those sons of Māgandikā spoke thus to the yakṣa Śailaka: "O beloved of the gods! We shall abide by whatever you command, according to your instruction and direction. Then that yakṣa Śailaka moved toward the north-eastern quarter; having moved there, he underwent a transformational emission (*veuvviyasamugghāēṇaṃ*) and, having undergone it, projected a staff (*daṇḍa*) for a measurable number of *yojanas*. A second time he underwent a transformational emission and, having undergone it, manifested a great form of a horse. Having manifested it, he spoke thus to the sons of Māgandikā: "Ho there, sons of Māgandikā! O beloved of the gods! Mount upon my back! Then those sons of Māgandikā, being delighted, paid homage to the yakṣa Śailaka and mounted his back. Then Śailaka, knowing that the sons of Māgandikā were mounted on his back, flew upward into the sky to the height of seven or eight stories. Having flown up, with that exalted, swift, divine, celestial gait, he set out on his journey through the very middle of the salt ocean toward Jambūdvīpa, toward the land of Bhārata, and toward the city of Campā.

Then that goddess of the Jewel Island circumnavigated the Salt Ocean twenty-one times, gathering whatever grass or [other] things were there and casting them aside in one place. She went to the palace-turret; not seeing those sons of Mākandika there, she went to the eastern grove and conducted a search and investigation everywhere on all sides. Not finding any news or trace of those sons of Mākandika anywhere, she likewise searched the northern and western groves. Failing to see them, she employed her clairvoyance (*avadhi-jñāna*) and saw those sons of Mākandika crossing through the very middle of the Salt Ocean with Śailaka. Seeing this, she became enraged, took up her sword and shield, and leaped into the air seven or eight *vyāmās* high. Flying up with that most exalted divine speed, she went to where the sons of Mākandika were and spoke thus:

"Ha! O Māgandiyaputra, you who desire what should not be desired, do you not know that you are passing through the very middle of the salt ocean together with the yakṣa Śailaka? Even though this is so, if you heed me, then you shall have life; but if you do not heed me, then I shall strike you with this [club] dark-blue like an elephant's tusk... Then those sons of Māgandiya, having heard and understood this matter from the presence of the deity of the Jewel Island, remained fearless, untroubled, undistressed, unperturbed, and unagitated. They did not respect, acknowledge, or heed the words of the deity of the Jewel Island. Without respecting, acknowledging, or heeding them, they continued to pass through the very middle of the salt ocean together with the yakṣa Śailaka.

When that goddess of the Jewel Island was unable to move, entice, disturb, or change the minds of those two sons of Mākandika through many contrary provocations and obstacles, she then began to employ sweet, amorous, and piteous enticements, saying: "O dear sons of Mākandika! If you had laughed, played, dallied, sported, wandered about, and enjoyed yourselves with me, then why, disregarding all of that, have you abandoned me and crossed the middle of the salt ocean with Śailaka? Then that goddess of the Jewel Island perceived Jinarakṣita’s mind through her clairvoyance (avadhi-jñāna), and having perceived it, she spoke thus: "I have always been undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, disagreeable, and repulsive to Jinapālita, and Jinapālita has always been undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, disagreeable, and repulsive to me. Yet I have always been desired, lovely, dear, pleasant, and agreeable to Jinarakṣita, and Jinarakṣita has always been desired, lovely, dear, pleasant, and agreeable to me. If Jinapālita does not take heed of me as I weep, wail, grieve, lament, and cry out, why then, O Jinarakṣita, do you also not take heed of me as I weep, wail, grieve, lament, and cry out?"

The deity of that island of supreme jewels, having perceived through her clairvoyance (avadhi-jñāna) that both sons of Māgandika were intent on killing Jinapālita, [acted] out of malice, gracefully scattering divine powder of various kinds mixed with fragrant dust. // Nāyā.
126 // Dōsakaliyā salaliyaṃ nāṇāviha-cuṇṇavāsa-mīsa divvaṃ।

Releasing a rain of fragrant flowers that satisfy the senses and the mind, she, filled with agitation, spoke these words while filling the quarters and intermediate directions with the sound of ornaments—various jewels, gold, gems, bells, tinkling anklets, bracelets, and girdles. (Nāyā. 127–128)
O Hala, Vasula, Gola, Nātha, Daitya-priya, Rāmaṇa!
O beloved, master, merciless one, and relentless one!
O you who have cast me out, you who are ungrateful, of loose character, shameless, and harsh;
O pitiless Jinarakṣita, you are the protector of my heart!
Indeed, it is not right for you [to abandon] me, all alone, helpless, and without kinsmen.
"O you who have performed service at my feet!
O mine of virtues! Deprived of you, I am not capable of living even for a moment. [Nāyā.
130] "But as for this [ocean], filled with many fish, crocodiles, and various predators..."
In the midst of the ocean, which is always agitated.
"I carry myself before you; come, turn back!
If you are angry, forgive me for this one transgression. [Nāyā.
131] "Your face is as beautiful as the stainless orb of the moon, free from clouds."
Her eyes resemble the mass of petals of fresh autumnal lotuses, white water-lilies, and blue lotuses.
"O Lord, my faith has come to drink in your face;
therefore, look upon me while I behold your lotus-like countenance.
Thus [she spoke] again and again with words that were affectionate, straightforward, sweet, and piteous.
Speaking such words, that wicked woman of sinful heart followed after him along the path. // Nāyā.133 //

Then that Jinarakṣita, his mind wavering, with his passion redoubled by that sound of ornaments which was pleasant to the ear and charming to the heart, and by those affectionate, straightforward, and sweet words, began to look back repeatedly and longingly toward the path. He did so while recollecting the splendor of the divine goddess of Ratnadvīpa’s beautiful breasts, hips, face, hands, feet, eyes, loveliness, beauty, and youth; her impetuous embraces; her playful gestures, amorous dalliances, smiles, side-long glances, sighs, languid movements, graceful stances, gait, endearments, and coquettish ways; and while his intellect was deluded by passion, he was helpless and subject to the power of karma.

Then, knowing that Jinarakṣita was filled with compassion, his mind agitated by the snare of death, and watching him [fall] in that very manner, the Yakṣa Śailaka slowly raised him up from his own back, his desire having been fulfilled. Then that goddess Ratnadvīpadevatā, pitiless and full of malice, seeing the compassionate Jinarakṣita falling from the back of Śailaka while crying out, "O slave, you are dead! seized him before he had reached the waters of the ocean. While he was screaming, she lifted him up into the sky; and as he was descending, she caught him with a sharp-edged discus and cut him into pieces with a supreme sword that was like a blue lotus, an ox-horn, a cluster of *gulikā* fruits, or an *ayasī* flower in color. Having cut him to pieces, she took the limbs of that one whose life-blood was still fresh—along with his blood—and offered them as a sacrifice in the four directions, her hands joined in reverence and her heart exultant.

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic! if a mendicant or a female mendicant, having gone forth in the presence of our teachers and preceptors, should again desire, long for, yearn for, and crave human sensual pleasures, then in this very life he becomes an object of contempt for many male ascetics, many female ascetics, many laymen, and many laywomen; and he shall wander again and again through the wilderness of *saṃsāra*, just like that Jinarakṣita, who looked back while crawling on his belly, whereas one who does not look back goes unhindered.
Therefore, one should become free from expectations regarding the essence of the teaching. (Nāyā.
136) Those who look back with longing for sensual pleasures fall into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra;
those who are free from expectations regarding pleasures cross over the wilderness of saṃsāra. (Nāyā. 137)

Then that goddess of the Jewel Island approached Jinapālita; with many favorable and unfavorable, harsh and gentle, seductive and piteous provocations, when she was unable to move him, disturb him, or change his mind, then—exhausted, weary, utterly spent, and despondent—she returned to the very same direction from which she had appeared.

Then that yakṣa Śailaka, together with Jinapālita, crossed through the very middle of the salt ocean; having crossed it, he went to where the city of Campā was, and upon arriving, he set Jinapālita down from his back in the eastern park of the city of Campā. Having set him down, he spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods, there you see the city of Campā. Having said this, he asked Jinapālita [for directions] and then departed in the same direction from which he had appeared.

Then that Jinapālita entered the city of Campā; having entered it, he went to his own house where his mother and father were, and upon arriving, while weeping and even lamenting, he reported the circumstances concerning Jinarakṣita. Then Jinapālita’s parents, together with their circle of friends, kinsmen, and attendants, weeping [and lamenting], performed many worldly funeral rites; having performed them, in time they became free from grief.

Then, on another occasion, while Jinapālita was seated upon his excellent throne, his parents spoke to him thus: "How was it, my son, that Jinarakṣita passed away? Thereupon, Jinapālita related to his parents exactly as it had happened—without error or doubt—the crossing of the salt ocean; the being overwhelmed by the Kālikā wind; the shipwreck of the vessel; the finding of the plank; the arrival at the Jewel Island; the seizing of the deity of the Jewel Island; the enjoyment of wealth and power; the exhortation of the deity of the Jewel Island; the sight of the man impaled on a stake; the climbing onto the Seleyaka Yakṣa; the assault by the deity of the Jewel Island; the rescue of Jinarakṣita; the crossing back across the salt ocean; the arrival at Campā; and the taking leave of the Seleyaka Yakṣa.

Then that Jinapāli became free from sorrow and, enjoying extensive sensual pleasures, lived his life. At that time, at that very moment, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra arrived. Having heard the Dharma, Jinapāli went forth as a monk; he became a master of the eleven *aṅgas*, practiced a month-long ritual of self-purification (*saṃlehaṇā*), and was reborn in the Saudharma Kalpa with a lifespan of two *sāgaropamas*. He will attain perfection in Mahāvideha. "In this very way, O venerable ascetic! one who no longer dwells upon human sensual pleasures shall transcend [the cycle of birth], just like that Jinapāli."
Thus indeed, Jambū! This is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, regarding the ninth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo; so I say.

"If, O Venerable Sir, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, regarding the ninth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo, then what, O Venerable Sir, is the meaning of the tenth?"

"Thus indeed, Jambū! At that time, at that moment, the Lord arrived in the city of Rājagṛha. Goyama spoke thus: 'Bhante, how do living beings increase or decrease? 'Goyama! It is just as, for example, the first-day moon of the dark fortnight, compared to the full-moon day, is deficient in color, deficient in gentleness, deficient in smoothness, deficient in brilliance; likewise deficient in radiance, splendor, shadow, light, glow, and hue; and deficient in its orb. And immediately following that, the second-day moon, compared to the first-day moon, is even more deficient in color, and so on, up to being even more deficient in its orb. And immediately following that, the third-day moon, compared to the second-day moon, is even more deficient in color, and so on, up to being even more deficient in its orb. And immediately following that, the fourth-day moon, compared to the third-day moon, is even more deficient in color, and so on, up to its orb. In this manner, by this sequence, as it continues to diminish and diminish until the new-moon day, compared to the fourteenth-day moon, it is lost in color, and so on, up to being lost in its orb.'"

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic! if a monk or a nun, having gone forth among us, is deficient in forbearance, and likewise in resolution, restraint, uprightness, gentleness, lightness, truthfulness, austerity, contentment, and possessionlessness; and if they are deficient in the practice of celibacy, and subsequently even more deficient in forbearance, and so on, up to being even more deficient in the practice of celibacy—then indeed, by this process of gradual decline and further decline, they are destroyed in forbearance, and so on, up to being destroyed in the practice of celibacy. It is just as, for example, the moon of the first day of the bright fortnight, compared to the moon of the new moon day, is superior in color, and so on, up to being superior in its orb; and the second-day moon, compared to the first-day moon, is even more superior in color, and so on, up to being even more superior in its orb.

In this very manner, indeed, as it increases step by step—just as the full moon, compared to the fourteenth-day moon, becomes complete in its color and so on, up to being complete in its orb—even so, O venerable ascetic, when one has gone forth, they increase further and further in forbearance and so on, up to the practice of celibacy; immediately thereafter, they increase even more in forbearance and so on, up to the practice of celibacy. In this way, indeed, increasing step by step, up to being complete in the practice of celibacy—it is thus that living beings increase or decrease.
Thus indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning of the tenth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahā as it was proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra; so I say.

"If this, O Venerable One, is the meaning of the tenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo* as taught by the Śramaṇa [Mahāvīra], then what is the meaning of the eleventh? "Thus it was, Jambū! At that time, at that moment, in the city of Rājagṛha, Gautama spoke thus: 'How, O Venerable One, do living beings become either fulfillers (*ārāhaka*) or transgressors (*virāhaka*)? 'Gautama! It is just as if, on a certain seashore, there were trees called *dāvaddava*, described as black [in color] up to being dense with foliage; they were leafy, flowering, fruit-bearing, green and shimmering, standing there exceedingly beautiful with their splendor. When the island-born winds—blowing from the front, blowing from behind, gentle winds, or great winds—blow, then many *dāvaddava* trees remain leafy up to [as before]; however, some *dāvaddava* trees remain withered, decayed, with their pale leaves and fruits fallen off, looking like dry trees, fading away, fading away. In exactly the same way, O venerable ascetic! If a monk or a nun of ours, having gone forth, while enduring, bearing, and patiently accepting [the hardships] of many monks, many nuns, many laymen, and many laywomen, does not properly endure, bear, or patiently accept [the provocations] of many heretics and many householders—this person, O venerable ascetic, is declared by me to be a partial transgressor (*deśavirāhaka*).'"

"O venerable ascetic! When the maritime winds—blowing from the east, from the west, gentle or violent—begin to blow, then many *dāvaddava* trees, being old and withered, remain withering away more and more; yet some *dāvaddava* trees, possessing leaves and flowers, remain looking beautiful. In the same way, O venerable ascetic! That monk or nun who, having gone forth, properly endures much from many followers of other sects and many householders, but does not properly endure much from many monks, many nuns, many laymen (*śrāvaka*), and many laywomen (*śrāvikā*), this person, O venerable ascetic, is declared by me to be a partial transgressor (*deśārādhaka*). When neither the island-born nor the maritime winds—blowing from the east, from the west, gentle or violent—blow, then all *dāvaddava* trees are old and withered. In the same way, O venerable ascetic! [That person] who, having gone forth, does not properly endure much from many monks, many nuns, many laymen, many laywomen, many followers of other sects, and many householders—this person, O venerable ascetic, is declared by me to be a total transgressor (*sarvavirādhaka*). When both the island-born and the maritime winds—blowing from the east, from the west, and so on—blow, then all *dāvaddava* trees possess leaves and flowers and remain [in full bloom]. In the same way, O venerable ascetic! That monk or nun who, having gone forth, properly endures much from many monks... [and] many followers of other sects and many householders—this person, O venerable ascetic, is declared by me to be a total fulfiller (*sarvārādhaka*). Thus indeed, Gautama, living beings become either fulfillers or transgressors."
Thus indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning of the eleventh [chapter] as proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra; so I say.

"If, venerable sir, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for the eleventh chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, then what, venerable sir, is the meaning declared for the twelfth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*? "Thus it was, Jambū: at that time, in that period, there was a city named Campā; [there was] the Punnabhadda shrine; King Jiyasattu; Queen Dhāriṇī; Prince Adīṇasattu, who was the crown prince; and the minister Subuddhi, who was in charge of the administration of the kingdom and a lay follower of the ascetics (*śramaṇopāsaka*). Outside that city of Campā, to the northeast, there was a certain cremation ground (*parihōdaē*), soaked with fat, marrow, blood, flesh, and layers of pus, strewn with corpses, unpleasant in color and even in touch. It was like, for example, a snake's carcass or a cow's carcass—up to: a corpse that is putrid, decomposed, infested with worms, and foul-smelling; swarming with webs of worms, full of filth, disgusting, and repulsive to look upon. Could it be of such a nature? No, that is not possible; it is declared to be even more undesirable and so on, up to its smell."

Then, on another occasion, King Jiyasattu—having bathed, performed his ritual offerings, and having adorned his body with many costly ornaments—together with numerous lords, ministers, and leaders down to the caravan chiefs, was seated upon an excellent comfortable throne in the dining pavilion at the time of the meal, partaking of abundant solid food and drink. When he had finished eating and drinking, and had become purified after that vast amount of solid food, drink, chewables, and delicacies, he was filled with wonder and spoke thus to those many lords, ministers, and caravan chiefs: "O dear ones, oh! This delicious solid food is endowed with pleasing color, and so forth, even to being endowed with pleasing texture; it is gratifying, delightful, nourishing, invigorating, exhilarating, intoxicating, thrilling, and a source of joy for all the limbs of the body."

Then those many lords, down to the caravan leaders and so forth, spoke thus to Jiyasattu: "It is even as you say, Lord! Indeed, this pleasant food—eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted—is endowed with color and is delightful to the palate."

Then King Jiyasattu said this to the minister Subuddhi: "O Subuddhi! This food is pleasant... [and so on] ...up to delightful. But Subuddhi did not acknowledge this matter of King Jiyasattu's; he remained silent. Then King Jiyasattu said this to Subuddhi a second and a third time: "O Subuddhi! This food is pleasant... [and so on] ...up to delightful."

When the minister Subuddhi had been addressed thus a second and a third time by King Jiyasattu, he spoke to King Jiyasattu as follows: “Indeed, my lord, we have no astonishment regarding this pleasant food, drink, chew, and taste. For it is thus, my lord: even particles (*poggala*) with pleasant sounds transform into unpleasant sounds; even particles with unpleasant sounds transform into pleasant sounds. Even particles with beautiful forms transform into ugly forms; even particles with ugly forms transform into beautiful forms. Even particles with pleasant fragrances transform into unpleasant fragrances; even particles with unpleasant fragrances transform into pleasant fragrances. Even particles with excellent tastes transform into bad tastes; even particles with bad tastes transform into excellent tastes. Even particles with pleasant touches transform into unpleasant touches; even particles with unpleasant touches transform into pleasant touches. Furthermore, my lord, particles are declared to be transformed through both application (*paoga*) and natural spontaneity (*vīsasā*).”
Then King Jiyasattu, while Subuddhi the minister was thus explaining, speaking, making it known, and demonstrating this matter, did not accept it, did not acknowledge it, and remained silent.

Then, on another occasion, King Jiyasattu—having bathed, mounted upon the neck of a horse, and accompanied by a great retinue of soldiers and a procession of cavalry—was passing by not far from that embankment.

Then King Jiyasattu, being overwhelmed by the foul odor of that ditch-water, covered his nose with his upper garment; having done so, he withdrew to one side and spoke thus to the many lords, down to the caravan leaders: "O beloved of the gods! This ditch-water is unpleasant in color, unpleasant in odor, unpleasant in taste, and unpleasant in touch; it is, for example, like a heap of dead snakes—or even more loathsome than that. Then those many lords, down to the caravan leaders, spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! This ditch-water is indeed unpleasant in color, unpleasant in odor, unpleasant in taste, and unpleasant in touch; it is, for example, like a heap of dead snakes—or even more loathsome than that."

Then King Jiyasattu said this to the minister Subuddhi: "O Subuddhi! This corpse is unpleasant in its color and so forth—just like, for example, a dead snake, or even more loathsome than that. Then the minister Subuddhi, [having heard this], remained silent and did not acknowledge it. Then King Jiyasattu said this to the minister Subuddhi a second and a third time: "O, it is exactly as you say!"

When the minister Subuddhi had been addressed thus a second and a third time by King Jiyasattu, he replied: "Indeed, my lord, we have no astonishment regarding this matter of the water in the moat. For it is thus, my lord: even particles (*poggala*) that possess pleasant sounds transform into unpleasant sounds; and so on, up to: 'my lord, particles are indeed described as transformed through application and natural spontaneity. Then King Jiyasattu said to Subuddhi: 'Do not, O beloved of the gods, persist in misleading and confusing yourself, others, and both together with many false assertions and dogmatic attachments to falsehood.'"

Then, this kind of internal reflection, thought, aspiration, and mental resolve arose in Subuddhi: "Alas! King Jiyasattu does not perceive those things that are real, true, factual, as they are, and proclaimed by the Jina. Therefore, it is indeed better for me to bring this matter to his attention so that King Jiyasattu may understand those things that are real, true, factual, as they are, and proclaimed by the Jina."

Reflecting thus, he had new jars and pots brought by his own men from the marketplace. Having taken them, at the time of twilight when few people were about and others had already gone home or were returning, he went to the salt-pond. Having arrived, he had the pond water drawn out; having had it drawn out, he had it strained through new cloth-filters; having had it strained, he had it poured into new jars; having had it poured in, he had rock-salt added; having had the salt added, he had them marked and sealed; having had them marked and sealed, he had them left to sit for seven nights. After seven nights, he again had it strained through new cloth-filters; having had it strained, he had it poured into new jars; having had it poured in, he had rock-salt added; having had the salt added, he had them marked and sealed; having had them marked and sealed, he had them left to sit for another seven nights. A third time, he had it poured into new jars and so on, until he had them left to sit.

Thus, indeed, by this method—alternately causing them to drink, alternately causing them to eat, and alternately causing them to dwell—he caused them to live for seven times seven years. Then, as that seventh year was coming to an end, a water-jewel (*udakarayaṇa*) arose in that Pharihoda lake; it was clear, pure, noble, thin, and possessed a color like that of crystal, endowed with fragrance, endowed with taste, and endowed with touch. It was delightful to the palate and so forth, up to being a source of gratification for all the senses and the body.

Then Subuddhi went to where that water-jewel was; having approached, he took it in his palms. Having taken that water-jewel—which was endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, endowed with taste, and endowed with touch; which was delicious and gratifying to all the senses and the body—he, joyful and delighted, prepared it by mixing it with many substances suitable for preparing water. Having prepared it, he summoned King Jiyasattu’s water-bearer and spoke to him thus: "O noble sir, take this water-jewel; having taken it, present it to King Jiyasattu at the time of his meal."

Then that water-bearer assented to this matter of Subuddhi’s; having assented, he took that water-jewel and, at the time of King Jiyasattu’s meal, presented it to him. Then King Jiyasattu, while tasting that exquisite food—drink, chewables, and delicacies—remained there enjoying himself. And when he had finished eating and was fully satisfied, having become supremely pure, he felt wonder regarding that water-jewel and spoke thus to those many lords of kings, down to the caravan leaders and others: “O beloved of the gods, how wonderful is this water-jewel! It is clear... [and so on]... refreshing to all the senses and the body. Then those many lords of kings, down to the caravan leaders and others, replied: “It is exactly as you say, Lord! It is indeed refreshing in that very way.”

Then King Jiyasattu summoned the water-vendor and, having summoned him, spoke thus: "My dear sir, from where did you obtain this water-jewel? Then that water-vendor spoke thus to Jiyasattu: "Sire, I obtained this water-jewel from Subuddhi."

Then Jiyasattu summoned the minister Subuddhi and spoke to him thus: "O Subuddhi! For what reason have I become so undesirable, unpleasant, unloved, disagreeable, and displeasing to you, that you do not set forth this water-jewel for me every day at the time of my meal? My dear sir, from where did you obtain this water-jewel? Then Subuddhi spoke thus to Jiyasattu: "My lord, it is from that moat-water. Then Jiyasattu spoke thus to Subuddhi: "For what reason, Subuddhi, is this moat-water [so excellent]?"

Then Subuddhi spoke thus to Jiyasattu: "Indeed, Lord, when you were previously being told, spoken to, instructed, and explained this matter by me, you did not believe it. Then, O Lord, there arose within me this internal reflection, thought, aspiration, and mental resolve: 'Alas! King Jiyasattu does not believe, does not trust, and does not find pleasure in these things that are true, as they have been proclaimed by the Jinas. Therefore, it is well for me to cause King Jiyasattu to understand this matter so that he may comprehend these things that are true and as they have been proclaimed by the Jinas. Having reflected thus, I [did] exactly as before... until I summoned the water-bearer and said: 'O beloved of the gods, bring the water-jewel to King Jiyasattu at the time of his meal. For this reason, O Lord, this is the pond-water."

While Subuddhi the minister was thus explaining, speaking, making known, and defining this matter, King Jiyasattu did not believe it, did not trust it, and did not accept it. Not believing, not trusting, and not accepting it, he summoned his inner-circle attendants and said to them: "Go, dear sirs, from the market and fetch new jars and pots; then prepare them with the materials required for filling with water. They likewise prepared them and brought them back to Jiyasattu.

Then King Jiyasattu took that water-jewel in his hand and tasted it; having tasted it, and knowing it to be worthy of being tasted—up to the point of being a delight to all his senses and limbs—he summoned the minister Subuddhi and spoke thus: "Subuddhi! From where did you obtain these true, real, and factual things? Then Subuddhi said this to Jiyasattu: "Sire, these true and factual things were obtained by me from the words of the Jina."

Then Subuddhi spoke thus to Jiyasattu: "O beloved of the gods! I desire to hear the words of the Jina from you. Then Subuddhi fully explained the manifold Dharma of the fourfold vows as proclaimed by the Kevalins to Jiyasattu; he expounded it, [describing] how living beings are bound, up to the five minor vows (*pañca-aṇuvvayāṇi*). Then Jiyasattu, having heard and understood the Dharma from Subuddhi, was joyful and delighted, and spoke thus to the minister Subuddhi: "I have faith, O beloved of the gods, in the Nirgrantha doctrine, even unto what you say. I desire to adopt and abide by the five minor vows and the seven disciplinary vows under you. [Subuddhi replied: "As is agreeable to you, O beloved of the gods! Do not hesitate."

Then Jiyasattu, in the presence of Subuddhi, accepted the five minor vows and the twelvefold duty of a lay follower (*śrāvaka-dharma*). Thereupon, Jiyasattu became a lay disciple (*śramaṇopāsaka*), one who had understood the nature of living beings and non-living beings, and he lived while providing for the needs [of the monks]. At that time, at that moment, the arrival of the Elders occurred; King Jiyasattu and Subuddhi went out [to meet them]. Having heard the Dharma, Subuddhi spoke thus: "Only this remains: I shall take leave of Jiyasattu and then go forth [into the religious life]. [Jiyasattu replied: "As it pleases you, dear sir."

Then Subuddhi went to where Jiyasattu was and, having approached him, spoke thus: "Truly, Lord, I have heard the Dharma in the presence of the Elders; that Dharma has been desired, accepted, and approved by me. Therefore, Lord, being terrified and agitated by the fear of *saṃsāra*, I desire, with your permission, to go forth as a monk."

Then King Jiyasattu said this to Subuddhi: "Dear friend, stay for a few years while enjoying these magnificent pleasures; after that, we shall together go before the elders, shave our heads, and go forth as ascetics. Then Subuddhi consented to this proposal of King Jiyasattu. Thereafter, twelve years passed while King Jiyasattu, together with Subuddhi, experienced extensive human sensual pleasures.

At that time, on that occasion, the Elders arrived. King Jiyasattu, having heard the Dharma, spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! Only this much remains: I shall summon my minister Subuddhi, install my eldest son in the kingdom, and then go forth into the religious life in your presence. "It is as you wish, O beloved of the gods! Then King Jiyasattu went to his own palace; having arrived, he summoned Subuddhi and spoke thus: "Indeed, I have listened to the Dharma in the presence of the Elders... [and] I shall go forth into the religious life. What will you do? Then Subuddhi spoke thus to King Jiyasattu: "If you, O beloved of the gods, being terrified by the fear of *saṃsāra*... go forth into the religious life, what other support would we have? I too shall go forth. "If it be so, O beloved of the gods, that you go forth, then go, O beloved of the gods! Install your eldest son in the household, and having installed him, mount a palanquin carried by a thousand men and appear before me in the palanquin. Then Subuddhi had the palanquin prepared, and it appeared.

Then King Jiyasattu summoned his household officials and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Go, dear sirs, and prepare the royal consecration for Prince Adīnasattu; [having done so,] he was consecrated until he eventually went forth as a mendicant."

Then King Jiyasattu, having studied the eleven Angas, and having observed the state of a śramaṇa for many years, attained perfection through a month-long ritual of self-mortification (*saṃlehaṇā*). Then Subuddhi, having studied the eleven Angas and observed the state of a śramaṇa for many years, likewise attained perfection.
Thus, indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning of the twelfth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahā as it was taught by the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra; so I say.

“If, O Venerable One, this is the meaning taught by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for the twelfth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, then what, O Venerable One, is the meaning taught for the thirteenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*? “Thus it was, Jambū: at that time, in that period, in the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇasīla shrine, there was a gathering; the assembly went out.”

At that time, in that period, in the Sōhamma kalpa, in the Daddura-vaḍiṁsaga vimāna, in the Sudhammā assembly hall, upon the Daddura lion-throne, the god Daddura dwelt, surrounded by four thousand *sāmānika* gods and four chief queens with their retinues. Just as described for Sūriyābha, he moved about enjoying divine pleasures and delights. And with his vast *avadhi*-knowledge, he surveyed this entire Jambudvīpa continent; [he performed the dance] up until he displayed the dance-ritual, and then departed just as Sūriyābha had done.

"Venerable Sir," the Blessed Gautama paid homage and reverence to the ascetic, the Blessed Mahāvīra; having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: "O Venerable Sir! The god Dardura was of great power, great splendor, great strength, great fame, great happiness, and great majesty. O Venerable Sir, where has that divine celestial power, that divine celestial glory, and that divine celestial majesty of the god Dardura gone? Where has it entered? "Gautama, it has entered the body; it has entered the body. It is like the analogy of the peaked-roofed house."

“Venerable sir, by what means was that divine celestial power, that divine celestial splendor, and that divine celestial majesty obtained by the god Daddura, up to [the point of] being fully attained? ‘Indeed, Gautama, in this very Jambudvīpa continent, in the region of Bhārata, in the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇasilaka shrine, there was King Śreṇika. There, in that city of Rājagṛha, there was a jewel-merchant guild-leader named Nanda, who was wealthy and prosperous.’”

At that time, O Gautama, on that occasion, I arrived [at Rājagṛha]. The assembly went out; Sreṇika also went out. Then Nanda, the merchant-prince of jewelers, having learned of this news, approached on foot to pay his respects. Having heard the Dharma, Nanda became a lay disciple (*śrāvakopāsaka*). Then I departed from Rājagṛha and wandered through the countryside for my travels.

Then, on a certain occasion, because of his failure to see holy men, his failure to attend upon them, his failure to receive instruction, and his failure to show respect, Nanda the chief jeweler’s son—while the states of right belief were steadily declining and the states of false belief were steadily increasing—became one who had fallen into false belief. Then, on another occasion during the summer season, in the month of Jyeṣṭha-Mūla, Nanda the chief jeweler’s son undertook the eighth meal-fast (a fast of two days) and, having undertaken it, remained in the *poṣadha* hall.

Then, as Nanda’s eighth meal was being digested, while he was overcome by thirst and hunger, there arose within him this kind of internal reflection, thought, aspiration, and mental resolve: "Blessed indeed are those lords and others; fulfilled indeed are those lords and others; successful indeed are those lords and others; possessed of merit indeed are those lords and others; endowed with good fortune indeed are those lords and others—for outside Rājagṛha, they have many ponds, lotus-pools, and even rows of lakes where many people bathe, drink, and transport water. Therefore, it would be well for me, tomorrow at dawn, having obtained permission from King Śreṇika, to cause a pond named 'Nanda' to be dug in a suitable location on a piece of ground near the Vebhāra mountain in the north-eastern direction outside Rājagṛha. Having thus reflected, he waited for the dawn. When the dawn had broken, he broke his fast, bathed, performed his religious duties, and, surrounded by friends, kinsmen, and others, took a great gift-offering. He went to King Śreṇika, presented the gift, and spoke as follows:

"I desire, Lord, that being permitted by you, I may have [the ground] dug outside Rājagṛha... 'As it pleases you, dear sir! Then Nanda, being permitted by King Śreṇika, was joyful and delighted; he went out through the very center of Rājagṛha and, at a site marked out by augurs and diviners, set about having the Nanda lotus-pond dug."

As that lotus pond, Nandā, was being gradually filled in, it became a pond with four corners and level banks; its water was gradually well-formed, clear, and cool; it was covered with leaves, lotus stalks, and roots; it was endowed with many blooming blue, red, white, and pink lotuses, as well as fragrant, sweet-smelling, and white lotuses—some with a hundred petals, some with a thousand petals, and others with filaments; it was filled with fish and turtles swimming about at will; it resounded with the sweet songs of many pairs of birds wandering there; it was delightful, beautiful to behold, lovely, and perfect in form.

Then that merchant-prince Nanda had four groves planted on the four sides of the Nandā lotus-pool. As those groves were gradually protected, guarded, and nurtured, they grew until they became dark like a mass of great clouds; covered with leaves and flowers, they remained there, looking exceedingly beautiful.

Then Nanda had a great picture-gallery (*cittasabhā*) constructed in the eastern grove, supported by many hundreds of pillars, beautiful to behold, and so forth. Therein, many black and even white wooden carvings (*kaṭṭhakamma*), woven works (*pōtthakamma*), and paintings—whether painted, modeled, embroidered, woven, stuffed, or composite—stood displayed, being repeatedly exhibited. Therein, many seats and couches were arranged in rows, one behind the other. There, many actors, dancers, and so forth, having been provided with gifts of food and wages, remained performing their work as musicians. People from Rājagṛha, having come out there, sat down together upon those aforementioned seats and couches; they stayed in great comfort, relaxing, sleeping, watching, conversing, and enjoying themselves.

Then Nanda, the merchant-prince of Maniyāra, had a great kitchen hall constructed in the southern grove—one provided with many pillars and so forth, up to being perfectly beautiful. There, many men, having been given wages for their labor, prepared abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies, and they remained distributing them repeatedly to many ascetics, brahmins, guests, the poor, and beggars.

Then Nanda, the chief merchant of jewelers, had a great *tigicchaya-śālā* (medical hall) constructed in the western grove—one provided with many hundreds of pillars, and so forth, up to "exquisite. There, many physicians and sons of physicians, leeches and sons of leeches, surgeons and sons of surgeons—having been granted fees, food, and wages—resided performing medical treatments for many who were afflicted, sick, diseased, and weak. Furthermore, many other men there, having been granted fees, food, and wages, resided performing the work of nursing those many who were afflicted, sick, diseased, and weak, by providing them with medicines, remedies, food, and drink.

Then Nanda, the chief jeweler, had a great hall for ornaments built in the northern grove, provided with many hundreds of pillars and so forth, up to being perfectly beautiful. There, many men employed as decorators, having been given abundant food, drink, and wages, lived while performing the work of decorating for many ascetics, the destitute, the sick, the diseased, and the weak.

In that Nanda lotus pond, many people—both those with protectors and those without, travelers and wayfarers, beggars, grass-gatherers, leaf-gatherers, and wood-gatherers—some bathe, some drink water, some wash their clothes, and some, having dispelled sweat, grime, fatigue, drowsiness, hunger, and thirst, dwell in great comfort. Even those who have departed from Rājagṛha go there; what more need be said? There, amidst various water sports, bathing, and pastimes, and amidst beds of kadalī leaves, lotuses, and flowers crowded with the warbling of flocks of diverse birds, the multitude dwells, taking their pleasure again and again in great comfort.

Now, while many people were bathing, drinking, and carrying away water in that Nandā pond, they spoke thus to one another: "Blessed indeed, O beloved of the gods, is Nanda, the chief jeweler! He has achieved his purpose; his birth and life have borne fruit, for he possesses such a Nandā pond—quadrangular and so forth, beautiful to behold. And regarding its eastern side [and likewise all four groves], everything is as described before, up until: where the people coming out from Rājagṛha, having sat down on seats and couches, resting, reclining, looking on, and conversing, dwell in great happiness. Therefore, blessed, successful, fortunate, meritorious, and truly lucky are the people of this world! Well-gained is the fruit of human birth and life for Nanda the jeweler. Then, in the crossroads, squares, and thoroughfares of Rājagṛha, many people spoke thus to one another, declared thus, explained thus, and defined thus: "Blessed, O beloved of the gods, is Nanda, the chief jeweler! The same account follows, up until: "...dwell in great happiness."

Then, having heard this matter from the mouths of many people and having reflected upon it, Nanda, the chief of jewel-merchants, became joyful and delighted; with the hair on his body standing on end like a *kalamba* flower struck by rain, he dwelt experiencing supreme pleasure and bliss.
Then, at another time, sixteen ailments appeared in the body of that Nanda, the chief of jewel-merchants, as follows:
asthma, cough, fever, burning sensation, abdominal pain, and fistula.
In indigestion, in eye diseases, in headaches,
in throat ailments, in pain of the eyes, in pain of the ears, in itching, in abdominal tumors, and in leprosy.

Then that merchant-prince Nanda, being afflicted by sixteen types of diseases, summoned his household servants and said to them: "Go, dear friends, through the triple-crossroads, squares, and thoroughfares of the city of Rājagṛha, and while making a great proclamation with a loud voice, say this: 'Indeed, dear friends, sixteen diseases have appeared upon the body of the merchant-prince Nanda, namely—from asthma up to leprosy. Therefore, dear friends, whatever physician, son of a physician, surgeon, son of a surgeon, or skilled practitioner, son of a skilled practitioner, desires to alleviate even a single one of those sixteen diseases from the merchant-prince Nanda, the merchant-prince Nanda shall grant him a generous reward of wealth. Having said this, proclaim this announcement a second and a third time, and then report back this command. They likewise reported back accordingly.
