Then, having heard and understood this proclamation in the city of Rājagṛha, many physicians, sons of physicians, and sons of craftsmen—some with surgical instruments in their hands, some with lancets in their hands, some with needles in their hands, some with pills in their hands, and some with medicinal herbs and remedies in their hands—departed from their respective homes. Having departed, they went through the middle of Rājagṛha to the house of the merchant Nanda the jeweler. Having arrived, they examined the body of Nanda and inquired about the cause of those sixteen ailments. With many applications of ointments, massages, oil treatments, emetics, purgatives, sedatives, cauterizations, baths, enemas, suppositories, bloodletting, scarifications, incisions, venesection, plasters, earth-remedies, bark, creepers, roots, tubers, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds, needles, pills, and medicinal herbs and remedies, they desired to alleviate even one of those sixteen ailments; yet they were not at all able to alleviate them.
Then, when those many physicians and sons of physicians were unable to alleviate even a single one of those sixteen types of ailments, they became weary and exhausted, and eventually departed.

Then Nanda, being overcome by those sixteen symptoms of disease, infatuated with, attached to, greedy for, and deeply immersed in the lotus pond Nandā—having his life-span bound to that animal existence and having his destiny fixed there—oppressed by distress and agony, at the time of death, passed away and was reborn as a frog in the womb of a female frog in the lotus pond Nandā.

When that frog, Nanda, had emerged from the womb, having cast off childhood, having attained maturity and reached youth, he lived enjoying himself in the Nandā lotus pond. Now, many people bathing, drinking, and washing their clothes in the Nandā lotus pond spoke thus, declared thus, explained thus, and defined thus to one another: "Blessed indeed, O beloved of the gods, is the jeweler Nanda, for whom there is this very Nandā lotus pond—quadrangular and so forth, up to 'exquisite'—and in whose eastern grove there is the Citra Hall with its many pillars, and likewise the four branches, up to 'the fruit of life itself. Then, having repeatedly heard and reflected upon this matter from the presence of those many people, this kind of internal thought, consideration, conviction, and mental resolve arose in that frog:

"Where indeed have I previously heard such a sound as this?"—having thought thus, through a wholesome transformation of thought, there arose in him the recollection of his former births; he correctly regained his memory of his previous life. Then, this kind of internal reflection, thought, aspiration, and mental resolve arose in that frog: "Truly, in this very city of Rājagṛha, I was a jeweler named Nanda, wealthy and prosperous. At that time, at that moment, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra arrived [in the city]."

Then, having received from the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, the five minor vows and the seven rules of training—up until their formal acceptance—at some other time, due to the sight of non-ascetics and so forth, I fell into wrong belief.

Then, on another occasion during the summer season, having undertaken the *poṣadha* vow, I lived [in that manner]. Just as before—[including] the reflection, the request for permission, the lotus pond, the grove, and the assembly hall—all that occurred until I was reborn as a frog in the Nandā pond. Then I thought: "Alas! I am unfortunate, meritless, and one who has not performed meritorious deeds; I have fallen away from, strayed from, and utterly lost the teaching of the Nirgranthas. Therefore, it is indeed better for me to personally undertake and live by the five minor vows (*pañcāṇuvrata*) which I previously accepted. Having reflected thus, he undertook the five minor vows he had previously accepted; having undertaken them, he took this kind of vow (*abhigraha*): "It is permissible for me to live for as long as life lasts, purifying myself through an unceasing ascetic practice of every sixth meal (*ṣaṣṭha-ṣaṣṭha*), and on the day of breaking the fast (*pāraṇaka*) of each sixth meal, it is permissible for me to sustain my life by means of pure bathing water and by rubbing and massaging along the banks of the Nandā pond. He took this kind of vow and lived for as long as life lasted, practicing every sixth meal.

At that time, Gautama, on that occasion, I had arrived at the Guṇasilaka shrine. The assembly had gone out. Then, at the Nandā lotus-pool, a great crowd of people—bathing, drinking, and carrying away water—was speaking thus to one another: "The ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, has arrived right here at the Guṇasilaka shrine. Therefore, dear ones, let us go and pay homage to the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, and attend upon him; this will be for my benefit in this life and the next, and will lead to my long-term welfare. Then, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the mouths of that great crowd of people, this kind of internal thought, consideration, desire, and mental resolve arose in that frog: "Truly, the ascetic [Mahāvīra] is there. I shall go and pay homage to the ascetic [Mahāvīra]. Having thus reflected, he slowly emerged from the Nandā lotus-pool, went toward the royal highway, and having approached it, traveling with that most excellent gait of a frog, he set out toward where I was.

And now King Śreṇika Bimbisāra, having bathed and performed his auspicious rites, adorned with all ornaments, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, with a parasol [bearing] a cluster of white lotuses and white chowries [waving], surrounded by a fourfold army consisting of horses, elephants, chariots, and foot soldiers, is coming quickly to pay homage at my feet.

Then, when that frog was stepped upon by the left foreleg of King Śreṇika’s horse, its internal organs were crushed. Thereupon, that frog—deprived of strength, power, heroism, and human effort, and thinking "I am no longer to be sustained"—stepped aside to one side. With palms joined together, he paid homage: "Homage to the Arhats, those who have attained the state named the destination of perfection (Siddhigati). "Homage to the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra, who desires to attain the state named the destination of perfection. "Previously, in the presence of the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra, I renounced gross violence toward living beings, up to gross possessiveness. Therefore, now too, in his very presence, I renounce all violence toward living beings, up to all possessiveness, for as long as life lasts. I renounce all food, drink, soft food, and solid food for as long as life lasts. And as for this body—which is desirable and pleasing—I renounce it even with my final breaths, saying: 'May [these things] not touch me. Having said this, that frog, at the time of death, passed away and was reborn in the Saudharma Kalpa, in the Daddura-vatinsa Vimāna, in the Assembly Hall of Rebirth, in the form of a Daddura god. Thus indeed, Gautama, did that frog obtain, attain, and fully realize that divine splendor of a god.

“Bhante, for how long a duration is the life-span of the god Daddura declared to be? Goyama, a life-span of four *palyopamas* is declared for him. That god Daddura will attain perfection (*sijjhihii*), awaken (*bujjhihii*), and so on, until he makes an end of suffering in the region of Mahāvideha. Thus indeed, Jambū, by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained liberation, this is the meaning declared in the thirteenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*. Thus I say.”

"If this, O Venerable One, is the meaning declared for the thirteenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahā*, what is the meaning declared for the fourteenth? "Thus it was, Jambū: at that time, in that period, there was a city named Teyalipura. In the Pamayavana garden lived King Kaṇagaraha. He had a queen named Paümāvaī. That King Kaṇagaraha had a minister named Tēyaliputta, who [exercised authority] through conciliation and force, and so forth, until he wandered about."

There, in the city of Tetalipura, there was a goldsmith’s son named Kalāda, who was wealthy and so forth, even unto being beyond reproach. His wife was named Bhaddā. That daughter of the goldsmith’s son Kalāda, the child of Bhaddā, was a girl named Pōṭṭilā, who was preeminent in beauty, youth, and loveliness, possessing an exceedingly excellent body.

Then, on another occasion, that maiden Pōṭṭilā—having bathed, adorned with all her ornaments, and surrounded by a circle of maidservants—was staying atop a magnificent palace on the roof-terrace, playing and amusing herself with a golden ball.

And while the minister Tēyaliputta was proceeding on his way, having bathed and mounted the neck of a state elephant in a great procession of troops, chariots, and cavalry, he passed not far from the house of Kalāya, the son of a jeweler. As he was passing by the vicinity of the jeweler’s son’s house, he saw the girl Pōṭṭilā playing with a golden ball on the upper terrace. Having seen her, he became captivated by the girl Pōṭṭilā’s beauty, youth, and charm, and he summoned his household officials and said this: "O beloved of the gods! Whose daughter is she, and what is her name? Then the household officials spoke thus to Tēyaliputta:

"Lord, this is Pōṭṭilā by name, the daughter of Kalāya the carpenter’s son and the granddaughter of Bhaddā; she is [endowed] with beauty and so forth, up to her physical form. Now, when Tēyaliputta had returned from the horse-racing grounds, he summoned his inner-circle attendants and spoke thus: 'Go, dear friends, and ask for Kalāya the carpenter’s daughter, the granddaughter of Bhaddā, Pōṭṭilā by name, as my wife. Then those inner-circle attendants, having been thus addressed by Tēyalin, were delighted and joyful; with palms joined [in reverence], saying 'So be it,' they went to the house of Kalāya the carpenter’s son."

Then that man, the son of a jeweler named Kalāya, saw him approaching; seeing him, he was delighted and joyful, rose from his seat, and went forward seven or eight paces. Having gone forward, he invited him to a seat, and once he was seated comfortably and at ease upon an excellent couch, he spoke thus: "May my lord deign to tell me: what is the purpose of your visit? Then those inner attendants said this to Kalāya, the son of the jeweler: "O dear sir, we wish to choose your daughter Pōṭṭilā, the granddaughter of Bhaddā, as a wife for Tēyaliputta. If you know it to be fitting, appropriate, praiseworthy, or a suitable match, O dear sir, let the maiden Pōṭṭilā be given to Tēyaliputta. Then say, dear sir: 'What dowry shall I provide?'"

Then Kalāya, the son of a jeweler, spoke thus to those inner officials: "O beloved of the gods, this very thing is my own profit, that Teyaliputta shows me such favor on account of my daughter. He then honored and respected those inner officials with abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies, as well as flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments; having honored and respected them, he dismissed them. Then those inner officials departed from the house of Kalāya, the son of a jeweler, and went to where the minister Teyaliputta was; having arrived, they reported this matter to the minister Teyaliputta.

Then, on another occasion, at an auspicious conjunction of lunar days, constellations, and moments, the goldsmith’s son Kalā took the maiden Pōṭṭilā—who had been bathed and adorned with all ornaments—mounted her upon a palanquin, and surrounded by friends, kinsmen, and others, he departed from his own house. With full magnificence, he proceeded through the middle of the city of Tēyalipura and arrived at the house of Tēyali. He gave the maiden Pōṭṭilā himself as a wife to Tēyaliputta. Then, seeing that the maiden Pōṭṭilā had been presented to him as a wife, Tēyaliputta was thrilled and delighted; he mounted a couch together with Pōṭṭilā. Having mounted it, he had himself bathed with white and blue jars, performed the fire-sacrifice, and took her hand in marriage. Then, having taken Pōṭṭilā as his wife, he dismissed her circle of friends, kinsmen, and attendants with abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies, as well as flowers, garments, and so forth. Thereafter, Tēyaliputta remained devoted and inseparable from his wife Pōṭṭilā, enjoying magnificent pleasures.

Then King Kaṇagaraha became infatuated with, obsessed by, greedy for, and deeply attached to his kingdom, realm, army, vehicles, treasury, storehouses, city, and harem. He caused every son born to him to be dismembered; he cut off the fingers of some, he cut off the thumbs of others, and likewise the toes and big toes. He slit open the nostrils and severed the limbs and members of their bodies. Then, on another occasion, during the time between the first and last watches of the night, this reflection, thought, desire, and intention arose within Queen Paumāvatī: "It is indeed true that King Kaṇagaraha, from his kingdom down to his sons, causes them to be dismembered, even severing their limbs and members. Therefore, if I give birth to a child, it would be better for me to dwell while secretly protecting and guarding that child from Kaṇagaraha. Having thus reflected, she summoned the minister Teyaliputta and spoke to him as follows:

"Truly, O beloved of the gods, King Kaṇagaraha rules the kingdom and so forth with great discernment. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, if I give birth to a son, you must, in secret and in due course, protect, guard, and bring him up for Kaṇagaraha."

"When that boy has outgrown childhood and reached youth, he shall become the recipient of alms for both you and me. Then the minister Teyaliputta accepted this proposal from Queen Paumāvatī and departed. Subsequently, Queen Paumāvatī and the minister’s wife Pōṭṭilā conceived at the same time and carried their pregnancies together. When nine months had fully elapsed, Queen Paumāvatī gave birth to a lovely and handsome son. On the very night that Queen Paumāvatī gave birth to her son, the minister’s wife Pōṭṭilā gave birth to a daughter who was afflicted by a physical deformity.

Then Queen Paumāvatī summoned her nurse and, having summoned her, spoke thus: "Go, my dear, and summon Teyaliputta in strict secrecy. Then the nurse, saying "So be it," assented; she departed through a side gate of the inner apartments, went to the house of Teyali where Teyaliputta was, and upon arriving, with palms joined [in reverence], spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods, Queen Paumāvatī summons you."

Then Teyaliputta, having heard this matter from his nurse, was delighted and joyful; together with the nurse, he departed from his own house and entered the inner apartments by a secret, unguarded passage. Having entered, he approached Queen Paumāvatī and, with palms joined [in reverence], spoke thus: "May my lords command what I must do! Then Queen Paumāvatī said to Teyaliputta: "King Kanakaratha has indeed passed away, and so on, until his son has vanished. And I, O my lord, have given birth to a boy. Therefore, my lord, take this boy; he shall be the vessel for the alms of both you and me. Having said this, she placed him in the hand of Teyaliputta.

Then Teyaliputta took the boy from the hands of Padmāvatī, covered him with his upper garment, and went out through a secret exit of the inner apartments. Having gone out, he went to his own house where his wife Pōṭṭilā was; having arrived, he spoke thus to Pōṭṭilā:

"Thus indeed, O beloved of the gods, King Kaṇagaraha has abdicated his kingdom and even his sons. This boy here is the son of Kaṇagaraha and the offspring of Paumāvatī. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, you must secretly protect, nurture, and bring this boy up in due course for King Kaṇagaraha. When this boy has reached the end of childhood, he shall become the support for you, me, and Paumāvatī. Having said this, he placed the boy at the side of Pōṭṭilā. Then, taking that girl who had met her death from the side of Pōṭṭilā, he wrapped her in his upper garment, entered through a side door of the inner apartments, approached Queen Paumāvatī, and placed her by the side of Queen Paumāvatī, and then departed.

Then the body-servants of Queen Padmāvatī, seeing that Queen Padmāvatī had given birth to a dead daughter, went to King Kanakaratha; having approached him, they joined their palms [in reverence] and spoke thus: "Truly, Lord, Queen Padmāvatī has given birth to a dead daughter. Then King Kanakaratha performed the funeral rites for that dead daughter and carried out many worldly funeral ceremonies; having done so, after some time, he became free from grief.

Then Teyaliputta summoned his household servants early in the morning and spoke to them thus: "Quickly perform the purification of the prison, and so forth, up to the establishment of the [royal] status. Since this son of ours was born during the reign of Kanakaraha, let this boy be named Kanagajjhaya. [This continued] until he became capable of enjoying pleasures.

Then, at another time, that Pōṭṭilā became undesirable, unloved, unpleasant, disagreeable, and offensive to Tēyaliputta. Tēyaliputta did not even wish to hear Pōṭṭilā’s name, let alone see her or enjoy her company. Then, at another time, during the period between the latter part of the night and the early part of the day, this kind of internal reflection, thought, aspiration, and mental resolve arose in Pōṭṭilā: "Formerly, I was indeed beloved, dear, pleasing, agreeable, and charming to Tēyali; now I have become undesirable [and so forth]. Tēyaliputta does not wish for my name, nor even for my enjoyment. Having said this, with her mind and resolve overwhelmed, she remained brooding.

Then Teyaliputta saw Pōṭṭilā with her mind and thoughts dejected, even to the point of brooding; having seen her, he spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods, do not remain with your mind and thoughts dejected, even to the point of brooding. You should have abundant food—edibles, drinks, chewables, and tastables—prepared in my great kitchen, and having had it prepared, you may dwell there giving and causing to be given to many ascetics, brahmins, and even to wandering mendicants. Then Pōṭṭilā, being thus addressed by the minister Teyaliputta, was delighted and consented to this matter of his. Having consented, she dwelt day after day in the great kitchen, having abundant food—edibles and so forth—prepared and causing it to be given.

At that time, in that period, there were certain nuns named Suvratā who were restrained in their conduct (*iryā-samitā*), and so forth, up to being chaste observers of celibacy (*gupta-brahmacāriṇī*). They were highly learned and possessed large retinues. Wandering in regular succession from place to place, they arrived at the city of Tetalipura. Having arrived, they took possession of a suitable lodging (*avagraha*) and dwelt there, cultivating themselves through self-restraint and austerity. Now, a certain group of two of those nuns Suvratā performed their study during the first watch of the night, and so on, until they entered the house of Tetalipura while wandering for alms.

Then Pōṭṭilā saw those noble ladies approaching; seeing them, she rose from her seat with joy and satisfaction, paid homage and saluted them. Having paid homage and saluted them, she provided them with abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies. Having so provided for them, she spoke thus: “Noble ladies, it is indeed true that formerly I was dear, beloved, pleasing, agreeable, and charming to Tēyaliputta, but now I am no longer so—indeed, I am neither desired nor even fit for his sight or enjoyment. Now, noble ladies, you are well-traveled, highly educated, and well-read; you wander through many villages and towns, and you enter the homes of many kings, lords, and others. Therefore, noble ladies, do you possess any powder-preparations, mantra-preparations, ritual-preparations, or magical charms; any means for causing attraction, for causing aversion, for subjugation, or for enchantment; any *kōuya* (magical) rites, *bhūti* (demonological) rites, roots, bulbs, bark, creepers, *siliyā*, pills, herbs, or medicinal remedies previously acquired, by which I might once again become dear, beloved, pleasing, agreeable, and charming to Tēyaliputta?”

When those nuns had been addressed thus by Pōṭṭilā, they covered both ears; having covered them, they spoke to Pōṭṭilā as follows: "O beloved of the gods! We are Śramaṇīs, Nigranthīs, [and so forth] up to] observers of the vow of guarded celibacy. It is not indeed permissible for us even to listen to such words with our ears, much less to teach them or to practice them. O beloved of the gods! We shall, however, expound to you the wonderful Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin. Then Pōṭṭilā spoke to those nuns as follows: "I wish, O nuns, to listen to the wonderful Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin in your presence. Then those nuns expounded the wonderful Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin to Pōṭṭilā. Then Pōṭṭilā, having heard and reflected upon the Dharma, being delighted, spoke as follows:

"I have faith in this, noble ladies! The teaching of the Nirgranthas, just as you describe it. I wish to receive from your presence the Dharma consisting of the five minor vows and so forth. "As it pleases you. Then Pōṭṭilā received from those noble ladies the Dharma of the householder consisting of the five minor vows and so forth. She paid homage and saluted those noble ladies; having paid homage and saluted them, she dismissed them. Then Pōṭṭilā became a female lay disciple (*śramaṇopāsikā*) and lived there, providing for [the community] with offerings.

Then, on another occasion, during the time between the latter part of the night and the early part of the morning, while she was awake out of concern for her household, this reflection arose within Pōṭṭilā’s mind: "Formerly, I was indeed beloved, dear, pleasing, agreeable, and charming to Tēyaliputta; but now I am no longer beloved... [as before] ...or even fit for his enjoyment. Therefore, it would be best for me to go forth into the religious life in the presence of the venerable nuns Suvvatā. Having thus reflected, at dawn when the light had appeared, she went to where Tēyaliputta was; having approached him, with her hands joined in reverence, she spoke as follows: "O Lord, it is indeed so! I have heard the Dharma in the presence of the venerable nuns Suvvatā... [as before] ...and I have been granted permission to go forth."

Then Teyaliputta said this to Pōṭṭilā: "O beloved of the gods, having thus become a shaven-headed renunciant, you will at the time of death pass away and be reborn as a deity in one of the celestial realms. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, if you come to me from that celestial realm and awaken me to the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins, then I shall release you; but if you do not awaken me, I will not release you."

Then Pōṭṭilā consented to this matter of Tēyaliputta. Then Tēyaliputta had abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies prepared; having had them prepared, he invited his friends, kinsmen, and so forth, and honored and respected them. Having honored and respected them, he had Pōṭṭilā bathed and so forth, and helped her mount a palanquin carried by a thousand men. Surrounded by his friends, kinsmen, and so forth, with full splendor and a great clamor, he proceeded through the middle of Tēyalipura toward the monastery of the Suvvayas. Having arrived, he descended from the palanquin. Having descended, he placed Pōṭṭilā in front and went toward the Suvvayas. Having approached, he paid homage and reverence; having paid homage and reverence, he spoke as follows:

"Thus indeed, O beloved of the gods! My wife Pōṭṭilā is dear, beloved, cherished, pleasing, and agreeable to me. She, being terrified by the fear of *saṃsāra*... [and so forth]... wishes to go forth into the religious life. May the beloved of the gods grant permission for her; I offer her the alms-request of a female disciple (*sissiṇī-bhikkhā*). "As it pleases you, do not create an obstacle. Then, having been addressed thus by the noble ladies Suvvatā, Pōṭṭilā was delighted and joyful. To the north-eastern quarter, she herself removed her jewelry, garlands, and ornaments. Having removed them, she herself performed the tonsure of five handfuls of hair. She went to where the noble ladies Suvvatā were, paid homage and reverence, and having paid homage and reverence, spoke thus: [End of excerpt]

"Venerable ones, the world is indeed afflicted, just as in the case of Devānandā; [she] studied the eleven *aṅgas*, maintained the state of a monastic for many years, and having completed that period, she performed a month-long ritual of emaciation (*saṃlekhanā*), reduced her body by sixty meals through fasting, and having confessed and repented, attained composure. Having passed away at the time of death, she was reborn as a deity in one of the celestial realms."

Then, at another time, that King Kaṇagaraha passed away due to the law of time. Thereupon, those kings, ministers, and others performed his funeral rites; having done so, they spoke thus to one another: "O beloved of the gods, King Kaṇagaraha was indeed infatuated with the kingdom and its affairs until he died, leaving no son behind. O beloved of the gods, we are dependent on the king, supported by the king, and our business is centered on the king. Now this minister Teyalī was one who had gained confidence in all positions and in all territories under King Kaṇagaraha, and he was the executor of all affairs. Therefore, it would be well for us to appoint the minister Teyalīputta as prince. Having said this, they agreed to this matter among themselves, and having agreed, they went to where the minister Teyalīputta was and spoke to him thus: [The rest of the text follows the narrative of their request to him.]

"Indeed, O Lord, King Kaṇagaraha is so infatuated with his kingdom, his realm, and everything up to the royal insignia that he has neglected his sons. O Lord, we are dependent on the king; indeed, all our affairs are centered on the king. And you, O Lord, have been the one responsible for all matters of state for King Kaṇagaraha, even down to the management of the royal treasury. Therefore, O Lord, if there is any prince endowed with the marks of royalty who is worthy of consecration, please grant him to us, so that we may consecrate him with the most magnificent royal consecration."

Then Teyaliputta agreed to this proposal of those lords and others. Having agreed, he had Prince Kanakajjhaya bathed and adorned until he was most magnificent; having done so, he presented him to those lords and others and spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! This is Prince Kanakajjhaya, the son of King Kanagaraha and the daughter of Queen Paumāvatī, endowed with the marks of royalty and worthy of consecration. He has been raised by me in secret from King Kanagaraha. You must now consecrate him with a grand and magnificent royal consecration. And he related to them the entire account of his birth and upbringing.

Then those lords and others performed the great, grand consecration of Prince Kanakadhvaja. Thereupon, that Prince Kanakadhvaja became king—[his description] like that of the great Himavat, the great Malaya, and so forth, up until: "he dwelt ruling his kingdom. Then Queen Padmāvatī summoned King Kanakadhvaja and spoke thus: "My son, this kingdom of yours, as well as the inner apartments and so forth, exists through the power of your minister Teyaliputra. Therefore, you must honor, recognize, revere, and respect the minister Teyaliputra; welcome him when he arrives, attend upon him when he stands, escort him when he departs, invite him to a seat of honor, and increase his enjoyments. Then Kanakadhvaja assented to Padmāvatī’s words, saying "So be it," and did everything as requested, up until increasing his enjoyments.

Then that god Pōṭṭila repeatedly exhorted Tēyaliputta to the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin, yet Tēyaliputta did not awaken to it. Thereupon, this kind of internal reflection, thought, aspiration, mental resolve, and intention arose in that god Pōṭṭila: "Indeed, King Kaṇagajjhaī honors Tēyaliputta and even increases his wealth and enjoyments; yet although he is being exhorted repeatedly to the Dharma, Tēyaliputta does not awaken to it. Therefore, it would be well for me to turn King Kaṇagajjhaī away from Tēyaliputta. Having thus reflected, he resolved to turn Kaṇagajjhaī away from Tēyaliputta. And having so resolved, he turned Kaṇagajjhaī away from Tēyaliputta.

Then Teyaliputta, having bathed and performed his religious rites, mounted the back of a noble horse and, surrounded by many men, departed from his own house and set out toward King Kanakadhvaja. As the many lords, ministers, governors, and other officials saw the minister Teyaliputta, they honored him, recognized him, rose up for him, and saluted him with joined palms; addressing him with pleasant, lovely, and delightful words, they followed him—some in front, some behind, some at his side, and some along the path.

Then that Teyaliputta the minister went to where Kanakadhvaja was. Upon seeing Teyaliputta approaching, Kanakadhvaja did not welcome him, did not acknowledge him, and did not rise for him; remaining indifferent, unacknowledging, and unarising, he stood with his face turned away. Then Teyaliputta the minister joined his palms in salutation to King Kanakadhvaja, but King Kanakadhvaja, remaining indifferent, unacknowledging, and unarising, stayed silent with his face turned away.

Then Teyaliputta, perceiving that King Kanakadhvaja had been turned against him, became afraid and, overcome with fear, spoke thus: "King Kanakadhvaja is enraged at me; King Kanakadhvaja has lost his favor toward me; King Kanakadhvaja intends to execute me. Therefore, it is not known by which prince he will have me killed. Thinking this, he became terrified and, while there, backed away very slowly. Having retreated, he mounted the same horse, and having mounted it, set out through the middle of Teyalipura toward his own home.

Then, when those people—ranging from the lords down to the caravan leaders—beheld Teyaliputta, they did not honor him, nor did they acknowledge him, nor did they rise for him, nor did they join their palms in salutation; they did not address him with pleasant words or greetings, nor did they converse with him; nor did they follow after him from the front, from behind, or from the sides.

Then the minister Teyaliputta went to his own house. There, his outer circle of attendants—namely, the slaves, messengers, and laborers—neither welcomed him, nor recognized him, nor rose to greet him. And his inner circle of attendants—namely, his father, mother, [and so on] up to his daughter-in-law—likewise neither welcomed him, nor recognized him, nor rose to greet him. Then Teyaliputta went to the bedchamber where his couch was; having arrived, he sat down upon the couch and spoke as follows:

"In this way, indeed, I have gone out from my own house... [as before] ...and the inner circle of attendants neither honors, nor welcomes, nor rises up for me. Therefore, it is better for me to deprive myself of life. Having thought thus, he reflects; having reflected, he puts a *tāla-ūḍa* poison into his mouth, but that poison does not take effect. Then that minister Tetaliputta takes a sword with a hilt like a blue lotus... [as before] ...and draws it toward his shoulder, but even there its edge turns away. Then that Tetaliputta goes to the Aśoka grove; having gone there, he ties a noose around his neck, ties it, climbs a tree, and having climbed it, ties the noose to the tree and hangs himself, but even there the rope snaps. Then that Tetaliputta ties a very large stone to his neck, ties it, and throws himself into water that is not deep, not fordable, and not waist-deep, but even there he remains afloat. Then that Tetaliputta throws a mass of fire onto a heap of dry grass and throws himself into it, but even there the fire is extinguished.

Then Teyaliputta said this: "Truly, O venerable ones, the ascetics speak what is to be believed; truly, O venerable ones, the brahmins speak what is to be believed; truly, O venerable ones, the ascetics and brahmins together speak what is to be believed. But I alone speak what is not to be believed. Thus, while I have sons, who will believe me when I say I have no sons? While I have friends, who will believe me when I say I have no enemies? Likewise regarding wealth, wives, slaves, messengers, and attendants."

Thus, indeed, when Prince Kanakadhvaja was about to be executed by the minister Teyaliputra, his father’s ring was thrown into his mouth, yet it did not pass through; who would believe this? When Teyaliputra drew a blue lotus from the water up to its stalk and placed it upon his shoulder, even there the stream of water flowed down; who would believe this? When Teyaliputra bound a noose around his neck and snapped the rope, who would believe this? When Teyaliputra tied him with a great stone slab and released him into water eight fathoms deep, even there he found firm ground; who would believe this? When Teyaliputra extinguished a fire on a heap of dry grass, who would believe this? With his mind thus dejected and his thoughts troubled, he broods in distress.

Then that god Pōṭṭila manifested the form of Pōṭṭila; having manifested it, he stood nearby beside Tēyaliputta and spoke thus: "O Tēyaliputta! Ahead there is a ford, but behind there is the fear of an elephant; on both sides there is no range of vision, while in the middle rain-clouds are pouring down. The village is burning and the forest is smoldering; the forest is burning and the village is smoldering. O venerable Tēyaliputta, which way shall we go? Then Tēyaliputta said this to Pōṭṭila: "O sir, for one who is afraid, renunciation is indeed a refuge; for one who is distressed, going to a safe place; for the hungry, food; for the thirsty, drink; for the sick, medicine; for the deceived, a secret; for one who is entangled, a means of release; for one exhausted by the road, a vehicle; for one wishing to cross, a boat; for one wishing to overcome an enemy, an ally; but for one who is patient, self-controlled, and has mastered his senses, not even one of these is necessary."

Then that god Pōṭṭila said this to the minister Tēyaliputta: "O Tēyaliputta, you have indeed understood this matter well. Having said this, and having spoken thus a second and a third time, he departed in the same direction from which he had appeared.

Then, through that auspicious transformation of thought, the memory of his former births arose within Teyaliputta. Thereupon, this kind of internal reflection, consideration, aspiration, and mental resolve arose in Teyaliputta: "Indeed, in this very Jambudvīpa continent, in the Mahāvideha region, in the Puskalāvatī district, in the capital city of Puṇḍarīkiṇī, I was formerly a king named Mahāpadma. Then, having gone forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elders and studied the fourteen Pūrvas, and having fulfilled the course of the ascetic life for many years, I underwent a month-long ritual of self-mortification and was reborn as a deity in the Mahāśukra heaven."

Then, having descended from that celestial world due to the exhaustion of my lifespan and [the other karmic factors], I was reborn right here in Teyalipura as the son of the minister Teyali and his wife Bhaddā. Thinking, "It is indeed best for me to personally undertake and dwell by the great vows previously prescribed," he reflected thus; having reflected, he himself ascended to the great vows. Having ascended them, he went to the Pramada grove garden; having arrived, while sitting comfortably beneath an Aśoka tree on a stone slab, as he contemplated, the fourteen *pūrvas*—beginning with the *Sāmāyika*—which he had studied before, were spontaneously realized within him.

Then, through the auspicious transformation of that ascetic Teyaliputta, and by means of the destruction and subsidence of the karma obscuring [the soul], he entered the unprecedented state (*apūrvakaraṇa*) which disperses the dust of karma; and thus, supreme and perfect knowledge and vision (*kevalavarajñānadarśana*) arose within him.

Then, in the city of Teyalipura, the Vānamantara gods and goddesses who were nearby sounded divine drums, scattered flowers of ten colors, and a celestial rain of parched grain fell, while a divine sound of song and music was made.

When King Kaṇagajjhaya had grasped the meaning of this report, he spoke thus: "Indeed, Teyaliputta has been executed by me; having become shaven-headed, he has gone forth as a renunciant. Therefore, I shall go to the anagāra Teyaliputta to pay homage and reverence him; having paid homage and reverence, I shall repeatedly ask forgiveness for this matter with humility. Having reflected thus, he bathed and, together with his fourfold army, went to the Pamayavana park where the anagāra Teyaliputta was. Upon arriving, he paid homage and reverence to Teyaliputta; having paid homage and reverence, he repeatedly asked forgiveness for that matter with humility. Then, approaching closely, he waited upon him.

Then that ascetic Teyaliputta preached the Dharma to King Kanakadhvaja and that very large assembly. Having heard and understood the Dharma from the presence of the kevalin Teyaliputta, King Kanakadhvaja adopted the twelvefold duty of a lay follower (*śrāvaka*), consisting of the five lesser vows (*anuvratas*) and the seven disciplinary vows (*śikṣāvratas*). Having adopted it, he became a lay disciple (*śramaṇopāsaka*) who had comprehended the nature of living beings and non-living beings. Then the kevalin Teyaliputta, having fulfilled the stage of a kevalin for many years, attained liberation (*siddha*).
Thus indeed, Jambū! by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained [liberation], this is the meaning declared in the fourteenth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahā; thus I say.

"If, venerable sir, this is the meaning declared by the Śramaṇa [Mahāvīra] in the fourteenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, what is the meaning declared in the fifteenth? "Thus it was, Jambū: at that time, in that period, there was a city named Campā; there was a shrine named Punnabhadda; and there was a king named Jiyasattu. In that city of Campā, there was a caravan leader named Dhaṇa, who was wealthy, prosperous, and beyond reproach. To the north-eastern quarter of that city of Campā, there was a city named Ahicchattā—rich, flourishing, and prosperous; its description is as follows. In that city of Ahicchattā, there was a king named Kaṇakaketu, whose description is extensive."

Then, at a certain time, during the period between late evening and the early hours of the night, this kind of reflection, thought, aspiration, and mental resolve arose within that caravan leader Dhanna: "It would indeed be well for me to take a vast quantity of merchandise and go to the city of Ahicchatrā for trade. Having thus reflected, he took four kinds of goods—those to be counted, those to be weighed, those to be measured, and those to be examined by touch; having taken them, he prepared his wagons and carriages, loaded the wagons and carriages, summoned his household servants, and spoke to them as follows:

"Go, dear ones! In the city of Campā, at the crossroads, and so forth, throughout the streets and great highways, proclaiming repeatedly, say this: 'Truly, dear ones, the caravan leader Dhana, having taken a vast amount of merchandise, desires to go to the city of Ahicchatrā for trade. Therefore, dear ones, whoever there may be—a Caraka, a Cīrika, a leather-clad ascetic (Carmakhaṇḍika), a mendicant (Bhikṣuṇḍa), a Paṇḍuraṅga, a Goyama, a Gōvatiya, a follower of the householder-dharma (Gṛhidharma), a contemplator of Dharma (Dharmacintaka), or any sectarian such as the Aviruddha, Viruddha, Vṛddha-śrāvaka, Raktapaṭa, Nirgrantha, or others, or even a householder—who goes to the city of Ahicchatrā together with the caravan leader Dhana: for him, the caravan leader Dhana will provide an umbrella if he is without one; he will provide shoes if he is without shoes; he will provide a water-pot if he is without one; he will provide provisions if he is without them; he will provide a companion if he is without one; and he will also provide assistance if anything is lost or broken along the way, so that he may reach Ahicchatrā in complete safety. Having made this proclamation twice and thrice, report back to me that you have carried out this command."

Then those householders’ men, having been addressed [by Dhanaka] up until the words “Listen, venerable sirs! The news from the city of Campā concerns many wandering mendicants...,” returned [with the message]. Then, having heard this matter from the presence of those householders’ men, many wandering mendicants and others, up to householders, in the city of Campā went to where Dhanaka, the caravan leader, was.

Then Ghaṇa the caravan leader gave an umbrella to those wandering mendicants and householders who were without umbrellas, and so on, up to giving provisions to those who lacked provisions; having given these, he spoke thus: "Go, dear sirs, and wait upon me while staying in the outer park outside the city of Campā. Then those wandering mendicants and householders, being thus addressed by Ghaṇa the caravan leader, remained there as instructed.

Then Ghaṇa the caravan leader, on an auspicious day and at a favorable conjunction of stars, had abundant food—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—prepared. Having prepared it, he invited his friends, kinsmen, and others; having invited them, he fed them; having fed them, he took leave of them; having taken leave, he yoked his wagons and carts and departed from the city of Campā. Departing, traveling along very long stretches of road, staying at various pleasant lodgings and resting places, he proceeded through the middle of the Aṅga country toward the region of Deśagrāma. Having arrived, he unyoked his wagons and carts and established the caravan encampment. Having established the camp, he summoned his household servants and said this to them: "O beloved of the gods! In my caravan encampment, you must announce with a very loud voice, repeatedly proclaiming: 'O beloved of the gods! In the middle of this vast, desolate, and long-stretched wilderness, there are many trees called Nandiphala. They are black [in trunk], up to being leafy, flowering, fruit-bearing, green, shimmering, and exceedingly beautiful with their splendor. They are delightful to the eye, [delightful] to the nose, [delightful] to the tongue, [delightful] to the body, and delightful to the touch; they are delightful in their shade.'"

"O beloved of the gods! Whoever eats the roots, bulbs, bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds, or green shoots of those *nandiphala* trees, or rests in their shade, his dwelling becomes auspicious; however, as time passes, they will prematurely deprive him of his life. Therefore, O beloved of the gods! Let no one eat the roots or [other parts] of those *nandiphala* trees, nor rest in their shade, lest he too be prematurely deprived of his life. O beloved of the gods! You should eat the roots and [other parts] of other trees, and rest in their shades. Having thus made this proclamation, they returned that command to the king.

Then the caravan leader Ghaṇa yoked his wagons and carts; having yoked them, he went to where the Nandiphalā trees were. Having arrived, he established the camp for the caravan not far from those Nandiphalā trees. Having done so, he called his household servants a second and a third time, and having called them, he spoke thus: "O dear ones, you must make a proclamation at my caravan camp with a very loud voice, saying: 'O dear ones, these Nandiphalā trees are black [and so on] up to being pleasant in their shade. Therefore, O dear ones, whoever among you eats the roots, or bulbs, or bark, or leaves, or flowers, or fruits, or seeds, or green shoots of these Nandiphalā trees—[he will suffer] up to being deprived of life prematurely. So, dear ones, avoid them from afar, staying as far away as possible, lest you be deprived of life prematurely. Instead, eat the roots and so on of other trees, and then rest. Having said this, they made the proclamation and reported back."

In that regard, some men there believe, trust, and have faith in this matter regarding the caravan leader Ghaṇa. Believing in this matter, they repeatedly avoid those *nandiphala* trees from afar; they rest at the roots of other trees and so forth. For them, no misfortune occurs. Then, as they are gradually digested, they transform again and again into a state of good health and so forth.

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic! that Nirgrantha or Nirgranthī who, up to [the point of] not being attached to or enamored by the five strands of sensual pleasure, becomes in this very life an object of worship for many ascetics and so forth; and in the next world, he does not return [to rebirth], but rather transcends it. Now, among those people there, some do not have faith in, do not trust in, and do not find pleasure in this matter of Ghaṇa’s. Having no faith, no trust, and no pleasure in Ghaṇa’s matter, they go to where those Nandiphala trees are, and having gone there, they rest at the roots of those Nandiphala trees and so forth. Their experience there is pleasant at first, but then, as it continues to transform, it eventually results in their destruction.

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic, a Nirgrantha or a Nirgranthī who has gone forth, if they become attached to the five strands of sensual pleasure... [they will wander again and again through the wilderness of saṃsāra], just like those men. Then that merchant leader Ghaṇa had his wagons and carts yoked; having yoked them, he went to the city of Ahicchatrā. Having arrived, he established his caravan camp outside the city of Ahicchatrā in the main park and unloaded his wagons and carts.

Then that caravan leader Dhanaka took up a gift of great significance, great value, and great worth, befitting a king; having taken it, surrounded by many men, he entered the city of Ahicchatrā through its very center. Having entered, he approached King Kanakaketu, and having approached, he saluted him with palms joined together [in reverence] and, having so saluted, presented that gift of great significance, great value, and great worth, befitting a king.

Then King Kanakaketu, joyful and delighted, accepted that great wealth from the caravan leader Dhana, and having accepted it, he honored and respected the caravan leader Dhana; having honored and respected him, he granted him leave to depart, and having granted leave, he exchanged his own goods for theirs; having exchanged them, he took the goods in return and, traveling in comfort, arrived at the city of Campā. Having arrived, surrounded by friends, kinsmen, and relatives, he lived there enjoying the abundant pleasures of human life.

At that time, on that occasion, having heard the Dharma from the arrival of the Elders, the caravan leader Dhana established his eldest son in the household and went forth as a monk. Having studied the eleven *aṅgas*, beginning with the *Sāmāyika*, and having fulfilled the course of the ascetic life for many years, he purified himself through a month-long process of austerity (*saṃlekhanā*) and was reborn as a deity in one of the celestial realms. Thereafter, he will attain perfection in the region of Mahāvideha and eventually make an end of suffering.
Thus indeed, Jambū! this is the meaning of the fifteenth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo as proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra; so I say.

"If, venerable sir, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for the fifteenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, then what, venerable sir, is the meaning declared for the sixteenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*? "Thus it was, Jambū: at that time, in that period, there was a city named Campā. Outside that city of Campā, in the northeastern quarter, there was a park named Subhūmibhāga. There, in the city of Campā, three Brāhmaṇa brothers lived, namely: Soma, Somadatta, and Somabhūti. They were wealthy, [and so on], until: 'unconquered'; they were well-perfected in the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda, [and so on]."

Those brahmins had three wives, namely: Nāgasirī, Bhūyasirī, and Jakkhasirī; they were delicate in hand and foot, and were beloved by those brahmins, [and so on], until they lived enjoying extensive human pleasures.

Then, on another occasion, when those brahmins had gathered together, there arose among them this conversation and discussion: "O beloved of the gods! We possess this vast wealth—[as described]—and even more than that; it is sufficient for seven generations of our family line to give as much as we wish, to eat as much as we wish, and to distribute as much as we wish. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, it would be well for us to prepare abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies in one another's homes every day and dwell enjoying them. They agreed to this proposal, and every day they had abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies prepared in one another's homes, and having prepared them, they dwelt enjoying them.

Then, on a certain occasion, it was the time for the meal of that Brāhmaṇī Nāgasirī. She prepared an abundance of food—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables. She prepared a large dish of *sālaïya* with bitter vegetables (*tittālāuya*), seasoned with many ingredients and saturated with oil. Taking a single drop on the palm of her hand, she tasted it; realizing it was salty, bitter, inedible, and like poison, she spoke thus: "Fie upon me, Nāgasirī! Wretched, luckless, unfortunate, of an unfortunate nature, and born of an unfortunate womb! I have prepared this *sālaïya* with bitter vegetables, mixed with many ingredients and saturated with oil, wasting a great deal of substance and oil. If my mother-in-law finds out, she will despise me. Therefore, as long as my mother-in-law does not know, it is better for me to hide this *sālaïya* with bitter vegetables, mixed with many ingredients and saturated with oil, in a secret place, and prepare another *sālaïya* with sweet vegetables, likewise saturated with oil. Having reflected thus, she hid that *sālaïya* and prepared another *sālaïya* with sweet vegetables. When those Brāhmaṇas had bathed and were seated comfortably on excellent seats, she served them that abundant food—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables. Then those Brāhmaṇas, having finished their meal and returned from the dining hall, being satisfied, clean, and supremely purified, became engaged in their own respective duties. Then those Brāhmaṇī women, having bathed and adorned themselves, ate that abundant food and returned to their own homes, where they too became engaged in their own respective duties.

At that time, in that period, there were elder monks named Dhammaghosas, who, having a large retinue, arrived at the Subhūmibhāga garden in the city of Campā. Having arrived, they stayed there in a manner appropriate to the occasion; the assembly went out, the Dharma was preached, and the assembly returned.

Now, among those elder monks (theras) named Dhammaghosa, there was a disciple, an ascetic (anagāra) named Dhammarūi, who was noble and possessed of great splendor, practicing a month-long fast (māsa-kṣapaṇa). Then, at the time of breaking his month-long fast, that ascetic Dhammarūi performed his recitation (svādhyāya) during the first watch of the night and meditated during the second watch. Just as Goyama-sāmī [did], he likewise entered the alms-bowl; just as [Goyama-sāmī did], he requested permission from the elder Dhammaghosa and, wandering through high, low, and middle-class families in the city of Campā, eventually entered the house of the Brāhmaṇī Nāgasirī.

Then that Brāhmaṇī Nāgasirī, seeing Dhammarui approaching, was delighted and thrilled; for the purpose of pouring out that Sālāiya-tittakaḍuya sauce—which was prepared with many ingredients and saturated with oil—she rose from her seat. Having risen, she went to the kitchen, and having arrived there, she poured all of that Sālāiya-tittakaḍuya sauce, along with the other highly oily substances, into the alms-bowl of the ascetic Dhammarui. Then the ascetic Dhammarui, thinking "it is sufficient," departed from the house of the Brāhmaṇī Nāgasirī. Having departed, he went through the middle of the city of Campā, and having exited, he went to the Subhūmibhāga park where the elder Dhammaghosa was. Approaching the vicinity of Dhammaghosa, he showed the food and drink to him; having shown it, he placed the food and drink in his palms.

Then the elder Dhammaghosa, being overcome by the smell of that *sālaïya* thick with oil, took a single drop from that *sālaïya* thick with oil onto the palm of his hand and tasted it. Knowing it to be bitter, pungent, astringent, inedible, unfit for consumption, and like poison, he spoke thus to the ascetic Dhammarūi: "O dear one, if you consume this *sālaïya* thick with oil, you will be deprived of life prematurely. Therefore, O dear one, do not consume this *sālaïya* thick with oil; lest you be deprived of life prematurely. Go, O dear one, and discard this *sālaïya* thick with oil in a secluded, uninhabited, and clean spot. Then, having accepted other pure and permissible food—namely, eatables, drinks, chewables, and lickables—consume it as your meal."

Then, having been addressed in this way by the elder Dharmaghoṣa, the ascetic Dharmaruci departed from the presence of the elder Dharmaghoṣa. Having departed, he inspected a bare patch of ground not far from the Subhūmibhāga garden. Having inspected it, he took a single drop from the *sālaiya*—[which was bitter, pungent, mixed with many ingredients, and thick with oil]—and poured it onto that bare patch of ground. Then, by the scent of that *sālaiya*, thousands of ants appeared; and whichever ant consumed it was deprived of life prematurely.

Then, this kind of internal reflection, thought, aspiration, and mental resolve arose in that ascetic Dhammaruci: "If even when a single drop of this *sālāiya*—which contains many ingredients, is saturated with oil, and has been prepared for a long time—is cast upon it, thousands of ants are destroyed; therefore, if I were to pour all of this *sālāiya*, bitter and pungent, mixed with many ingredients and saturated with oil, onto a bare patch of ground, it would result in the killing of many living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings. It is therefore better for me to consume this *sālāiya*, which is saturated with oil, by myself alone; let it be digested within my own body. Having thus resolved, he...

Reflecting thus, he reflected; having reflected, he inspected his mouth-cloth; having inspected it, he wiped his body, including the head and upper garment. Having wiped it, he took that salted, bitter, and pungent food, thick with oil, and, like a snake entering its hole, he thrust it all into the cavity of his body. Then, as that salted food—up to being thick with oil—was being consumed by Dhammaruci, after a short interval, while it was being digested within his body, a pain arose that was intense, up to being difficult to endure.

Then that ascetic Dhammarūī, being powerless, weak, devoid of vigor, lacking manly effort and prowess, and thinking himself unable to maintain his vows, set aside his monastic requisites to one side. Having set them aside, he inspected the bare ground, spread out a mattress of *darbha* grass, and climbed upon it. Sitting there with his legs crossed (*sampaliyaṅka*), facing eastward, and with his hands joined in reverence, he spoke thus: "Adoration be to the Arhats, up to those who have attained perfection; adoration be to the elders Dhammaghosa, my teachers of the Dharma and instructors in the Dharma. Previously, in the presence of the elders Dhammaghosa, I renounced all killing of living beings for as long as life lasts, up to the renunciation of possession. Now, too, in the presence of those very same Blessed Ones, I renounce all killing of living beings and renounce possession for as long as life lasts. Just as Khaṇḍaka [did], up to 'I shall relinquish [my body] with my final breaths. Having said this, having confessed and repented, and having attained meditative absorption, he passed away."

Then those elder monks, Dharmaghosa, knowing that the ascetic Dhammaruci had been gone for a long time, summoned the Śramaṇas and Nirgranthas and spoke to them thus: "Indeed, dear sirs, the ascetic Dhammaruci, on the day of breaking his month-long fast, went outside for the purpose of seeking out food—such as *sālāgriya* and so forth, up to that which is steeped in oil—and has been gone for a long time. Therefore, dear sirs, go and conduct a search and inquiry for the ascetic Dhammaruci in every direction and on all sides."

Then those śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, having assented, departed from the presence of the elder Dharmaghoṣa. Having departed, they conducted a search and inquiry for the anagāra Dharmaruci in every direction and on all sides. They arrived at the very spot where the bare ground was. Having arrived, they saw the body of the anagāra Dharmaruci—lifeless, motionless, and abandoned by the soul. Seeing this, they cried out, "Alas! Alas! Oh, what a tragedy! and performed a *kāyotsarga* (meditative posture) for the sake of the final liberation of the anagāra Dharmaruci. They took up the belongings of the anagāra Dharmaruci and went to where the elder Dharmaghoṣa was. Having arrived, they performed the ritual of confession for their coming and going, and spoke as follows:

"Indeed, having departed from your presence, we went along the perimeter of the Subhūmibhāga garden; performing [our duties] toward the ascetic Dhammarūi, we arrived at the very spot where he was lying on the bare ground, and thus have come here quickly. Therefore, Venerable Sir, since the ascetic Dhammarūi has passed away, this is his collection of requisites."

Then those elder monks, Dhammadhosa by name, directed their attention to the past and summoned the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas and Nirgranthīs, and having summoned them, they spoke thus: "Venerable ones, my disciple, the ascetic named Dhammarūī, who is naturally auspicious, naturally tranquil, with naturally slight anger, pride, deceit, and greed; endowed with gentleness and humility; modest and well-behaved—while practicing self-discipline through a month-long penance that was never interrupted, he entered the house of the Brāhmaṇī Nāgasirī. Then that Brāhmaṇī Nāgasirī [prepared food] and served it to him. Thereupon, the ascetic Dhammarūī, thinking 'this is sufficient,' remained there without desiring death."

When that ascetic Dhammarūī, having fulfilled the course of the ascetic life for many years, had confessed his faults and repented, attained meditative absorption, and passed away at the time of death, he was reborn as a deity in the great celestial mansion Sarvārthasiddha, situated above [the world]. There, the lifespan is declared to be thirty-three *sāgaropamas*, neither less nor more; there, the lifespan of the deity Dhammarūī is also declared to be thirty-three *sāgaropamas*. That deity Dhammarūī, from that divine world, will eventually attain liberation in the region of Mahāvideha.

"Shame on that unfortunate, meritless, and wretched Brahmin woman Nāgaśrī, by whom such a holy man as Dharmaruci was deprived of his life at an improper time with ghee and oil—so thick with fatness—during the breaking of his month-long fast!"

Then those śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, having heard and reflected upon this matter in the presence of the elder Dhammaghosa, went through the crossroads, triple-forks, and so on, in Campā, and spoke thus to the great multitude: "Fie upon her, O beloved of the gods! Fie upon Nāgasirī, that wretched, ill-fated woman, by whom such a holy man, a man in the likeness of a sage, was caused to be deprived of his life by Sālaika!"

Having heard and reflected upon this matter from those ascetics, many people spoke thus to one another, declared thus, explained thus, and defined thus: "Fie upon that Brahmin woman Nāgasirī! ... [she who] has been deprived of life! Then those Brahmins, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the many people in the city of Campā, became enraged and, burning with indignation, went to where the Brahmin woman Nāgasirī was. Having approached her, they spoke thus to the Brahmin woman Nāgasirī: "Ha! O Nāgasirī! You who pray for what is undesired! You whose characteristics are wretched and miserable! You who are devoid of merit, like the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight! You who are bereft of fortune, modesty, courage, and fame! Fie upon you, the unfortunate and meritless one, you who are as worthless as a rotten gourd! For it was by you—that you have deprived such a worthy ascetic, a true sage, a lover of Dharma, during his breaking of the month-long fast, of his life with salt... [and so on]. They reviled him with various insults; they insulted him with various threats; they reviled him with various censures; they reviled him with various blows; they threatened him, they struck him, and having threatened and struck him, they cast him out from their own house."

Then, having been expelled from her own home, that Nāgasirī wandered about in the city of Campā, being mocked, reviled, censured, reproached, threatened, intimidated, scorned, and spat upon by the multitude of people at the street corners, trijunctions, crossroads, squares, and four-way junctions. Finding no place to stay or a dwelling anywhere, dressed in tattered rags with a broken water-jar and a small bowl in her hand, her head shorn and bald, her path blocked by swarms of flies, she subsisted by begging for morsels of food from house to house.

Then, in that very same existence, sixteen afflictions of disease appeared in that Brāhmaṇī Nāgasirī, namely: asthma, cough, uterine pain, and so on, up to leprosy. Then, that Brāhmaṇī Nāgasirī, being overcome by those sixteen afflictions of disease and tormented by the distress of agonizing suffering, passed away at the time of death and was reborn as a denizen of hell in the hells of the sixth earth, with a maximum lifespan of twenty-two *sāgaropamas*.

Immediately after that, having transmigrated, she was reborn among fish. There, being destined for slaughter by the sword and succumbing to a feverish affliction, she died at the time of death and was reborn as a denizen of hell in the seventh hell below, with a maximum lifespan of thirty-three *sāgaropamas*. Having transmigrated from there, she was reborn among fish for a second time. There too, being destined for slaughter by the sword and succumbing to a feverish affliction, she was reborn for a second time as a denizen of hell in the seventh hell below, with a maximum lifespan of thirty-three *sāgaropamas*. Having transmigrated from there, she was reborn among fish for a third time. There too, being destined for slaughter... [as before] ...having died, she was reborn for a second time in the sixth hell below, with a maximum [lifespan]. Immediately after that, having transmigrated, she was reborn among serpents; this should be understood in the same manner as Gosāla’s account, until: having transmigrated from the *Ratnaprabhā* hell, she was reborn among sentient beings (*saṇṇī*). Having transmigrated from there, [she passed through various states] up to these species of winged creatures, and furthermore, she was born many hundreds of thousands of times as coarse and gross earth-bodied organisms.

Immediately after that, having transmigrated, she was reborn right here in this Jambudvīpa continent, in the land of Bhārata, in the city of Campā, in the womb of Bhaddā, the wife of the caravan leader Sāgaradatta, as a female child. Then, when nine months had fully elapsed, the caravan leader’s wife Bhaddā gave birth to a girl who was delicate and soft, like the palate of an elephant. When twelve days had passed for that girl, her parents gave her this appropriate name derived from her qualities: "Since this girl of ours is delicate and soft, like the palate of an elephant, let the name of this girl be Sukumālikā—Sukumālikā."

Then her parents gave that girl the name Sūmālikā. Thereupon, the girl Sūmālikā was attended by five nurses, namely: a milk-nurse, and so forth, until she was like a *campaka* creeper clinging to the peak of a mountain; she grew up happily and without hindrance. Then, as the girl Sūmālikā emerged from childhood, she became preeminent in beauty, youth, and loveliness, possessing a most excellent body.

There, in the city of Campā, lived a caravan leader named Jinadatta, who was wealthy and prosperous. His wife was Bhaddā, who was delicate, beloved, and so forth; she lived enjoying human sensual pleasures. Jinadatta had a son by his wife Bhaddā named Sāgara, a youth with tender hands and feet, and so forth, who was handsome. Then, on a certain occasion, that caravan leader Jinadatta went out from his own house and passed by the vicinity of Sāgaradatta’s house. And at that time, the maiden Sūmālikā—having bathed and surrounded by a circle of maidservants—was playing, repeatedly tossing a golden ball, upon the upper terrace.

Then that caravan leader Jinadatta, seeing the maiden Sūmālikā, was filled with wonder at her beauty, youth, and loveliness; he summoned his household servants and spoke thus: "O dear ones! Whose daughter is this maiden, and what is her name? Then those household servants, being thus addressed by the caravan leader Jinadatta, were delighted and joyful; with palms joined [in reverence], they spoke as follows: "O dear one! This is the daughter of the caravan leader Sāgaradatta and the granddaughter of his wife Bhadrā, named Sūmālikā—a maiden with delicate hands and feet, and so forth, most excellent."

Then Jinadatta, the caravan leader, having heard this matter from those householders, went to his own home. Having arrived, he bathed and, surrounded by friends and kinsmen, proceeded through Campā to the house of Sāgaradatta, the caravan leader. Then Sāgaradatta, the caravan leader, saw Jinadatta, the caravan leader, approaching; seeing him, he rose from his seat, and having risen, invited him to a seat. Once he was comfortably seated, at ease, and settled upon an excellent seat, Sāgaradatta spoke thus: "Speak, dear sir! What is the purpose of your visit?"

Then Jinadatta spoke thus to Sāgaradatta: "O dear sir, I indeed request your daughter Bhadrā’s offspring, Sūmālikā, as a wife for Sāgara. If you deem it fitting, appropriate, praiseworthy, or if the union is suitable, O dear sir, let Sūmālikā be given to the youth Sāgara. And what, O dear sir, shall we give to Sūmālikā as a dowry? Then the caravan leader Sāgaradatta said this to the caravan leader Jinadatta: "O dear sir, the maiden Sūmālikā is my only child, born of one [mother], beloved, and so forth—how much more so when she is seen! I certainly do not wish for even a moment's separation from the maiden Sūmālikā. Therefore, O dear sir, if the youth Sāgara becomes my son-in-law in my own house, then I shall give Sūmālikā to Sāgara. When the caravan leader Sāgaradatta had spoken thus, the caravan leader Jinadatta went to his own home. Having arrived, he summoned the youth Sāgara and said this: "O son, the caravan leader Sāgaradatta has told me this: 'The maiden Sūmālikā is beloved... [as before] ...if the youth Sāgara becomes my son-in-law in my own house, then I shall give her. When the youth Sāgara was thus addressed by the caravan leader Jinadatta, he remained silent. Then, on another occasion, at an auspicious time, lunar day, constellation, and moment, the caravan leader Jinadatta prepared abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies. Having prepared them, he honored his friends, kinsmen, and others. He had the youth Sāgara bathed and adorned with all ornaments. He had him mount a palanquin carried by a thousand men. Surrounded by his friends, kinsmen, and others, and accompanied by great splendor, he departed from his own house, proceeded through the middle of the city of Campā, and arrived at the house of the caravan leader Sāgaradatta. Having arrived, he descended from the palanquin and presented the youth Sāgara to the caravan leader Sāgaradatta.

Then that caravan leader Sāgaradatta had abundant food, drink, chewables, and delicacies prepared; having prepared them, and having honored [the guests] as was fitting, he had the boy Sāgara mount a palanquin together with the girl Sūmālikā. Having had him mount it, he had him bathed with white and blue jars; having had him bathed, he had an oblation to the fire performed; and having had the oblation performed, he had the boy Sāgara take the hand of the girl Sūmālikā in marriage.

Then Sāgara experienced that touch of the maiden Sūmālikā as being like, for example, the touch of a sword-blade, or [as described] up to glowing embers; indeed, he experienced a touch even more undesirable than those, and so on. Then Sāgara, against his will and without autonomy, remained still for a mere moment. Thereupon, the caravan leader Sāgaradatta, along with Sāgara’s parents, friends, kinsmen, and others, honored them with abundant food, drink, edibles, delicacies, flowers, and garments, and then dismissed them.

Then Sāgara went with the maiden Sūmālikā to the bedchamber; having arrived, he lay down upon a couch together with the maiden Sūmālikā. Then that youth Sāgara experienced such a touch of the maiden Sūmālikā’s body as was like, for example, the blade of a sword—indeed, he remained experiencing a touch of the body even more unpleasant than that. Unable to endure the touch of the maiden Sūmālikā’s body and losing all self-control, he remained there for a mere moment. Then, knowing that the maiden Sūmālikā was sleeping soundly, the youth Sāgara rose from the side of the maiden Sūmālikā; having risen, he went to his own bed, and having arrived, he lay down upon it.

Then, after a short while, the maiden Sūmālikā woke up. Being devoted to her husband and deeply enamored of him, she did not see him by her side; she rose from the couch, went to where her bed was, and searched for Sāgara’s side. Then the young man Sāgara experienced that same touch of Sūmālikā’s body for a second time, and so forth, until—being unwilling and lacking self-control—he remained there for a moment. Then, knowing that the maiden Sūmālikā was sleeping soundly, the young man Sāgara rose from the bed, opened the door of the chamber, and like a body released from a garden, he departed in the very direction from which he had appeared.

Then, after a short while, the maiden Sūmālikā woke up. Having woken, she arose from her bed and, not seeing [Sāgara], began searching for and seeking him everywhere. While searching all around, she saw that the door of the bedchamber was opened. Seeing this, she said: "Sāgara has gone! Thinking thus, with her mind and intentions overwhelmed, she remained brooding. Then, when the night had turned into dawn, Bhaddā the merchant’s wife summoned her maidservant and said: "Go, dear girl, and bring the water for washing the bridegroom's face. Thus addressed by Bhaddā the merchant’s wife, the maidservant consented to this matter, saying "So be it. She took the water for washing the face and went to the bedchamber. There she saw the maiden Sūmālikā brooding, and seeing her, she said: "Why, dear lady, are you brooding with your mind and intentions overwhelmed?"

Then that maiden Sūmālikā spoke thus to the female slave: "O beloved of the gods! Indeed, while I was sleeping soundly, the boy Sāgara rose from my side; having risen, he opened the door of the bedchamber and departed. A moment later, I woke up and saw the door wide open. Seeing this, I thought, 'Sāgara has gone,' and with a dejected mind and purpose, I remained brooding. Then that female slave, having heard this matter from the maiden Sūmālikā, went to where the merchant Sāgaradatta was and, having approached him, informed Sāgaradatta of this matter.

Then Sāgaradatta, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the mouth of the maidservant, became enraged and, proceeding directly to the house of the caravan leader Jinadatta, spoke thus to the caravan leader Jinadatta: "O beloved of the gods! Is this right, is it proper, is it worthy of our lineage, or is it consistent with our family, that the boy Sāgara, having abandoned the maiden Sumālikā—who was free from any perceived fault and his own wife—should come here and be reproached by you with many censures and outbursts of lamentation?"

Then Jinadatta, having heard this matter from the merchant Sāgaradatta, went to where Sāgara was and spoke thus to the boy Sāgara: "It was ill done by you, my son, that you came here so hastily from the house of Sāgaradatta. Therefore, go back, my son, to the house of Sāgaradatta. Then the boy Sāgara spoke thus to the merchant Jinadatta: "Even if I were to undergo, father, a fall from a mountain, a fall from a tree, a desert storm, entering water, entering fire, consuming poison, being impaled on a stake, hanging, being devoured by vultures, renunciation [of life], or going to a foreign land, I would certainly not go to the house of Sāgaradatta."

Then that caravan leader Sāgaradatta heard this matter from Kuṇḍantariyā; having heard it, he was ashamed, abashed, and humiliated. He departed from the house of the caravan leader Jinadatta and went to his own home. Having arrived, he summoned the girl Sukumālikā, placed her on his lap, and spoke thus: "Why, my daughter, have you been abandoned by the boy Sāgara? I shall give you to whoever will be dear to you, even as much as you desire. Thus he consoled the girl Sukumālikā with those pleasing and affectionate words, and having consoled her, he dismissed her.

Then, on another occasion, while the merchant Sāgaradatta was sitting comfortably upon the upper terrace of his palace, looking down repeatedly at the royal highway, he saw a certain beggar man. He was dressed in tattered rags, holding a broken bowl and a broken jar in his hands; his head was bald and withered, and he was being driven along the road by thousands of flies. Then the merchant Sāgaradatta summoned his household servants and spoke to them thus: "O beloved ones, entice this beggar man with abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies, and lead him into the house. Once he has entered, put away his broken bowl and broken jar to one side. Then have him adorned; have him bathed, performed his ritual offerings, and decked out in all his ornaments. After that, feed him delicious food and bring him into my presence."

Then those householders' servants, having assented, went to where that beggar was; having approached, they tempted that beggar with food, drink, snacks, and delicacies; having tempted him, they brought him into their own house; having brought him in, they hid that broken bowl and broken jar in a secluded spot for that beggar. Then, as that broken bowl and broken jar were being hidden away, the beggar let out a very loud cry. Then the caravan leader Sāgaradatta, having heard and perceived that very loud crying-out of the beggar, spoke thus to the householders' servants: "O dear ones, why is this beggar crying out with such a very loud sound? Then those householders' servants said: "Master, it is because that broken bowl and broken jar are being hidden away that he is crying out with such a very loud sound."

Then Sāgaradatta, the caravan leader, spoke thus to those householders: "O dear ones, do not give that piece [of cloth] to this beggar; rather, place it near him so that he does not believe it. They did exactly as they were told. Having placed it there, they performed the act of adorning the beggar. Having adorned him, they anointed him with oils of a hundred and a thousandfold potency. Once anointed, they rubbed his body with fragrant scented powder. Having rubbed it, they bathed him with hot perfumed water and then with cold water. They dried his limbs with a fine, soft, scented powder. Then they dressed him in a pair of garments marked with the swan-pattern and adorned him with every kind of ornament. They fed him with abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies. Having fed him, they presented him to Sāgaradatta.

Then that caravan leader Sāgaradatta, having bathed the maiden Sūmālikā and adorned her with all ornaments, spoke thus to that beggar: "O dear one, this daughter of mine is beloved, charming, dear, pleasing, and delightful; I give her to you as your wife. O auspicious one, may you become blessed through her. Then that beggar accepted this proposal from Sāgaradatta; having accepted it, he entered the bedchamber together with the maiden Sūmālikā and lay down upon the couch with her. Then that beggar experienced such a touch of the limbs of Sūmālikā—the rest is as in the account of Sāgara—until he rose from the bed, departed from the bedchamber, took his broken bowl and broken jar, and like a tree cast off by a garden, went back in the very direction from which he had appeared. Then Sūmālikā, [realizing] that the beggar had gone, became despondent in mind and intent, and remained brooding.

Then, when the night had turned to dawn, Bhaddā [the mother] summoned her maidservant and spoke thus, [and so on], until she informed Sāgaradatta of this matter. Then Sāgaradatta, being likewise agitated, went to the bedchamber; having arrived, he placed the girl Sūmālikā on his lap and spoke thus: "Alas, my daughter! You are experiencing the fruits of your past deeds, both ancient and [recent]. Therefore, my daughter, do not remain with a dejected mind and intent, nor brood over it. My daughter, you shall dwell distributing abundant food and drink in my kitchen—just as Puṭṭilā did—until it is exhausted. Then the girl Sūmālikā accepted this proposal. Having accepted it, day after day she dwelt distributing abundant food and drink in the kitchen, and so forth. At that time, at that very moment, the nuns of the Govālika order—who were highly learned—arrived [at the city], just as the Suvvayā nuns had previously arrived for Teyaliṇā. Just as before, a group of them entered [the house], and so forth, until they had been offered alms by Sūmālikā. Having been offered alms, they spoke thus: "O Noble Ones, I am indeed disliked and unpleasant to Sāgara; Sāgara does not desire even my name, much less my touch or my enjoyment. To whomever I am given, I become disliked and unpleasant to him as well. But you, Noble Ones, are of great lineage—just as Puṭṭilā was—and you have previously obtained [such power] whereby I might become beloved and dear to the boy Sāgara."

Then those noble ladies spoke just as before; she became a lay follower just as before; she had the same reflections just as before; she took leave of the caravan leader Sāgaradatta just as before, until she went forth into homelessness in the presence of the noble ladies of Govālikā. Then that noble lady Sūmālikā became one who was restrained in her movements (iryā-samiti) and so forth, up to being a practitioner of guarded celibacy (gupta-brahmacāriṇī), and she dwelt practicing many [austerities] such as the fourth, sixth, and eighth [fasts].

Then, on a certain occasion, the noble lady Sūmālikā approached the noble ladies of the Gōvāliya group; having approached, she paid homage and reverence to them, and having paid homage and reverence, she spoke thus: "O noble ladies!
