With your permission, I wish to dwell outside the city of Campā, not far from the Subhūmibhāga park, performing the penance of fasting every sixth meal, without interruption, facing the sun while practicing heat-exposure."

Then those cowherd girls said this to the noble lady Sūmālikā: "O Noble Lady! We are Śramaṇīs, Nigranthīs, restrained in our conduct (*īryā-samitā*), and so forth, up to being chaste in our conduct (*gupta-brahmacāriṇī*). It is not indeed permissible for us to wander outside a village or even a settlement every sixth day and so forth. However, it is permissible for us to perform the *āyāva* (exposure to heat) within the enclosure of the residence, walking in a line along a level path. Then Sūmālikā did not believe, did not trust, and did not accept this matter from the cowherd girls; not believing, not trusting, and not accepting it, she continued her practice every sixth day and so forth in the vicinity, not far from the Subhūmibhāga garden.

There, in Campā, lived a gang named Laliyā; they had been granted leave by the king, were beloved by the citizens, free from personal thirst [for wealth], made their home in the pleasure quarters of courtesans, were preeminent in various kinds of misconduct, wealthy, and so forth, up to being beyond reproach.

There, in Campā, there was a courtesan named Devadattā, beautiful as described in the *Aṇḍanāya* [story]. Once, on a certain occasion, five companions from that group were enjoying the splendor of the Subhūmibhāga garden together with the courtesan Devadattā. There, one companion held the courtesan Devadattā on his lap; one held a sunshade over her back; one arranged a flower garland for her; one adorned her feet; and one performed the waving of a fly-whisk.

Then, the noble lady Sūmālikā saw the courtesan Devadattā enjoying magnificent human pleasures in the company of those five libertine men; having seen her, this thought arose within her: "Aha! This woman is experiencing the results of her ancient and long-standing karmas... [as previously described] ...and so she dwells. If there is indeed a specific auspicious fruit and result of this well-practiced life of austerity, discipline, and celibacy, then may I too, in a future birth, enjoy such magnificent [pleasures] as these. Having thus made a formal vow (*niyāṇa*), she descended from the terrace for self-mortification.

Then that noble lady Sūmālikā became obsessed with her physical body; she repeatedly washed her hands, washed her feet, washed her head, washed her face, washed the space between her breasts, washed the space between her armpits, and washed the space of her private parts. Furthermore, whenever she occupied a standing place, a bed, or a sitting area, she would first sprinkle it with water and only afterwards occupy that standing place, bed, or sitting area.

Then those cowherd nuns said this to the noble Sūmālikā: "Indeed, noble lady, we are Śramaṇīs, Nigranthīs, restrained in our conduct (*iryāsamiti*), and so forth, up to being observers of the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). It is not permissible for us to indulge in bodily adornment. Yet you, noble lady, are constantly washing your hands and so forth, and even applying ointments. Therefore, dear lady, confess this matter and renounce it. Then Sūmālikā neither accepted nor acknowledged this matter from the cowherd nuns; not accepting it and not acknowledging it, she continued her life as before.

Then those nuns frequently reviled, insulted, and disparaged the noble Sūmāliyā, repeatedly forbidding her from this matter. While being thus reviled and forbidden by the Śramaṇī Nigaṇṭhīs, this reflection arose within the mind of Sūmāliyā: "When I lived in the midst of the household life, I was my own mistress; but now that I have become shaven-headed and gone forth, I am under the control of others. Formerly the nuns honored me and recognized me, but now they neither honor nor recognize me. Therefore, it is best for me to depart tomorrow at dawn from the presence of the noble Gopālikā nuns, and having entered a separate dwelling, to dwell there. Having reflected thus, she departed at dawn from the presence of the noble Gopālikā nuns, entered a separate dwelling, and dwelt there.

Then that noble lady Sūmālikā, unrestrained, unforbidden, and acting according to her own will, frequently washed and anointed her hands; yet even there, she was one who lived near [the laity], living like those who live near; she was lax, living in laxity; she was indolent, living in indolence; she was attached, living in attachment. Having completed the ascetic career for many years, and having performed the half-monthly *saṃlekhanā* (austerity), without having examined or repented for that state, when the time came, she passed away and was reborn as a celestial courtesan in a certain celestial mansion in the Īśāna heaven. The lifespan of some goddesses there is declared to be nine *palyopamas*; the lifespan of the goddess Sūmālikā there is also declared to be nine *palyopamas*.

At that time, in that very era, here in Jambūdvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, in the country of Pañcāla, there was a city named Kampillapura—its description [is as follows]. There, a king named Duvaia reigned—his description [is as follows]. His queen was Culaṇī, and Prince Dhaṭṭhajjuṇa was the crown prince.

Then, that queen Sūmālikā, upon the exhaustion of her lifespan in that celestial world, having passed away, was reborn right here on the island of Jambudvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, in the country of Pañcāla, in the city of Kampillapura, in the womb of Queen Culaṇī, the wife of King Duvaya, as a female child. Then, after nine months had passed, Queen Culaṇī gave birth to a daughter. When twelve days had elapsed for that girl, they gave her this name: "Since this girl is the daughter of King Duvaya and Queen Culaṇī, let the name of this girl be Dōvaī. Then her parents gave her this appropriate name, derived from her qualities: Dōvaī, Dōvaī.

Then that maiden Dovaī, attended by five nurses, grew up happily and without hindrance like a *campaka* creeper clinging to a mountain cave; she flourished in comfort until she reached the end of childhood and attained a fully developed body. Then, on another occasion, the women of the inner apartments bathed the noble princess Dovaī, adorned her with all ornaments, and sent her to pay homage at the feet of King Duvaī. Thereupon, the noble princess Dovaī went to where King Duvaī was, and having approached him, she took hold of King Duvaī’s feet.

Then King Duvaya placed the maiden Dovaī upon his lap; having placed her there, he was filled with wonder at the beauty, youth, and loveliness of Dovaī, the excellent royal maiden, and spoke thus to her: "My daughter, for whichever king or crown prince I myself shall give you as a wife, whether you become happy or unhappy under him, that will cause me a burning in my heart for as long as I live. Therefore, my daughter, I grant you a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage). Since you have been granted a *svayaṃvara*, whatever king or crown prince you yourself choose, he shall be your husband. Having said this, he comforted her with those pleasing words and so forth, and having comforted her, he dismissed her.

Then King Duvaya summoned a messenger and spoke to him thus: "Go, dear sir, to the city of Dvārāvatī. There, you must—with palms joined, ten fingers extended, and the head bowed in salutation—greet with cries of 'Victory! and 'Prosperity! Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva; the ten Dāśārhas headed by Samudravijaya; the five great heroes headed by Baladeva; the sixteen thousand kings headed by Ugrasena; the four and a half million princes headed by Pradyumna; the sixty thousand wild warriors headed by Śamba; the twenty-one thousand heroic men headed by Vīrasena; the fifty-six thousand soldiers headed by Mahāsena; and many others, including the lords of regions, provincial governors, district officials, householders, wealthy merchants, guild-leaders, and caravan chiefs. Having greeted them thus, speak as follows:"

"Thus indeed, O beloved of the gods! In the city of Kampillapura, there will be a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage) for Queen Dōvaī, the daughter of King Duvaia, the granddaughter of Cūlaṇī, and the sister of Prince Dhaṭṭhajjuṇa. Therefore, showing favor to King Duvaia, you must arrive at the city of Kampillapura without delay. Then the messenger, having grasped [the command] with his palms together, assented to this matter of King Duvaia. Having assented, he went to his own home and summoned his household servants. Having summoned them, he spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, prepare a four-bell chariot drawn by horses! They likewise prepared it. Then that messenger, having bathed and adorned his body with many costly ornaments, mounted the four-bell chariot. Surrounded by many men equipped with armor and bearing weapons, he departed through the middle of the city of Kampillapura. He traveled through the middle of the Pañcāla country and arrived at its border. He traveled through the middle of the Suraṭṭha country and arrived at the city of Bāravaī. Having entered the city of Bāravaī through its center, he went to the outer assembly hall of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva. Having arrived, he stopped the four-bell chariot, descended from the chariot, and—surrounded by a throng of men—proceeded on foot to where Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was. Having arrived, he [announced] Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, Samudravijaya and the other ten Daśārhas, and up to the fifty-three thousand Bāhlika warriors, with his palms joined together, and so forth, until [he delivered the message]: "Please come."

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the mouth of that messenger, with a heart joyful, satisfied, and glad, honored and respected that messenger; having honored and respected him, he dismissed him.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva summoned his household servants and spoke to them thus: "Go, dear ones, and strike the *sāmudāyika* drum in the Sudharmā assembly hall. Then those household servants, with palms joined [in reverence], assented to this matter of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva’s and went to where the *sāmudāyika* drum was in the Sudharmā assembly hall; having arrived, they struck the *sāmudāyika* drum with a very great sound.

When that *sāmudāyikā* drum was struck, the ten *daśārhas* headed by Samudravijaya, up to the fifty-six thousand *balavaga* warriors headed by Mahāsena, bathed and adorned themselves according to their wealth, prosperity, and honor. Some on horseback, others on elephants, and some on foot, they proceeded to where Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was; having arrived, with palms joined in reverence, they greeted Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva with cries of "Victory! and "Triumph! (jaya-vijaya).

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva summoned his household servants and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Prepare the royal elephant for the consecration ceremony. [The servants] prepared the horses, elephants, and so forth, and returned [to report]. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva went to the bathing hall; having gone there, he mounted the lord of elephants—which was beautiful with its complete lattice-work and ornaments, and resembled a peak of the Añjana mountain—the king of men.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, surrounded by the ten Dāsārhas headed by Samudravijaya, and accompanied by many thousands of courtesans headed by Anaṅgasenā, set out from the city of Dvārakā through its very center with full splendor and a great roar. He traveled through the middle of the Surāṣṭra country until he reached the border of the region; then, traveling through the middle of the Pañcāla country, he directed his course toward the city of Kampilyapura.

Then King Duvaya summoned a second messenger and spoke thus: "Go, dear sir, to the city of Hastināpura. There, you must—with palms joined in reverence and so forth—bring together King Pāṇḍu along with his sons: Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva, and Duḥśāsana; as well as Bhīṣma, Vidura, Droṇa, Jayadratha, Śakuni, Kīva, and Āśvatthāman, accompanied by their entire retinue of brothers. Then depart just as before! Then that messenger replied: "Just as [described] regarding Vāsudeva, except that there is no war-drum (bhērī); [he departed] toward the city of Kampillapura."

In this very order: as the second messenger, go to the city of Campā; there you must, with palms joined [in reverence], approach King Kṛṣṇa, the ruler of Aṅga, and likewise [deliver my message] until you have arrived. As the fourth messenger, go to the city of Suttimati; there you must, with palms joined, approach Śiśupāla, the son of Damaghosa, who is surrounded by five hundred brothers, and likewise [deliver my message] until you have arrived. As the fifth messenger, go to the city of Hastiśīrṣa; there you must, with palms joined, approach King Damadanta, and likewise [deliver my message] until you have arrived. As the sixth messenger, go to the city of Mathurā; there you must, with palms joined, approach King Dhara, and likewise [deliver my message] until you have arrived. As the seventh messenger, go to the city of Rājagṛha; there you must, with palms joined, approach Sahadeva, the son of Jarāsandha, and likewise [deliver my message] until you have arrived. As the eighth messenger, go to the city of Koṭiṇṇa; there you must, with palms joined, approach Rūpin, the son of Bheṣaka, and likewise [deliver my message] until you have arrived. As the ninth messenger, go to the city of Virāṭa; there you must, with palms joined, approach Kīyaga, together with his assembly of brothers, and likewise [deliver my message] until you have arrived. As the tenth messenger, go to all the remaining villages, towns, and cities, and approach the many thousands of kings there, and likewise [deliver my message] until you have arrived.

Then that messenger departed in the same manner and arrived at the villages, towns, and so forth, until he reached the assembly. Then those many thousands of kings, having heard and understood this matter from the mouth of that messenger, were delighted; they honored and respected that messenger and dismissed him.

Then those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, each having bathed and being equipped with fastened armor and breastplates, mounted upon the best of elephant-shoulders, surrounded by a great multitude of horses, elephants, chariots, foot soldiers, and crowds of attendants, set out from their respective cities and proceeded toward the Pañcāla country.

Then King Duvaia summoned his household officials and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Go, dear friends! Outside the city of Kampillapura, not far from the great river Gaṅgā, construct a great self-choice pavilion (svayaṃvara-maṇḍapa), supported by many hundreds of pillars, adorned with graceful statues of Salibhañjikā figures, and so forth, until [the completion of its description]. They did as they were told and returned.

Then King Duvaya summoned his household officials for a second time, and having summoned them, spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, prepare dwellings for many thousands of kings, with Vāsudeva at their head! They, having prepared them, reported back to him.

Then King Duvaya, having learned of the arrival of many thousands of kings headed by Vāsudeva, mounted each on the back of an elephant and surrounded by [his retinue], took tribute and offerings and, with full majesty, departed from Kampillapura. Having departed, he went to where those many thousands of kings headed by Vāsudeva were; having arrived, he honored and respected those headed by Vāsudeva with tribute and offerings, and he assigned separate lodgings for each of those headed by Vāsudeva.

Then those [leaders], headed by Vāsudeva, went to their respective dwellings; having arrived, they dismounted from the backs of their elephants, and having dismounted, each established his own military camp. Having done so, they entered their respective dwellings, and having entered, they sat down and reclined upon their seats and beds in their respective dwellings, and they dwelt there while being entertained with many songs and dances.

Then those two kings entered the city of Kampillapura; having entered, they had abundant solid food, soft food, chewable food, and tastable food prepared. Having had it prepared, they summoned their household officials and spoke thus: "Go, dear sirs, and distribute the abundant solid food, etc., as well as liquor, wine, meat, *sīdhu* spirit, and *prasanna* spirit, along with a great quantity of flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, to the residences of the thousands of kings headed by Vāsudeva. And they distributed them accordingly.

Then those people, headed by Vāsudeva, remained there eating, tasting, relishing, and enjoying that abundant food and drink with a serene mind. And when they had finished their meal and retired from the table, having come back and sat upon excellent comfortable seats, they remained there engaged in various musical performances and other diversions.

Then, in the late afternoon, King Duvaya summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "Go, dear friends, through the triple-crossroads, the squares, and the thoroughfares of Kampillapura, and at the residences of the thousands of kings headed by Vāsudeva, mounted upon the backs of excellent elephants, proclaim with a very loud voice, and so on, making a proclamation, saying: 'Listen, dear friends! Tomorrow, when the night has turned to dawn, there will be a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage) for Queen Dōvaī, the daughter of King Duvaya, the granddaughter of Queen Culaṇī, and the sister of Ghaṭṭajjuṇa. Therefore, dear friends, out of favor toward King Duvaya, you should come having bathed, adorned with all ornaments, mounted upon the backs of excellent elephants, holding white lotuses and excellent white chowries, accompanied by horses, elephants, and chariots, surrounded by a great multitude of soldiers and attendants, and proceed to the *svayaṃvara* pavilion. Having arrived, each of you shall sit down on seats marked with your respective names, and remaining there, wait upon Queen Dōvaī, the princess. Proclaim this announcement, and having done so, report back to me that my command has been carried out. Then those household officials did exactly as instructed, and so on, until they reported back."

Then King Duvaya summoned his household officials and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Go, dear friends! Prepare the Svayaṃvara pavilion—sprinkled, swept, and smeared [with cow dung], perfumed with the scent of excellent fragrances, adorned with offerings of five-colored flowers, made fragrant by black aloe-wood, the finest *kundurukka*, *turukka*, and so forth, up to incense-sticks; and furnished with tiered couches. Have it prepared, and once prepared, have it completed. Then prepare individual seats engraved with the names of the many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, arranged in rows one after another. Having done so, report back that this command has been fulfilled. They likewise did so, up until they reported back.

Then those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, having risen early at dawn, bathed, and adorned themselves with all ornaments, mounted upon the backs of excellent elephants, holding white fly-whisks with golden handles, surrounded by horses, elephants, and [other retinues], proceeded with full splendor and a great clamor to the Svayaṃvara pavilion. Having arrived, they entered; having entered, they sat down each on his own seat marked with his name, waiting and waiting for the noble princess Dōvaī.

Then, on the following day, King Paṇḍuka—having bathed and being adorned with all ornaments—mounted upon the back of a preeminent elephant, holding a white lotus and fanned by two excellent white chowries, proceeded through the very center of the city of Kampillapura amidst a multitude of horses and elephants. He went to the self-choice pavilion where many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, were gathered; having arrived, he greeted them with palms joined in reverence, and standing in attendance, he held a white chowrie for Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.

Then, on the following day, that princess Dōvaī went to the bath-house; having arrived there, she bathed, performed her ritual offerings (*balikamma*), and completed the auspicious purificatory rites (*kōuya-maṅgala-pāyacchitta*). Having put on pure, clean, and auspicious garments of excellent quality, she emerged from the bath-house. She went to the temple of the Jina; having arrived, she entered the temple and paid homage to the images of the Jinas upon seeing them. She took hold of a brush for cleaning hair (*lōmahatthaya*) and, just as Sūriyābha worships the Jina images, so too should it be described here, up until the burning of incense. She lowered her left knee, placed her right knee upon the surface of the ground, and bowed her head three times to the earth. Rising slightly, she joined her palms together [in reverence] and spoke thus: "Homage be to the Arhats, the Blessed Ones, [and so forth,] unto those who have attained perfection. She paid homage and prostrated herself; having done so, she departed from the temple of the Jina and went to the inner apartments.

Then the women of the inner apartments adorned Dōvaī, the excellent daughter of the king, with all kinds of ornaments. What [ornaments] were they? Excellent anklets for her feet, and so forth, until she was surrounded by a circle of maidservants and a multitude of great ladies. Having departed from the inner apartments, she went to the outer assembly hall where the four-bell chariot stood; having approached it, she mounted the four-bell chariot along with Kiḍḍāviyā and Lēhiyā. Then the prince Dhaṭṭajjuṇa acted as the charioteer for Dōvaī, the excellent daughter of the king. Then Dōvaī, the excellent daughter of the king, proceeded through the middle of the city of Kampillapura to the Svayaṃvara pavilion. Having arrived, she stopped the chariot and descended from it. Having descended, she entered the Svayaṃvara pavilion together with Kiḍḍāviyā and Lēhiyā. With palms joined in reverence, ten-fingered and turned toward her head, she placed them at her forehead and paid homage to those many thousands of excellent kings, headed by Vāsudēva. Then Dōvaī, the excellent princess, took a large cluster of garlands—what [flowers]? Pāṭala, Mallikā, Campaka, and so on, up to Saptacchada trees—emitting a fragrant scent, supremely pleasant to the touch, beautiful to behold. Then Kiḍḍāviyā, who was beautiful, and so forth, took a small mirror in her left hand and, with graceful movements, showed the reflection of the image in the mirror to him with her right hand, saying, "O lion among excellent kings! With speech that was clear, distinct, pure, resonant, deep, and sweet, she described the lineage, power, capability, clan, valor, splendor, various traditional sciences, greatness, beauty, family, and character of all those monarchs, as well as their mothers and fathers. First, she praised the heroes of the Daśārhas, the bulls among men, the foremost warriors of the three worlds, the subduers of hundreds of thousands of enemies, the excellent white lotuses of the Bhavasiddhiya clan, describing their strength, heroism, beauty, youth, virtues, and charm. Then she spoke of the Yādavas beginning with Ugrasēṇa: "Choose, O lady endowed with good fortune and beauty, from these excellent men who are like scent-elephants, him who shall become the lord of your heart."

Then Dōvaī, the princess, as she moved through the midst of many thousands of excellent kings, being repeatedly urged on by her own past karmic causes (niyāṇa), approached the five Pāṇḍavas. Having approached them, she surrounded and encircled those five Pāṇḍavas with a garland of flowers of ten colors. Having done so, she spoke thus: "These five Pāṇḍavas have been chosen by me. Then those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudēva, crying out with a very great sound, exclaimed: "Well-chosen indeed is Dōvaī, the princess! Having said this, they departed from the Svayaṃvara pavilion. Having departed, they went each to his own respective residence.

Then Dhaṭṭhajjuṇa the prince caused the five Pāṇḍavas and the princess Dōvaī to mount the four-bell chariot; having mounted them, he entered his own palace through the very center of the city of Kampillapura.

Then King Druvaya had the five Pāṇḍavas and the princess Dōvaī ascend the throne; having had them ascend, he had them bathed with white and yellow jars; he had the fire-oblation performed and caused the marriage ceremony of the five Pāṇḍavas and Dōvaī to be conducted. Then King Druvaya bestowed this kind of gift of joy upon Dōvaī, the princess: namely, eight crores of gold coins, and so on, up to eight maidservants who perform domestic tasks; and he bestowed other abundant wealth, gold, and so forth. Then King Druvaya dismissed those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudēva, after providing them with abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies, as well as flowers, garments, perfumes, and so on.

Then King Paṇḍu, with his palms joined [in reverence] toward those many thousands of kings headed by Vāsudeva, spoke thus: "Truly, dear sirs, in the city of Hastināpura, there will be a festival of auspiciousness for the five Pāṇḍavas and Queen Dōvaī. Therefore, dear sirs, out of favor toward me, please assemble here without delay."

Then those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, each individually prepared themselves for the journey. Then King Paṇḍu summoned his household officials and said to them: "Go, dear friends, and have five magnificent palaces constructed in the city of Hasthināura for the five Pāṇḍavas—palaces that are lofty, towering, [described] as in the standard description, and beautiful. Those household officials assented and had them built. Then King Paṇḍu, accompanied by the five Pāṇḍavas and Queen Dōvaī, surrounded by horses, elephants, and [the rest], departed from Kampillapura and arrived at Hasthināura.

Then King Paṇḍu, having learned of the arrival of those [guests] headed by Vāsudeva, summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "Go, dear friends! Outside the city of Hastināpura, prepare dwellings for the many thousands of kings headed by Vāsudeva—dwellings provided with many hundreds of pillars—and having done so, report back to me as before. They did exactly so and reported back.

Then those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, arrived at Hastināpura. When King Pāṇḍu learned that those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, had arrived at Hastināpura, he was delighted and overjoyed; having bathed and performed the ritual offerings (*balikamma*), as described in the *Duvālasaṅga* [scripture], he provided them with dwellings according to their rank.

Then those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, went each to his own respective residence and stayed there as previously described. Then King Paṇḍu entered the city of Hastināpura; having entered, he summoned his household officials and spoke to them thus: "O beloved of the gods, prepare abundant food, drink, edibles, and delicacies," and so on, until they had finished their preparations. Then King Paṇḍu had the five Pāṇḍavas and Queen Dōvaī ascend a palanquin. Having made them ascend, he bathed them with white and blue jars; having bathed them, he performed auspicious rites. He then honored and respected those many thousands of kings, headed by Vāsudeva, with abundant food, flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Having honored and respected them, he dismissed them. Then those many [kings], headed by Vāsudeva, departed as they had come.

Then those five Pāṇḍavas, together with Queen Draupadī and the entire retinue of the inner apartments, spent their time day after day, taking turns, enjoying magnificent pleasures. Then, on another occasion, King Pāṇḍu, surrounded by the five Pāṇḍavas, Queen Kuntī, and Queen Draupadī, as well as the entire retinue of the inner apartments, was seated upon his excellent lion-throne.

And this Kacchulla Nārada—by his very appearance most auspicious and disciplined, yet inwardly turbid-hearted; appearing outwardly as one who is impartial, friendly, and pleasant to behold; handsome, dressed in clean and whole garments; with a black antelope skin draped over his chest as an upper garment; holding a staff and a water-pot in his hands; with matted locks shining upon his head; wearing a sacrificial thread, a girdle of muñja grass, and a deer-skin; carrying a hand-made lute (*kacchapī*); fond of perfumes; preeminent among those who move upon the earth; renowned for his fame in many *vidyādhari* spells such as those for concealment, protection, descending, ascending, and adhesion, as well as for the *saṅkāṇī*, *ābhiyogī*, *prajñaptī*, *gamaṇī*, and *stambhinī* spells; beloved by Rāma and Keśava; the heart’s darling of the half-million Yādava youths including Pradyumna, Pṛthu, Sāmba, Aniruddha, Niṣadha, Umraya, Sāraṇa, Gaja, Sumukha, Durmukha, and others; fond of quarrels, battles, and tumultuous noise; longing for strife; delighting in the sight of many hundreds of battles; constantly seeking out quarrels along with their rewards; a source of unrest to the noble heroes of the Daśārhas and the strongest men in the three worlds—he, having summoned that venerable *pakkamaṇī* (the "quick-going" spell) which is skilled in traveling through the sky, flew up and soared into the heavens. Crossing over villages, towns, cities, market towns, hamlets, mountain settlements, ports, and royal capitals, he traversed the beautiful land of the earth, which was adorned with thousands of settlements and teeming with people. He arrived at the lovely city of Hastināpura and descended suddenly and swiftly into the palace of King Pāṇḍu.

Then King Paṇḍu, seeing Kacchulla Nārada approaching, rose from his seat together with his five sons and Queen Kuntī; having risen, he went forward to meet Kacchulla Nārada seven or eight paces; having gone forward to meet him, he performed three circumambulations from left to right; having performed them, he paid homage and saluted him; having paid homage and saluted him, he invited him to a most worthy seat.

Then that Kacchulla Nārada sat down upon a cushion made of Darbha grass moistened with water and spread out over it; having sat down, he inquired after the welfare of King Paṇḍu, as well as [the welfare] of the queen Kuntī, the five Pāṇḍavas, and the harem. Then King Paṇḍu, Queen Kuntī, and the five Pāṇḍavas honored Kacchulla Nārada and so forth, and attended upon him. But Queen Draupadī, perceiving that Kacchulla Nārada was uncontrolled, unrestrained, and had not renounced or turned away from sinful deeds, did not honor him, nor acknowledge him, nor rise for him, nor attend upon him.

Then, this kind of internal reflection, thought, aspiration, and mental resolve arose in that Kacchulla Nārada: "Alas! Queen Dōvaī, though endowed with such beauty and loveliness, being attended by the five Pāṇḍavas, does not honor me nor wait upon me. Therefore, it is indeed better for me to do what is displeasing to Queen Dōvaī. Having thus reflected, he took leave of King Paṇḍu; having taken leave, he invoked the *Uppayaṇī* (flight) spell. Having invoked it, with great speed and by way of the flight of the Vidyādharas, he set out to cross through the very middle of the salt ocean toward the east.

At that time, in that period, on the island of Ghātaiṣaṇḍa, in the southern half of the eastern region of Bharata, there was a royal capital named Aparakaṅkā. There, in that royal capital of Aparakaṅkā, there was a king named Padmanābha—[described] with the standard epithet beginning with "great like Himavat" (*mahāhimavanta*). That King Padmanābha had seven thousand queens in his harem. That King Padmanābha also had a son named Sunābha who was the crown prince (*yuvarāja*). Then, that King Padmanābha, surrounded by his harem within the inner apartments, was dwelling upon an excellent lion-throne.

Then that Kacchulla Nārada went to the royal capital of Aparakanka, to the palace of King Padmanābha; having arrived, he descended with great speed and haste into King Padmanābha’s palace. Then King Padmanābha saw Kacchulla Nārada approaching; seeing him, he rose from his seat and, having risen, invited him with honor and so forth, including offering him a seat. Then Kacchulla Nārada sat down on a cushion spread over a layer of Darbha grass sprinkled with water, and [the king] inquired after his welfare and well-being.

Then King Padmanābha, his curiosity aroused by his own retinue, spoke thus to Kacchulla Nārada: "O beloved of the gods, you enter many villages and even houses; have you ever, O beloved of the gods, seen anywhere a retinue such as this one of mine? When he had been addressed thus by Padmanābha, Kacchulla Nārada smiled slightly and said: "O Padmanābha, you are like that frog in the pit! Who, O beloved of the gods, is that frog? [The rest of the narrative proceeds] just as in the case of Mallī: "Truly, O beloved of the gods, on the island of Jambudvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, in the city of Hastināpura, there was the daughter of King Duppaya, the granddaughter of Queen Culaṇī, the daughter-in-law of Paṇḍu, and the wife of the five Pāṇḍavas—the queen named Draupadī. In beauty and so forth, she possessed an exceedingly excellent body. Compared to even a severed toe-nail of Queen Draupadī, this entire retinue of yours does not equal even a sixteenth part," and so on, until having spoken thus, he took leave of Padmanābha and departed in the same direction from which he had appeared.

Then King Padmanābha, having heard and reflected upon this matter from the presence of the rogue Nārada, became infatuated with, attached to, greedy for, and obsessed by the beauty, youth, and loveliness of Queen Dōvaī. He went to the fasting hall (*pōsahasālā*), and having arrived, he spoke thus to the deity formerly associated with him within the fasting hall: "O beloved of the gods! In Jambūdvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, in Hastināpura... [there is a woman] with such a body. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, I desire that Queen Dōvaī be brought here quickly."

Then that former associate deity spoke thus to Paumanābha: "O beloved of the gods! It is certainly not possible—nor has it ever been, nor will it ever be—that Queen Dovaī, having left the five Pāṇḍavas, shall sport with any other man in such magnificent [pleasures]. Nevertheless, for the sake of your pleasure, I shall quickly bring Queen Dovaī here. Having said this, he took leave of Paumanābha; and having taken his leave, with great speed and so forth, he traveled through the very middle of the salt ocean toward the city of Hastināura.

At that time, in that very moment, King Yudhiṣṭhira was sleeping soundly on the upper terrace of his palace together with Queen Draupadī. Then that deity who had been his former associate went to where King Yudhiṣṭhira and Queen Draupadī were; having arrived, he removed the bedding from Queen Draupadī, took her, and departed by means of that same exalted celestial gait toward Aparakankā, to the palace of Padmanābha. Having arrived, he placed Queen Draupadī in the Aśoka grove within Padmanābha’s palace, removed the bedding, and went to where Padmanābha was. Having arrived, he spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods, this Queen Draupadī has been brought here by me from Hastināpura; she stays here in your Aśoka grove. From now on, you shall know her. Having said this, he departed in the same direction from which he had appeared.

Then, after a short while, Queen Dōvaī awoke; not recognizing that palace or the Aśoka grove, she spoke thus: "This is certainly not our own palace, nor is this our own Aśoka grove. It is not known by whom—whether by a god, a *dānava*, a *kiṃnara*, a *kimpuruṣa*, a *mahoraga*, or a *gandharva*—I have been brought to the Aśoka grove of another king. Having said this, with her mind and intentions overwhelmed, she remained brooding.

Then that Padmanābha, having bathed and being adorned with all ornaments, surrounded by his harem and retinue, went to where the Aśoka grove was and where Queen Dōvaī was. Having arrived, he saw Queen Dōvaī with a dejected mind and intent, sighing deeply. Seeing her, he spoke thus: "Why, O beloved of the gods, are you dejected in mind and sighing so deeply? Indeed, O beloved of the gods, you have been carried away from Jambudvīpa, from the continent of Bhārata, from the city of Hastināpura, and from the palace of King Yudhiṣṭhira, by a god who was your former companion. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, do not be dejected in mind and intent, nor sigh so deeply; rather, enjoy with me abundant pleasures and delights."

Then Queen Dōvaī spoke thus to Paümanābha: "O dear Lord! In Jambūdvīpa, in the land of Bhārata, in the city of Bāravaī, there dwells one named Kaṇha Vāsudēva, who is my beloved brother. If he does not come to my well within six months, then, O dear Lord, I shall abide by your command, favor, word, and instruction. Then Paümanābha consented to this matter of Queen Dōvaī; having consented, he established Queen Dōvaī in the inner apartments of his harem. Thereafter, Queen Dōvaī lived while cultivating her soul through a penance consisting of uninterrupted *āyambila* fasts performed every sixth meal-time.

Then, after a short while, King Yudhiṣṭhira woke up; not seeing Queen Draupadī by his side, he rose from his bed. Having risen, he conducted a search and inquiry for Queen Draupadī everywhere and on all sides. Failing to find any trace, sign, or news of Draupadī anywhere, he went to where King Pāṇḍu was and spoke to him thus: "O Father, while I was sleeping comfortably on the upper terrace, Queen Draupadī has disappeared from my side. It is not known whether she has been carried off, taken away, or abducted by some god, dānava, kinnara, kimpuruṣa, mahoraga, or gandharva. Therefore, O Father, I wish to conduct a search and inquiry for Queen Draupadī everywhere and on all sides."

Then King Paṇḍu summoned his household officials and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Go, dear sirs, through the triple-crossroads, triads, quadrangles, squares, crossroads, and highways in the city of Hastināpura, and making a great proclamation with a loud voice, say this: 'O dear sirs, while King Yudhiṣṭhira was sleeping comfortably on the upper terrace, Queen Draupadī has been carried off—whether by a god, a Dānava, a Kiṇṇara, a Kimpuruṣa, a Mahoraga, or a Gandharva; it is not known who took her, or whether she was stolen, abducted, or carried away. Therefore, O dear sirs, whoever reports news of Queen Draupadī’s ear, or even a single virtuous word concerning her, to him King Paṇḍu shall grant a vast reward of wealth. Having made this proclamation, report back that the command has been executed. Then those household officials [did as they were told] and reported back.

Then King Paṇḍu, finding no news, nor even a whisper, nor any report whatsoever concerning Queen Dōvaī, summoned Queen Kōntī and spoke to her thus: “Go, dear lady, to the city of Bāravaī and inform Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva of this matter: ‘May Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva undertake a search and inquiry for Queen Dōvaī; otherwise, it is not known whether one might obtain news, a whisper, or any report concerning Queen Dōvaī. Then Queen Kōntī, having been thus addressed by King Paṇḍu, agreed and assented. Having bathed and performed the ritual offerings (*balikamma*), she mounted the back of an elephant and departed through the middle of the city of Hatthiṇāura. She traveled through the middle of the Kuru country toward the Surāṣṭra country, toward the city of Bāravaī, and toward the royal garden (*aggujjāṇa*). Upon arrival, she dismounted from the elephant’s back and summoned her household servants, saying to them: “Go, dear friends, enter the city of Bāravaī. Having entered, with palms joined [in reverence], speak thus to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: ‘Indeed, Lord, your paternal aunt Kōntī has come here in haste from the city of Hatthiṇāura and longs for a sight of you.’”

When those householders’ men had reported this matter, Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, having heard and understood it from the presence of those householders’ men, was joyful and delighted. Mounted upon the back of an elephant, he proceeded through the middle of the city of Dvārāvatī toward Queen Kuntī. Having arrived, he dismounted from the elephant’s back; having dismounted, he took hold of Queen Kuntī’s feet. Having done so, he mounted the elephant together with Queen Kuntī. Having mounted it, he proceeded through the middle of the city of Dvārāvatī toward his own house. Having arrived, he entered his own house.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to Queen Kuntī, who had bathed, performed her ritual offerings, finished her meal, and was seated comfortably on an excellent couch: "Command me, O Mother! What is the purpose of your visit? Then Queen Kuntī spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: "Truly, my son, while King Yudhiṣṭhira was sleeping soundly on the roof-terrace of his palace in the city of Hastināpura, Queen Draupadī disappeared from his side. It is not known by whom she has been carried off, nor whether she has been abducted or simply left behind. Therefore, my son, I desire that a search and investigation for Queen Draupadī be conducted everywhere and in all directions."

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to his paternal aunt Kuntī: "O aunt, as soon as I obtain news or [other information] regarding Queen Draupadī, I shall personally bring Queen Draupadī from her feet, or from her palace, or from all parts of half-Bharata. Having said this, he honored and respected his paternal aunt Kuntī and dismissed her. Then Queen Kuntī, having been dismissed by Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, returned to the very direction from which she had appeared.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva summoned his household servants and said to them: "Go, dear ones, and cause a proclamation to be made in the city of Dvārakā, just as Paṇḍu did," and so on, until they returned and reported it just as Paṇḍu had. Then, on another occasion, while Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was staying within the inner apartments, seated upon a couch and so forth, the rogue Nārada arrived there; having sat down, he inquired after the welfare of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva said this to Kacchulla Nārada: "O dear one! You enter many villages, towns, and so forth; have you ever heard of, or indeed obtained any news regarding Queen Dōvaī? Then Kacchulla Nārada said this to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: "Indeed, O dear one! On another occasion, I went to the eastern half of the island of Ghāyatisaṇḍa, to the southern half of Bhārata-varṣa, to the capital city of Aparakaṅkā. There, in the palace of King Paümanābha, I saw Queen Dōvaī exactly as she had been seen before."

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva said this to Kacchulla Nārada: "O dear one, this is indeed the result of your own past karma. When Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva had spoken thus, Kacchulla Nārada summoned the magic power of flight (*uppayaṇi-vijjā*), and having summoned it, he departed in the very same direction from which he had appeared.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva summoned a messenger and spoke to him thus: "Go, dear sir, to the city of Hastināpura and inform King Pāṇḍu of this matter: 'O dear sir, news has been received regarding Queen Dvāpī from the palace of Padmanābha in the city of Aparakāñcī, in the southern half of the eastern region of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa island. Therefore, let the five Pāṇḍavas go, surrounded by their fourfold army, and wait for me at the eastern gate. Then that messenger said [as instructed], "Wait," and they likewise remained waiting.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva summoned his household servants and spoke to them thus: "Go, dear ones, and beat the battle-drum! They beat it. Then, having heard the sound of that battle-drum, the ten Dāśārhas headed by Samudravijaya, up to the fifty-six thousand soldiers, equipped with armor and fastened [with belts], having taken up their weapons and armaments—some mounted on horses, some mounted on elephants, and so forth, surrounded by hunting-nets—went to where the Sudharmā assembly hall was, and to where Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was; having arrived, they saluted him with palms joined together, and so forth.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, mounted upon the back of an elephant, with a parasol adorned with *koraṇṭa* flowers and garlands, under a white canopy, amidst a great multitude of horses, elephants, and a throng of infantry, chariots, and cavalry, departed through the very center of the city of Dvāravatī. Having departed, he went to the eastern gate; having arrived there, he met the five Pāṇḍavas together at one place. Having met them, he established his military camp and entered the fasting hall (*poṣadhaśālā*). Having entered, he remained there meditating upon the deity Suṣṭhita. Then, as the eighth meal-time (fast) of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was passing, the deity Suṣṭhita appeared before him and said, "O beloved of the gods! Tell me what must be done by me. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to the deity Suṣṭhita: "O beloved of the gods! Queen Dvāpāvatī has been carried away to the palace of Padmanābha. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, grant a path for me and my five Pāṇḍavas—six chariots in total—in the salt ocean, so that I may go to the well of Dvāpāvatī in the capital city of Aparakaṅkā."

Then that god Suṣṭhita spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: "O beloved of the gods! Just as Queen Dṛṣadvatī was carried away by the god who was formerly associated with King Padmanābha, even so shall I carry away Queen Dṛṣadvatī from Dhātakīkhaṇḍa Island in Bhārata to Hastināpura; or else, shall I cast King Padmanābha along with his city, army, and vehicles into the salt ocean? Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to the god Suṣṭhita: "O beloved of the gods! Do not carry away Queen Dṛṣadvatī from the city of Hastināpura or from the palace of King Yudhiṣṭhira; rather, O beloved of the gods, grant me a path through the salt ocean for six chariots—myself being the sixth along with the five Pāṇḍavas—and I myself shall go to the well of Dṛṣadvatī."

Then that god Suṣṭhita spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: "Let it be so; he shall grant passage through the salt ocean for six chariots, including himself as the sixth, together with the five Pāṇḍavas. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva dismissed his fourfold army; having dismissed it, he proceeded through the very middle of the salt ocean in six chariots, including himself as the sixth, together with the five Pāṇḍavas. Having passed through, he went to where the royal city of Aparakankā was, and to where the eastern garden of the royal city of Aparakankā was; having arrived, he stopped the chariot, and having stopped it, he summoned the charioteer Dāruka and spoke to him thus.

"Go, dear one! Enter the capital city of Aparakaṅkā. Having entered, kick King Padmanābha’s footstool with your left foot, and present the letter with the point of your spear. Having presented it, knitting your brows into three furrows on your forehead, furious, enraged, agitated, fierce, and hissing like a serpent, speak thus: 'O Padmanābha! You who seek what should not be sought, you whose characteristics are wretched and miserable, you who are devoid of merit, the fourteenth day of the moon, and destitute of fortune, modesty, steadfastness, and fame—you shall no longer exist today! Do you not know that Queen Dōvaī is the sister of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva? Since you have brought her here so hastily, now that this has happened, either return Queen Dōvaī to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, or else go forth prepared for battle. This Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, together with the five Pāṇḍavas, himself as the sixth, has come here in haste to the very well of Queen Dōvaī.'"

When the charioteer Dāruka had been thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, he was delighted and satisfied; he gave his assent, and having given his assent, he entered the capital city of Aparakaṅkā. Having entered, he went to where Padmanābha was, and having approached him, with palms joined [in reverence] and having offered salutations, he spoke as follows: "O Lord, this is my humble service, but this other matter is a command from my Lord. Having said this, he became enraged and stepped upon the footstool with his left foot. Having stepped upon it, he presented the letter with the point of his spear. Having presented it, he quickly returned to the well.

When Pauṣamanābha had been addressed thus by the charioteer Dāruka, he became enraged and, knitting his brows into three furrows upon his forehead, spoke as follows: "O beloved of the gods, I shall not surrender Draupadī to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva; rather, I myself will go out prepared for battle. Having said this, he spoke to the charioteer Dāruka: "Furthermore, O sir, among royal retinues, an envoy is not to be slain. Having said this, he dismissed him without honor or respect and expelled him through a side gate. Then the charioteer Dāruka, having been dishonored and expelled by King Pauṣamanābha, went to where Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was. Upon arriving, with palms joined [in reverence], he approached Kṛṣṇa and spoke as follows: "It is indeed so, Lord; at your command, [I was sent], and he has expelled me."

Then Pauṣmanābha summoned his commander-in-chief and said to him: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, prepare the royal elephant for the consecration. Immediately thereafter, through the skillful instructions, mental calculations, and deliberations of the master artisans, [the elephant] was brought forth. Then Pauṣmanābha, having equipped himself for battle, mounted the royal elephant for the consecration and, accompanied by horses and elephants, set out toward where Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva saw King Padmanābha approaching, and having seen him, he spoke thus to those five Pāṇḍavas: "Ho, young men! Will you fight with Padmanābha, or will you merely look on? Then those five Pāṇḍavas spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: "O Lord, we shall fight; you may look on. Then those five Pāṇḍavas, equipped with armor and weapons, mounted their chariots. Having mounted them, they went to where King Padmanābha was, and having arrived, they spoke thus: "Whether it be us or King Padmanābha! Having said this, they engaged in combat with Padmanābha.

Then King Padmanābha quickly caused those five Pāṇḍavas to be driven away in every direction, their excellent horses slain, their preeminent heroes killed, and their banners, standards, and flags cast down. When they had been thus driven away by King Padmanābha—having their horses slain, their preeminent [heroes] killed, and so forth—they became powerless and, concluding that it was impossible to hold out, went to where Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to those five Pāṇḍavas: "How indeed, dear friends, did you engage in battle with King Padmanābha? Then the five Pāṇḍavas spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: "It was thus, dear friend: having been permitted by you, we equipped ourselves for battle, mounted our chariots, and went to where King Padmanābha was... [and so on] until he repelled us. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to those five Pāṇḍavas: "If, dear friends, you had spoken thus—'We shall not engage in battle with King Padmanābha'—and had not engaged him, then you would not have been repelled by Padmanābha with your horses slain, your men crushed, and your finest [troops] destroyed. Behold, dear friends, how I, thinking 'I shall not engage King Padmanābha,' mount my chariot with the intent, 'I will fight with King Padmanābha. Having mounted it, I go to where King Padmanābha is; having approached, I grasp the Pañcajanya conch—which is as white as a stream of cow's milk, resembling Sinduvāra flowers and jasmine buds, which brings joy to one's own army and causes the destruction of the enemy host—and having grasped it, I blow it with the breath of my mouth."

Then, by that sound of the conch, one-third of Paumanābha’s army—consisting of horses and so forth—was repelled. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva took up his bow; having taken it up, he drew the bow, and having drawn it, he made the sound of the bowstring.

Then, by that sound of the bow, the second third of Paumanābha’s army was struck down, crushed, and so forth, until it was repelled. Consequently, King Paumanābha, with only one-third of his army remaining, being powerless, weak, devoid of heroism, and lacking manly effort and prowess, thinking, "This is unsustainable," quickly and hurriedly went to Avarakaṅkā. Having arrived, he entered the capital city of Avarakaṅkā; having entered, he closed the gates and remained prepared for defense. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva went to Avarakaṅkā; having arrived, he halted his chariot, descended from the chariot, and underwent a transformational emission (*vaikriyasamudghāta*). He manifested the form of a great lion-man and, with a very loud roar, made a great earth-shaking stampede with his feet.

When Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva raised a great, tumultuous roar with his feet, the royal capital of Aparakanka—with its walls, gate-towers, battlements, archways, and magnificent palaces shattered—collapsed onto the surface of the earth with a loud crash. Then King Padmanābha, seeing the royal capital of Aparakanka thus shattered and destroyed, became terrified and sought refuge with Queen Dvāpāṛī.

Then Queen Dōvaī said this to King Paümanābha: "O beloved of the gods! Do you not know that by doing what is displeasing to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudēva, the Supreme Being, you have caused me to be brought here? Since this is so, go now, O beloved of the gods! Having bathed, wearing wet garments and fresh clothes, surrounded by your harem attendants, and taking the finest and most excellent jewels, place me before you and go for refuge to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudēva, prostrating yourself with palms joined at his feet; for, O beloved of the gods, Supreme Beings are affectionate toward those who bow before them."

Then Pauṣmanābha, having assented to this matter of Queen Dōvaī, bathed and [performed his daily rites] until he approached Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva for refuge. Having approached him, with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus: "The power, wealth, and prowess of the Lord are truly seen! Therefore, O Lord, I beg your pardon; may you forgive me so that I shall not act in such a way again and again. Having said this, with palms joined and prostrating at his feet, he personally presented Queen Dōvaī to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to Pauṣmanābha: "Ha! O Pauṣmanābha, you who pray for what is undesired, you whose characteristics are wretched and miserable, you who are devoid of merit like the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, and you who are abandoned by fortune, modesty, steadfastness, and glory—do you not know that Dōvaī, my sister, is a queen? Even though you have brought her here by force, even so, there is no longer any fear for you from me. Having said this, he dismissed Pauṣmanābha, took Queen Dōvaī, mounted his chariot, and drove to where the five Pāṇḍavas were. Having arrived, he personally presented Queen Dōvaī to the five Pāṇḍavas.

Then that Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, together with the five Pāṇḍavas—six in all, including himself—set out in six chariots through the middle of the salt ocean toward Jambūdvīpa, specifically toward the region of Bhārata.

At that time and on that occasion, in the eastern half of the island of Ghātakīkhaṇḍa, in the region of Bhārata, there was a city named Campā and a shrine named Pūrṇabhadra. There, in the city of Campā, there was a king named Kapila Vāsudeva, [possessing] the great Himavat-like [splendor]; his description is as follows.

At that time, in that period, the Arhat Munisuvrata had arrived at Campā in the Punnabhadda park. Kaviḷa Vāsudeva was listening to the Dharma. While Kaviḷa Vāsudeva was listening to the Dharma in the presence of the Arhat Munisuvrata, he heard the sound of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva’s conch shell. Then, this kind of reflection arose within Kaviḷa Vāsudeva: "I wonder, has a second Vāsudeva appeared in Bhārata-varṣa on the island of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa? For the sound of his conch shell spreads forth, filled by the breath of his mouth, just like mine. Kaviḷa Vāsudeva heard [the sound]. The Arhat Munisuvrata spoke thus to Kaviḷa Vāsudeva: "O Kaviḷa Vāsudeva, while you were listening to the Dharma in my presence, having heard the sound of the conch shell, did this kind of reflection arise within you... [as before] ...until 'it spreads forth'? O Kaviḷa Vāsudeva, is this matter true? "Yes, it is true," [he replied]. "O Kaviḷa, it is certainly not possible—nor has it ever been, nor will it ever be—that two Arhats, or two Cakravartins, or two Baladevas, or two Vāsudevas should appear, do appear, or will appear in one field, in one age, at one time. Indeed, O Vāsudeva, from Jambūdvīpa, from Bhārata-varṣa, from the city of Hastināpura, Queen Draupadī—the daughter-in-law of King Paṇḍu and the wife of the five Paṇḍavas—was carried away to the city of Aparakaṅkā by a god who was formerly associated with you, King Padmanābha."

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, together with the five Pāṇḍavas—six in all—quickly arrived at the well of Queen Dvāravatī in the capital city of Aparakaṅkā. While that Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was engaged in battle with King Pauṣamanābha, this sound of the conch, produced by the blowing of his own mouth, became as dear and beloved to him as if it were manifesting right here [in the presence of the Arhat]. Then that Kapila Vāsudeva paid homage and reverence to the Arhat Munisuvrata; having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: "I shall go, O Blessed One, to see Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, that supreme man, that peerless man."

Then the Arhat Munisuvrata spoke thus to Kāvila Vāsudeva: "Indeed, O Devānupriya, it has not happened, nor will it ever happen, that an Arhat should see another Arhat, a Cakravartin should see another Cakravartin, a Baladeva should see another Baladeva, or a Vāsudeva should see another Vāsudeva; nevertheless, you shall see the white and yellow tops of the banners of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva as he passes through the very middle of the salt ocean."

Then that Kappila Vāsudeva paid homage and reverence to the sage Suvrata Arhat; having paid homage and reverence, he mounted the back of his elephant. Having mounted it, he proceeded swiftly until he arrived at the port of Vellāula. Upon arriving, he saw the white and yellow tops of the banners of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva as he was passing through the middle of the salt ocean. Having seen them, he spoke thus: "This is my peer, this supreme man, Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, who is passing through the middle of the salt ocean. Having said this, he took hold of his five-toned conch shell and blew it with the breath of his mouth.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, having heard the sound of Kapila Vāsudeva’s conch, grasped his own five-ringed conch; having grasped it, he blew it with his mouth. Then both Vāsudevas performed the ritual convention regarding the sounding of the conch.

Then that Vāsudeva Kapila went to where the royal capital Avarakaṅkā was; having arrived, he saw the royal capital Avarakaṅkā with its gateways shattered and so forth. Having seen it, he spoke thus to Paümanābha: "O beloved of the gods! Why is this royal capital Avarakaṅkā shattered and so forth, reduced to ruins? Then Paümanābha spoke thus to Vāsudeva Kapila: "Truly, my lord! Having come swiftly here from the island of Jambūdvīpa, from the region of Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva has humiliated you and reduced Avarakaṅkā to ruins."

Then that Vāsudeva Kapila, having heard this matter from Paumanābha, spoke thus to Paumanābha: "Oho! Paumanābha! You who desire what is undesired... [as before] ... why do you not know that you are doing something displeasing to me, Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, a man equal to yourself? Enraged... [as before] ... he orders Paumanābha to be banished from his territory; he consecrates Paumanābha’s son with a very grand royal consecration in the capital city of Avarakaṅkā, and then returns home.

As Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva was thus crossing through the middle of the salt ocean, he arrived at the Gaṅgā. Having arrived, he spoke thus to the five Pāṇḍavas: "Go, dear ones, cross the great river Gaṅgā; meanwhile, I shall wait until I have seen Suṣṭhita, the lord of the salt ocean. Then, having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, the five Pāṇḍavas went to where the great river Gaṅgā was. Having gone there, they searched for a single path; having found it, they crossed the great river Gaṅgā on that single path. Having crossed, they said to one another: "Is Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva able, dear ones, to cross the great river Gaṅgā with his arms, or is he not able? Having said this, they pushed their boat onto the single path and stood waiting, looking toward Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, seeing that Suṣṭhita was the lord of the salt ocean, went to where the great river Gaṅgā was; having arrived, he conducted a search and investigation all around for the *egaṭṭhiyā* (the boat). Not seeing the *egaṭṭhiyā*, he took the chariot, along with the horses and the charioteer, in one arm, and proceeded to cross the great river Gaṅgā, which was sixty-two *yojanas* and half a *yojana* in width, using his other arm.
When Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva had reached the middle of the great river Gaṅgā, he became exhausted, weary, and utterly fatigued, and his strength was bound.

Then, this reflection arose within the mind of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: "Aha! How mighty are the five Pāṇḍavas, by whom the great river Gaṅgā—sixty-five yojanas wide—was crossed with their arms; yet, even though they so desired, King Padmanābha was not restrained by those five Pāṇḍavas."

When Gaṅgādevī perceived this internal thought of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, she granted him passage. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva comforted her for a moment; having comforted her, he crossed the great river Gaṅgā at a depth of sixty-eight [fathoms], and having crossed it, he went to where the five Pāṇḍavas were and spoke to them thus: "O dear ones, you are indeed possessed of great strength, since you have crossed the great river Gaṅgā at a depth of sixty-eight [fathoms]. Had you so desired, you could have prevented Padmanābha from crossing."

Then those five Pāṇḍavas, having been thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, spoke to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva as follows: "It is indeed so, O beloved of the gods! Having been dismissed by you, we went to where the great river Gaṅgā is; having arrived there, we searched for and sought out that very path [to the hermitage], and while waiting for you, we remained there until we reached the hermitage."

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, having heard and reflected upon this matter from those five Pāṇḍavas, became enraged and, knitting his brows threefold, spoke thus: "Aha! When I crossed the salt ocean two hundred thousand *yojanas* wide, subdued Paumanābha, [and] having destroyed Avarakaṅkā, brought back Draupadī with my own hands, at that time you did not recognize my greatness; now you shall know it! Having said this, he seized an iron club and dismantled the chariots of the five Pāṇḍavas. Having dismantled them, he ordered the five Pāṇḍavas to dwell there; they were settled in the fortress named Rahamadda.

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva went to where his own military camp was; having arrived, he joined together with his own army. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva went to where the city of Dvārakā was; having arrived, he entered his own palace.

Then those five Pāṇḍavas went to the city of Hastināpura; having arrived, they went to where King Pāṇḍu was, and having approached him with palms joined, they spoke thus: "Truly, father, we have been ordered by Kṛṣṇa to leave the country. Then King Pāṇḍu said to those five Pāṇḍavas: "How is it, my sons, that you have been ordered by Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva to leave the country? Then those five Pāṇḍavas said to King Pāṇḍu: "Truly, father, having returned from Aparakanka, we crossed two hundred thousand yojanas of the salt ocean."

Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva said to us: "Go, dear friends! Cross the great river Gaṅgā; meanwhile, I shall remain here exactly as before. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, having seen Suṣṭhita, the lord of the salt ocean, [did] all that very same thing—except that no mention is made of Kṛṣṇa’s anxiety—until he commands him to depart.

Then King Paṇḍu said this to those five Pāṇḍavas: "O sons, you have acted wickedly by doing what was displeasing to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva. Then King Paṇḍu summoned Queen Kuntī and, having summoned her, spoke thus: "Go, dear lady, to the city of Bāravaī and inform Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva as follows: 'O dear lord, the five Pāṇḍavas have indeed been ordered by you to leave the country, and you, dear lord, are the sovereign of the southern half of Bharata. Therefore, dear lord, please instruct them—toward which region, direction, or intermediate direction shall those five Pāṇḍavas go?'"

When Kuntī had been addressed thus by Pāṇḍu, she mounted the back of an elephant. Having mounted it, [she proceeded] as described below until: "May my maternal uncles grant leave! What is the purpose of your visit? Then Queen Kuntī spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva: "Indeed, my son, you have ordered the five Pāṇḍavas to leave the kingdom, and you yourself [have ordered] that they go to the southern half of Bhārata, even to the intermediate directions. Then Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva spoke thus to Queen Kuntī: "O maternal aunt, the words of the supreme men—the Vāsudevas, Baladevas, and Cakravartins—are never in vain. Therefore, let the five Pāṇḍavas go to the southern Vaitāḍhya mountain; there let them settle at Paṇḍumathurā and remain as those who serve me without being seen by me. Having said this, he honored and respected Queen Kuntī and dismissed her.

Then Queen Kunti reported this matter to Pāṇḍu. Thereupon, King Pāṇḍu summoned the five Pāṇḍavas and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Go, my sons! To the southern Veyālī; there you shall establish the city of Pāṇḍumathurā."

Then those five Pāṇḍavas, having heard King Pāṇḍu’s command, replied, “So be it. Having assented, they departed from Hastināpura with their armies and vehicles, including horses and elephants. They proceeded to the southern Veyālī and settled there at the city of Paṇḍumathurā. There too, they came to possess abundant enjoyments and wealth.

Then, at another time, Queen Dōvaī became pregnant. When nine months had fully elapsed, Queen Dōvaī gave birth to a handsome boy—delicate, and so forth—and when twelve days had passed, they performed his naming ceremony with this intention: "Since this boy is the son of the five Pāṇḍavas and the offspring of Queen Dōvaī, let the name of this boy be Paṇḍusēṇa. Then his parents gave him the name Paṇḍusēṇa. He mastered the seventy-two arts and became capable of enjoyment; he lived as a crown prince and so forth.

The elders arrived; the assembly went out; the people of Paṇḍava went out. Having heard the Dharma, they spoke thus: "Venerable Sirs, we would first like to take leave of Queen Dōvaī and establish Prince Paṇḍusēṇa on the throne; after that, Venerable Sirs, we shall go forth from home into homelessness in the presence of the Venerable Ones. [The Teacher replied: "As it pleases you, O Venerable Ones!"

Then those five Pāṇḍavas went to their own home; having arrived, they summoned Queen Draupadī and spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! We have heard the Dharma from the presence of the Elders... [and so forth]... until we shall go forth into the religious life. Now, O beloved of the gods, what will you do? Then Draupadī spoke to those five Pāṇḍavas: "If you, O beloved of the gods, being terrified by the fear of *saṃsāra*... [and so forth]... go forth into the religious life, who else will there be for me as a support... [and so forth]...? I too, being terrified by the fear of *saṃsāra*, shall go forth into the religious life together with you, O beloved of the gods."
Then those five Pāṇḍavas [anointed] Paṇḍusena as king; he became a king and dwelt while ruling the kingdom.

Then those five Pāṇḍavas and Queen Dōvaī, at another time, took leave of King Paṇḍusēṇa. Then King Paṇḍusēṇa summoned his household servants and said to them: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods, prepare the consecration for renunciation... [and so on] until they descend from the palanquin. They went to where the Elders were... [and so on] until they became ascetics. Having studied the fourteen *Pūrvas*, and having studied them, they dwelt for many years, disciplining themselves with the sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth [fasts], and with month-long and half-month-long fasts."

Then Queen Dōvaī descends from her palanquin and, having become a female ascetic under the guidance of the nun Suvvatā, she studies the eleven *aṅgas*. For many years, she dwells cultivating herself through fasts of the sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth meals, as well as fortnightly and monthly fasts.
Then, at another time, those venerable elders depart from the city of Paṇḍumathurā and the Sahassambavana park; having departed, they wander for their alms-tour in the surrounding countryside.

At that time, in that period, the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi went to the Surāṣṭra country; having arrived, he dwelt in the Surāṣṭra country, disciplining himself through self-restraint and austerity. Then, many people spoke thus to one another: "O beloved of the gods! The Arhat Ariṣṭanemi is indeed dwelling in the Surāṣṭra country," and so forth.

Then those five ascetics, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard this matter from the mouths of many people, called one another and spoke thus: "It is indeed so, dear friends! The Arhat Ariṣṭanemi is wandering from place to place in regular succession... Therefore, it would be well for us to take leave of the venerable elders and go to pay homage to the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi. They agreed to this proposal of one another, went to where the venerable elders were, and upon arrival, they paid homage and reverence to the venerable elders. Having paid homage and reverence, they spoke thus: "We wish, with your permission, to go to pay homage to the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi. "As it pleases you, dear friends," [the elders replied]. Then those five ascetics, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, being permitted by the elders, paid homage and reverence to the venerable elders; having paid homage and reverence, they departed from the presence of the elders. Departing, and practicing an uninterrupted penance month after month, wandering from village to village, they eventually arrived at the city of Hastakalpa. Upon arrival, they stayed in the Sahasrāmravana park outside of Hastakalpa, and so forth.

Then those four ascetics, with Yudhiṣṭhira as their leader, performed their study during the first watch of the night on the day of breaking their month-long fast, and practiced meditation during the second watch; in this manner, just as Goyama-sāmī [did], with the exception that they took leave of Yudhiṣṭhira and so forth, until while wandering they heard the voice of a great multitude: "O beloved of the gods, the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi, on the peak of Mount Ujjanta, having fasted for a month without water, together with five hundred and thirty-six ascetics, has passed away and reached final liberation."

Then those four ascetics, with the exception of Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard and reflected upon this matter in the presence of the great multitude, departed from the city of Hastikalpa. Having departed, they went to the Sahasrāmra grove, and to where the ascetic Yudhiṣṭhira was, they approached him. Having approached, they examined their food and drink; having examined them, they performed the ritual of confession for their coming and going (*gamana-āgamana*); having performed it, they announced what was permissible and what was not permissible in alms-food (*eṣaṇā-an-eṣaṇā*); having announced it, they presented the food and drink, and spoke thus: "Truly, O Venerable Ones, [the King] has passed away. Therefore, O Venerable Ones, it is well for us to discard this previously taken food and drink, and having slowly ascended Mount Śvetavya, to dwell there, having perfected ourselves through the practice of self-mortification (*saṃlekhanā*) and meditation, without regard for the time of death. Having said this, they agreed to this proposal of one another. Having agreed, they discarded that previously taken food and drink in a secluded place. Having discarded it, they went to Mount Śvetavya. Having gone there, they slowly ascended Mount Śvetavya, and dwelt there without regard for the time of death.

Then those five ascetics, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, having studied the fourteen *pūrvas* beginning with the *Sāmāyika*, having fulfilled the stage of asceticism for many years, and having emaciated themselves through a two-month *saṃlekhanā*, attained the purpose for which the state of nakedness is practiced; having attained that goal, they produced infinite, supreme, absolute knowledge and vision, and finally became perfected ones (*siddhas*).

Then that noble lady Dōvaī, having studied the eleven *aṅgas* beginning with the *Sāmāyika* in the presence of the noble ladies Suvvatā, and having fulfilled the stage of asceticism for many years, performed a month-long ritual of self-restraint (*saṃlēhaṇā*). Having confessed her faults and repented, she passed away at the time of death and was reborn in the *Brahmaloka* heaven. There, the lifespan of certain gods is declared to be ten *sāgaropamas*; there, the lifespan of the god Duvaē was also ten *sāgaropamas*. "Venerable sir, where will that god Duvaē go from there... [and so on]... until he makes an end in the region of Mahāvidēha?"
Thus indeed, Jambū! this is the meaning of the sixteenth chapter on Knowledge (Nāyajjhayaṇa) as proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra; so I say.

“If, venerable sir, this is the meaning taught by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained liberation, regarding the sixteenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, then what is the meaning taught, venerable sir, regarding the seventeenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*? “In this way, Jambū: At that time, in that period, there was a city named Hatthisīsa. [Its description is as follows. There, there was a king named Kaṇakaketu. [His description is as follows. In that city of Hatthisīsa, many sea-faring ship-traders resided; they were wealthy, [and so forth], and they were not held in contempt by the multitude.”

Then, at another time, those merchants of the sea-going vessel gathered together—just as in the case of Arahanṇaka—and having entered the salt ocean for many hundreds of *yojanas*, there arose against them many hundreds of portents, just as in the case of the sons of Māgandiya, including a black storm (*kāliyavāta*). Then that ship, being tossed about, shaken, agitated, and thrown into turmoil by that black storm, began to founder right there. Consequently, the navigator became one whose memory was lost, whose hearing was lost, and whose discernment was lost; he became confused regarding the directions and regions. Not knowing which country, direction, or intermediate point the ship had reached, he fell into despair and remained brooding with a dejected mind.

Then those many helmsmen, steersmen, sailors, and ship-merchants approached that navigator; having approached, they spoke thus: "Why, O beloved of the gods, are you dejected in mind and intent, even to the point of brooding? Then that navigator spoke thus to those many helmsmen and others: "Indeed, O beloved of the gods, because my memory has failed and I have become distracted, I am therefore dejected in mind and intent, even to the point of brooding."

Then those helmsmen and others, having heard and understood this matter from that navigator, became terrified; they bathed, performed their ritual offerings, and with palms joined together—as described in the *Mallināya* passage up to—stood waiting and paying homage to many Indras and Skandhas. Then, after a short while, that navigator regained his mental composure, recovered his hearing, regained his presence of mind, and became oriented toward the cardinal directions. Thereupon, that navigator spoke thus to those many hold-fasters, helmsmen, sailors, and merchant ship-captains: "O dear ones, I have indeed regained my mental composure and become oriented toward the cardinal directions. O dear ones, we have been driven by the Kāliya Island, and there Kāliya Island appears in sight."

Then those merchants, from the time they were pregnant [with their horses] until they heard this matter from the mouth of that navigator, became joyful and delighted. With a wind favorable for circumambulation, they went to where the island of Kāliya was; having arrived, they moored the ship, and with a single-minded effort, they crossed over to the island of Kāliya. There they saw many mines of silver, mines of gold, mines of jewels, and mines of diamonds, as well as many horses. What were they like? They were marked with the *harirēṇu* dust, had manes like threads, and were adorned with *āīṇa* wool. Then those horses saw the merchants; smelling their scent, they became terrified, alarmed, agitated, and with agitated minds, they bolted away for many *yojanas*. But there, having abundant grazing and plenty of grass and water, they lived happily, free from fear and agitation.

Then those merchants, having boarded their ships, said to one another: "O dear ones, what need have we for horses? Here are many mines of silver, mines of gold, mines of jewels, and mines of diamonds. It would be better for us to load our ship with silver, gold, jewels, and diamonds. Having agreed upon this matter, they loaded their ship with silver, gold, jewels, diamonds, grass, wood, food, and water. Once the ship was loaded, they set sail with a favorable wind and arrived at the port of Gambhīra. Upon arrival, they moored the ship, prepared their wagons and carts, and transferred the silver, gold, jewels, and diamonds from the ship onto the wagons and carts. Having yoked the wagons and carts, they proceeded to the city of Hasthisīsa. Arriving there, they established their camp in the outer park outside the city of Hasthisīsa. They unyoked the wagons and carts, took up a great and precious gift, and entered the city of Hasthisīsa. Having entered, they went to where King Kanakaketu was and presented him with that great and precious gift.
Then King Kanakaketu accepted that great wealth and so forth from those merchants and ship-owners.

Those ship-merchants said this to him: "O beloved of the gods! You wander through villages, towns, and so forth, and you frequently navigate the salt ocean by means of sea-going vessels. Have you ever seen any wonders anywhere? Then those ship-merchants said this to Kanakaketu: "O beloved of the gods! We indeed reside right here in the city of Hastiśīrṣa... [and so on] ...until we were driven by a storm onto the Kāliya Island. There, O Lord, we saw many mines of gold and silver, and many horses. What kind of horses? Horses with hair like dust (harirēṇu) that rise up for many yojanas. Thus, O Lord, we have previously seen those horses as a wonder on the Kāliya Island."

Then, having heard and reflected upon this matter from those ship-owning merchants, Kanakaketu spoke thus to those ship-owning merchants: "Go, dear sirs, together with my household servants, and bring those horses from Kālika Island. Then those merchants, saying "So be it, Master," respectfully assented to his command. Then Kanakaketu summoned his household servants and said to them: "Go, dear sirs, together with the ship-owning merchants, and bring my horses from Kālika Island. They, too, assented.

Then those householders prepared their carts and carriages; having prepared them, they loaded the carts and carriages with many lutes (*vīṇā*), harps (*vallakī*), *bhāmarī* lutes, *kacchabhī* lutes, *bhambhā* drums, *chabbhāmarī* lutes, various other lutes, and many other substances suitable for the sense of hearing.
