They loaded the carts and carriages with many black [objects] up to white ones, including woodwork and so forth, up to knotted items and so forth, and many other substances suitable for the sense of sight. They loaded the carts and carriages with many bags of spices (*koṭṭhapuḍa*) and bags of *keyaya* (fragrant herbs), up to many other substances suitable for the sense of smell. They also loaded much sugar, molasses, *sakkāra* (a type of sweet), *macchaṇḍikā* (sour gruel), *pupphuttara*, and *paümuttara*.

They load wagons and carriages with various substances suitable for the sense of taste, such as many kinds of sweets, blankets, woolen cloths, cotton fabrics, *malaya* cloth, *masūra* cloth, stone slabs, and even those as fine as *haṃsagarbha*. Having loaded them, they yoke the wagons and carriages and proceed to the port of Gambhīrā. Upon arrival, they unload the wagons and carriages, prepare the ship, and load it with those excellent sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells, as well as wood, grass, water, rice, salt, milk products, and many other items suitable for the ship. With a favorable wind from the south, they set sail and arrive at Kāliya Island. They anchor the ship and disembark those excellent sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells onto the island using rafts. Wherever those horses rest, lie down, stand, or roll about, there the householders place lutes and other many instruments suitable for the sense of hearing, producing their sounds repeatedly. They station their feet around the perimeter of the horses and remain motionless, still, and silent.

Wherever those horses rest, lie down, stand, or stretch out their limbs, there those household servants place many black [objects]—up to wooden carvings—and various other substances suitable for the sense of sight; having placed them around the perimeter, they remain motionless, still, and silent. Wherever those horses rest, lie down, stand, or stretch out their limbs, there those household servants make heaps and piles of many pouches of *koṭṭha* flowers up to *pāṭala* flowers, and of many other substances suitable for the sense of smell; having made them, they remain around the perimeter, and so forth.

Wherever those hopes of theirs settle, there those householders' men make heaps and stores of molasses, and so forth, as well as of many other substances suitable for the tongue; having done so, they dig out pits, and having dug them, they fill the pits with molasses drinks, sugar-candy drinks, date drinks, and many other kinds of beverages; having filled them, they place seats around their perimeters and remain standing there.

And wherever those hopes settled upon him, there those householders' men set up many traps, snares, and even stone-slabs, as well as other objects suitable for the sense of touch, arranged one after another; having set them up, they placed seats around their perimeter and remained standing there.

Then those horses go toward where those excellent sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells are. There, some of those horses—thinking, "These sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells are unprecedented"—being uninfatuated, unattached, ungreedy, and undeluded by those excellent sounds through to smells, retreat very far away from those excellent sounds through to smells. They, having abundant grazing grounds and abundant grass and water there, dwell in happiness, fearless and undisturbed.

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic, that Nirgrantha or Nirgranthī who does not become attached to sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells—up to that point—he, in this very world, becomes one to be honored by many ascetics and [others], and he shall cross over the wilderness of the fourfold saṃsāra.

There, some of those horses went right to where the most excellent sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells were; having gone there, they became infatuated with those excellent sounds, touches, and so on, up to being completely absorbed in them, and they began to indulge in them. Then, while those horses were indulging in those excellent sounds and so on, they were bound by those merchants with many snares, traps, nooses, and fetters around their necks and legs. Then those householders seized the horses, and having seized them, they loaded them onto a ship. Having loaded them, they filled [the ship] with grass, wood, and so on. Then those merchants, whose ships were well-equipped, with a favorable wind from the south, arrived at the port of Gambhīraka. Having arrived, they moored the ship; having moored it, they unloaded the horses. Having unloaded them, they went to the city of Hastiśīrṣa, to where King Kanakaketu was, and having arrived, they saluted him with palms joined together and so forth, and presented the horses to him. Then King Kanakaketu bestowed great favor upon those merchants, honored them, and showed them respect. Having honored and shown them respect, he dismissed them.

Then King Kanakaketu summoned his household officials; having summoned them, he honored them and dismissed them. Then King Kanakaketu summoned his horse-trainers and spoke to them thus: "O beloved of the gods, you must train my horses. Then those horse-trainers, saying "So be it," assented. Having assented, they trained those horses by means of many mouth-restraints, ear-restraints, nose-restraints, mane-restraints, hoof-restraints, bit-restraints, and bridle-restraints; and by means of rubbing, striking with the feet, marking with the body, blows with canes, blows with whips, blows with switches, blows with whips of leather, blows with sticks, and blows with goads. Having trained them, they presented them to King Kanakaketu. Then King Kanakaketu honored those horse-trainers and dismissed them.

Just as those horses experience many physical and mental sufferings through numerous bites and even blows from sticks, O venerable ascetic, so too a monk or a nun who has gone forth, if they become attached to, enamored of, infatuated with, deluded by, and obsessed with desirable sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells, will in this very world be an object of contempt for many ascetics and [the like], and will wander through the wilderness of saṃsāra.
Those who are enslaved by the sense of hearing take delight in sounds that are charming with sweet strings, cymbals, flutes, and drums;
being captivated by these sounds, they revel while under the sway of the sense of hearing.
This, indeed, is the fault arising from the lack of restraint over the sense of hearing. // Nāyā. 187 //
Unable to endure the beauty of the sky, the partridge fell into the snare of the hunter.
// Nāyā.188 Delighting in forms—the prideful and graceful movements of the breasts, hips, face, hands, feet, and eyes—those enslaved by the sense of sight take their pleasure. // Nāyā.189
Furthermore, this is the fault arising from the lack of restraint regarding the faculty of sight:
that the foolish moth falls into the blazing fire.
[This occurs despite] the methods of using excellent aloe-wood incense, superior perfumes, seasonal garlands, and ointments.
Delighting in odors, those overcome by the sense of smell find pleasure [in them]. (Nāyā.
191) Furthermore, this is the fault arising from the lack of control over the sense of smell:
that a serpent emerges from its hole at the scent of medicinal herbs. (Nāyā. 192)
In bitter, pungent, astringent, and sweet foods—among many things to be chewed, drunk, and licked—the tongue-bound ones, enslaved by the organ of taste, take delight in the craving for flavors.
This is the fault that arises from the unruliness of the organ of taste. (Nāyādhammakahāo 193)
Just as a fish, when cast upon the ground and writhing, gasps with its mouth agape;

so too do those overcome by the sense of touch, finding pleasure in tactile sensations that are pleasant in the seasons and which bring satisfaction to the heart and mind through their full abundance, delight in them while being enslaved by the faculty of touch. (Nāyā. 194–195)
Furthermore, there is this fault arising from the lack of restraint of the sense-faculties:
that the sharp iron goad digs into the head of the elephant.
// Nāyā.196 // Amidst those things delightful with sweet strings, cymbals, drums, flutes, and lutes, played in rhythmic harmony...
Those who are not greedy for sounds do not die the death of one overcome by passion. (Nāyā.
197) Those who are not attached to forms—the breasts, hips, faces, hands, feet, eyes, and the graceful, coquettish gait—do not die the death of one overcome by passion. (Nāyā. 198)

Those who are not greedy for fragrances— the methods of incense such as agallochum and the finest aloeswood, nor for garlands and ointments— do not die a death of passion (vasaṭṭa-maraṇa). [Likewise, those who are not attached] to bitter,
pungent, astringent, or sweet tastes, nor to many kinds of foods to chew, drinks, and things to lick...
Those who are not greedy for tastes do not die a death of passion’s affliction.

// Nāyā.200 And those who are not greedy for tactile sensations—which bring seasonal delights, physical comforts, and peace to the heart and mind—do not die a death of passion’s affliction. // Nāyā.201
When sounds, whether pleasant or unpleasant, have come within the range of hearing,
a monk should never be either delighted or enraged.
When forms, whether pleasant or unpleasant, have come within the range of sight...

A śramaṇa should never be [affected] by either pleasure or anger when encountering fragrances, whether they be pleasant or foul, that come within the range of the sense of smell. (Nāyā. 203) A śramaṇa should never be [affected] by either pleasure or anger when encountering fragrances, whether they be pleasant or foul, that come within the range of the sense of smell. (Nāyā. 204)
When tastes, whether pleasant or unpleasant, come within the range of the tongue,
a monk should never be affected by them, whether feeling joy or anger.
When tactile sensations, whether pleasant or unpleasant, come within the range of the body...
A śramaṇa should never be [either] pleased or angry.
Thus indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning declared by the śramaṇa, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained liberation, in the seventeenth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo. Thus I speak.

“If, O Venerable One, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, regarding the seventeenth chapter of the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, what is the meaning declared regarding the eighteenth? “Thus it was, Jambū: At that time, in that period, there was a city named Rājagṛha, [described] as in the standard description. There lived a caravan leader named Dhana, whose wife was Bhaddā. That caravan leader Dhana had five sons by his wife Bhaddā, who were caravan-leader’s children, namely: Dhana, Dhanapāla, Dhanadeva, Dhanagopa, and Dhanarakṣita. That caravan leader Dhana also had a daughter by his wife Bhaddā, born after his five sons, a girl named Suṃsumā, with delicate hands and feet. That caravan leader Dhana also had a slave-boy named Cilāta, whose body possessed all five senses intact, who was well-fleshed, and skilled in the play of children.”

Now, that servant-boy became the fosterer of the girl Suṃsumā; he would take the girl Suṃsumā upon his hip, and having taken her, he would dwell taking his pleasure with many boys and girls, children and children, lads and lads. Then that servant-boy Cilāta would steal from some of those many boys [and so on] up to... their balls, their loincloths, their *āḍōliyās*, their *tindūsas*, their *pōttullas*, and their *sāḍōllas*; he would steal the ornaments, garlands, and finery of some; he would mock, laugh at, belittle, revile, threaten, and strike some. Then those many boys [and so on] up to... weeping, crying out, grieving, shedding tears, and lamenting, informed each of their own mothers and fathers.

Then the mothers and fathers of those many boys, girls, infants, infant girls, youths, and young maidens went to where the caravan leader Dhana was; having arrived, while grieving, lamenting, and entreating him with many consolations, reproaches, and entreaties, they informed the caravan leader Dhana of this matter. Then that caravan leader Dhana repeatedly tried to dissuade the slave-boy Cilāta from this matter, yet the slave-boy Cilāta did not desist at all.

Then that Cilāta would seize some of those many boys and girls, even the very small ones, and beat them with sticks. Then those many boys and girls, weeping and so forth, informed their parents. Thereupon, they became enraged and, burning with anger, went to where Dhana the caravan leader was; having arrived, they informed him of this matter with many reproaches and so forth. Then Dhana the caravan leader, having heard this matter from the presence of the parents of those many boys and girls, became enraged and so forth; he reviled, insulted, rebuked, and threatened the slave-boy Cilāta with various harsh words, and beat him with various blows, and finally expelled him from his house.

Once that servant-boy Cilāta had been expelled from his own house, he wandered about quite comfortably in the city of Rājagṛha—through its main streets, crossroads, and thoroughfares, as well as in temples, assembly halls, taverns, gambling dens, brothels, and drinking establishments. Thereupon, that servant-boy Cilāta became one who was unrestrained, uncurbed, acting according to his own whims, moving about at will, and addicted to liquor, dice, gambling, prostitutes, and the wives of others.

Not far from the city of Rājagṛha, in the south-eastern direction, there was a bandit settlement named Siṃhaguhā. It was situated on rugged mountain ridges and peaks, surrounded by a rampart of bamboo thickets, hidden by a moat consisting of precipices and uneven rocky slopes, accessible through a single gate, divided into many sections, with its exits and entrances known only to trusted people, possessing water within its interior, having its outer limits difficult to reach due to a scarcity of water, and it was also difficult to overcome even for a large force of thieves who had arrived.

There, in the bandit settlement of Siṃhaguha, lived a bandit leader named Vijaya—unrighteous, [and so forth], a banner of unrighteousness, one who had risen up, whose fame had spread through many cities, valiant, a striker of firm blows, daring, and a man of his word. He dwelt there in that bandit settlement of Siṃhaguha, exercising authority over five hundred bandits, and so forth.

Now, that Vija, the thief and leader of a band of robbers, was the chief among many thieves, adulterers, cutpurses, burglars, tunnel-diggers, royal oppressors, murderers of the innocent, murderers of children, betrayers of trust, gamblers, and guards of gambling dens—as well as many others who were maimed, wounded, or cast out from society—and he was their very stronghold.

Then that Vijaia, the thief and leader of the band of robbers, wandered about repeatedly plundering and destroying the southeastern district of Rājagṛha by means of many village raids, city raids, cattle seizures, captivities, highway robberies, and the digging of pits, leaving it destitute and impoverished.

Then that slave-boy Cilāta, being repeatedly harassed by many wealthy men, gamblers, and others in Rājagṛha who were suspicious of his wealth, suspicious of his ornaments, suspicious of his wife, and suspicious of his property, departed from the city of Rājagṛha. Having departed, he went to the bandit camp of Siṃhaguhā; having arrived there, he joined the bandit leader Vijaya and lived with him. Then that slave-boy Cilāta became a sword-bearer in the presence of the bandit leader Vijaya. Whenever the bandit leader Vijaya went out to plunder villages or to commit highway robbery, the slave-boy Cilāta would repel even a very large force of thieves—beating them, crushing them, and so forth—and having regained their position, accomplished his task, and returned safe and sound, he would quickly return to the bandit camp of Siṃhaguhā. Then the bandit leader Vijaya instructed the thief Cilāta in many bandit arts, bandit spells, bandit deceptions, and bandit stratagems. Then, on a certain occasion, the bandit leader Vijaya met his end through the law of time (died). Thereupon those five hundred bandits performed the funeral rites for the bandit leader Vijaya with great pomp and honor; having performed many worldly funeral duties, they eventually became free from grief.

Then those five hundred thieves called one another and, having called, spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! Our leader of the band of thieves, Vijaya, has indeed been united with the law of time (passed away). This Cilāta, the robber, was taught many arts of thievery and so forth by Vijaya, the leader of the band of thieves. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, it is well for us to consecrate Cilāta, the robber, as the leader of the band of thieves in the stronghold of Siṃhaguhā. Having said this, they agreed to this matter among themselves. Having agreed, they consecrated Cilāta as the leader of the band of thieves in the stronghold of Siṃhaguhā. Then that Cilāta became the leader of the band of thieves; he lived as one who was unrighteous and so forth.

Now, that Cilāta, the leader of the band of thieves and chief of the robbers, was also a master of ambushes. There, in the robber settlement of Siṃhaguha, he ruled over five hundred thieves; and just as Vijaya had done, so did he do everything—up to making the region to the southeast of the city of Rājagṛha destitute and devoid of wealth.

Then, on another occasion, that bandit chief Cilāta had abundant food, drink, chewables, and delicacies prepared and invited those five hundred bandits. He remained there eating, tasting, relishing, and enjoying them with a joyful heart. When they had finished their meal and were satiated, he honored and respected those five hundred bandits with abundant incense, flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments; having honored and respected them, he spoke thus: "O dear ones, in the city of Rājagṛha there is a caravan leader named Dhana, who is wealthy. His daughter, the granddaughter of Bhadrā, born after five sons, is a maiden named Suṃsumā—endowed with all limbs, beautiful, and lovely. Therefore, O dear ones, let us go to the house of the caravan leader Dhana and plunder it; you shall take abundant wealth, gold, jewels, gems, pearls, conchs, crystals, and corals, while I shall take the maiden Suṃsumā."

Then those five hundred thieves agreed to this proposal of Cilāta. Thereupon, Cilāta, the leader of the bandits, mounted his wet hide together with those five hundred thieves. Having mounted it, at the time of evening, he—along with the five hundred thieves—fully armored and having taken up weapons and missiles, with their *gomuṣṭika* clubs sharpened, their swords polished, their bows strung, and their small drums being beaten, set forth from the Sīhaguha bandit camp with a great, loud, exultant lion-roar and a tumultuous clamor, making a sound like the roar of the ocean. Having departed, they went to the vicinity of the city of Rājagṛha; having arrived, they entered a large thicket not far from Rājagṛha, and having entered, they remained there, passing the day.

Then that bandit chief, Cilāta, at the time of midnight, when all were resting and quiet, together with five hundred bandits—some carrying *māiya* and *gomuḥī* fruits, and others with *mūiyā* thigh-bells—went to the eastern gate of the city of Rājagṛha. He took up a water-skin, and having rinsed it and become perfectly pure, he invoked the spell for opening locks. Having invoked it, he sprinkled the gate-leaves of Rājagṛha with water; having sprinkled them, he opened the leaves. Having opened them, he entered Rājagṛha, and having entered, he made a great clamor, shouting aloud as he spoke thus: "O beloved of the gods! I am indeed the bandit chief named Cilāta, who has come here in haste from the bandit camp of Siṃhaguha with five hundred bandits, desiring to plunder the house of the caravan leader Dhana. Therefore, whoever wishes to drink the milk of his own mother, let him go out! Having said this, he went to the house of the caravan leader Dhana and opened the door of Dhana’s house.

Then Dhanas, seeing his house being plundered by the bandit chief Cilāta together with five hundred thieves, became afraid, terrified, agitated, and seized with fear; he then withdrew to a secluded spot along with his five sons. Thereupon, the bandit chief Cilāta plundered the house of the caravan leader Dhanas, and having plundered it, he took a great quantity of wealth, gold, and so forth, as well as the maiden Suṃsumā; having taken these, he departed from Rājagṛha and set out toward Siṃhaguha.

Then that caravan leader Ghaṇa went to his own home. Upon arriving and learning that a great deal of gold and the maiden Suṃsumā had been carried off, he took a gift of great value, high price, and great worth, and went to where the city officials were. Having arrived, he presented that gift of great value and spoke thus: "Truly, O lords, the bandit chief Cilāta came here in haste from the bandit stronghold of Siṃhaguha together with five hundred bandits; having plundered my house, he took a great deal of gold and the maiden Suṃsumā, and has departed. Therefore, O lords, we wish to go to the well of the maiden Suṃsumā. As for that vast wealth of gold and jewels, O lords, it is mine, and the maiden Suṃsumā is yours."

Then those city guards agreed to this proposal of Dhanas. Having agreed, they equipped themselves in armor and, taking up their weapons and armaments, set out from Rājagṛha with a great and tumultuous clamor, as if making the very ocean roar. Having departed, they went to where Cilāta, the bandit chief, was located; having arrived, they engaged in combat with Cilāta, the bandit chief. Then those city guards struck down, overpowered, and finally subdued Cilāta, the bandit chief.

Then those five hundred thieves, having been struck, beaten, and even repelled by the city guards, scattered and dispersed that vast wealth and gold in all directions and fled away. Then those city guards took that vast wealth and gold, and having taken it, they went right back to the city of Rājagṛha.

Then that Cilāta, having had that band of thieves beaten, struck, and seized by those city guards, entered a great, trackless, and long-stretched forest. Then the merchant Dhanna, seeing his daughter Suṃsumā terrified and standing there, being carried away by Cilāta toward the forest, together with his five sons—six in all—clad in armor and equipped for battle, set out following Cilāta’s path; pursuing him, shouting, calling out, crying out, threatening, and terrifying him, he followed behind.

Then that Cilāta saw Dhanaka, the caravan leader, together with his five sons—himself being the sixth—all equipped and armored, pursuing him. Seeing this, and finding himself powerless, weak, devoid of heroism, lacking manly effort and prowess, and unable to rescue the maiden Suṃsumā, he became exhausted, weary, and distressed; he then seized his sword, which was like a blue lotus, and having seized it, he cut off the head of the maiden Suṃsumā. Having taken it, he entered that trackless forest.

Then that Cilāta, being overcome by thirst and hunger in that trackless forest, having lost his sense of direction and failing to reach the bandit stronghold of Siṃhaguhā, passed away right along the way.

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic! if a Nirgrantha of ours who has gone forth... having taken food for the sake of its color, or [for its strength, beauty, or pleasure], of this physical body which is full of impurities and subject to decay, he indeed becomes an object of contempt for many ascetics and laywomen in this very world, and he will wander through the wilderness of *saṃsāra*—just like that thief Cilāta.

Then that caravan leader Dhanu, together with his five sons—six in all—while repeatedly searching everywhere and on all sides for Cilāta in that trackless forest, became exhausted, weary, and utterly fatigued; he was unable to capture the bandit chief Cilāta with his own hands, so he turned back. Having returned, he went to the very place where the maiden Suṃsumā had been deprived of life by Cilāta. Upon arriving, he saw the maiden Suṃsumā, deprived of life by Cilāta, like a *campaka* tree felled by an axe. Then that caravan leader Dhanu, together with his five sons—six in all—sitting down, wailing, lamenting, and crying out with a great, loud voice, wept and wailed in deep distress for a long time, shedding tears from his eyes.

Then that caravan leader Ghaṇa, together with his five sons—himself being the sixth—while wandering about in every direction within that trackless forest, exhausted by thirst and hunger, searching everywhere in that trackless forest for water, became weary, distressed, exhausted, and despondent. Not finding water in that trackless forest, he went to the very place where Suṃsumā had been deprived of her life. Having arrived, he called his eldest son, Dhaṇa, and spoke to him thus: "Truly, my dear son, for the sake of the maiden Suṃsumā, while we were wandering about in every direction within this trackless forest, we were overcome by thirst and hunger. Though we searched for water in this trackless forest, we did not find any. Since we have not found water, we are unable to reach Rājagṛha. Therefore, my dear ones, you must deprive me of my life; eat my flesh and blood. With that food, being sustained, you will afterwards cross over this trackless forest, reach Rājagṛha, meet with your friends and kinsmen, and become partakers of wealth, merit, and righteousness."

When the eldest son had been addressed thus by the caravan leader Dhana, he spoke to the caravan leader Dhana as follows: "O father! You are our beloved, our elders, our deities, our establishers, our founders, our protectors, and our guardians. How then, O father, could we deprive you of life and consume your flesh and blood? Therefore, O father, deprive me of my life and consume my flesh and blood; then you shall cross the wilderness ahead. [He said all that] until: you will become partakers of wealth, of Dharma, and of merit."

Then the second son spoke thus to the caravan leader Dhana: "O father, let us not deprive our eldest brother—our elder, our teacher, our deity—of life; rather, O father, you should deprive me of life so that [the rest of] us may remain alive. This was repeated by each of the sons up to the fifth. Then the caravan leader Dhana, knowing the desire of his five sons' hearts, spoke to those five sons: "O sons, let us not deprive even one of us of life. This body of the maiden Suṃsumā is breathless, motionless, and abandoned by life. Therefore, O sons, it is better for us to consume the flesh and blood of the maiden Suṃsumā. By means of that food, being sustained, we shall reach Rājagṛha. Then those five sons, having been addressed thus by the caravan leader Dhana, accepted this matter.

Then the caravan leader Dhana, together with his five sons, prepared the fire-drill wood; having prepared it, he made a cavity in the wood; having made the cavity, he rubbed the fire-drill with the stick; having rubbed it, he struck out the fire; having struck it out, he kindled the fire; having kindled it, he threw pieces of wood into it; having thrown them in, he caused the fire to blaze up. He then offered the flesh and blood of the girl Suṃsumā as an oblation. Having been sustained by that food, they reached the city of Rājagṛha and were reunited with their friends and kinsmen. They became partakers of that vast wealth, gold, jewels, and so forth. Then the caravan leader Dhana, regarding the girl Suṃsumā, performed many worldly rites until he was freed from his grief.

At that time, at that moment, the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra arrived at the Guṇasilaka shrine in the city of Rājagṛha. Then, the merchant Dhanasārthavāha, together with his son, having heard the Dharma, went forth as a monk. He became a master of the eleven *aṅgas* and, through a month-long process of self-mortification (*saṃlekhanā*), was reborn in the Saudharma heaven. He will attain perfection in Mahāvideha. And just as, O Jambū, the merchant Dhanasārthavāha did not consume the flesh and blood of the maiden Suṃsumā for the sake of beauty, nor for the sake of form, nor for the sake of strength, nor for the sake of sensual pleasure, but solely for the purpose of reaching Rājagṛha; even so, O venerable ascetic, whatever monk or nun—up to the point of this physical body which flows with vomit, bile, phlegm, semen, and blood, and which must inevitably be abandoned—does not consume food for the sake of beauty, nor for the sake of form, nor for the sake of strength, nor for the sake of sensual pleasure, but solely for the purpose of attaining the state of perfection (*siddhigamana*), he indeed becomes in this very life worthy of worship by many monks, many nuns, many laymen, and many laywomen, and he shall cross over the wilderness of the fourfold cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), just like that merchant Dhanasārthavāha together with his son.
Thus indeed, Jambū! by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained [liberation], this is the meaning declared in the eighteenth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo. Thus I say.

"If, O Venerable Sir, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained [liberation] in the eighteenth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo, then what is the meaning declared, O Venerable Sir, in the nineteenth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo?"

Thus indeed, Jambū! At that time, at that moment, right here on this continent of Jambūdvīpa, in Pūrvavideha, on the northern bank of the great river Sītā, to the south of the Nīlavanta range of boundary mountains, to the west of the northern Sītāmukhavana forest grove, and to the east of the Ekaśailaka range of bordering mountains—therein lies the region named Puṣkalāvatī. Therein lies the royal capital named Puṇḍarīkiṇī, nine yojanas in width and twelve yojanas in length, [described] up to: it is like a manifest divine world, delightful, beautiful to behold, lovely, and perfect in form.

To the northeast of that city of Puṇḍarīkiṇī was a park named Nalinivana. There, in that royal capital of Puṇḍarīkiṇī, there was a king named Mahāpadma; he had a queen named Padmāvatī. King Mahāpadma had two sons by Queen Padmāvatī, both of whom were very delicate in their hands and feet: namely, Puṇḍarīka and Kaṇḍarīka. Of these, Puṇḍarīka was the crown prince.

At that time, on that occasion, the Elders arrived. King Mahāpadma went out [to meet them], and having heard the Dharma, he installed Puṇḍarīka upon the throne and went forth as a monk. Puṇḍarīka became king and Kaṇḍarīka became crown prince. The ascetic Mahāpadma studied the fourteen Pūrvas. Then the Elders wandered for their residence in the countryside outside. Thereafter, that Mahāpadma, after many years, attained perfection (siddha).

Then, at another time, those elders arrived once again in the capital city of Puṇḍarīkiṇī, in the Nalinavana park. King Puṇḍarīka went out [to meet them], and Kaṇḍarīka, having heard the great sound of the crowd, [approached] just as Mahābala had done, until he paid his respects. The elders preached the Dharma; Puṇḍarīka became a lay disciple (*śramaṇopāsaka*) and departed. Then Kaṇḍarīka rose from his seat, and having risen, [said]: "Just as you say, [I wish to renounce the world]; however, I must first take leave of King Puṇḍarīka, and then I shall go forth. [The elders replied: "As it pleases you, O beloved of the gods."

Then Kaṇḍarīka, having paid homage and salutation to the elders, departed from their presence. He mounted that same four-bellied horse-chariot, [proceeded,] and then dismounted. Having dismounted, he went to where King Puṇḍarīka was, and upon arrival, with palms joined [in reverence], he spoke thus to Puṇḍarīka:

"It is indeed so, O beloved of the gods! In the presence of the elders, the Dharma has been heard by me... that Dharma is desired, accepted, and approved by me. Therefore, O beloved of the gods, I wish to go forth [into the religious life]."
Then King Puṇḍarīka spoke thus to Kaṇḍarīka: "O beloved of the gods, do not now go forth as a shaven-headed ascetic; rather, I shall consecrate you with the great royal inauguration.
Then Kaṇḍarīka neither accepted nor approved this proposal from King Puṇḍarīka, but remained silent. Then King Puṇḍarīka spoke thus to Kaṇḍarīka a second and a third time, [but] he remained silent.

When Puṇḍarīka was unable, despite many explanations, instructions, admonitions, and entreaties, to persuade Prince Kaṇḍarīka—whether to explain or even to entreat him—he then, though unwillingly, consented to this matter. [The king] consecrated him with the consecration for renunciation, and so on, until he offered him as a gift of discipleship to the Elders. He became a wandering monk (*anagāra*), learned in the eleven *aṅgas*. Then, at another time, the venerable Elders departed from the city of Puṇḍarīkiṇī and the Nalinivana garden, and wandered abroad through the countryside.

Then, for that ascetic Kaṇḍarīya, because of those extreme and harsh [practices], just as in the case of Śailaka, he even came to dwell with a feverish affliction. Then, at another time, the elders arrived at the city of Puṇḍarīkiṇī and, having arrived, settled in the Nalinīvana grove.

Puṇḍarīka heard the Dharma from Nigga. Then King Puṇḍarīka, having heard the Dharma, went to where the ascetic Kaṇḍarīka was; having approached, he paid homage and reverence to Kaṇḍarīka. Having paid homage and reverence, he saw that the body of the ascetic Kaṇḍarīka was free from all affliction and disease. Having seen this, he went to where the venerable elders were; having approached, he paid homage and reverence to the venerable elders. Having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: "Venerable sirs, I am providing for the ascetic Kaṇḍarīka medical treatment, medicines, and remedies as they are required. Therefore, venerable sirs, please come to my carriage-sheds. Then the venerable elders consented to this request of Puṇḍarīka, and having accepted it, they dwelt there.

Then King Puṇḍarīka, like Maṇḍuka, became as strong-bodied as Śailaka had been. Then the venerable elders took leave of King Puṇḍarīka, and having taken leave, they wandered in the wandering of the countryside outside.

Then Kaṇḍarīka, having been freed from that royal illness, became infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and obsessed by those pleasant foods—eatables, drinks, chewables, and tastables—and he was unable to take leave of Puṇḍarīka to wander in the wandering of the countryside outside; he remained settled right there.

When Puṇḍarīka had grasped the meaning of this speech, he bathed and, surrounded by his harem and retinue, went to where the ascetic Kaṇḍarīka was. Having approached, he performed three circumambulations—rightward and leftward—of Kaṇḍarīka; having done so, he paid homage and reverence. Having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: "Blessed indeed are you, O beloved of the gods! You have achieved your goal, you are meritorious, you possess auspicious marks; truly well-obtained, O beloved of the gods, is the fruit of your human birth and life, since you have abandoned your kingdom and even your harem, and have gone forth as a wanderer. As for me, I am unfortunate, one who has not achieved his goal, one who is not meritorious, and one who lacks auspicious marks; being infatuated with my kingdom and even my harem, and with human sensual pleasures, I am unable—even though I desire it—to go forth. Therefore, blessed indeed are you, O beloved of the gods! [Truly well-obtained is] the fruit of your human birth and life."
Then that ascetic Kaṇḍarīka neither accepted nor understood this matter from Puṇḍarīka, but remained silent.

When Kaṇḍarīka the ascetic had been addressed thus by Puṇḍarīka for a second and even a third time, being unwilling and lacking self-control, yet out of shame and respect, he took leave of Puṇḍarīka; having taken leave, he wandered abroad with the elders through the countryside. Then, after Kaṇḍarīka had spent some time practicing severe austerity with the elders, he became weary of the state of a śramaṇa, disgusted with the state of a śramaṇa, and indifferent toward the state of a śramaṇa; having abandoned the application of the qualities of a śramaṇa, he slowly withdrew from the presence of the elders. Having withdrawn, he went to the city of Puṇḍarīkiṇī, to the palace of Puṇḍarīka, and arrived there. He sat down upon a stone slab beneath an excellent Aśoka tree in the Aśoka grove; having sat down, he remained there brooding, with his mind and intentions overwhelmed.

Then the nurse of the prince Puṇḍarīka went to where the Aśoka grove was; having arrived, she saw the ascetic Kaṇḍarīka beneath a noble Aśoka tree on a stone slab on the ground, with his mind dejected and his intentions frustrated, even to the point of brooding. Having seen him, she went to where King Puṇḍarīka was and, having approached, spoke thus to King Puṇḍarīka: "O beloved of the gods, it is thus: your paternal cousin, the ascetic Kaṇḍarīka, is in the Aśoka grove beneath a noble Aśoka tree on a stone slab on the ground, with his mind dejected and his intentions frustrated, even to the point of brooding."

Then, having heard and understood this matter from his nurse, Puṇḍarīka became agitated; rising up, he went forth surrounded by his harem and attendants to the Aśoka grove, where Kaṇḍarīya was, and after approaching him three times, he spoke thus: "Blessed indeed are you, O beloved of the gods, that you have gone forth into the religious life; I, however, am unfortunate, for I am unable to go forth. Therefore, blessed indeed are you, O beloved of the gods, for such is the fruit of your life. When Kaṇḍarīya had been addressed thus by Puṇḍarīka, he remained silent; and a second and a third time, he likewise remained silent.

Then Puṇḍarīka spoke thus to Kaṇḍarīya: "Is there need, venerable sir, for enjoyments? "Yes, indeed, there is need. Then King Puṇḍarīka summoned his royal officers and, having summoned them, spoke thus: "Quickly, O beloved of the gods! Prepare a grand royal consecration for Kaṇḍarīya... [and so on] until he was consecrated with the royal consecration.

Then that Puṇḍarīka himself performed the tonsure of five handfuls of hair; he himself adopted the fourfold law (*cāujjāma-dhamma*), and having adopted it, he took the ascetic requisites belonging to Kaṇḍarīka. Having taken them, he undertook this kind of vow (*abhiggaha*): "It is permissible for me to go to the elders, to salute and honor them, and having fully embraced the fourfold law in the presence of the elders, only after that shall I take food. Having undertaken this vow, he departed from the city of Puṇḍarīkiṇī; departing, wandering in regular succession and traveling from village to village, he set out toward where the venerable elders were.

When King Kaṇḍarīka had consumed that choice food and drink, due to excessive wakefulness and excessive indulgence in eating, that food did not digest properly. Then, as that food remained undigested within King Kaṇḍarīka, during the time between the first and last watches of the night, a pain appeared in his body—intense, vast, deep, and difficult to endure. With his body overcome by bilious fever, he wandered about afflicted by a burning heat.

Then that King Kaṇḍarīka, having renounced his kingdom, realm, harem, and so forth, became a monk; yet, overcome by distress and anguish, lacking self-control and subject to external power, he passed away at the time of death and was reborn as a denizen of hell in the seventh underworld, the lowest hell, for the maximum duration of existence.

In exactly the same way, O venerable ascetic, a Nirgrantha of our order who has gone forth into homelessness, if he again hankers after human sensual pleasures and so forth, he will wander through the cycle of rebirth—just like that King Kaṇḍarīka.

Then that anagāra Puṇḍarīka went to where the venerable elders were; having approached, he paid homage and reverence to the venerable elders. Having paid homage and reverence, he received the fourfold dharma a second time from the presence of the elders. On the day of breaking his sixth fast, during the first watch of the night, he performed his study (*svādhyāya*). [He then went out for alms] and while wandering, he accepted cool and coarse food and drink. Having accepted it, thinking "it is sufficient," he returned. He went to where the venerable elders were; having approached, he presented the food and drink. Having presented it, being permitted by the venerable elders, he—uninfatuated, unattached, not greedy, and not overcome by passion—like a snake entering its hole, with his own self, placed that pure and acceptable food and drink into the storehouse of his body.

Then, as that food—out of season, tasteless, flavorless, cold, and coarse—was being consumed by the ascetic Puṇḍarīka, it did not properly digest while he was practicing spiritual vigilance during the first and last watches of the night. Consequently, intense pain, difficult to endure, arose in the body of the ascetic Puṇḍarīka; his body was overcome by a bilious fever, and he remained in a state of burning heat.
Then that ascetic Puṇḍarīka, being without strength, without power, without heroism, and lacking manly effort and exertion, [placed his hands together] and spoke thus:

Homage be to the Arhats, the Blessed Ones, up to those who have attained the state named the destination of perfection; homage be to the Elders, the Blessed Ones, my teachers of Dharma and instructors in Dharma. Previously, in the presence of the Elders, I renounced all violence toward living beings, up to the thorn of false view; having confessed and repented, at the time of death, I passed away and was reborn in Sarvārthasiddha. Thence, after descending, I shall attain realization in Mahāvideha and bring an end to all suffering.

In the very same way, O venerable ascetic! when one has gone forth as a renunciant, he does not become attached to or enamored by human sensual pleasures, and so on, until he does not fall into opposition. In this very life, he becomes worthy of worship, salutation, reverence, honor, respect, and veneration by many ascetics, many female ascetics, many laymen, and many laywomen; he becomes an object of auspiciousness, a source of blessing, a deity, and a shrine to be served with humility. Furthermore, in the next world, he does not undergo many punishments, shavings of the head, censures, or beatings, and he will cross over the wilderness of the fourfold cycle of existence—just like that ascetic Puṇḍarīka.

Thus indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning set forth by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—the pioneer, the Tīrthaṅkara, [and so on] up to him who has attained the state named Siddhigati—in this nineteenth chapter of the Nāyādhammakahāo.

Thus indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning set forth by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—[and so on] up to him who has attained [the goal]—in this first book (śrutaskandha) of the sixth Aṅga. Thus I speak.
Of that Śrutaskandha, there are nineteen chapters consisting of single verses, which are completed over the course of nineteen days.

At that time, in that era, there was a city named Rājagṛha; [its] description [follows]. Outside that city of Rājagṛha, in the northeastern quarter, there was a shrine named Guṇasilaka; [its] description [follows]. At that time, in that era, the venerable elder Ārya-Sudharmā, a disciple of the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra—endowed with noble birth, endowed with a noble family, [and so on], up to] possessing the fourteen *pūrvas* and endowed with the four types of knowledge—was wandering in regular succession from village to village, traveling comfortably, together with five hundred monks. He arrived at the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇasilaka shrine, and stayed there, disciplining himself through self-restraint and austerity. The assembly went out, the Dharma was preached, and the assembly returned to the same direction from which it had come.

At that time, at that moment, the senior disciple of the venerable monk Ajja Suhamma, the monk named Ajja Jambū, while paying homage, spoke thus: "If, O Venerable One, this is the meaning set forth by the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra—attained to perfection—in the first book of the sixth Aṅga, titled the *Jñātādharmakathā*, then what, O Venerable One, is the meaning set forth by the Śramaṇa—attained to perfection—in the second book of the *Dharmakathā*?"

Thus indeed, Jambū! By the Śramaṇa [Mahāvīra], who has attained perfection, ten sections of the *Dharmakathās* have been proclaimed, namely: the first section on the chief queens of Camara; the first section on the chief queens of Bali; the second section on the chief queens of Bali, the Vaiśravaṇa Indra and King of the Vaiśravaṇas; the third section on the chief queens of the southern Indras, excluding the Asura-indra; the fourth section on the chief queens of the northern Indras of the Bhavanavāsins, excluding the Asura-indra; the fifth section on the chief queens of the southern Vāṇamantara Indras; the sixth section on the chief queens of the northern Vāṇamantara Indras; the seventh section on the chief queens of Candra (the Moon); the eighth section on the chief queens of Sūra (the Sun); the ninth section on the chief queens of Śakra; and the tenth section on the chief queens of Īśāna.

“If, O Venerable One, ten sections of the Dharma-discourses have been taught by the Ascetic [Mahāvīra], who has attained perfection, what is the subject matter of the first section, O Venerable One, as taught by the Ascetic who has attained perfection?
“Thus indeed, Jambū, five chapters of the first section have been taught by the Ascetic who has attained perfection, namely: Kālī, Rāī, Rayaṇī, Vijjū, and Mehā.”

"If, venerable sir, five chapters have been taught by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained [liberation], for the first book, then what, venerable sir, is the meaning taught by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, who has attained [liberation], for the first chapter?

"Thus indeed, Jambū: at that time, in that period, in the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇasilaka shrine, King Śreṇika was reigning; Queen Cellaṇā was his queen. The Lord arrived [at the shrine]; the assembly went out [to meet him]... until the assembly sat in attendance upon him."

At that time, at that moment, the goddess named Kālī was residing in the palace known as Kālivaḍeṃsaga in the royal city of Camaracañcā, seated upon the throne Kāla. She was surrounded by four thousand *sāmānika* gods, four chief queens with their retinues, the three assemblies, the seven armies and the seven army commanders, sixteen thousand *ātmarakṣa* (bodyguard) gods, and many other asura-kumāra gods and goddesses dwelling in the Kālivaḍiṃsaga palaces. Amidst great music and festivities, she was wandering about. And while repeatedly surveying the entire Jambudvīpa continent with her vast clairvoyant power (*avadhi-jñāna*), she beheld it.

There he saw the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, on the island of Jambudvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, in the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇasilaka shrine; having taken formal possession of a suitable lodging, he was dwelling there, cultivating his self through self-restraint and austerity. Having seen him, with a heart full of joy, contentment, and delight, with a mind overflowing with bliss and a heart thrilled, he rose from his lion-throne. Having risen, he descended from the footstool. Having descended, he removed his shoes. Having removed them, he approached the Tīrthaṅkara, walking seven or eight steps toward him. Having approached, he lowered his left knee and placed his right knee upon the surface of the earth. He bowed his head to the ground three times. Rising slightly, he drew back his arms which were adorned with bracelets and armlets. Joining the palms of his hands together [in reverence], he spoke thus:

"Homage be to the Arhats, [and so on] up to those who have attained perfection; homage be to the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra, [and so on] up to him who desires to reach the state named the destination of the Siddhas. Standing here, I pay homage to the Bhagavān who is there; may the Śramaṇa Bhagavān Mahāvīra, who is there, see me who am here. Having said this, he paid homage and reverence; having paid homage and reverence, he sat down upon his excellent lion-throne facing the east.

Then, this thought occurred to Queen Kālī: "It is indeed fitting for me to go to pay homage to the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, and so forth, to serve him. Having reflected thus, she summoned the *ābhiyogika* gods and said to them: "O beloved of the gods! The ascetic Lord Mahāvīra has given an order—just as Sūryābha did—down to: 'Prepare a divine vehicle suitable for the approach of the best of gods,' and so forth, until 'report back. They likewise performed it and reported back; however, the chariot was a thousand *yojanas* in width, and the rest was exactly as before. She announced her name and clan, displayed the dance performance just as before, and then they departed."

"Venerable Sir," [said] the Blessed Gautama, having paid homage and reverence to the Blessed Śramaṇa Mahāvīra; having paid homage and reverence, he spoke thus: "Venerable Sir, where has that divine divine-magic, divine divine-splendor, and divine divine-power of Queen Kālī gone? Where has it entered? [This is explained by] the simile of the peaked-roofed hall. Oh, Venerable Sir, Queen Kālī is of great power! Venerable Sir, by whom was that divine divine-magic, divine divine-splendor, and divine divine-power of Queen Kālī obtained? By whom was it attained? By whom was it fully acquired?"

Thus, as in the case of Sūryābha, up to: "In this way indeed, Gautama, at that time and at that occasion, here in Jambūdvīpa, in the land of Bhārata, there was a city named Āmalakappā—[its] description. There was a shrine called Ambasālavaṇa, and King Jiyasattu [ruled]. There, in that city of Āmalakappā, there was a householder named Kāla—wealthy, up to, invincible. That householder Kāla had a wife named Kālasirī, who had delicate hands and feet, up to, beautiful. That householder Kāla had a daughter, the offspring of his wife Kālasirī, named Kālī, a young girl. She was grown, a grown-up maiden; she was aged, an aged maiden; her breasts were sagging; she was despondent regarding marriage and avoided by suitors."

At that time, at that moment, the Arhat Pārśva, the leader of men, the founder [of the order]—just as Lord Vardhamāna [is described], with this difference: surrounded by sixteen thousand monks and thirty-eight thousand female ascetics—arrived at the Amba-śālavana grove; the assembly went out [to meet him] and worshipped him.

Then, having learned of this news, Kālī the maiden was thrilled and her heart was filled with joy; she went to where her mother and father were, and having approached them, with palms joined [in reverence], spoke thus: "Mothers, it is indeed so: the Arhat Puruṣādānīya, the founder [of the order], is staying nearby... Therefore, O mothers, I wish, being permitted by you, to go and pay homage at the feet of the Arhat Puruṣādānīya Pārśva. "As it pleases you, dear child! Do not hesitate."

Then, having been granted permission by her mother and father, the maiden Kālī—delighted and joyful at heart—bathed, performed the ritual offerings, completed the auspicious purificatory rites, and put on clean, festive garments. Her body adorned with costly ornaments and surrounded by a circle of female attendants, she departed from her home. Having departed, she went to the outer assembly hall where the excellent religious chariot was; having arrived, she ascended the excellent religious chariot.

Then that maiden Kālī mounted the excellent religious chariot just as Dōvaī had done, and so on until she waited upon him. Then the Arhat Pārśva, the one who subdues men, preached the Dharma to the maiden Kālī and to that very large assembly. Then the maiden Kālī, having heard and absorbed the Dharma from the presence of the Arhat Pārśva, the one who subdues men, was joyful and her heart was filled with happiness; she paid homage and reverence to the Arhat Pārśva, the one who subdues men, three times. Having paid homage and reverence, she spoke thus: "I have faith, O Venerable One, in the Nirgrantha doctrine, even as you say it. However, O Beloved of the Gods, I must first ask my parents for permission; then, O Beloved of the Gods, I shall go forth into the religious life in your presence. "As it pleases you, O Beloved of the Gods! Then the maiden Kālī, being addressed thus by the Arhat Pārśva, the one who subdues men, was joyful and her heart was filled with happiness; she paid homage and reverence to the Arhat Pārśva, and having paid homage and reverence, she ascended that same excellent religious chariot. Having ascended, she departed from the Ambasālavaṇa shrine in the presence of the Arhat Pārśva, the one who subdues men. She went to the city of Āmalakappā, entered the middle of the city of Āmalakappā, and arrived at the outer assembly hall. Having arrived, she stopped the excellent religious chariot, descended from the excellent religious chariot, and approached her parents. With palms joined in reverence, she spoke thus:

"Truly, O mothers! I have heard the Dharma in the presence of Pārśva, the Arhat; that Dharma has been desired, accepted, and approved by me. Therefore, O mothers, being terrified by the fear of *saṃsāra* and afraid of birth and death, I desire, with your permission, to go forth from the home to the homeless state, having become a female renunciant in the presence of Pārśva, the Arhat. 'As it pleases you, beloved goddesses! Do not place any obstacle in my way.'"

Then, at that time, the householder had abundant food, drink, snacks, and delicacies prepared; having had them prepared, he invited his friends, kinsmen, relatives, family members, and attendants. After inviting them, he bathed and, having done so, honored and venerated them with an abundance of flowers, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Having honored and venerated them, in the presence of those very friends, kinsmen, relatives, family members, and attendants, he had the maiden Kālī bathed with jars of white and yellow water. Having bathed her, he adorned her with all ornaments. He then mounted a palanquin carried by a thousand men. Mounted upon it and surrounded by his friends, kinsmen, relatives, family members, and attendants, he went out through the very center of the city of Āmalakappā with full splendor and a great clamor. Having gone out, he proceeded to the Ambasālavana park. Upon arriving, he beheld the parasol and other signs of the excellence of a Tīrthaṅkara. Having seen them, he halted the palanquin. Having halted it, he helped the maiden Kālī descend from the palanquin.

Then the parents, placing the maiden Kālī before them, went to where the Worthy One, the Puruṣādānīya, was; having approached, they paid homage and reverence, and having paid homage and reverence, they spoke thus: "It is indeed so, O Devānupriya! This maiden Kālī is our daughter, dear and beloved to us... how much more so when seen in person! O Devānupriya, she is terrified by the fear of *saṃsāra* and desires to go forth into homelessness under the guidance of the Devānupriya after having shaved her head. Therefore, O Devānupriya, we offer her to you as a candidate for discipleship (*śiṣṇibhikṣā*). May the Devānupriya accept this candidate for discipleship! [The Lord replied: "As it pleases you, O Devānupriya! Do not hesitate."

Then that maiden Kālī paid homage and reverence to Pārśva, the Arhat, and having done so, she departed toward the north-eastern direction. Having departed, she herself removed her ornaments, garlands, and finery; having removed them, she herself performed the tonsure. Then, approaching the place where Pārśva, the Arhat, was, she paid homage and reverence to Pārśva, the Arhat, three times, and spoke as follows: "The world, O Blessed One, is on fire," and so on, just as in the account of Devānandā, until: "She herself has been initiated. Then Pārśva, the Arhat, the leader of men, gave Kālī over to the nun Puṣpacūlā to be her pupil. Then the nun Puṣpacūlā herself initiated the maiden Kālī, and [having been instructed], she dwelt there, having fully undertaken the practice.

Then that Kālī was herself initiated by the noble lady Puṣpacūlā, [and having been instructed] until she had fully adopted [the life of a nun], she lived there. Then that noble lady Kālī became one who is restrained in her movements (iryā-samitā) and so forth, up to being a practitioner of guarded celibacy (gupta-brahmacāriṇī). Then that noble lady Kālī studied the eleven *aṅgas*, beginning with the *Sāmāyika*, in the presence of the noble lady Puṣpacūlā, and she lived practicing many [austerities], such as the fourth [meal-interval fast], and so forth.

Then, at another time, that noble lady Kālī became afflicted by a bodily ailment; she frequently washed her hands, washed her feet, washed her head, washed her face, washed the space between her breasts, washed the space between her armpits, and washed the space between her thighs. And wherever she established a place for standing, a bed, or a seat, she would first sprinkle it with water and only thereafter sit or lie down.

Then the venerable Puṣpacūlā said this to the venerable Kālī: “It is indeed not permitted, O Goddess, for Nigaṇṭhī śramaṇīs who are devoted to bodily mortification to be so. And you, O Goddess, have become one devoted to bodily mortification; yet you wash your hands repeatedly, and even lie down or sit down. Therefore, O Goddess, confess this state, undergo penance, and undertake the appropriate atonement.”

Then that nun Kālī did not accept the meaning of what the nun Puṣpacūlā said; she remained silent. Then those nuns, Puṣpacūlā and the others, repeatedly reviled, censured, despised, reproached, and insulted the nun Kālī, and they repeatedly tried to dissuade her from this matter. While the nun Kālī was being repeatedly reviled and [despised] by the Śramaṇī Nigranthīs and repeatedly being dissuaded, there arose within her this kind of internal reflection: "When I lived in the midst of a household, I was my own mistress. But ever since I shaved my head and went forth from home to homelessness, I have become dependent on others. Therefore, it would be best for me to stay tomorrow night in a separate dwelling when the night has turned into dawn and the sun is shining. Having reflected thus, she took up a separate dwelling when the night had turned into dawn and the sun was shining. There, unobstructed, unimpeded, and acting according to her own will, she repeatedly washed her hands and [performed other acts], until she sat or lay down.

Then that noble lady Kālī—being one who dwelt near [the laity], dwelling in proximity; being lax, dwelling in laxity; being indolent, dwelling in indolence; acting according to her own whims, dwelling according to her whims; being attached, dwelling in attachment—completed the course of the ascetic life for many years. Having completed it, she emaciated herself through a half-monthly *saṃlekhanā*. Having emaciated herself, she terminated thirty meals by means of fasting. Without having reflected upon or repented for that state, at the time of death, she passed away during the month of Kāla and was reborn in the celestial bed within the assembly hall of rebirth in the palace of Kālivaḍiṃsa in the capital city of Camaracañcā. There, clothed in divine raiment, with a body-measure of an infinitesimal fraction of a finger-breadth, she was reborn as the goddess Kālī. Then, having just been reborn, that goddess Kālī, like Sūriyābha, attained the fivefold full development, up to the full development of speech.

Then that goddess Kālī exercised authority over four thousand *sāmānika* gods, and so forth, as well as over many other asura-kumāra gods and goddesses dwelling in the Kālivaḍeṃsaga forest, and she lived [there] in this manner.

"Indeed, Gautama, that divine celestial power, divine celestial splendor, and divine celestial majesty was obtained, attained, and fully realized by the goddess Kālī. Venerable sir, for how long is the lifespan of the goddess Kālī declared to be? Gautama, her lifespan is declared to be two and a half *palyopamas*. Venerable sir, having passed away from that celestial world, where will the goddess Kālī go? Where will she be reborn? Gautama, in the region of Mahāvideha, she will attain perfection [and so forth]."
Thus, indeed, Jambū, by the ascetic [Mahāvīra], who has attained perfection, this is the meaning declared in the first chapter of the first section. So I say.

"If, venerable sir, this is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, who has attained perfection, in the first chapter of the first section of the *Dhammakahā*, then, venerable sir, what is the meaning declared by the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, who has attained perfection, in the second chapter?"
Thus indeed, Jambū! At that time, at that moment, in the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇasilaka shrine, the Lord arrived; the assembly went out and worshipped him.

At that time, at that moment, Queen Rāī came from the royal city of Camaracañcā in the same manner as Kālī had; she displayed her dance performance and departed. [Gautama asked: "Venerable One, what was the previous birth of Bhagavān Gautama? [The Lord replied: "In this way, Gautama: At that time, at that moment, there was a city named Āmalakappā and a shrine named Ambasālavaṇa. There was a king named Jiyasattu, a householder named Rāī, and his wife was Rāyasirī. Their daughter was Rāī. There was a gathering of Pārśva, and the girl Rāī went forth [into the religious life] just as Kālī had. She became emaciated in body in the same way; all of that [is to be told] exactly as before, until she shall make an end."

Thus indeed, Jambū, is the summary of the second chapter. If, O Venerable One, you ask for the summary of the third chapter: Thus indeed, Jambū, in the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇasilaka shrine—just as it was with Rāī, so too with Rayanī—with this difference: the city is Āmalakappā; the householder is Rayanī; the wife is Rayanīśrī; the daughter is Rayanī. The rest is exactly the same until she brings about an end [to rebirth]. Thus also with Vijjū—the city is Āmalakappā; the householder is Vijjū; the wife is Vijjūśrī; the daughter is Vijjū. The rest is exactly the same.

Thus, in the city of Viāmalakappā, there was the householder Mēha, his wife Mēhasirī, and their daughter Mēhā; the rest is exactly as before. Thus indeed, Jambū! by the Śramaṇa, up to the one who has attained perfection, this meaning of the first section of the *Dhammakahā* has been proclaimed.

"If, O Venerable One, the exposition of the second chapter has been delivered by the Ascetic [Jina] who has attained perfection, then indeed, Jambū, five lessons have been declared by the Ascetic who has attained perfection for the second chapter of the Dhammakahā. They are as follows: Sumbhā, Nisumbhā, Rambhā, Nirambhā, and Madanā. If, O Venerable One, five lessons have been declared by the Ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for the second chapter of the Dhammakahā, then, O Venerable One, what is the subject matter declared for the first lesson of the second chapter?"
Thus indeed, Jambū! At that time, at that moment, in the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇasilaka shrine, the Lord arrived; the assembly went out and paid homage, as described previously.

At that time, in that period, the goddess Sumbhā was dwelling in the palace Sumbhavaḍeṃsa in the royal capital Balicañcā, upon the lion-throne Sumbha. Kālī, by way of a song, having displayed her dance-performance, departed. [The goddess] asked about her previous birth: in the city of Sāvatthī, at the Koṭṭhaka shrine, King Jiyasattu reigned; there was a householder named Sumbha and his wife Sumbhasirī; their daughter was Sumbhā. The rest is as in the account of Kālī, with the exception that her lifespan is four and a half *palyopamas*.

Thus indeed, Jambū, is the meaning of this chapter; in the same way, the remaining four chapters [are set] at Sāvatthī, with the only difference being that the mother and father have names corresponding [to those of the respective chapters].
Thus indeed, Jambū, has this matter of the second section of the *Dhammakahā* been proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra.

[The summary follows. Regarding the third section: thus indeed, Jambū, has this matter of the third section—comprising fifty-four chapters—been proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for those who have attained [the goal], namely: from the first chapter up to the fifty-fourth chapter.

"If, venerable sir, fifty-four chapters have been taught by the Ascetic [Mahāvīra], who has attained perfection, in the third section of the Discourses on Dharma, then what, venerable sir, has been taught as the meaning of the first chapter by the Ascetic, who has attained perfection?
"Thus it is, Jambū! At that time, at that period, in the city of Rājagṛha, at the Guṇaśila shrine, the Lord arrived. The assembly went out, and [the people] paid their respects."

At that time, in that period, Queen Ilā, in the city of Dharaṇī, in the palace of Ilāvaṭaṃsa, on the lion-throne of Ilā—following the same sequence as Kālī up to the display of the dance, she departed. [Then follows] the inquiry regarding her previous birth: in the city of Vāṇārasī, in the Kāmamahāvana shrine, there was a householder named Ilā; his wife was Ilasirī; their daughter was Ilā. The rest is as in the case of Kālī, with the exception that her rebirth was as the chief queen of Dharaṇa, and her lifespan was slightly more than half a *palyopama*. The rest is exactly the same. Thus indeed is the summary of the first chapter. In this same order, Satērā, Soyāmaṇī, Indā, Dhaṇā, and Vijjuyā are also mentioned; all of these are the chief queens of Dharaṇa. These six chapters are to be recited without distinction for Veṇudēva as well. Likewise, for Ghōsa too, there are these same six chapters each. Thus, these constitute fifty-four chapters for the southern [Nāgas]. All of them take place in the city of Vāṇārasī, at the Kāmamahāvana shrine; such is the summary of the third section (*varga*).

And the summary of the fourth [chapter]: Thus indeed, Jambū, by the ascetic... having attained [enlightenment], forty-four lessons have been proclaimed in the fourth section of the *Dharmakathās*, namely: from the first lesson up to the forty-fourth lesson. The summary of the first lesson: O Gautama, thus indeed, Jambū, at that time, at that moment, there was a gathering in Rājagṛha; [the assembly] sat in attendance upon the Teacher.

At that time, in that period, there was the goddess Rūpā, the royal capital Rūpānandā, and the palace Rūpakāvataṃsaka. On the Rūpaka throne, [the narrative] is just as it was for Kālī; however, the differences are as follows: in her previous birth, she was at the Pūrṇabhadra shrine in Campā; her father was the householder Rūpaka, her wife was Rūpaśrī, and her daughter was Rūpā. The rest is exactly the same; however, she was born as the chief queen (agramahiṣī) of Bhūtānanda, with a lifespan of slightly less than a palyopama. This is the conclusion. In this very same manner, Surūpā, Rūpyā, Rūpakavatī, Rūpakāntā, and Rūpaprabhā are also to be described as the northern queens of the Indras, up to Mahāghoṣa. This is the conclusion of the fourth chapter.
The summary of the fifth chapter: Thus indeed, Jambū, thirty-two lessons are proclaimed, namely:
Kamalā, Kamalappabhā, Uppalā, Sudaṃsaṇā, Rūpavaī, Vahurūvā, Surūvā, and Subhagā. (Nāyā. 229)
Puṇṇā, Bahuputtiyā, Uttamā, and Tārayā;
Paümā, Vasumaī, Kaṇagā, and Kaṇagappabhā;
Vaḍēṁsā, Kēumaī, Vaïrasēṇā, and Raïppiyā. // Nāyā.230 //
Rohiṇī, Navamiyā, Hirī, and Pupphavaī;
Bhuyagā, Bhuyagāvaī, Mahākacchā, and Phuḍā; Sughosā, Vimalā, Sussarā, and Sarasvatī. (Nāyā. 231–232)

The summary of the first chapter: Thus indeed, Jambū! At that time, at that moment, there was a gathering in Rājagṛha; [the Lord arrived] until the assembly worshipped him. At that time, at that moment, Queen Kamalā was in the capital city of Kamalā, in the palace of Kamalāvataṃsaka, upon the lion-throne of Kamalā. The rest is exactly as for Kālī, with this difference: in her previous birth, she was in the city of Nāgapura, in the Sahasrāmravana garden, the daughter of the householder Kamala and his wife Kamalaśrī. She went forth into the presence of Pārśva and became the chief queen of Kāla, the lord of the Piśāca-kumāras. Her lifespan is half a *palyopama*. In this same manner, the remaining chapters regarding the southern Vānamantara lords are to be recited; all [of them] were in Nāgapura, in the Sahasrāmravana garden; their mothers and fathers have names corresponding to their daughters', and their lifespan is half a *palyopama*.

The sixth chapter is similar to the fifth; the only difference is that it concerns the chief queens of the northern Indras, such as Mahākāla and others. In their previous births, they were in the city of Sāgēya, in the Uttarakuṛu garden; their mothers and fathers had names similar to those of their daughters. The rest is exactly the same. This is the summary of the seventh chapter: "Thus indeed, Jambū! ... up to four lessons are proclaimed, namely: Sūrappabhā, Āyava, Accimālī, and Pamhakarā.
"Thus indeed, Jambū! At that time, at that moment, there was an assembly in Rājagṛha... up to the congregation paid homage."

At that time, in that period, Queen Sūrappabhā was in the celestial vehicle Sūra, upon the lion-throne Sūrappabha. The rest is as it was for Kālī; however, [the difference is]: her previous birth was in the city of Arakkhurī, as the daughter of the householder Sūrappabha and his wife Sūrasirī; she was the chief queen of Sūra. Her lifespan was half a *palyopama* increased by five hundred years. The rest is as it was for Kālī. In this same way, all the others were also from the city of Arakkhurī.

The summary of the eighth [chapter]: Thus indeed, Jambū, four chapters have been proclaimed, namely: Candappabhā, Dōsiṇābhā, Accimālī, and Pabhaṅkarā. The summary of the first chapter: Thus indeed, Jambū, at that time, at that moment, there was a gathering in Rājagṛha; [the Lord arrived] until the assembly waited upon him. At that time, at that moment, Queen Candappabhā was in the Candappabha celestial palace, on the Candappabha lion-throne. The rest is as in the case of Kālī, with this difference: her previous birth was in the city of Mathurā, in the Bhaṇḍivaḍeṃsaka garden. [Her father was] the householder Candappabha, [her mother] Candasirī, [and she herself] the maiden Candappabhā. She became the chief queen of Candra. Her lifespan was half a *palyōpama* plus fifty thousand years. The same applies to the others. [Their birth was] in the city of Mathurā; their parents were likewise, and the daughters had names similar to their own.

The summary of the ninth [chapter]: Thus indeed, Jambū, eight chapters are proclaimed, namely: Paumā, Sivā, Saī, Añjū, Rohiṇī, Navamiyā, Ayalā, and Accharā. The summary of the first chapter: Thus indeed, Jambū, at that time, at that moment, there was an assembly in Rājagṛha... until the congregation paid homage. At that time, at that moment, Queen Paumāvatī was in the Sōhamma heaven, in the Paumavaḍeṁsaga palace, in the Sudhamma hall, upon a lotus-throne. Just as it was told of Kālī, so too all eight chapters are to be understood according to the model of Kālī. However—the two women were in Sāvatthī, the two in Hatthiṇāura, the two in Kampillapura, and the two in Sāēya. Their fathers were named Pauma and their mothers Vijayā. All of them went forth into homelessness in the presence of Pārśva. They were the chief queens of Śakra; their life-span was seven *palyōpamas*, and they will bring an end to rebirth in Mahāvidēha.
The summary of the ninth [chapter]: Thus indeed, Jambū, eight lessons have been proclaimed, namely:
Kaṇhā, Kaṇharāī, Rāmā, and likewise Rāmarakkhiyā; Vasū, Vasuguttā, Vasumittā, and Vasundarā in Īsāṇa. (Nāyā. 239)

The introductory summary of the first chapter: Thus indeed, Jambū, at that time, at that moment, there was a gathering in Rājagṛha, [and] the assembly waited upon [the Lord]. At that time, at that moment, Queen Kṛṣṇā was in the Kalpa Īśāna, in the celestial mansion Kṛṣṇāvataṃsaka, in the Sudharmā assembly hall, on the Kṛṣṇa lion-throne; the rest is as in the case of Kālī. In this manner, all eight chapters are to be understood according to the model of Kālī. However—the previous births: two women in the city of Vārāṇasī, two women in the city of Rājagṛha, two women in Śrāvastī, and two women in the city of Kauśāmbī. Rāma was their father and Dharmā their mother. They all went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Arhat Pārśva, becoming female disciples under the nun Puṣpacūlā. They became the chief queens of Īśāna. Their lifespan is nine *palyopamas*. In the region of Mahāvideha, they will attain perfection, awaken, be liberated, and bring an end to all suffering.
Thus indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning set forth by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, in the tenth chapter of the *Dhammakahā*.

Thus indeed, Jambū, this is the meaning set forth by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra—the pioneer, the founder of the order, the self-enlightened one, the supreme among men, and so forth, up to the one who has attained perfection—in the *Dhammakahā*. The *Suyakkhandha* (Scriptural Collection) of the *Dhammakahā* is complete with its ten chapters; the *Nāyādhammakahā* is complete.
